title: Interview Study Plan
text: How to use this handbook: what to read for which interview round, in what order, and how to know you're ready. ML interviews are not one exam. Most loops have four or five distinct rounds, each graded on something different: breadth of fundamentals, depth on models, coding, open-ended system design, and (increasingly) LLMs. The notes here are organized by topic, but you should study by round . This page maps one to the other. What you'll get from this page A reading order for each interview round, from must-know to nice-to-have. Three priority tiers so you know what to cut when time is short. A self-test for each round: if you can answer these out loud, you're ready. # How the notes are built Every topic comes in two sizes: Chapters go deep: intuition, math, worked examples, interview angles, and a one-page summary at the end. Read these once, carefully. Quick answers are one-minute cards with a say it in 30 seconds answer, key points, and the follow-ups interviewers ask. Re-read these the night before. Tick Mark as reviewed at the bottom of a page to track progress; the sidebar greys out what you've finished. Press / to search. Interview angle Interviewers rarely ask define X . They ask why X and not Y? and what breaks X? . Every chapter ends with traps and trade-offs for exactly this reason. Practise answering out loud, not just reading. # Round-by-round reading order # ML fundamentals / breadth round The rapid-fire round: 20–30 short questions across the whole field. Fundamentals — ERM, generalization, bias-variance, problem framing. Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Overfitting Underfitting , Regularization , Generalization — the four cards you'll use in every other round. Data Preparation Feature Engineering with Data Leakage and Class Imbalance . Model Evaluation Validation with Precision Recall , ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC , Cross-Validation , Calibration . Loss Functions and Cross-Entropy Loss . # Theory / math round Math — linear algebra, probability, statistics, optimization, information theory. Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Gradient Descent . Eigenvectors, PCA and SVD . Probability Statistics and p-Values Statistical Power — statistics questions show up in almost every loop. Probability Math Drills — practise out loud. # Models round Regression Methods and Classification Methods . Decision Trees, Random Forests Gradient Boosting — the most-asked model family for tabular data. Clustering, Dimensionality Reduction Anomaly Detection . Cards to drill: Logistic Regression , Support Vector Machines , Naive Bayes , k-Nearest Neighbors , Decision Trees , Bagging vs Boosting , Gradient Boosting , k-Means Clustering , Generative vs Discriminative . # Coding round Implement-from-scratch problems, usually in numpy or PyTorch. Coding Round: ML From Scratch — 14 problems (regression, k-means, attention, AUC, training loop) with tested solutions. PyTorch and TensorGym Study Notes — tensor shapes, eval() vs no_grad() , mixed precision. Tutorials Cheatsheets — runnable scikit-learn and PyTorch guides. # Deep learning round Training Neural Networks — activations, backprop, optimizers, normalization, debugging. PyTorch and TensorGym Study Notes — for the implementation round. Architectures: Vision beyond CNNs , CNNs , RNNs → LSTM / GRU , GNNs . Cards: Backpropagation , Optimizers: SGD, Momentum Adam , BatchNorm vs LayerNorm , Dropout , Vanishing Exploding Gradients , Activation Functions . # LLM / GenAI round Transformers Attention — non-negotiable for any modern ML role. LLM Training: Pretraining, Fine-Tuning Alignment . LLM Inference: Decoding, KV Cache Serving . Retrieval-Augmented Generation . LLM Evaluation . Cards: Self-Attention , Tokenization: BPE, WordPiece SentencePiece , Decoding Strategies , KV Cache , LoRA Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning , RLHF vs DPO , Embeddings Vector Search , Hallucination . # ML system design round ML System Design Framework — the six-step spine to drive every answer. ML System Design Interview Prep — each stage in depth. Recommender Systems — the most common prompt family (feeds, ads, search). ML in Production — serving, monitoring, drift, retraining. A/B Testing Online Experimentation — how you prove the system works. Models and Loss Functions Reference — the lookup table. Worked cases: Search Ranking , Fraud and Abuse Detection , RAG Assistant ; also Responsible ML , Bandits RL , Causal Inference . Cards: Two-Tower Retrieval , Cold Start , Training-Serving Skew , Data Drift vs Concept Drift , Ranking Metrics: NDCG, MAP MRR . # Forecasting (role-dependent) Time Series Stationarity , then Stationarity , ARIMA vs Exponential Smoothing , Time-Series Validation Backtesting . # Priority tiers When time is short, cut from the bottom. Tier Read Why 1 — Must know Fundamentals, Model Evaluation, Loss Functions, Trees Ensembles, Training Neural Networks, Transformers Attention, ML System Design Framework, and every quick answer Asked in nearly every loop; weak answers here are disqualifying 2 — Expected for mid/senior Math, Regression/Classification Methods, A/B Testing, Recommender Systems, ML in Production, LLM Training, RAG, Data Preparation Separates knows the words from has shipped models 3 — Role-dependent CNN/RNN/LSTM/GRU/GNN, LLM Inference, LLM Eval, Unsupervised Learning, Time Series, PCA/SVD Go deep only if the job description points there Memory hook Breadth first, then depth where the job is. One shallow pass over Tier 1 beats a perfect read of one chapter. # Self-test: are you ready? Answer each out loud in under two minutes, without notes. Fundamentals Decompose expected squared error into bias, variance, and noise. What moves each term? Your validation AUC is great and production performance is poor. List five causes. Why is accuracy the wrong metric at 1% prevalence, and what would you use? Models Walk through how gradient boosting fits the next tree. What does XGBoost add? Why do random forests rarely overfit as you add trees, but boosting can? When would you pick logistic regression over gradient boosting in production? Deep learning Why does Adam need bias correction? What does AdamW change? What does BatchNorm do differently at train and eval time, and why do transformers use LayerNorm? Your loss is NaN after 200 steps. What do you check, in order? LLMs Write scaled dot-product attention and explain the ​ ​ . What is stored in the KV cache, how big is it, and how does GQA shrink it? RLHF vs DPO: what does DPO remove, and what does it give up? Your RAG system answers confidently but wrong. How do you find out whether retrieval or generation is at fault? System design Design a feed recommender: objective, metrics, candidate generation, ranking, serving, and how you'd A/B test it. How do you detect and respond to data drift when labels arrive two weeks late? How many users per arm do you need to detect a 1-point lift on a 10% conversion rate? Rapid fire — How to study Study by round, not by chapter order. Chapters once, deeply; quick answers repeatedly. Say answers out loud; interviews grade explanation, not recognition. For every concept, know one trade-off and one failure mode. In system design, drive the structure yourself. # Related Overview: Foundations · Overview: Models · Overview: Deep Learning · Overview: LLMs · Overview: System Design

title: scikit-learn Tutorial
heads: 2. Split first, touch nothing before it
7. Choose the decision threshold (on training data, not test)
8. Final evaluation on the test set (once)
9. Calibrate if you need real probabilities
Cheat list of mistakes this workflow prevents
text: A complete tabular-ML workflow in one pass: build a leak-free pipeline, validate it, tune it, pick a threshold, calibrate, and save it. The whole tutorial uses one synthetic dataset with a numeric column that has missing values, two categorical columns and a ~10% positive class, so every step mirrors a real problem. # 0. The mental model scikit-learn has three kinds of objects, and almost everything is one of them: Object Key methods Examples Transformer fit , transform StandardScaler , SimpleImputer , OneHotEncoder Estimator / model fit , predict , predict_proba LogisticRegression , HistGradientBoostingClassifier Pipeline the same API as its last step Pipeline , ColumnTransformer Golden rule: anything that learns from data (means, medians, category lists, a threshold) must be fit on the training portion only. A Pipeline enforces this automatically inside cross-validation. # 1. Make the data import numpy as np, pandas as pd rng = np.random.default_rng( 0 ) n = 3000 df = pd.DataFrame({ age : rng.integers( 18 , 80 , n).astype( float ), income : rng.lognormal( 10 , 0.5 , n), plan : rng.choice([ free , pro , team ], n, p=[ .6 , .3 , .1 ]), country : rng.choice([ US , IN , DE , BR ], n), }) df.loc[rng.random(n) .1 , income ] = np.nan # inject missing values logit = - 3 + 0.02 * (df.age - 40 ) + (df.plan == pro ) * .8 + (df.plan == team ) * 1.2 + (df.country == BR ) * .5 y = (rng.random(n) 1 / ( 1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype( int ) # 2. Split first, touch nothing before it from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( df, y, test_size= 0.2 , stratify=y, random_state= 42 ) # stratify keeps the 10% positive rate The test set is locked away until the very end. Every decision (model, hyperparameters, threshold) is made with the training data and cross-validation. # 3. Build the preprocessing + model pipeline from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression num, cat = [ age , income ], [ plan , country ] pre = ColumnTransformer([ ( num , Pipeline([( imp , SimpleImputer(strategy= median )), ( sc , StandardScaler())]), num), ( cat , OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown= ignore ), cat), # unseen category at predict time → all zeros, no crash ]) clf = Pipeline([( pre , pre), ( model , LogisticRegression(max_iter= 1000 , class_weight= balanced ))]) Why a pipeline? One object holds every step, so clf.fit(X_train, y_train) and clf.predict(new_df) do the same preprocessing, and cross-validation refits the imputer and scaler inside each fold. No leakage. # 4. Validate with cross-validation from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_validate cv = StratifiedKFold( 5 , shuffle= True , random_state= 42 ) res = cross_validate(clf, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring=[ roc_auc , average_precision ]) print (res[ test_roc_auc ].mean(), res[ test_average_precision ].mean()) With a 10% positive rate, average precision (PR-AUC) is the more honest number. A random model scores about 0.10 on it, versus 0.50 for ROC-AUC. Always compare against that baseline. See ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC . # 5. Tune hyperparameters Step names are the key: model__C means parameter C of the step named model . from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV grid = GridSearchCV(clf, { model__C : [ 0.01 , 0.1 , 1 , 10 ]}, cv=cv, scoring= average_precision , n_jobs=- 1 ) grid.fit(X_train, y_train) print (grid.best_params_, grid.best_score_) best = grid.best_estimator_ # already refit on all of X_train For larger spaces use RandomizedSearchCV(..., n_iter=30) . It is usually as good for far less compute. # 6. Try a stronger model Gradient boosting handles missing values natively and needs no scaling, but still needs categoricals encoded in this setup. from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier gb = Pipeline([( pre , pre), ( model , HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state= 0 ))]) print (cross_validate(gb, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring= average_precision )[ test_score ].mean()) Compare it to the linear model on the same folds and metric . On small or mostly linear data, the simple model often wins, which is a legitimate result. # 7. Choose the decision threshold (on training data, not test) predict() uses 0.5, which is rarely right for imbalanced problems. Pick the threshold from out-of-fold predictions so the test set stays untouched: from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve oof = cross_val_predict(best, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, method= predict_proba )[:, 1 ] p, r, t = precision_recall_curve(y_train, oof) f1 = 2 * p * r / (p + r + 1e-12 ) thr = t[np.argmax(f1[:- 1 ])] # or choose by business cost instead of F1 If a false negative costs more than a false positive, pick the threshold that minimizes expected cost rather than maximizing F1. # 8. Final evaluation on the test set (once) from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score, classification_report proba = best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1 ] print ( AUC , roc_auc_score(y_test, proba), AP , average_precision_score(y_test, proba)) print (classification_report(y_test, proba = thr)) If this number is much worse than the cross-validation score, suspect leakage or a distribution shift between train and test. # 9. Calibrate if you need real probabilities class_weight= balanced distorts predicted probabilities. If downstream code treats the score as a probability (expected value, risk), recalibrate: from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV cal = CalibratedClassifierCV(clf, method= isotonic , cv= 5 ).fit(X_train, y_train) cal.predict_proba(X_test)[: 3 , 1 ] Use method= sigmoid when the data is small (isotonic overfits). See Calibration . # 10. Inspect and save import joblib names = best.named_steps[ pre ].get_feature_names_out() # num__age, cat__plan_pro, ... coefs = best.named_steps[ model ].coef_[ 0 ] # linear-model feature effects joblib.dump(best, model.joblib ) # saves preprocessing + model together model = joblib.load( model.joblib ) model.predict(X_test.iloc[: 3 ]) Because the pipeline is saved as one object, serving code cannot forget a preprocessing step. Load a saved model only from sources you trust, and with the same scikit-learn version it was saved with. # Cheat list of mistakes this workflow prevents Fitting a scaler or imputer on all data before splitting (leakage). Reporting accuracy on a 10% positive problem. Tuning the threshold or hyperparameters on the test set. Forgetting stratify=y and getting a split with almost no positives. A crash in production on an unseen category ( handle_unknown= ignore ). Next: sklearn Quick Reference for compact lookups, then the PyTorch Tutorial .

title: sklearn Quick Reference
text: Compact lookups. For the guided walkthrough read the scikit-learn Tutorial ; for the searchable three-level version open the full interactive cheat sheet . # Pick the right tool Need Use Fill missing numbers SimpleImputer(strategy= median ) , or KNNImputer Scale numeric features StandardScaler (most models), RobustScaler (outliers) Encode low-cardinality categories OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown= ignore ) Encode high-cardinality categories TargetEncoder (cross-fitted internally) or hashing Different steps per column type ColumnTransformer Chain steps without leakage Pipeline / make_pipeline Strong tabular default HistGradientBoostingClassifier / Regressor Simple, interpretable baseline LogisticRegression , Ridge # Splitting Situation Splitter Classification, imbalanced StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0) Several rows per user/group GroupKFold (keeps a group in one fold) Time-ordered data TimeSeriesSplit (train always before validation) Quick holdout train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0) # Metrics Task Metric Function Balanced classification accuracy, F1 accuracy_score , f1_score Imbalanced classification PR-AUC average_precision_score Ranking quality ROC-AUC roc_auc_score Probability quality log loss, Brier log_loss , brier_score_loss Regression MAE, RMSE, R² mean_absolute_error , root_mean_squared_error , r2_score Scoring strings for cross_validate / GridSearchCV : roc_auc , average_precision , f1 , neg_log_loss , neg_mean_absolute_error . Sklearn maximizes scores, so error metrics are negated. # Snippets Pipeline with column types pre = ColumnTransformer([ ( num , make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy= median ), StandardScaler()), num_cols), ( cat , OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown= ignore ), cat_cols), ]) model = make_pipeline(pre, LogisticRegression(max_iter= 1000 )) Cross-validate several metrics cross_validate(model, X, y, cv= 5 , scoring=[ roc_auc , average_precision ]) Tune (step name + __ + parameter) GridSearchCV(model, { logisticregression__C : [ 0.1 , 1 , 10 ]}, cv= 5 , scoring= average_precision ) Out-of-fold predictions (for threshold choice or stacking) cross_val_predict(model, X, y, cv= 5 , method= predict_proba )[:, 1 ] Class imbalance LogisticRegression(class_weight= balanced ) Then tune the decision threshold and judge by PR-AUC. Resampling must happen inside each training fold, never before splitting. Calibration CalibratedClassifierCV(model, method= isotonic , cv= 5 ) # sigmoid for small data Feature names after preprocessing model[:- 1 ].get_feature_names_out() Save and load joblib.dump(model, model.joblib ); model = joblib.load( model.joblib ) Permutation importance (model-agnostic) from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance permutation_importance(model, X_val, y_val, n_repeats= 10 , random_state= 0 , scoring= average_precision ) # Common errors Symptom Likely cause Test score far below CV score leakage in CV, or train/test shift ValueError: Found unknown categories forgot handle_unknown= ignore Perfect CV score target leaked into a feature, or group split needed Scores change every run missing random_state or non-shuffled folds Invalid parameter in a grid step name wrong; check model.get_params().keys() See also Data Leakage , Class Imbalance , Cross-Validation .

title: PyTorch Tutorial
text: From a tensor to a saved, evaluated model: one complete, runnable training workflow. For the theory of how weights get updated, see PyTorch: Weights, Gradients Backprop . This page is the practical counterpart. # 1. Tensors A tensor is an n-dimensional array that can live on a GPU and can track gradients. import torch torch.manual_seed( 0 ) a = torch.tensor([[ 1. , 2. ], [ 3. , 4. ]]) b = torch.randn( 2 , 2 ) a.shape, a.dtype, a.device # torch.Size([2, 2]), torch.float32, cpu a @ b # matrix multiply (not a * b, which is elementwise) a. sum (dim= 0 ) # reduce over rows → shape [2] a[:, 0 ] # indexing works like NumPy Shapes cause most bugs. Print x.shape often. Convention: batch dimension first, [B, features] . # 2. Autograd Mark a tensor requires_grad=True and PyTorch records operations so it can differentiate them. x = torch.randn( 3 , 4 , requires_grad= True ) y = (x ** 2 ). sum () y.backward() # computes dy/dx torch.allclose(x.grad, 2 * x) # True Gradients accumulate into .grad on every backward() , which is why training loops call zero_grad() each step. # 3. Data: Dataset and DataLoader from torch.utils.data import TensorDataset, DataLoader, random_split N = 2000 X = torch.randn(N, 10 ) w = torch.randn( 10 ) y = ((X @ w + 0.5 * torch.randn(N)) 0 ). float () # binary labels as float for BCE ds = TensorDataset(X, y) train_ds, val_ds = random_split(ds, [ 1600 , 400 ], generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 )) train_loader = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size= 64 , shuffle= True ) # shuffle only for training val_loader = DataLoader(val_ds, batch_size= 256 ) For real data, subclass Dataset and implement __len__ and __getitem__ . DataLoader handles batching, shuffling and (with num_workers ) parallel loading. # 4. Define a model import torch.nn as nn class MLP (nn.Module): def __init__ ( self, d_in, hidden= 32 ): super ().__init__() self .net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(d_in, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout( 0.1 ), nn.Linear(hidden, 1 ), ) def forward ( self, x ): return self .net(x).squeeze(- 1 ) # raw logits, shape [B] Return logits , not probabilities. The loss below applies the sigmoid internally in a numerically stable way. # 5. Loss, optimizer, device device = torch.device( cuda if torch.cuda.is_available() else mps if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else cpu ) model = MLP( 10 ).to(device) loss_fn = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr= 1e-3 , weight_decay= 1e-2 ) sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max= 20 ) Data and model must be on the same device. Move each batch with .to(device) . # 6. The training loop best = float ( inf ) for epoch in range ( 20 ): model.train() # enables dropout, batchnorm training mode for xb, yb in train_loader: xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device) opt.zero_grad(set_to_none= True ) # 1. clear old gradients loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb) # 2. forward + loss loss.backward() # 3. backprop nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0 ) # optional stability opt.step() # 4. update weights sched.step() # once per epoch for this scheduler model. eval () # disables dropout total, correct, n = 0.0 , 0 , 0 with torch.no_grad(): # no graph, less memory for xb, yb in val_loader: xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device) logits = model(xb) total += loss_fn(logits, yb).item() * len (yb) correct += ((logits 0 ). float () == yb). sum ().item() n += len (yb) val_loss = total / n if val_loss best: # keep the best checkpoint best = val_loss torch.save(model.state_dict(), best.pt ) print (epoch, round (val_loss, 4 ), round (correct / n, 4 )) The four-line core ( zero_grad , forward/loss, backward , step ) is the same for every PyTorch model, from this MLP to a transformer. # 7. Save and load model2 = MLP( 10 ) model2.load_state_dict(torch.load( best.pt , map_location= cpu , weights_only= True )) model2. eval () Save the state_dict (weights only), not the whole model object. It survives code refactors and weights_only=True avoids loading arbitrary pickled code. # 8. Predict model2. eval () with torch.no_grad(): probs = torch.sigmoid(model2(X[: 5 ])) # Debugging checklist Overfit one small batch first. If loss will not go near zero on 32 examples, the bug is in the code, not the data. Loss is NaN → learning rate too high, bad input values, or log(0) ; try gradient clipping and a smaller lr . Loss does not move → forgot opt.step() , wrong zero_grad placement, or parameters not passed to the optimizer. Validation much worse than train → regularize (dropout, weight decay), get more data, stop earlier. Results differ between runs → set torch.manual_seed ; some GPU ops stay non-deterministic. Next: keep the PyTorch Cheatsheet open while you build.

title: PyTorch Cheatsheet
heads: Loss ↔ output ↔ target (the most common mismatch)
text: Lookups for shapes, losses, optimizers and the mistakes that cost hours. New to PyTorch? Start with the PyTorch Tutorial . # Loss ↔ output ↔ target (the most common mismatch) Task Last layer outputs Loss Target dtype and shape Binary classification 1 logit, [B] nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() float , [B] Multi-class C logits, [B, C] nn.CrossEntropyLoss() long (class index), [B] Multi-label C logits, [B, C] nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() float , [B, C] Regression 1 value, [B] nn.MSELoss() / nn.L1Loss() / nn.HuberLoss() float , [B] Do not put softmax or sigmoid before CrossEntropyLoss / BCEWithLogitsLoss . They apply it internally. Apply it only at prediction time when you need probabilities. # Tensor basics x = torch.zeros( 2 , 3 ) # also ones, randn, arange, linspace x.shape; x.dtype; x.device x.view( 3 , 2 ) # same data, needs contiguous memory x.reshape( 3 , 2 ) # view if possible, else copy x.unsqueeze( 0 ) # add dim → [1, 2, 3] x.squeeze() # drop size-1 dims x.permute( 1 , 0 ) # reorder dims torch.cat([a, b], dim= 0 ) # join along an existing dim torch.stack([a, b], dim= 0 ) # join along a NEW dim x.to( cuda ) # or .to(device); x.cpu().numpy() back to NumPy x. float (); x.long() # dtype casts x.detach() # cut from the autograd graph x.item() # one-element tensor → Python number # Training loop skeleton model.train() for xb, yb in loader: xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device) opt.zero_grad(set_to_none= True ) loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb) loss.backward() opt.step() model. eval () with torch.no_grad(): ... # validation / inference # model.eval() vs torch.no_grad() model.eval() torch.no_grad() Effect switches dropout off, batchnorm uses running stats stops building the autograd graph Saves memory no yes Need both at inference yes yes # Optimizers and schedulers Choice Typical use AdamW(lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-2) strong default, transformers SGD(lr=0.1, momentum=0.9) CNNs with a tuned schedule CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max=epochs) smooth decay, step once per epoch OneCycleLR fast training; step once per batch ReduceLROnPlateau sched.step(val_loss) Call opt.step() before sched.step() . # Useful layers Layer Notes nn.Linear(in, out) input [B, in] → [B, out] nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, k) input [B, C, H, W] nn.BatchNorm1d/2d behaves differently in train vs eval nn.LayerNorm(d) standard in transformers nn.Dropout(p) active only in train() mode nn.Embedding(vocab, d) integer ids [B, T] → [B, T, d] nn.LSTM(..., batch_first=True) set batch_first=True to keep [B, T, F] # Initialization and freezing nn.init.kaiming_normal_(layer.weight) # ReLU networks nn.init.xavier_uniform_(layer.weight) # tanh / sigmoid for p in backbone.parameters(): # freeze (transfer learning) p.requires_grad = False opt = torch.optim.AdamW( filter ( lambda p: p.requires_grad, model.parameters()), lr= 1e-4 ) # Saving and loading torch.save(model.state_dict(), model.pt ) model.load_state_dict(torch.load( model.pt , map_location= cpu , weights_only= True )) # resume training: also save optimizer and epoch torch.save({ model : model.state_dict(), opt : opt.state_dict(), epoch : epoch}, ckpt.pt ) # Speed and memory # mixed precision on GPU scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler( cuda ) with torch.autocast( cuda , dtype=torch.float16): loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb) scaler.scale(loss).backward() scaler.step(opt); scaler.update() # gradient accumulation (effective batch = batch_size * accum) (loss / accum).backward() if (i + 1 ) % accum == 0 : opt.step(); opt.zero_grad(set_to_none= True ) DataLoader(ds, batch_size= 64 , num_workers= 4 , pin_memory= True ) # faster input pipeline If you hit out-of-memory: lower the batch size, use mixed precision, accumulate gradients, or checkpoint activations. # Pitfalls Pitfall Fix Forgot zero_grad() → gradients accumulate call it every step Forgot model.eval() at inference dropout noise, wrong batchnorm stats softmax before CrossEntropyLoss remove it; feed raw logits Class targets as float for CrossEntropyLoss use long indices Accumulating loss in a list for logging use loss.item() so the graph is freed Model and data on different devices .to(device) both In-place op breaks autograd avoid x += ... on tensors needed for backward Non-reproducible runs torch.manual_seed(...) ; GPU ops may still vary See also Gradient Descent , Regularization , PyTorch: Weights, Gradients Backprop .

title: Fundamentals
heads: Generalization: Why Held-Out Data Is Sacred
Regularization, Inductive Bias & No Free Lunch
Turning a vague problem into a crisp one: I-O-L-M
text: Foundations: the learning problem. Simplified illustrated edition. This is the bedrock the rest stands on. We answer four questions: what machine learning actually is , how supervised learning is set up as an optimization problem, why held-out data is sacred, and what the bias-variance tradeoff really means. Nail these and most fundamentals round questions become a handful of ideas you apply, not facts you memorize. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Define ML as function approximation under a generalization constraint . Name the five learning settings by their supervision signal . Explain why we minimize empirical risk but care about true risk. Diagnose underfitting vs overfitting from a learning curve. Turn any vague use ML for X prompt into a crisp problem with I-O-L-M . # What Machine Learning Is Classical software is rules in, answers out : a human writes the logic, the computer applies it. Machine learning flips the second half: answers in, rules out . You hand it worked examples and it reverse-engineers an approximate procedure. Classical code applies rules you wrote; ML infers the rules from examples. Why bother? For a huge class of problems nobody can write the rules by hand: telling a cat from a dog in pixels, predicting loan default, translating English to Japanese. The rules exist in human intuition but are too tangled to articulate. ML recovers an approximation of them from data. One subtlety to carry through: ML never learns the true rule. It learns a function that fits the data you showed it and, hopefully, behaves well on data you haven't. That gap between fits what I saw and works on what I haven't seen is the single most important theme in the field. Regularization, validation, and the bias-variance tradeoff are all machinery for managing it. Memory hook Classical programming = rules in, answers out . Machine learning = answers in, rules out . Interview angle What is machine learning? is a softball you can fumble. Weak: computers learning from data. Strong: we use data to pick a function from a hypothesis space, and we care about expected performance on unseen data, not training accuracy. Saying generalization in your first sentence signals seniority. # The five learning settings Learning problems are grouped by what kind of supervision signal the algorithm gets — how much, and what kind of, labeled feedback is available. The map of learning settings, organized by supervision signal. Setting Supervision signal Goal Examples Supervised Labeled pairs Learn a mapping that generalizes Spam detection, credit scoring, demand forecasting Unsupervised Inputs only, no labels Find structure in the data Clustering, PCA/UMAP, density estimation Self-supervised Labels forged from the input itself Pretrain rich representations BERT (mask a word), GPT (next token), contrastive image learning Semi-supervised Few labels + lots of unlabeled data Spread few labels over data structure Pseudo-labeling, label propagation Reinforcement Reward from an environment Learn a policy maximizing cumulative reward AlphaGo, robotics, RLHF Memory hook Self-supervised learning is supervised learning that forges its own labels : hide a piece of the input, predict it, repeat a billion times. It's the engine behind foundation models. Interview angle A classic trap: is this supervised or unsupervised? for an ambiguous task. Don't name a box — name the supervision signal . Recommendation can be supervised (predict the rating), self-supervised (predict the next item), or RL (optimize long-term engagement). The signal is the discriminator. Go deeper (optional) The boundaries are porous. The dominant modern recipe — self-supervised pretraining then supervised fine-tuning — is neither purely one nor the other. Treat the taxonomy as vocabulary for describing the components of a system, not exclusive boxes. # Discriminative vs generative models A second axis, orthogonal to supervision, cuts across how a model represents the problem. People fumble this one constantly. Discriminative models draw the border; generative models learn each class's shape and derive the border. Discriminative Generative Learns — or just a decision boundary — the full data story Answers Which side of the line is this? How is each class generated? then applies Bayes' rule Can it sample? No Yes — can generate new , detect outliers, handle missing features Examples Logistic regression, SVM, random forest, most NN classifiers Naive Bayes, GMM, HMM, VAE, diffusion, autoregressive LLMs Wins when You only need the label and have ample data Small data (assumptions hold), or you need to sample Memory hook Discriminative draws the border ; generative paints the countries . Generative knows enough to forge a new passport (sample data); discriminative only checks which side of the line you're on. Go deeper (optional) Ng Jordan's classic result: a generative model (Naive Bayes) has higher asymptotic error than its discriminative pair (logistic regression), but reaches that asymptote with far fewer samples. So generative can win in the small-data regime and lose in the large-data regime — they converge to different places at different speeds. Rapid fire — What ML is ML infers rules from examples; classical code applies hand-written rules. Reframe what is ML as function approximation under a generalization constraint . Five settings by supervision signal: supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement. Self-supervised = supervised with manufactured labels; it powers foundation models. Discriminative models (border); generative models (countries, can sample). Generative wins small-data / sampling; discriminative wins large-data accuracy. # The Supervised Setup, Formally The formalism is exactly what separates a crisp answer from hand-waving. Supervised learning has six objects: Object What it is Example Input space The set of possible inputs Feature vectors, images, sentences Output space The set of possible labels for binary, for regression Distribution Unknown source of all data; we only see samples The real world we never observe directly Training set examples drawn i.i.d. from Your labeled dataset Hypothesis space Functions you're willing to consider Linear models? Depth-3 trees? A given NN? Loss How wrong a single prediction is Squared loss, 0-1 loss, cross-entropy The goal: use to pick an that performs well on the whole distribution , not just on . # True risk vs empirical risk What we actually care about is the true risk — the average loss over the entire distribution, for a fresh example drawn from the real world. The problem is fatal: we cannot compute it , because we don't have , only the finite sample . So we approximate it with the only data we have — the average loss on the training set. This is the empirical risk : ​ ( h ) = n 1 ​ i = 1 ∑ n ​ ℓ ( h ( x i ​ ) , y i ​ ) By the law of large numbers, for a fixed it converges to the true risk as grows. It's the visible shadow cast by the invisible true risk. True risk Empirical risk ​ ( h ) Defined over The whole distribution The finite training sample Can we compute it? No — is unknown Yes — it's just an average Role What we want to minimize The proxy we actually minimize Catch Invisible Unbiased but noisy for a fixed ; optimistically biased for the picked by minimizing it # Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) Since we can't minimize the true risk directly, we minimize the empirical risk instead. That principle is Empirical Risk Minimization : pick the hypothesis with the smallest average error on your training data. Almost every model you've trained does a version of this — linear regression minimizes squared loss, logistic regression minimizes log-loss, a neural net minimizes cross-entropy via SGD. ERM minimizes the wiggly empirical risk, but the minimum we actually want belongs to the smooth true risk. Here's the crucial gap: ERM minimizes ​ , but we want to minimize , and the minimizer of one isn't the minimizer of the other. When is rich and is small, ​ can hit zero (perfect training fit) while stays large. That is overfitting , and it's why naive ERM on an unconstrained fails. Managing this gap is the entire game. Memory hook True risk is your score on the real exam; empirical risk is your score on the practice test. ERM means study to ace the practice test — it works only if the practice test resembles the real one and you didn't memorize the answer key. Interview angle What does training a model actually do? Senior answer: it performs regularized empirical risk minimization over a chosen hypothesis space, using the training sample as a proxy for the unknown distribution — and the whole challenge is that the proxy is imperfect, which is why we hold out data and regularize. Rapid fire — Supervised setup Objects: input space , output space , distribution , i.i.d. sample , hypothesis space , loss . True risk is what we want but can't compute. Empirical risk ​ ( h ) = n 1 ​ ∑ ℓ is the computable proxy. ERM picks the hypothesis minimizing empirical risk; nearly all training is regularized ERM. The gap between and ​ is the source of overfitting and the reason for held-out data. # Generalization: Why Held-Out Data Is Sacred Generalization is performance on data the model wasn't trained on. It's the only thing that matters: a model that memorizes its training set and fails on everything else is worthless. This section is about measuring it honestly — mostly a matter of discipline. # The i.i.d. assumption The license to even hope for generalization is the assumption that training and future data are drawn i.i.d. from the same distribution . Identically distributed : test data looks statistically like training data. Independent : examples don't leak information about each other. When this breaks — the world shifts after you train, the test set comes from a different population, a time series is autocorrelated — generalization estimates turn optimistic and models silently degrade. Distribution shift is the number-one reason good offline models disappoint in production. Memory hook i.i.d. is the contract that says the future will be sampled from the same urn as the past. Every ML guarantee is voided the moment that contract breaks. # The train / validation / test split Because training error is an optimistically biased estimate of true risk, we estimate generalization on data the model never saw while fitting. Standard practice splits three ways. Three-way split (left) and the learning curve whose gap diagnoses bias vs variance (right). Split Typical % What it's for Training ~60–80% Fit the parameters (weights). The model directly minimizes loss here. Validation ~10–20% Tune hyperparameters and make model decisions: architecture, regularization, when to stop, which features. Test ~10–20% Used once , at the very end, for an honest unbiased estimate of real-world performance. Why do we need both validation and test? Every time you use the validation score to make a decision, you fit it a little. After trying a hundred configurations and keeping the best, the winner's validation score is optimistic — you've partly overfit the validation set through selection. The untouched test set restores honesty. The golden rule Never touch the test set until the very end. Not to peek, not to just check, not to engineer features, not to pick a threshold. The moment a test observation influences any decision, the test set stops being an unbiased estimate and becomes just another training signal. Treat it as locked in a vault. Violating this is called data snooping (or leakage). It's insidious: it inflates your reported metrics while the model is secretly worse. The classic traps: Leakage type What goes wrong Fix Preprocessing on full data Normalization stats / imputation / feature ranks computed before the split leak test info into training Fit every transform on the training fold only , then apply Target leakage A feature is a proxy for or downstream of the label (e.g. account closed date for churn) Drop features unknown at prediction time Temporal leakage Random shuffling trains on the future to predict the past Always split by time for temporal problems Group leakage Same patient/user/doc in both train and test; model memorizes the entity Split by group Interview angle Your model scores 99% offline but tanks in production. What happened? Walk the checklist: distribution shift, target leakage, temporal/group leakage, normalization fit on full data, validation overfitting from too many trials. A systematic suspicion of suspiciously good numbers is the senior instinct interviewers screen for. # Reading a learning curve A learning curve plots error against training-set size (or epochs). It's a cheap diagnostic. As you add data, training error rises slightly and validation error falls; the two converge, and the vertical gap between them is the generalization gap . What you see What it means → the fix Big gap that doesn't close with more data High variance / overfitting → more data, more regularization, or a simpler model Both curves plateau high and sit close together High bias / underfitting → a more expressive model or better features (more data won't help) Rapid fire — Generalization Generalization = performance on unseen data; it's the only goal. i.i.d. (same distribution, independent samples) licenses generalization; distribution shift breaks it. Train fits parameters, validation tunes choices, test is the one-shot honest estimate. You need both val and test because repeated validation selection overfits the validation set. Golden rule: never touch the test set until the end. Leakage (preprocessing on full data, target/temporal/group) inflates offline metrics and kills production. Learning curve: persistent gap = variance; high converged floor = bias. # Overfitting, Underfitting the Bias-Variance Tradeoff Underfitting : the model is too simple to capture the pattern — high error on both train and test. Overfitting : the model is so flexible it captures noise as if it were signal — low train error, high test error. The art of ML is steering between the two. The same 18 noisy points fit by polynomials of degree 1, 4, and 14. Note the overfit model has the lowest training error and the worst test error. Model capacity (complexity) is the knob: polynomial degree, tree depth, number of NN parameters, the inverse of regularization strength. Low capacity → underfit; high capacity → overfit; the right spot depends on how much data you have (more data supports more capacity). Memory hook Underfitting is a student who didn't study (wrong on practice and exam). Overfitting is a student who memorized the practice answer key (perfect on practice, lost on the exam). You want the one who learned the concept . # The bias-variance decomposition For squared-error regression the tradeoff is exact. If data is with zero-mean noise of variance , then the expected error at a point, averaged over all training sets you might draw, splits cleanly: ​ ( x ) ) 2 ] = too simple Bias 2 ​ ​ + too flexible Variance ​ ​ + irreducible σ 2 ​ ​ Term Plain English Signals Bias² How far the average prediction sits from the truth — systematic error in the same direction Model too simple Variance How much the prediction jumps around as you swap training sets Model too flexible, chasing noise (noise) The floor — the label is partly random; no model beats it Irreducible The tension: simplifying lowers variance but raises bias ; enriching lowers bias but raises variance . You can't drive both to zero with finite data — push one down and the other comes up. Total error is their sum, so you minimize by trading off. Go deeper (optional) The clean additive split is special to squared loss . For 0-1 loss or cross-entropy the decomposition is messier and not additive the same way — a subtlety interviewers occasionally test. Don't claim bias-variance decomposes cleanly for classification accuracy: it doesn't. # The dartboard picture The most durable mental image: throwing darts at a target. The bullseye is the truth; each dart is a prediction from a model trained on one random dataset. Bias is aim (is the cluster centered?); variance is grouping (how tight is it?). Memory hook Bias = aim (is the cluster centered on the bullseye?). Variance = grouping (how tight is the cluster?). A sniper with a bent scope: low variance, high bias. A jittery shooter with good aim: low bias, high variance. # The U-curve Plot expected test error against complexity and you get the famous U. As complexity rises, bias² falls steeply but variance climbs; their sum plus the noise floor is U-shaped. The minimum is the optimal capacity for your data. Bias falls and variance rises with complexity; total error bottoms out at the sweet spot. Training error (not shown) keeps falling monotonically to the right — which is exactly why you can't pick complexity by training error . You pick it by validation error, which traces this U. Interview angle — which lever moves which term Expect how do you reduce variance without adding much bias? Knowing which lever moves which term is the actual test. To reduce VARIANCE (overfitting) To reduce BIAS (underfitting) More data A richer / more expressive model Bagging / ensembling (averages variance away) Boosting (fits the residual error) Regularization (trades a little bias for a lot of variance) Better features / less regularization # Double descent — the modern asterisk The clean U is the classical story, and mostly right. But in modern deep learning, as you grow a model past the point where it can perfectly fit (interpolate) the training data, test error often goes down again after a spike at the interpolation threshold . Double descent: error dips, spikes where the model exactly fits the data, then dips a second time. This is why a neural net with far more parameters than data points can still generalize beautifully. The leading explanation: among the many settings that perfectly fit the data, gradient descent has an implicit bias toward simple, low-norm solutions — so huge models effectively self-regularize. Go deeper (optional) Don't oversell this as overfitting isn't real. The classical U holds for a fixed effective complexity; double descent is a phenomenon of overparameterized interpolating models with optimizer-induced regularization. Both pictures are true in their regimes — saying so reads as well-calibrated rather than buzzword-chasing. Rapid fire — Bias, variance, capacity Underfit = high train AND test error (high bias). Overfit = low train, high test (high variance). Capacity (degree, depth, #params, 1/regularization) is the knob; more data supports more capacity. Squared error Bias² + Variance + (this clean split is special to squared loss). Bias = aim off-center; variance = loose grouping; noise = the floor you can't beat. U-curve: pick the minimum via validation error, never training error. Lower variance: more data, bagging, regularization. Lower bias: richer model, boosting, better features. Double descent: overparameterized nets can improve again past the interpolation threshold. # Regularization, Inductive Bias No Free Lunch Three tightly linked ideas explain why and how we deliberately constrain models. Idea What it means Regularization Any change to learning that reduces variance/overfitting, usually by penalizing complexity. Minimize ​ ( h ) + λ Ω ( h ) instead of ​ ( h ) alone, where measures complexity ( ridge, ​ lasso) and sets the strength. It trades a little bias for a larger drop in variance — sliding you left toward the U-curve's sweet spot. Early stopping, dropout, weight decay, data augmentation, and ensembling are all regularizers in spirit. Inductive bias The assumptions a model uses to generalize beyond the data. Every model that generalizes has one. A linear model assumes linearity; a CNN assumes locality and translation invariance; an RNN/Transformer assumes sequence structure; a tree assumes axis-aligned split

title: Data Preparation & Feature Engineering
text: Models learn from what you feed them — garbage features beat clever algorithms every time. Feature work is where many interviews go deep: not because formulas are hard, but because judgment is — knowing when a transform helps, when it leaks, and when imbalance demands a different loss and metric. The best candidates narrate a pipeline end to end: audit the table, define the label at the right time, split without cheating, encode for the model family, and pick metrics that match the business asymmetry — then show the sklearn Pipeline that enforces it. This chapter walks data quality through encoding, transforms, selection, leakage ( Data Leakage ), class imbalance ( Class Imbalance ), and honest train/validation/test splits aligned with cross-validation and evaluation practice. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Run a data quality checklist before modeling. Handle missing data (MCAR/MAR/MNAR) and pick imputation vs missing indicators. Scale and encode features for the right model family without leakage. Engineer numeric, text, and datetime signals; select features with filter/wrapper/embedded tools. Classify leakage types with examples and prevent them with pipelines. Address imbalance and split data by groups and time correctly. # Data quality checks Before featurizing, interrogate the table: Check What to look for Why it matters Schema types IDs stored as floats, dates as strings Silent coercion bugs in training Duplicates Exact dupes, same user-timestamp Inflated metrics, wrong splits Cardinality Constant columns, near-unique junk Zero information or memorization Outliers range Negative ages, 10⁹ seconds Breaks scaling and linear models Label sanity Prevalence, temporal gaps Wrong baseline, wrong metric Join integrity Orphan keys after merges Missing-not-at-random bias Profile train and (future) production separately — drift in quality often precedes drift in model scores. Automate checks in a validation gate before each training run: assert label column never null, assert timestamp monotonicity for event streams, and alert when categorical cardinality jumps (new enum values in production). These gates catch silent schema breaks that models cannot learn around. Interview angle Walk me through starting a new tabular problem. Open with data quality and label definition, not I'll try XGBoost. # Target definition and label hygiene Before featurizing, freeze what you predict and when the label is known. Churn at 30 days is not the same problem as churn at 7 days — horizons change prevalence and feature eligibility. Document inclusion rules (active users only, minimum activity) so train and serve use the same population. Wrong labels poison every downstream step; no amount of regularization fixes a label that encodes the wrong business question. Interview angle How do you predict churn? — answer with label definition and prediction time first, then features. Interviewers listen for eligibility filters and whether features exist at scoring time. # Missing data MCAR (missing completely at random): drop or simple impute without much bias. MAR (missing at random): missingness depends on observed columns — model it or impute with care. MNAR (not at random): missingness depends on the hidden value itself — no imputation is unbiased without extra structure (e.g. Tobit, explicit missingness model). Strategy When Caveat Listwise delete MCAR, few missing Wastes data if not MCAR Mean / median impute Quick baseline Shrinks variance; use + missing indicator Model-based (KNN, MICE) MAR, structured Fit inside CV folds only Learned missing token Trees, deep nets Let splits handle absent values Separate category Unknown Categoricals Don't confuse with a real level A missing-indicator feature (1 if imputed) lets linear models recover different slopes for imputed rows. Decision rule of thumb : if missing and MCAR plausible, median impute + indicator is fine for tree/linear baselines. If missingness correlates with the label (MNAR suspicion), model whether missingness is informative — or drop features you cannot defend at inference time. Memory hook MCAR = dropped coins; MAR = missingness you can explain from other columns; MNAR = the secret itself drives absence. # Scaling numeric features Method Formula (per column) Robust to outliers? Standardization No Min–max No — dominated by extremes Robust Better for heavy tails Needs scaling : distance models (k-NN, SVM RBF), neural nets, linear/logistic with gradient descent, k-means. Often indifferent : tree ensembles (splits are rank-invariant). Rule : if the algorithm cares about magnitude or dot products, scale; fit scaler on training only . Rapid fire — Missing scale Name MCAR/MAR/MNAR before imputing. Indicators + imputation for MAR tabular. Robust scaling when outliers matter. Trees don't need scale; linear and NN do. Fit transforms on train. # Encoding categoricals Encoding High-cardinality? Leakage risk One-hot Poor if thousands of levels Low if fit on train categories only Ordinal When order is real Wrong order hurts linear models Target / mean encoding Strong for high card High — needs out-of-fold stats Hashing Very high card, streaming Collisions trade bias for memory Embeddings Very high card, deep nets Learned; watch rare levels Target encoding replaces category with smoothed mean label ​ c ​ estimated on training rows with label only — compute per fold on the other folds' training portion (K-fold target encoding) to avoid label leakage into validation. Add smoothing toward global mean for rare categories. For high cardinality (user ids, zip codes): hash, frequency encoding, bucket rare levels to Other , or embeddings in tree/NN hybrids. Frequency encoding maps a level to its training count or log-count — smooth for trees, leaky if computed on train+val together. Embedding layers learn dense vectors for sparse IDs in neural nets; rare levels need min-frequency cutoffs or a shared UNK bucket. In interviews, tie encoding choice to data volume and model family : one-hot blows up sparse linear models; target encoding helps GBDT on categoricals when done out-of-fold. Target encoding on full train before CV The validation fold sees its own labels in the encoding — classic leakage. Always out-of-fold. # Numeric transforms, interactions, and binning Log / Box–Cox : right-skewed counts, multiplicative effects → approximate normality for linear models. Binning : capture nonlinearities for linear models; trees do this implicitly. Interactions : ​ × x 2 ​ when domain says joint effect (price × discount); explosive dimension — prefer models that learn interactions (GBDT, NNs) when data is ample. Pair transforms with interpretability needs: stakeholders may want monotonic bins; NNs may want raw + embeddings. # Text and datetime features Text : tokenization, n-grams, TF–IDF for classical baselines; pretrained embeddings or fine-tuned encoders for depth ( classification pipelines). Normalize case and unicode consistently with production. Datetime : decompose into hour, day-of-week, month , holidays, time-since-event; for series, lags and rolling stats with strict causal windows (only past data). See time series splitting below. Cyclic encoding helps linear models respect wrap-around: for hour, same for day-of-week. Raw integers imply hour 23 is far from hour 0. For recency features, compute ​ − t last event ​ using the same clock as serving — training backfills with warehouse as_of timestamps prevent subtle future peeking. # Text feature ladder Stage Representation When Bag-of-words / TF–IDF Sparse n-grams Strong baseline, interpretable Char n-grams Subword robustness Typos, morphology Pretrained embeddings Average or pool token vectors Medium data, transfer Fine-tuned encoder End-to-end task loss Enough labels, compute budget Start simple: TF–IDF + logistic regression often beats an under-trained BERT in interviews because it's fast, debuggable, and pairs with logistic regression intuition. Move up the ladder when offline metrics plateau and latency budget allows. Interview angle Features for fraud? Mix velocity (counts in 1h), device graph signals, and time since last event — always ask what's known at decision time ( leakage ). # Feature selection Family Idea Cost Filter Correlation, mutual information, chi-square Cheap; ignores model Wrapper Forward/backward stepwise on validation score Expensive; overfits small Embedded L1 (lasso paths), tree importance Built into training Permutation importance Shuffle one column, measure metric drop Model-aware; compute on validation Drop collinear features for linear models; trees tolerate redundancy but importance gets muddy. Permutation on test once at the end; tune selection on validation inside CV. Wrapper vs embedded trade-off : stepwise selection with logistic regression can overfit when is small — each added feature is tuned on the same validation slice. L1 ( lasso ) path gives a sparse model in one shot; gradient boosting importance is fast but favors high-cardinality columns — use permutation importance to sanity-check. For interviews, name one filter method (mutual information), one embedded (L1), and permutation as the honest check. # Data leakage Full taxonomy — see Data Leakage card: Type Example Fix Target leakage Refund issued predicting purchase Drop post-outcome fields Train–test contamination Same user in train and test Group split Temporal leakage Random shuffle on time series Time-based split Preprocessing leakage StandardScaler on all data before split Pipeline fit on train only Aggregate leakage : target encoding or global counts computed including test users — fix with per-fold or streaming estimators. Walk the same checklist when tuning hyperparameters : if each trial refits encoders on train+validation labels, you leak selection signal. Nested cross-validation separates outer honest estimation from inner tuning — expensive but correct when stakes are high ( Cross-Validation , overfitting ). Rapid fire — Leakage Features must exist at prediction time. Split before fit. Groups and time are not optional. Target encoding = out-of-fold only. Suspicious offline AUC → audit joins first. # Class imbalance Rare positives break accuracy and default thresholds ( Precision Recall , PR-AUC ): Technique Role Class weights Reweight loss — cheap, no duplicate rows Undersample majority Faster training; loses data Oversample / SMOTE Synthetic minority points along borders — overuse blurs boundaries ; only inside train folds Threshold move Tune on PR curve on validation Focal loss Down-weight easy negatives in deep nets ([[loss-functions Pick metrics that reflect the business: PR-AUC, recall at fixed precision, cost-sensitive utility. After resampling, recalibrate if probabilities matter ( Calibration ). # SMOTE caveats (expanded) SMOTE interpolates between a minority point and its k nearest minority neighbors — synthetic points lie on chords in feature space. It helps when the minority class is tiny and the boundary is smooth; it hurts when features are mostly categorical or when noise dimensions dominate (synthetic points land in nonsense regions). Never apply SMOTE before splitting — duplicates the minority into validation. Prefer class weights first on large data; SMOTE is a scalpel for small tabular sets with continuous features. Cost-sensitive learning bakes business asymmetry into the loss: false negative cost 100× false positive → weight positives 100× or optimize a custom utility at a chosen threshold. This is cleaner than resampling when costs are asymmetric but known ( Loss Functions ). # Train, validation, and test splitting Problem type Split strategy i.i.d. tabular Random 60/20/20 or nested CV ([[cross-validation Grouped (user, patient) GroupKFold — all rows of a group in one fold Temporal Train on past, validate on future; expanding window Spatial / market Hold out geos for true generalization Fundamentals golden rule: touch test once. Hyperparameters and thresholds consume validation only. # Leakage-safe sklearn pipeline Fit preprocessors on training data only; chain with the estimator: from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression num_cols = [ age , income ] cat_cols = [ country ] preprocess = ColumnTransformer( transformers=[ ( num , Pipeline([ ( imputer , SimpleImputer(strategy= median )), ( scaler , StandardScaler()), ]), num_cols, ), ( cat , Pipeline([ ( imputer , SimpleImputer(strategy= constant , fill_value= Unknown )), ( onehot , OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown= ignore )), ]), cat_cols, ), ] ) model = Pipeline(steps=[ ( preprocess , preprocess), ( clf , LogisticRegression(max_iter= 1000 )), ]) # X_train, y_train only — never fit on validation or test model.fit(X_train, y_train) y_val = model.predict(X_val) In cross-validation, wrap the entire pipeline in cross_val_score so each fold refits imputer and scaler on that fold's train slice only. # Leakage stories interviewers love Scenario Leakage type One-line fix Predicting hospital readmission using length of stay after discharge Target Feature not known at discharge scoring time Email spam with duplicate forwards in train and test Contamination Split by message id or hash Stock prediction with random 80/20 row split Temporal Walk-forward validation Feature selection ranked by correlation on full dataset Preprocessing Select inside each CV train fold # Feature engineering vs feature stores In production ( ML system design ), point-in-time correct features come from a feature store: every training row joins attributes as they were known at that timestamp , not today's snapshot of the user. Training on current aggregates (total lifetime spend) to predict past events is subtle temporal leakage — offline AUC soars, live model flatlines. Go deeper (optional) Polynomial features explode dimension on wide tables; use only with strong regularization or low-dimensional domain picks. Entity embeddings pre-trained on co-occurrence can transfer cold-start signal for recommender-style problems ( Recommender Systems ). Memory hook Pipeline = every transform is part of the model, trained where the model is trained. Interview angle How do you prevent leakage in sklearn? — ColumnTransformer + Pipeline , fit on train or inside CV; never fit on concatenated train+val. Rapid fire — Splits imbalance Group split for repeated entities. Time split for series. SMOTE only in train folds. Class weights often enough. Threshold ≠ 0.5. Pipeline fit on train. # Model-aware feature choices Different learners expose different failure modes — feature prep should match. Model family Encoding / scaling notes Linear / logistic Scale continuous; one-hot or OOF target encode; watch multicollinearity k-NN, SVM (RBF) Scale mandatory; distance metrics suffer from mixed units Tree / GBDT Unscaled OK; target encoding helps high-cardinality categoricals Neural nets Standardize inputs; embeddings for sparse IDs; watch embedding dimension vs data Naive Bayes Discretize heavy tails; independence assumption hates redundant copies Classification and regression chapters assume these prep choices; mismatches (linear on unscaled dollar amounts) show up as the model didn't learn when the pipeline was wrong. # Worked split example (groups + time) E-commerce click prediction: rows are impression-level, but users repeat. Wrong : random 80/20 row split — same shopper in train and test. Right : GroupKFold by user_id for validation; hold out the last 7 days globally for test so features use only past behavior. Imputation and scaling live in the pipeline fitted on train users only; future users with unseen countries hit handle_unknown='ignore' on the one-hot encoder. Validation optimism on grouped data If groups are huge (enterprise accounts), a single fold may contain entire whales — report variance across folds, not one lucky split. Rapid fire — Model-aware prep Linear needs scale + careful categoricals. Trees eat raw-ish tables with good encodings. NNs need normalized inputs + embeddings. Match prep to the inductive bias. Group+time splits for behavioral data. # One-page summary Concept The one thing to remember Data quality Profile types, dupes, label prevalence before modeling. Missingness MCAR/MAR/MNAR drives strategy; add missing indicators. Scaling For distance/linear/NN; fit on train; robust if heavy tails. Encoding One-hot for low card; hashed/target/emb for high card — OOF for target. Transforms Log/Box–Cox for skew; interactions when domain demands. Text/datetime TF–IDF or embeddings; causal lags for time. Selection Filters cheap; L1/permutation model-aware; avoid test peeking. Leakage Time, group, target, and preprocessing — pipeline fixes the last. Imbalance Weights, resampling, threshold, PR metrics — not accuracy. Splits Random vs group vs time; test locked until the end. Model-aware prep Scale for distance/linear/NN; trees need encoding more than scaling. Document each feature in a feature contract : dtype, null policy, allowed range, and whether it exists at serve time. Contracts ride with system design reviews so batch backfills and online routers apply the same rules — otherwise you debug metric drops that are just inconsistent null handling. # Related Data Leakage Class Imbalance Fundamentals Cross-Validation Model Evaluation Validation Classification Methods Regression Methods Logistic Regression Regularization Trees Ensembles Time Series Stationarity ML System Design Framework

title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
text: Say it in 30s: For squared-error regression, expected test error decomposes exactly into bias² + variance + irreducible noise. Bias is error from wrong assumptions (too simple a model, underfits); variance is error from sensitivity to the training sample (too flexible a model, overfits). Lowering one usually raises the other, so the goal is the sweet spot, not zero of either. Key points More capacity (deeper tree, higher polynomial degree, less regularization) → lower bias, higher variance. More data lets you afford more capacity without paying as much variance. The dartboard picture: bias = is the cluster centered on the target; variance = how tight the cluster is. The U-curve: total test error falls then rises as complexity grows; minimum = optimal capacity. Modern asterisk: double descent — past the interpolation point, very overparameterized models can improve again. The math Data with , . Learner ​ ( x ) trained on random . At fixed , expected squared error: ​ ( x ) ) 2 ] = E [ ( f ( x ) + ε − f ^ ​ ( x ) ) 2 ] . Add and subtract ​ ( x )] : ​ ] + E [ f ^ ​ ] − f ^ ​ + ε ) 2 ] = Bias 2 ( E [ f ^ ​ ( x )] − f ( x ) ) 2 ​ ​ + Variance E [ ( f ^ ​ ( x ) − E [ f ^ ​ ( x )] ) 2 ] ​ ​ + σ 2 . Cross terms vanish because ​ and ​ − E [ f ^ ​ ]] = 0 . Bias² = systematic miss; Variance = spread across training sets; = label noise floor. Common follow-ups / traps How do you reduce variance? → more data, regularization, simpler model, bagging/ensembling. How do you reduce bias? → richer model, better features, boosting. Don't confuse this with the bias/variance of an estimator in statistics (related, not identical framing). See depth: Fundamentals (§4). title: Empirical Risk Minimization
text: Say it in 30s: We want to minimize true risk — expected loss over the real data distribution — but we can't see that distribution. So we minimize empirical risk , the average loss on our training sample, as a stand-in. ERM is pick the hypothesis with lowest average training loss. Why it works (and when it doesn't) Justified by the i.i.d. assumption : training and future data come from the same distribution, so empirical risk estimates true risk. Pure ERM overfits, so in practice we use regularized risk minimization : empirical loss + λ·penalty. When i.i.d. breaks (distribution shift, autocorrelated time series, sampling bias), empirical risk becomes an optimistic, misleading estimate. The math True (expected) risk over distribution : ​ [ L ( f ( x ) , y ) ] is the per-example loss; is unknowable because is hidden. title: Generalization
text: Say it in 30s: A model generalizes if it performs well on data it never saw during training. The whole point of ML is low error on the true distribution, not low error on the training set. Held-out data is how we estimate it. Key points The i.i.d. assumption is the license to even hope for generalization: test data is statistically like training data. Train / validation / test split : train fits parameters, validation tunes hyperparameters and model choice, test is touched once for an unbiased final estimate. Distribution shift is the #1 reason good offline models disappoint in production — the i.i.d. assumption quietly fails. The generalization gap = test error − training error; large gap signals overfitting. The math Let be the true risk and n ​ ( f ) = n 1 ​ ∑ i ​ L ( f ( x i ​ ) , y i ​ ) the average loss on a sample. The gap is n ​ ( f ) . Evaluated on the training sample the fit was chosen on, n ​ is optimistically biased (gap on average); evaluated on fresh held-out data, n ​ is an unbiased estimate of . Same finite-class bound as ERM: for and , with probability , n ​ ( f ) + 2 n ln ∣ H ∣ + ln ( 2/ δ ) ​ ​ ∀ f ∈ H . VC-style (qualitative): for richer , uniform convergence scales like ​ / n ​ — you need ​ for n ​ to track everywhere in . Estimating accuracy on held-out points: if true rate is , the binomial std of the sample mean is ​ . Example: , → , so pp is one–σ noise — don't chase 0.1 pt swings on a small test set. Trap: any decision made by looking at the test set leaks information and inflates your estimate. Guard the test set. See depth: Fundamentals (§3). title: Overfitting & Underfitting
text: Say it in 30s: Underfitting = the model is too simple to capture the signal (high training error AND high test error). Overfitting = the model memorizes the training sample including its noise (low training error, high test error). You diagnose which one you have from the gap between training and validation curves. Reading the learning curve Big gap that doesn't close with more data → high variance / overfitting → more data, regularization, simpler model. Both curves plateau high and sit close together → high bias / underfitting → richer model or better features (more data won't help). Fixes Overfitting: regularization, dropout, early stopping, data augmentation, more data, ensembling. Underfitting: more capacity, better/more features, train longer, reduce regularization. The math Train vs validation error: underfitting → both high and close; overfitting → training low, validation high (the gap widens with capacity). Polynomial degree : rich fits noise → n ​ ↓ , past some . Tame it with regularized ERM: min ​ n 1 ​ i ∑ ​ L ( w ⊤ ϕ d ​ ( x i ​ ) , y i ​ ) + λ ∥ w ∥ 2 2 ​ . Complexity penalties when comparing models fit by MLE / least squares (residual SSE, params, points): SSE ​ + 2 k , BIC = n ln n SSE ​ + k ln n . BIC penalizes extra parameters harder for large — favors simpler models when the gap is mostly noise. Trap: a low training error alone tells you nothing. Always quote the validation gap. See depth: Fundamentals (§3–4). Related: Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Regularization , Cross-Validation , Generalization , Dropout , Data Leakage .

title: Regularization
text: Say it in 30s: Anything that constrains a model to reduce variance at the cost of a little bias. Most often an added penalty on model complexity: minimize (empirical loss + λ·penalty). λ trades fit against simplicity. L1 vs L2 (the classic question) L2 / Ridge (penalize Σwᵢ²): shrinks weights smoothly toward zero, never exactly zero. Handles correlated features by sharing weight. Has a closed form. L1 / Lasso (penalize Σ|wᵢ|): drives some weights exactly to zero → built-in feature selection / sparsity. The corner of the diamond constraint is why. No closed form (subgradient / soft-thresholding at zero). Elastic Net : L1 + L2, gets sparsity plus stability with correlated features. Beyond penalties: early stopping, dropout, data augmentation, weight decay, ensembling are all variance-fighting regularizers. The math Ridge (L2) on weights : min ​ i ∑ ​ L ( f ( x i ​ ; w ) , y i ​ ) + 2 λ ​ ∥ w ∥ 2 2 ​ . Lasso (L1): same with ​ — sparsity via subgradients at zero. Linear regression + MSE: closed form = ( X ⊤ X + λ I ) − 1 X ⊤ y (for 1 ​ ( y − w ⊤ x ) 2 ; the also makes X + λ I invertible even when is rank-deficient). SGD implements this as weight decay: ​ L (the gradient of λ ​ ∥ w ∥ 2 is ) (decoupled from the loss gradient in AdamW). MAP view: Gaussian prior 2 ​ / ( 2 τ 2 ) gives ∑ ​ lo g p ( y i ​ ∣ x i ​ , w ) − 2 λ ​ ∥ w ∥ 2 2 ​ with — MAP MLE L2. Laplace prior ​ / b yields the L1 penalty the same way. Trap: larger λ = more regularization = more bias, less variance. Tune λ on validation, not test. See depth: Loss Functions (§2.5–2.6), Regression Methods (§3.3), Fundamentals (§5). Related: Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Overfitting Underfitting , Dropout , Decision Trees, Random Forests Gradient Boosting .

title: Data Leakage
text: Say it in 30s: Leakage is any path for test or future information to influence training or model selection, so offline metrics lie and production tanks. Taxonomy: target leakage (features that encode the label or its future), train–test contamination (duplicate users/docs across splits), temporal leakage (training on the future), and preprocessing leakage (scalers, encoders, or feature selection fit on the full dataset). Fix by splitting first, then fitting every transform inside the training fold only. Key points Target leakage example: “account closed date” predicting churn — only known after the user left. Group splits when rows correlate (patient, user, session); random shuffles let the model memorize entities. Time series: always train on past, validate on future — random k-fold is invalid. The math Preprocessing leakage: fit scaler on train only. Train mean ​ = n tr ​ 1 ​ ∑ i ∈ tr ​ x i ​ ; leaked full-data 1 ​ ∑ all ​ x i ​ folds test rows into the statistic, so scaled test values for different points are coupled through shared — optimistic CV. Target encoding: naive category mean ​ cat ​ = n cat ​ 1 ​ ∑ i ∈ cat ​ y i ​ uses the row’s own label in the average when that row is included → leakage. Leave-one-out / out-of-fold fix with global mean and smoothing : cat ​ = n cat ​ + m n cat ​ y ˉ ​ cat ​ + m μ ​ Compute ​ cat ​ only on other rows in the training fold (or LOO neighbors); shrinks small categories toward . Common follow-ups / traps We scaled before splitting — is that bad? → Yes — test statistics leaked into train normalization. CV score is 99% — suspicious? → Walk the leakage checklist before celebrating. See depth: Data Preparation Feature Engineering (§Leakage), Fundamentals (§Generalization), Model Evaluation Validation . Related: Cross-Validation , Time Series Stationarity , Generalization .

title: Class Imbalance
text: Say it in 30s: When positives are rare (fraud, disease, clicks), accuracy is useless and default 0.5 thresholds waste recall. Responses: class weights or resampling (undersample majority, oversample minority — SMOTE synthesizes borderline positives but can blur decision boundaries if overused), threshold tuning on validation, focal loss for hard examples in deep nets, and metrics that ignore the TN flood: PR-AUC , precision/recall, or cost-sensitive scores. Always align the metric with the cost of a miss vs a false alarm. Key points Lower threshold → higher recall, lower precision; pick the operating point by business cost, not default 0.5. Resampling changes the training distribution — recalibrate probabilities if you care about calibrated scores. Report PR curve , not ROC alone, when prevalence is skewed ( ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC ). The math Weighted cross-entropy (classes ): ​ w c ​ y c ​ lo g p c ​ , with ​ = K N c ​ N ​ so rare classes up-weight ( = total samples, ​ = class count). Focal loss down-weights easy examples: ​ = − ( 1 − p t ​ ) γ lo g p t ​ , ​ = probability assigned to the true class. At : ​ = 0.9 ⇒ L ≈ 0.001 ; ​ = 0.1 ⇒ L ≈ 1.87 — hard mistakes dominate gradients. Prior / threshold shift: if training downsampled negatives at keep-rate , map served score ​ to the true-rate probability ( ML System Design Prep ): ​ = p s ​ + ( 1 − p s ​ ) / w p s ​ ​ Equivalent to adding to the logit. Since that shift is negative: downsampling negatives made positives look more common, so the sampled model overestimates and has to be pulled back down. Cost-sensitive threshold: minimize with FN cost ​ , FP cost ​ → optimal = c FP ​ + c FN ​ c FP ​ ​ on ​ . Example: , ​ = 0.5 → ​ ≈ 0.091 . Common follow-ups / traps SMOTE on the full data before CV? → Leakage — resample inside each training fold only. 99% accuracy on 1% positives → Likely predicting all-negative; check PR-AUC and recall at your threshold.
