title: Math
heads: Linear algebra — the words for data
Matrix calculus — gradients you must be able to derive
Statistics — from data back to the model
The bootstrap — uncertainty without a formula
Information theory — where loss functions come from
text: Four languages — linear algebra, probability, statistics, optimization — plus information theory, where loss functions secretly come from. After this chapter you can Read any model as matrix operations on data; state Bayes' rule and explain MLE vs MAP; say what a p-value and a confidence interval actually mean; explain why gradient descent works and when it doesn't; and derive cross-entropy from first principles. # Linear algebra — the words for data Almost every model is linear algebra with a nonlinearity sprinkled on top. A dataset is a matrix of shape : rows (examples) by columns (features). A single example is a vector; a batch is a matrix; an image or a sequence of embeddings is a tensor. Once you see data as a matrix, a linear layer is just — a matrix multiply that maps one vector space into another. Object Shape What it is Scalar A single number (a learning rate, a loss value) Vector One example, one feature column, one embedding Matrix A dataset ( ), a weight layer, a covariance ( ) Tensor 3D+ A batch of images, a sequence of token embeddings Two operations carry most of the weight. The dot product measures alignment: large when two vectors point the same way, zero when orthogonal. Normalize it and you get cosine similarity — the backbone of search, embeddings, and attention. Matrix–vector multiplication is a linear transformation that rotates, scales, and projects the input; stacking these with nonlinearities is the entire forward pass of a neural net. Norms measure size. The L2 norm ​ is Euclidean length and underlies ridge regression; the L1 norm ​ sums absolute values and drives sparsity (lasso). The choice of norm decides whether your regularizer shrinks weights smoothly or zeroes them out. The two ideas interviewers probe are eigendecomposition and SVD . An eigenvector is a direction a transformation only stretches, never rotates. The eigenvectors of a covariance matrix are the axes of greatest variance — which is exactly PCA . The singular value decomposition factors any matrix into rotate–scale–rotate, and powers PCA, low-rank approximation, recommender systems, and pseudo-inverses. Understand SVD and half of classical ML stops looking like separate tricks. PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance; keep the top-k for the best linear summary. Interview cue Why does PCA use eigenvectors of the covariance matrix? Because they are the orthogonal directions that maximize retained variance; the eigenvalues say how much each captures, so the top-k give the best rank-k linear summary of the data. # Eigen-everything: directions that don't rotate Most vectors are knocked off course by a matrix transformation, but a few stay perfectly aligned. An eigenvector is a special direction that a square matrix only scales, never rotates. The scaling factor is the eigenvalue . Formally, . Take 1 ​ 1 2 ​ ] . Solving the characteristic equation yields roots at ​ = 3 and ​ = 1 . The corresponding unit eigenvectors are ​ = [ 2 ​ 1 ​ , 2 ​ 1 ​ ] ⊤ and ​ = [ 2 ​ 1 ​ , − 2 ​ 1 ​ ] ⊤ . Notice that ​ = 3 v 1 ​ = [ 2 ​ 3 ​ , 2 ​ 3 ​ ] ⊤ — the vector is simply stretched by a factor of 3 along its original axis. The eigenvector defines the space's orientation, while the eigenvalue measures the magnitude of variance or spread along that specific axis. # Matrix calculus — gradients you must be able to derive Backprop is applied matrix calculus. Fix a shape convention and stick to it: if is a column vector, then ​ f ( x ) ∈ R d has the same shape as , and the Jacobian for is (row is ​ y i ⊤ ​ ). Expression Gradient (column ) x ​ = a A x (symmetric gives ) ​ = ( A + A ⊤ ) x 2 ​ w.r.t. ​ = 2 X ⊤ ( X w − y ) The Hessian f is the matrix of second partials; for MSE in linear regression, ​ = 2 X ⊤ X (PSD). One layer, chain rule. Forward with , . Given upstream (same shape as ): ∂ L ​ = ∂ y ∂ L ​ x ⊤ , ∂ x ∂ L ​ = W ⊤ ∂ y ∂ L ​ , ∂ b ∂ L ​ = ∂ y ∂ L ​ Shapes check: for ; for . Softmax + cross-entropy (one example). Logits , , one-hot , ​ y i ​ lo g p i ​ . Then — the error between predicted and true class probabilities. No separate term; that cancellation is why training uses logits + CrossEntropyLoss in one fused op. Memory hook Outer product for weights, transpose for inputs: ; softmax+CE = . Interview angle Weak: backprop is automatic. Strong: derive ​ ∥ X w − y ∥ 2 and on the board, and state Jacobian shapes so dimensions never surprise you in a transformer block. # Probability — measuring uncertainty Probability is the language for everything a model doesn't know. A random variable takes values with a distribution: a pmf for discrete outcomes, a pdf for continuous ones (where probability lives in areas, not points). A few distributions show up constantly: Distribution Models Shows up as Bernoulli / Binomial One / many yes-no trials Binary labels, click/no-click Categorical / Multinomial One-of-k outcomes Softmax outputs, class labels Gaussian (Normal) Sums of many small effects Noise, weight init, CLT Poisson / Exponential Counts / waiting times Arrivals, rare events, survival Uniform No prior preference Initialization, sampling From a distribution you get expectation (mean), variance (spread), and covariance (co-movement). Discrete: ​ p ( x , y ) , . Continuous: replace sums with integrals — , . For random vectors : ​ ) ( Y − μ Y ​ ) ⊤ ] , ρ ij ​ = σ i ​ σ j ​ Cov ( X i ​ , X j ​ ) ​ Variance of a sum (not additive unless independent): The multivariate Gaussian in with mean and SPD covariance : ∣Σ ∣ 1/2 1 ​ exp ( − 2 1 ​ ( x − μ ) ⊤ Σ − 1 ( x − μ ) ) Independence means — knowing one tells you nothing about the other. The single most important formula in the chapter is Bayes' rule : p ( data ∣ θ ) p ( θ ) ​ ⟹ posterior ∝ likelihood × prior The prior belief, reshaped by the likelihood of the data, yields the posterior. Two estimation principles fall out of it. Maximum Likelihood (MLE) picks the that makes the observed data most probable — ignoring the prior. Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) maximizes the posterior — MLE plus a prior, and that prior term is exactly regularization (a Gaussian prior gives L2, a Laplace prior gives L1). This is the bridge between probability and the losses you minimize. Interview cue — the base-rate trap A test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific for a disease with prevalence 1 in 10,000. You test positive — , not 99%, because false positives dominate: , and the posterior is . Reaching for Bayes instead of the headline number is the signal. # Statistics — from data back to the model Probability reasons from a known model to data; statistics runs it backwards — from a finite sample to claims about the population. An estimator is any rule computed from data (the sample mean estimates the true mean). Estimators have their own bias and variance: unbiased means right on average. Law of large numbers (weak): n ​ = n 1 ​ ∑ i = 1 n ​ X i ​ converges in probability to as (i.i.d., finite mean). Central limit theorem: For i.i.d. ​ with mean and variance , as , ​ ( X ˉ n ​ − μ ) d ​ N ( 0 , σ 2 ) ⟹ SE ( X ˉ n ​ ) = n ​ σ ​ That's what lets us attach error bars without knowing the true population shape — n ​ ± z α /2 ​ SE is a frequentist confidence interval procedure. Efficiency and MLE. For model , Fisher information (scalar parameter): ∂ 2 lo g p ( X ∣ θ ) ​ ] Cramér–Rao bound: for i.i.d. observations, ) ≥ 1/ ( n I ( θ )) for an unbiased . Under regularity conditions, the MLE MLE ​ is asymptotically normal: ​ ( θ ^ MLE ​ − θ ) d ​ N ( 0 , 1/ I ( θ )) — efficient in the large- limit. Bayesian vs frequentist intervals (one line each). A 95% CI is a recipe: repeat sampling, 95% of intervals trap the true parameter. A 95% credible interval is a Bayesian statement: given the prior and data, the parameter lies in the interval with probability 0.95 after seeing this dataset. Same arithmetic can look similar on a Normal posterior, but the interpretation differs. Beta–Bernoulli conjugacy. Prior , observe successes in trials → posterior . MAP and mean are closed form — the clean bridge from Bayes to count plus pseudocount regularization. Medical test (full Bayes arithmetic). Prevalence , sensitivity , specificity : 0.99 π ​ ≈ 0.0098 ( ≈ 1% ) Even a skewed population produces a near-Gaussian distribution of the sample mean. A confidence interval is a procedure that traps the true value 95% of the time over repeated sampling — not 95% probability the truth is in this particular interval. Hypothesis testing assumes a null (no effect) and asks how surprising the data would be under it; that surprise is the p-value : . It is not the probability the null is true, and not the false-positive rate. A Type I error is a false alarm, a Type II error is a miss, and power is the chance of catching a real effect. Two traps: correlation is not causation (a confounder can drive both), and Simpson's paradox (a within-group trend can reverse when pooled). The thread to ML: MLE is the statistical backbone of training — squared error is MLE under Gaussian noise; cross-entropy is MLE for a categorical model. Interview cue What does a p-value mean? is the most failed stats question. Say: . A small p-value means the data is surprising under the null — evidence against it, nothing more. # The bootstrap — uncertainty without a formula Sometimes you need the uncertainty of an estimator with no clean formula. The bootstrap treats your sample as a stand-in for the population, then resamples from it with replacement many times, recomputing the statistic each time. The spread of those values approximates the true sampling distribution — standard errors and intervals by brute force instead of algebra. It works because a large sample resembles the population. Each bootstrap sample contains about 63.2% of the distinct original points, leaving ~36.8% out-of-bag — a free held-out set. This is the basis of bagging and random forests: each tree trains on a resampled dataset, averaging cuts variance, and out-of-bag points give a built-in validation estimate. # Optimization — how models actually learn Training is optimization: define a loss, then search for parameters that make it small. The workhorse is gradient descent — compute the gradient (steepest increase) and step the opposite way: ​ L . The learning rate sets the step size: too large overshoots or diverges, too small crawls. The learning rate is the whole game: the right size converges, too large diverges. Variant Uses per step Trade-off Batch GD All data Stable, accurate; slow, memory-heavy Stochastic (SGD) One example Fast, noisy; noise escapes bad minima Mini-batch A small batch The default — GPU-efficient, stable enough Plain SGD is slow on ravine-shaped losses, so modern optimizers add memory. Momentum accumulates velocity to power through flat regions; RMSProp scales each parameter's step by its recent gradient magnitude; Adam combines both and is the deep-net default. A convex loss has one global bowl (linear/logistic regression, SVMs); deep nets are non-convex, but the real obstacle is usually saddle points and plateaus, not bad local minima — exactly what momentum and adaptive methods escape. Interview cue Why mini-batch SGD? It fits in memory, updates far more often per epoch, and its gradient noise mildly regularizes. Why Adam? Per-parameter adaptive steps plus momentum make it robust to learning-rate choice and fast to converge. # Convexity and second-order methods A function is convex if for — the chord lies above the graph. For smooth : first-order condition ( y − x ) ; second-order condition (Hessian PSD) everywhere. Examples: MSE for linear regression and logistic NLL are convex in the weights; deep nets are not. If is -strongly convex and -smooth (Hessian eigenvalues in ), plain gradient descent with shrinks the optimality gap like — condition number sets the rate. Newton: step ∇ f — quadratic convergence near the root, but each step needs an ) solve and a definite Hessian. Too expensive per step for billion-parameter models. Quasi-Newton (BFGS, L-BFGS) builds low-rank Hessian approximations — great for moderate (logistic on thousands of features), rarely for full deep nets. # Information theory — where loss functions come from Information theory answers how surprising is an outcome, and how many bits to encode it? Entropy is a distribution's average surprise — high when outcomes are unpredictable, low when one dominates. Cross-entropy is the average bits to encode data from the true using a model . KL divergence is the gap ​ ( p ∥ q ) = H ( p , q ) − H ( p ) : how much worse your model is than the truth, zero only when . This is why cross-entropy is the classification loss , not an arbitrary choice. Minimizing cross-entropy between true labels and predicted probabilities equals minimizing KL divergence to the true distribution, which equals maximum likelihood for a categorical model — three framings, one objective. Squared error is the same story under a Gaussian assumption. Entropies and dependence. Shannon entropy ; KL ​ ( p ∥ q ) = E p ​ [ lo g p − lo g q ] ≥ 0 ; mutual information ​ ( p ( x , y ) ∥ p ( x ) p ( y ) ) — how much knowing shrinks uncertainty about , and equals the KL from the joint to the product of marginals. Interview cue Why cross-entropy and not MSE for classification? Cross-entropy is the MLE/KL-minimizing loss for probabilities, and its gradient stays strong when the model is confidently wrong; MSE's gradient vanishes there (via the sigmoid), so it learns slowly and is non-convex for logistic models. # One-page summary Topic The one thing to remember Linear algebra Data is a matrix; models are matrix multiplies. Dot product = similarity; SVD/eigen = PCA, low-rank, recommenders. Matrix calculus ​ ∥ X w − y ∥ 2 = 2 X ⊤ ( X w − y ) ; layer ; softmax+CE → . Norms L2 shrinks smoothly (ridge); L1 zeroes out (lasso). Probability Joint/marginal/conditional (sum or integrate). adds ; MVN = quadratic form in . MLE vs MAP MLE = fit data; MAP = MLE + prior, and the prior is regularization (Gaussian→L2, Laplace→L1). Statistics LLN → sample mean; CLT → ​ . Fisher ; Cramér–Rao ; MLE asymptotically normal. CI = procedure; credible = posterior mass. p-value . Not P(null true), not the false-positive rate. Bootstrap Resample with replacement for uncertainty without a formula; ~63% in-bag. Basis of bagging. Optimization Gradient descent; mini-batch default; Adam = momentum + adaptive steps. Convex: rate ; Newton needs (too big for DNNs). Information theory Cross-entropy = KL-to-truth = MLE for classification. . # Related Gradient Descent Maximum Likelihood Estimation Eigenvectors, PCA and SVD p-Values Statistical Power A/B Testing Online Experimentation Optimizers: SGD, Momentum Adam Clustering, Dimensionality Reduction Anomaly Detection

title: Probability & Statistics
heads: Key distributions and where they show up in ML
Law of large numbers and central limit theorem
text: Statistics Experimentation: the inference toolkit behind every metric, test, and model claim. Most ML interview questions about is this result real? , how much data do we need? , or why does this loss make sense? reduce to probability and statistical inference. This chapter covers the rules of probability, the distributions that recur in ML, how estimators are judged, how likelihood-based fitting connects to regularization, and how confidence intervals and hypothesis tests are built and (mis)interpreted. The companion chapter A/B Testing Online Experimentation applies all of this to online experiments. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Apply Bayes' theorem to a base-rate problem and explain why a positive test on a rare condition is usually a false alarm. Match a distribution (Bernoulli, Binomial, Poisson, Normal, Exponential, Beta) to a modeling situation. State the LLN and CLT with their conditions , and say what each does and does not guarantee. Judge an estimator by bias, variance, and consistency, and relate MLE and MAP to loss functions and regularizers. Interpret a confidence interval and a p-value correctly, and name the error types and power. Pick a t-test, z-test, or chi-square test, and correct for multiple comparisons. # Probability rules Probability assigns a number in to events, with and additivity over disjoint events. Everything else is derived. Rule Statement Condition / note Complement ) = 1 − P ( A ) None Addition Subtract the overlap; drops to a plain sum only if are disjoint Conditional P ( A ∩ B ) ​ Needs Multiplication (chain rule) Extends to ​ , … , A k ​ ) = ∏ i ​ P ( A i ​ ∣ A 1 ​ , … , A i − 1 ​ ) Independence , equivalently Independent is not the same as disjoint; disjoint events with positive probability are dependent Total probability ​ P ( B ∣ A i ​ ) P ( A i ​ ) ​ } must partition the sample space Conditional independence Underlies Naive Bayes; neither implies nor is implied by marginal independence Common slips Treating and as interchangeable (the prosecutor's fallacy ). They are related only through Bayes' theorem and the base rates. Multiplying probabilities of events that are not independent. Check whether the chain rule's conditionals actually equal the marginals. Confusing pairwise independence with mutual independence. Three events can be pairwise independent yet jointly dependent. # Bayes' theorem Memory hook Posterior odds = prior odds x likelihood ratio; the base rate is the anchor. Rearranging the chain rule in two ways gives P ( E ∣ H ) P ( H ) ​ = P ( E ∣ H ) P ( H ) + P ( E ∣ H c ) P ( H c ) P ( E ∣ H ) P ( H ) ​ Read it as: posterior likelihood prior . The denominator is just the normalizer, computed with total probability. # Worked base-rate example A screening model flags a rare condition. Suppose: Prevalence (prior): . Sensitivity (true positive rate): . False positive rate: ) = 0.05 (specificity ). Given a positive flag, the probability of the condition is 0.90 × 0.01 ​ = 0.009 + 0.0495 0.009 ​ = 0.0585 0.009 ​ ≈ 0.154. Only about 15% of flagged cases are true positives, despite 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity. A natural-frequency check with 10,000 people: 100 have the condition, 90 of them flag; 9,900 do not, and 495 of those flag. So . The result is driven by the prior. Precision depends on prevalence, which is why a classifier with fixed TPR/FPR has very different precision on a balanced test set than in production where positives are rare. This links directly to precision-recall trade-offs in imbalanced problems such as fraud or abuse detection. Interview angle When given a 99% accurate test puzzle, state the three inputs (prior, sensitivity, false positive rate) before computing, then give the answer in natural frequencies. Mention that the conclusion changes with prevalence: the same model has higher precision in a high-prevalence slice. Interviewers often follow up with what if the test is repeated? Under conditional independence of repeated tests given the true state, the posterior odds multiply by the likelihood ratio per positive result. The odds form makes sequential updating clean: . # Key distributions and where they show up in ML Distribution Support / parameters Mean, variance Typical use in ML Bernoulli , A single binary label or click; logistic regression's output model; per-user conversion Binomial , Count of conversions in independent trials with common ; basis for proportion tests Poisson , Event counts in a fixed window (requests, arrivals) with independent events at constant rate; Poisson regression Normal ) , Sample means via the CLT; noise in linear regression; weight priors; latent variables in VAEs Exponential , Waiting time between Poisson events; memoryless; survival and time-to-event baselines Beta α ​ , ( α + β + 1 ) α β ​ Prior over a probability; conjugate to Bernoulli/Binomial; Thompson sampling for bandits; smoothing of rates Useful connections, each with its condition: Binomial to Poisson. If is large and small with , then . Binomial to Normal. For large with and both reasonably large (a common guide is at least about 10), . This is the CLT applied to a sum of Bernoullis. Poisson and Exponential. If events arrive as a Poisson process with rate , the counts in a window are Poisson and the inter-arrival times are Exponential . Memorylessness. The Exponential satisfies . It is the only continuous distribution with this property, which is why it implies a constant hazard rate. Real lifetimes often violate it. Beta-Binomial conjugacy. With prior and successes in trials, the posterior is . The prior acts like pseudo-observations, a handy way to smooth click-through rates for items with few impressions. Overdispersion. Real count data often has variance greater than its mean, which a Poisson cannot represent (it forces variance equal to mean). Negative binomial or quasi-Poisson models relax this. Interview angle A frequent follow-up: what distribution would you use for X? Answer by asking what is being counted or measured and what the generative story is. Conversion per session: Bernoulli. Conversions out of sessions: Binomial. Support tickets per hour: Poisson, if arrivals are roughly independent and the rate is stable; check for overdispersion. Time until next event: Exponential, if hazard is roughly constant. Unknown rate with prior beliefs: Beta. # Expectation, variance, covariance Memory hook Expectation is always linear; variance of a sum needs the covariance term. Expectation is linear without any independence condition : Variance measures spread: ] = E [ X 2 ] − ( E [ X ] ) 2 . Covariance and correlation : ​ = σ X ​ σ Y ​ Cov ( X , Y ) ​ ∈ [ − 1 , 1 ] . Variance of a sum needs the covariance term: Var ( X ) + b 2 Var ( Y ) + 2 ab Cov ( X , Y ) . If ​ , … , X n ​ are uncorrelated with common variance , then ) = σ 2 / n . With a common pairwise correlation , ) = σ 2 [ ρ + ( 1 − ρ ) / n ] , so averaging correlated quantities (bagged trees, repeated measures from the same user) reduces variance less than and plateaus at . Other identities that come up: Law of total expectation: . Law of total variance: . Used to split variance into within-group and between-group parts, for example in stratification arguments. Zero correlation does not imply independence. and are uncorrelated yet fully dependent. The implication does hold for jointly Gaussian variables. Jensen's inequality: for convex , . Example: the sample standard deviation is a biased (low) estimator of even though is unbiased for . # Law of large numbers and central limit theorem Let ​ , X 2 ​ , … be i.i.d. with mean and variance , and n ​ the sample mean. Law of large numbers Central limit theorem Statement n ​ → μ as ​ ( X ˉ n ​ − μ ) / σ d ​ N ( 0 , 1 ) Conditions Finite mean (weak form for i.i.d.); weaker conditions exist for non-i.i.d. cases Finite variance 0 , with independence (i.i.d. version) Tells you Where the average ends up The shape and scale of fluctuations around : about ​ Does not tell you How fast, or anything about the distribution of a single observation That the data are normal, or that is always enough Points worth stating precisely: The CLT is about the distribution of the mean (or sum), not of the data. A skewed variable stays skewed; its average becomes approximately normal. How large must be depends on the skewness and tails of the data. Heavy-tailed variables (revenue per user, session duration) can require far more than the folk figure of 30 for the normal approximation to be good, and with infinite variance the classical CLT does not apply at all. The standard error of the mean is ​ . Halving the standard error needs four times the data. Dependence breaks the standard error formula. If observations are clustered (many sessions per user) and treated as independent, standard errors are too small. Cluster at the true randomization or dependence unit. The LLN is what justifies empirical risk as a proxy for true risk for a fixed hypothesis ; uniform convergence over a hypothesis class needs additional machinery (see Fundamentals ). Go deeper (optional) The Berry-Esseen theorem bounds the error of the normal approximation by a term of order ​ / ( σ 3 n ​ ) , where ​ is the third absolute central moment. It quantifies why skewed or heavy-tailed data converge more slowly. # Estimators: bias, variance, consistency An estimator is a function of the sample, so it is itself a random variable with a sampling distribution. Three properties: Property Definition Intuition Bias ) = E [ θ ^ ] − θ Systematic miss, averaged over repeated samples Variance ) How much the estimate moves from sample to sample Consistency n ​ p ​ θ as Converges to the truth with more data These combine in the mean squared error: ) = E [( θ ^ − θ ) 2 ] = Bias ( θ ^ ) 2 + Var ( θ ^ ) . This is the same decomposition behind the bias-variance trade-off in Fundamentals , here applied to a parameter estimate instead of a prediction. Examples: The sample mean is unbiased and consistent for (finite variance). The sample variance with divisor is biased: 1 ​ ∑ ( X i ​ − X ˉ ) 2 ] = n n − 1 ​ σ 2 . Dividing by (Bessel's correction) removes the bias, because is fitted from the same data, costing one degree of freedom. The biased version is still consistent. Unbiased does not mean better. Ridge regression or shrinkage estimators accept bias to cut variance and can have lower MSE. Consistent does not mean unbiased: a consistent estimator can be biased at every finite (the divisor- variance above). An unbiased estimator need not be consistent (for example, using only the first observation ​ to estimate ). Under regularity conditions, the MLE is consistent, asymptotically normal, and asymptotically efficient, attaining the Cramér-Rao lower bound ) ≥ 1/ ( n I ( θ )) with the Fisher information per observation. # MLE vs MAP Maximum likelihood picks the parameter that makes the observed data most probable: MLE ​ = ar g θ max ​ i = 1 ∑ n ​ lo g p ( x i ​ ∣ θ ) . Maximum a posteriori adds a prior : MAP ​ = ar g θ max ​ [ i = 1 ∑ n ​ lo g p ( x i ​ ∣ θ ) + lo g p ( θ ) ] . The prior acts as a regularizer, and MAP reduces to MLE under a flat prior. Model / prior Resulting objective Gaussian noise, no prior MLE equals least squares (minimize squared error) Gaussian noise + Gaussian prior on weights I ) MAP equals ridge (L2), with / τ 2 Gaussian noise + Laplace prior on weights MAP equals lasso (L1) Bernoulli outputs with sigmoid link, no prior MLE equals minimizing cross-entropy (logistic loss) Worked example: for a Bernoulli parameter with successes in trials, ​ MLE ​ = k / n . With a prior, ​ MAP ​ = n + α + β − 2 k + α − 1 ​ (for ). With 0 successes in 3 trials, the MLE says , which is usually an overconfident claim, while the MAP is pulled toward the prior mean. Interview angle Why is cross-entropy the right loss for classification? is answered by MLE: minimizing it is maximizing the Bernoulli/categorical likelihood. What is L2 regularization, probabilistically? is MAP under a Gaussian prior. The prior's influence fades as grows, so MAP and MLE agree asymptotically in standard settings. See Regression Methods for the regularization side. Go deeper (optional) MAP is a point summary of the posterior and is not invariant under reparameterization (the mode of a density changes with the parameterization), whereas the MLE is invariant. A fully Bayesian treatment keeps the whole posterior, for example to report credible intervals or to average predictions. # Confidence intervals Memory hook The parameter is fixed and the interval is random: coverage belongs to the procedure. A confidence interval is a procedure that, over repeated sampling, produces intervals containing the true parameter with the stated long-run frequency. For a mean with large (or normal data with known variance): ± z 1 − α /2 ​ n ​ s ​ , z 0.975 ​ ≈ 1.96 for 95% . With normal data and unknown variance, replace by the quantile with degrees of freedom, which has heavier tails for small . For a proportion, a Wald interval is ​ ± z p ^ ​ ( 1 − p ^ ​ ) / n ​ ; it behaves poorly for small or ​ near 0 or 1, where Wilson or exact (Clopper-Pearson) intervals have better coverage. Correct interpretation. The parameter is fixed and the interval is random. If we repeated the study many times, about 95% of intervals constructed this way would contain the true value. After the interval is computed, it either contains the parameter or it does not. Incorrect readings There is a 95% probability that the true mean lies in this interval. That is a Bayesian credible-interval statement; it requires a prior and is a different object. 95% of the data lie in the interval. That describes a prediction or reference range, not a CI for the mean. If two 95% CIs overlap, the difference is not significant. Overlap is a conservative, unreliable check; build a CI for the difference directly. CI width shrinks like ​ , grows with , and grows with the confidence level. A CI is more informative than a bare p-value because it shows effect size and precision together. It is also dual to testing: a two-sided level- test of ​ : θ = θ 0 ​ rejects exactly when ​ is outside the CI, for tests and intervals built from the same statistic. # Hypothesis testing The setup: a null hypothesis ​ (typically no effect , ​ ) and an alternative ​ (two-sided = θ 0 ​ or one-sided). Choose a test statistic whose distribution under ​ is known, and a significance level fixed before seeing data. p-value: the probability, computed assuming ​ (and the model assumptions) are true, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. What a p-value is not It is not ​ ∣ data ) . Getting that requires a prior, via Bayes' theorem. It is not the probability the result occurred by chance alone in any direct sense. It is not a measure of effect size or practical importance. With large enough , trivially small effects yield tiny p-values; with small , large effects can yield large ones. is insufficient evidence against ​ , not evidence that ​ is true. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, especially when power is low. # Error types and power ​ true ​ true Reject ​ Type I error (false positive), probability Correct, probability = power Fail to reject Correct, probability Type II error (false negative), probability Power depends on four linked quantities: the effect size , the noise , the sample size , and . Larger , larger , smaller , or larger each raise power. For a two-sample comparison of means, the required per-group sample size is derived in A/B Testing Online Experimentation . Low power has a second cost besides missed effects: among results that do reach significance, effect estimates are inflated (the winner's curse or Type M error), and a larger fraction of significant findings are false positives. The latter follows from Bayes: the positive predictive value of a significant result depends on the prior probability that the effect is real, which is the same base-rate logic as the screening example. # Choosing the test Situation Test Key conditions One or two means, known, or large z-test Approximately normal sampling distribution of the mean (CLT) One or two means, estimated, smaller t-test Roughly normal data, or enough for the mean to be near-normal; Welch's version does not assume equal variances Paired measurements (same unit before and after) Paired t-test Differences are the unit of analysis; roughly normal differences Two proportions Two-proportion z-test Large enough expected counts in each cell; Fisher's exact test for small counts Association between two categorical variables Chi-square test of independence Independent observations; expected counts usually at least about 5 per cell Categorical counts vs expected proportions Chi-square goodness of fit Same count condition; used for the sample ratio mismatch check Skewed data, small , outliers matter Mann-Whitney / permutation test Tests a different hypothesis (stochastic dominance or exchangeability), not equality of means, unless extra assumptions hold The Welch t-statistic for two groups is 2 ​ / n 1 ​ + s 2 2 ​ / n 2 ​ ​ x ˉ 1 ​ − x ˉ 2 ​ ​ . Practical default: prefer Welch over the pooled-variance t-test unless there is a reason to assume equal variances, since it loses little when variances are equal and protects when they are not. Interview angle Asked which test? , name the outcome type (continuous, binary, count, categorical), the design (independent vs paired), and whether the sample is large enough for the normal approximation. Then state the assumption most at risk (independence of observations is usually the one that fails). # Multiple testing Memory hook Bonferroni divides alpha by m; Benjamini-Hochberg sorts and compares p(k) to kq/m. Running independent tests each at level gives a family-wise false-positive probability of under all nulls true. At and this is about . Two error rates are commonly controlled: FWER (family-wise error rate): . FDR (false discovery rate): the expected fraction of rejections that are false, with false rejections out of total. Method Controls Procedure Trade-off Bonferroni FWER Reject test if ​ ≤ α / m Valid under any dependence; conservative, low power for large Holm FWER Step-down on sorted p-values Uniformly at least as powerful as Bonferroni, same guarantee Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) FDR at level Sort ​ ≤ ⋯ ≤ p ( m ) ​ ; find the largest with ​ ≤ m k ​ q ; reject hypotheses More power; guarantee holds under independence or positive dependence (PRDS) Which to use depends on the cost of a false positive. For a confirmatory decision where one wrong call is expensive (a launch decision on a single primary metric family), FWER control fits. For exploratory screening of many metrics or many segments, where a small fraction of false leads is tolerable, FDR control keeps more power. Related practice: designate one primary metric in advance, treat guardrail and secondary metrics as supporting evidence, and treat post hoc subgroup findings as hypotheses for follow-up. The forking paths problem arises whenever analysis choices depend on the data, even without an explicit list of tests. # Bootstrap The bootstrap approximates a statistic's sampling distribution by resampling the observed data with replacement. Draw samples (commonly 1,000 or more) of size with replacement from the data. Compute the statistic on each. Use the spread of the values to estimate the standard error, or their percentiles for an interval (the percentile bootstrap). When it is useful: statistics without a convenient closed-form variance (median, quantiles, ratios, AUC, differences in percentiles), and checking that a CLT approximation is adequate. Conditions and limits: It assumes the sample represents the population and observations are i.i.d. For dependent data, resample at the dependence unit (users, clusters) or use block bootstrap for time series. It can fail for extremes such as the sample maximum, and

text: Worked problems turn formulas into reflexes; every numeric answer below was checked by calculation or simulation. Interview math questions rarely ask for a theorem. They ask for a number or a derivation under time pressure, and the scoring is on setup, sanity checks, and clean statements of assumptions. This chapter collects 26 practice problems with full solutions, grouped by the skill they train. Try each problem before reading the solution. Background lives in Probability Statistics , Math , Maximum Likelihood Estimation , and Eigenvectors, PCA and SVD . What you'll be able to say after this chapter Set up a Bayes problem with natural frequencies and update sequentially with likelihood ratios. Use indicator variables and linearity of expectation to avoid hard joint distributions. Pick between Poisson, exponential, geometric, and binomial from the generative story, and use memorylessness correctly. Derive the MLE for Bernoulli, Gaussian, and Poisson models in a few lines and state the bias of each. Derive the gradient of least squares, softmax with cross-entropy, and the ridge closed form from scratch. Read PCA and SVD facts off a covariance matrix, check convexity with a Hessian, and apply Jensen and tail bounds. Memory hook Name the model, write the likelihood or the indicator, simplify, then sanity-check against a limiting case. # Bayes and conditional probability # Problem 1: repeated positive tests A condition has prevalence . A test has sensitivity and false positive rate . Two independent tests (independent given the true state) both come back positive. What is the probability of the condition? Solution. Use odds. Prior odds are . Each positive multiplies the odds by the likelihood ratio . Posterior odds are 0.01 ​ ⋅ 1 8 2 = 99 324 ​ , so the probability is 324 ​ ≈ 0.766 (one positive gives about ). The strong answer states the independence-given-state assumption and multiplies by the likelihood ratio. # Problem 2: two children A family has two children. (a) Given at least one is a boy, what is the probability both are boys? (b) Given at least one is a boy born on a Tuesday? Solution. (a) The equally likely outcomes are BB, BG, GB, GG; conditioning removes GG, leaving three outcomes of which one is BB: . (b) Enumerate (sex, weekday) pairs: = 196 outcomes. A contestant picks a door, the host (who knows where the prize is) opens a different door without the prize, and offers a switch. What is the winning probability of switching? Solution. The first pick is right with probability . If it was wrong (probability ), the host's reveal leaves the prize behind the one remaining door, so switching wins. title: Eigenvectors, PCA and SVD
heads: PCA = eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix
PCA as constrained optimization (first principal direction)

text: A worked summary that walks from eigenvectors up to PCA and SVD, reusing the same small matrices throughout so the numbers stay easy to follow. One-line summary PCA finds the directions of greatest variance by eigendecomposing the covariance matrix; SVD on the centered data matrix gives the same principal components in one step, more stably, because X = V Σ 2 V T . # Eigenvectors and eigenvalues A square matrix acts on vectors. For most vectors it changes their direction; for a special few it only stretches them. Those are the eigenvectors , and the stretch factor is the eigenvalue . 1 ​ 1 2 ​ ] Solve : − 1 = λ 2 − 4 λ + 3 = ( λ − 3 ) ( λ − 1 ) = 0 Eigenvalues ​ = 3 , λ 2 ​ = 1 , with unit eigenvectors ​ = 2 ​ 1 ​ [ 1 1 ​ ] , v 2 ​ = 2 ​ 1 ​ [ 1 − 1 ​ ] Keep the two roles separate: the eigen vector is the direction (the axis); the eigen value is the spread along that direction. Why the eigenvectors land on the data's natural axes: the covariance matrix encodes how features vary together. Its eigenvectors are the directions along which it acts as pure stretching (no rotation) — exactly the directions where variance is self-contained and uncorrelated, i.e. the directions of maximum spread. # PCA as constrained optimization (first principal direction) Maximize the variance of the projections x subject to . Ill-conditioned → prefer SVD on centered . # Why do this? (not just dimensionality reduction) Ranking the directions of variance is the core operation. Dimensionality reduction is the common payoff, but the same computation also gives: Decorrelation — the new axes are uncorrelated by construction. Denoising / compression — low-variance directions are often noise and can be dropped. Visualization — project many features down to the top 2–3 components to plot. Interpretable structure — the principal directions themselves can be meaningful. PCA is worth it because it finds the best directions to keep, not just any. # SVD — decomposition of the data matrix directly SVD factors the data matrix itself (any shape, samples × features), not the covariance matrix: = principal directions (same axes PCA finds). = singular values, sorted largest first — the spread along each direction, equal to ​ up to the scaling. = where each data point sits along the new axes. SVD runs on any matrix, but uncentered data makes the first singular vector swing toward the mean (the offset from the origin) instead of the direction of maximum variance. title: Gradient Descent
text: Say it in 30s: An iterative optimizer. Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters, then step in the negative gradient direction. Repeat. The learning rate sets the step size. It converges to a stationary point of differentiable losses (the global minimum if the loss is convex) without solving for it in closed form. Variants Batch GD : gradient over the whole dataset each step — stable, slow, memory-heavy. SGD : one example (or mini-batch) at a time — noisy but fast, and the noise can help escape sharp minima. Mini-batch SGD : the practical default. Momentum / Adam / RMSProp : adapt the step using past gradients to go faster and handle ill-conditioning. The one update step: w ← w − η · ∂L/∂w . For linear regression with MSE, ∂L/∂w = (2/n) Xᵀ(Xw − y) . The math Update: ​ = w t ​ − η ∇ w ​ L ( w t ​ ) . First-order Taylor: for small , . If is -smooth, descent lemma with : η ​ ∥ ∇ L ∥ 2 . Linear regression + MSE: ​ L = n 2 ​ X ⊤ ( X w − y ) . Quadratic 1 ​ w ⊤ H w with eigenvalues ​ : along eigen-direction , error shrinks by factor ​ ) per step. Need ​ ; ill-conditioning ​ / λ m i n ​ slows convergence on stiff directions. Mini-batch : gradient noise variance (full batch = lowest variance). Traps Learning rate too high → diverge; too low → crawl. Non-convex losses (neural nets) → only convergence to a stationary point (often a saddle or plateau), not a global minimum; that's usually fine in practice. Always scale/standardize features so the loss surface isn't a stretched ravine. See depth: Math (§5), TensorGym Study Notes . title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text: Say it in 30s: Pick the parameters that make the observed data most probable. Maximize the likelihood (equivalently, minimize negative log-likelihood). Most common losses are NLL in disguise: the assumed noise model determines the loss. The key insight interviewers want Assume Gaussian noise on a regression target → MLE gives MSE / least squares . Assume Bernoulli/categorical labels → MLE gives cross-entropy / log loss . So every loss is a hidden assumption about the noise — the loss is not arbitrary. MLE vs MAP MLE maximizes P(data | θ). MAP maximizes P(θ | data) ∝ P(data | θ)·P(θ) — adding a prior. A Gaussian prior on weights = L2 regularization ; a Laplace prior = L1 . MLE minimize NLL: for discrete , is cross-entropy vs the model; vs truth , excess risk is KL ​ ) . Asymptotics: ≈ N ( θ 0 ​ , I ( θ 0 ​ ) − 1 / n ) ; Cramér–Rao: ) ≥ 1/ ( n I ( θ 0 ​ )) for unbiased estimators. text: The ML Interview Bible — analogy first, then the exact math, for every loss an interviewer can name. Notation used throughout = true value, ​ = prediction, ​ (error / residual). = raw model score before it becomes a probability (the logit ): p ​ , the inverse of the sigmoid; also called the pre-softmax score. To get a probability: ​ ) = ∑ j ​ e z j ​ e z i ​ ​ . = predicted probability, 1 ​ (sigmoid). For margin losses: , = raw score, margin . = number of examples, = weights, = regularization strength. # The one big idea Analogy. A loss function is the scorecard in golf. Every swing (prediction) gets a number for how far you landed from the hole (the truth). You don't need the scorecard to play — you need it to improve . Training = adjusting your swing to lower the average score. Definition. A loss ​ ) ≥ 0 scores one prediction: ~0 when right, growing as it gets more wrong. Training minimizes the average loss over the data — the empirical risk : 1 ​ i ∑ ​ ℓ ( y i ​ , f ( x i ​ ; θ ) ) All of supervised learning in one line: pick a model family , pick a loss , run an optimizer downhill on . Add a penalty and you get the full objective : (see L1 vs L2 below). Loss vs cost vs metric — know the difference cold: Term What it is Needs gradient? Example Loss Error of ONE example ✓ log loss of one prediction Cost / objective What the optimizer minimizes = avg loss + regularizer ✓ 1 ​ ∑ CE + λ ∥ w ∥ 2 Metric What you report / decide with ✗ accuracy, AUC, NDCG, revenue The surrogate idea: The thing you truly care about (accuracy, ranking) is flat or step-shaped → gradient almost everywhere → un-trainable. Why it's flat: for one example the model outputs a logit; if score threshold → class 1, so the 0/1 loss of that sample is a step. Across the dataset, accuracy is the average of many step functions — a staircase. Each time you nudge a parameter enough to flip one sample, accuracy jumps by ; between flips it's completely flat. So the gradient is zero almost everywhere. You'd need to land exactly on the knife-edge where a sample flips to get a nonzero gradient, and even then it's undefined (a discontinuity). Gradient-based optimizers just see a flat landscape and have no idea which way to move. So you train on a smooth surrogate loss pointing the same direction, and evaluate on the real metric. Production issue — loss/metric mismatch. A ranking team trains on log loss but is judged on NDCG@10. Log loss improves, NDCG doesn't — most of the gradient goes to easy negatives that never appear in the top 10. Fixes: switch to a pairwise/listwise ranking surrogate, or reweight examples that matter to the metric. Always plot loss AND business metric per epoch; if they diverge, the surrogate is wrong. # What's happening with log loss in this case? Log loss applies uniform weight, treating every document as an isolated binary classification task. Thousands of easy negatives each leak a small but nonzero loss ; in aggregate, their gradients overwhelm the update . Say we have 2 positives, 5 hard negatives, 1000 easy negatives. The optimizer focuses on driving these already-low scores to zero to minimize loss, ignoring the ranking struggle. Crucially, NDCG@10 is sensitive only to the relative ordering at the top . Hard negatives lingering in positions 5–10 must be demoted to improve the metric, yet they receive negligible gradients because they are statistically rare compared to the vast sea of easy pairs. Fixes: Strategy How it works Why it fixes the issue 1. Hard negative mining (data level) Prune the massive tail of trivial negatives ( ​ 0.01 ). Deliberately stock the dataset with difficult samples currently at ranks 11–100. Sanitizes the training pool so easy examples can no longer overwhelm the update or silence the signal from the few that matter. 2. Pairwise loss (loss level) Abandon point-wise labels for relative ordering. Optimize the logit gap: ​ − s − ​ ) ) . For trivial negatives the gap ​ − s − ​ is large positive, so vanishes, driving loss and gradient to zero — focusing the update on rank inversions where a negative ​ threatens the positive ​ . 3. LambdaRank (metric level) A listwise strategy: weight pairwise gradients by their leverage on the business metric: . Pairwise ranking is indifferent to which pairs matter; inversions far below the cutoff contribute nothing useful. LambdaRank makes the optimizer target only rank shifts that materially change the final metric. # Every loss is a hidden assumption about the noise Analogy. Choosing a loss is choosing insurance. Believe damages are always small? Accept a policy where rare big losses cost you quadratically (MSE). Believe wild outliers happen? You want one whose price grows only linearly (MAE). Your loss reveals what error weather you expect. The theory (MLE view): Assume data is generated as , noise drawn from density . Maximizing likelihood = minimizing negative log-likelihood (NLL) : ​ ln p ( y i ​ ∣ f ( x i ​ ) ) . Plug in a noise distribution → out pops a familiar loss: Assumed noise / label model Density (up to constants) collapses to Resulting loss Gaussian /2 σ 2 MSE Laplace MAE Bernoulli( ) ( 1 − p ) 1 − y Binary cross-entropy Categorical y k ​ ​ Multiclass CE Poisson( ​ ) ​ y e − y ^ ​ / y ! ​ − y ln y ^ ​ ) Poisson loss Tweedie ( ) compound Poisson–Gamma ​ 1 − ρ / ( 1 − ρ ) + y ^ ​ 2 − ρ / ( 2 − ρ ) ) Tweedie loss The interview sentence: Choosing a loss function is choosing a probabilistic model of the noise. Prove it for MSE in two lines: Gaussian density ​ ) 2 /2 σ 2 → take → constants drop → ​ ) 2 . Done. Same trick, applied to weights (MAP view — preview of regularization): MAP = MLE + prior on : maximize . Gaussian prior /2 τ 2 → L2 penalty . Laplace prior → L1 penalty . Summary: loss ↔ noise model; regularizer ↔ prior on weights. Production issue. A payments team predicted settlement time with MSE. A few multi-day bank-holiday outliers dominated the gradient (off by 5 → penalty ; gradient descent tries to minimize this by overpredicting, sacrificing the mode/median to appease outliers). Huber loss fixed median performance overnight. Root cause: the Gaussian (thin-tail) assumption was false — the real noise was heavy-tailed. # Regression losses (predicting a number) Analogy. Three managers reviewing the same mistake. MSE gets disproportionately angrier the bigger the miss — 2× the miss earns 4× the scolding. MAE scolds in exact proportion, no drama. Huber is the reasonable one: squared scolding for small errors (smooth feedback), flat-rate for big ones (one disaster can't dominate the meeting). Optimal constant prediction = -th quantile of . → median ( 1 ​ ·MAE). Train and → a 90% prediction interval with no distribution assumption (watch for quantile crossing). Quantile crossing A logically impossible state where a model predicts a lower percentile (e.g. 10th) as larger than a higher one (e.g. 90th) — it implies a non-monotonic CDF, a frequent failure in multi-quantile models. Root cause: most setups minimize separate pinball losses independently; the models don't communicate, so they intersect under data sparsity (blind extrapolation) or misspecified priors (independent linear planes are destined to cross if the true trend is non-linear). The fix: post-hoc isotonic sorting (sort predictions at inference — a cheap bandage); non-negative deltas (train on offsets from the median via ReLU/Softplus — monotonic by design); simultaneous constraints enforcing ​ τ k ​ ​ ≤ y ^ ​ τ k + 1 ​ ​ ; or structural deep nets whose output nodes feed sequentially via additive positive units. Figure 2 — Pinball loss: tilting the V encodes asymmetric business costs # Rapid-fire facts interviewers probe Best constant prediction is the most asked follow-up: MSE → mean, MAE → median, quantile( ) → -quantile, -insensitive → anything within of the median region, log loss → base rate. RMSE vs MSE: same minimizer; RMSE is just MSE in interpretable units → a reporting convention, not a different loss. MSLE = MSE on : measures ratio errors; penalizes under-prediction more than over-prediction (log compresses the high side); undefined for . MAPE: unbounded penalty for over-prediction (can exceed 100%), capped at 100% for under-prediction with ​ = 0 → models trained on it systematically under-predict ; explodes when . Log-target trick: train MSE on , predict − 1 → you've estimated the conditional geometric mean of , which is the median only if log-noise is symmetric, and is biased low for the mean (Jensen's inequality) — classic senior-level probe. Why the log-target trick works For data with a massive right tail, outliers dominate the loss — taking the log compresses the scale of the target. MSE assumes homoscedasticity (constant residual variance), which is false for skewed targets. MSE optimizes for the mean, but on a logged target it optimizes the mean of , which back-transforms to the geometric mean (the median only under symmetric log-noise; biased low for the mean by Jensen's inequality). If you need a mean, apply a smearing correction to account for the lost variance. Production examples. Food-delivery ETA: a few orders stuck for hours wreck MSE training → Huber loss and/or winsorize the target. Winsorization Replacing outliers with a specific percentile value rather than deleting them — no gradient explosion. You lose the nuance of how extreme the outlier is, but you reduce variance and shift the mean toward the center. Inventory / demand: stockout costs 5× overstock → don't predict the mean; train quantile loss with — the newsvendor critical ratio ​ / ( C u ​ + C o ​ ) maps the cost asymmetry directly to . Insurance claim amounts / ad spend: mostly zeros + occasional large positives → Tweedie loss ( ) is the standard in GBDT libraries (XGBoost/LightGBM tweedie ). House prices / durations spanning orders of magnitude: MSE on ≈ optimizing relative error. # Classification losses (predicting a label) Analogy. The loss you WANT is the exam grade: 0 if right, 1 if wrong ( 0–1 loss ). But the exam gives no feedback — every wrong answer scores the same whether you were nearly right or absurdly wrong, so there is no slope to learn from. Every classification loss below is a tutor standing in for the exam : a smooth upper bound on the grade that always tells you which way to improve. 0–1 loss (the real goal): ​ = 1 [ sign ( f ( x ))  = y ] = 1 [ m 0 ] , m = y ⋅ f ( x ) Non-convex, gradient 0 almost everywhere, NP-hard to optimize directly → we use convex surrogates that upper-bound it (margin-based ones; log loss only after rescaling by , i.e. ​ ( 1 + e − m ) , which equals 1 at ). The log-sum-exp trick — surviving float precision Computing naively is like measuring the ocean with a teaspoon: limited bits, and extreme numbers overflow or underflow. Overflow: large positive logits ( ) make explode past the float limit → inf . Underflow: deeply negative logits ( ) force → 0 , and . Either way you get NaN gradients that poison the weights. title: Cross-Entropy Loss
text: Say it in 30s: The standard loss for classification. It measures the distance between the true label distribution and the predicted probability distribution. For a true class, it's −log(predicted probability of that class) — you're penalized by how surprised the model was about the right answer. Why it beats MSE for classification It pairs with softmax/sigmoid to give a well-behaved loss (convex in the logits, and in the weights for a linear model such as logistic regression) with strong gradients even when the model is confidently wrong (MSE's gradient vanishes there → slow learning). It's the maximum-likelihood loss under a Bernoulli/categorical model, so it's the principled choice. Forms Binary: −[y·log p + (1−y)·log(1−p)] , paired with sigmoid . Multiclass: −Σ yᵢ log pᵢ , paired with softmax . The math Binary ( , ): Multiclass (one-hot , logits , softmax ​ = e z k ​ / ∑ j ​ e z j ​ ): ∑ ​ y k ​ ln p k ​ . If true class is : ​ — e.g. , → . Gradient w.r.t. logits: chain rule on softmax + log gives the compact form ∂ L ​ = p − y (componentwise; same for binary with scalar ). Information view: ; for hard labels , CE is KL to the one-hot target. Traps Feed logits to the loss (e.g. CrossEntropyLoss in PyTorch already applies softmax) — don't softmax twice. Numerically unstable if you compute log(softmax) naively; use log-sum-exp / built-in fused versions. See depth: Loss Functions (§2.3–2.4), TensorGym Study Notes . title: Regression Methods
heads: The four classical assumptions (and what breaks)
Regularization: OLS vs Ridge vs Lasso vs Elastic Net
Choosing features and going beyond a straight line
text: Notation used throughout = examples, = features, = design matrix (first column of 1s for the intercept). = coefficient vector, ​ = X w , residual ​ , = regularization strength. = true noise term, = noise variance. # Linear regression: the straight line Analogy. Linear regression is a recipe with fixed ingredient prices. The prediction is a shopping bill: each feature (quantity) times its coefficient (unit price), plus a base charge (intercept). Training = figuring out the prices that best explain past bills. Model: ​ = w 0 ​ + w 1 ​ x 1 ​ + w 2 ​ x 2 ​ + ⋯ + w p ​ x p ​ = X w Assumed truth: , with noise . How to read a coefficient (say it precisely in interviews): ​ = expected change in for a one-unit increase in ​ , holding all other features fixed . Holding others fixed is exactly what breaks under multicollinearity — correlated features can't be moved independently, so individual coefficients become unstable and uninterpretable. Standardize features → coefficients become comparable importance per standard deviation. Why it's everyone's baseline: Closed-form training, exact reproducibility, interpretable coefficients with confidence intervals, fast at serving time, and a strong sanity check — if a deep model can't beat linear regression, the features (not the architecture) are the problem. Closed form Finding the optimal parameters directly via a mathematical formula, without an iterative optimization process like gradient descent. # How it finds the line (OLS) Analogy. Stretch vertical rubber bands from every data point to a rigid rod. Each band pulls with force proportional to its stretch (squared-error physics). OLS is where the rod settles — the equilibrium of all the pulls. One point dragged far away (an outlier) pulls linearly harder (its energy grows quadratically) and tilts the whole rod: that's MSE sensitivity from Loss Functions , now geometric. Figure 1 — OLS minimizes the sum of squared vertical residuals Objective (ordinary least squares): minimize the residual sum of squares = i ∑ ​ ( y i ​ − x i ⊤ ​ w ) 2 This is MSE from Loss Functions , summed. Derivation → normal equations (do this on a whiteboard once): ​ RSS = − 2 X ⊤ ( y − X w ) = 0 ⇒ X ⊤ X w = X ⊤ y ⇒ w ^ = ( X ⊤ X ) − 1 X ⊤ y The solution exists when X is invertible — i.e. full column rank (no perfect multicollinearity), typically with an intercept. Geometric view (the elegant answer): ​ = X w ^ is the orthogonal projection of onto the column space of . Residual vector is perpendicular to every column: e = 0 — the same statement as the normal equations. Two ways to solve it: Method Cost When Normal equations / QR or Cholesky + p 3 ) small–medium ( ); exact Gradient descent / SGD per epoch huge, huge, streaming; approximate Gauss–Markov theorem (the why OLS credential): IF errors have zero mean, constant variance, and no correlation, THEN OLS is BLUE : the B est (minimum-variance) L inear U nbiased E stimator. Note what's NOT required: normality. Normality is only needed for exact small-sample t-tests/CIs. Also know: ridge (below) deliberately gives up U (unbiased) to reduce variance — and usually wins on test error. That's the bias–variance trade from Fundamentals , in one sentence. # The four classical assumptions (and what breaks) Analogy. The assumptions are the warranty card, not the on/off switch. The line still fits if you violate them — but the warranty (unbiased coefficients, trustworthy p-values and intervals) is void, often silently. The four (mnemonic LINE) + the practical fifth: # Assumption Meaning Diagnostic What breaks if violated Fix L Linearity really is residuals vs fitted: curve pattern coefficients biased — model is just wrong transforms, polynomials, splines, interactions I Independence of errors errors don't influence each other Durbin–Watson; residuals vs time show waves SEs too small → fake significance time-series models; clustered/robust SEs N Normality of errors Gaussian Q–Q plot small-sample p-values/CIs off (predictions fine) rarely fatal; bootstrap; large → CLT rescues you E Equal variance (homoscedasticity) constant across funnel in residuals vs fitted; Breusch–Pagan wrong SEs → wrong inference; inefficient log-transform , WLS, robust (White/HC) SEs + No perfect multicollinearity no feature is a linear combo of others VIF, condition number X ) − 1 blows up → huge, sign-flipping coefficients drop/combine features, PCA, ridge Figure 2 — Residual-plot signatures: healthy, funnel, curve, waves Multicollinearity — the deep-dive interviewers love: ​ = 1 − R j 2 ​ 1 ​ , where 2 ​ comes from regressing feature on all other features. Rule of thumb: → trouble. Symptoms: great but no individual feature significant; coefficients flip sign when you add/remove a feature; tiny data changes swing coefficients wildly. Key subtlety: multicollinearity inflates coefficient variance but barely hurts predictions . If you only predict, you can often ignore it; if you must explain, you can't. Cleanest fix: ridge — X + λ I ) is always invertible (see Regularization ). Production issues. Silent heteroscedasticity: revenue-prediction errors grow with customer size. Point forecasts look fine; the ± bands are fiction for big accounts. Fix: model , or use quantile regression for honest intervals. Duplicated features in a feature store: two teams register near-identical signals (e.g. 7-day and weekly averages) → multicollinearity → an important feature shows a negative coefficient in the explanation dashboard and stakeholders panic. Fix: VIF audit + ridge. Extrapolation: linear models happily predict far outside the training range (a house with 50 bathrooms). Clamp inputs and monitor feature ranges in serving. # Regularization: OLS vs Ridge vs Lasso vs Elastic Net Analogy (recap from Loss Functions ). Airline L1 charges per item → you drop items (sparse). Airline L2 charges by weight squared → everything lighter, nothing dropped. Elastic Net is a codeshare of both. The four estimators, one table: Objective Solution Sparsity Best at OLS X ) − 1 X ⊤ y ✗ , clean, low collinearity Ridge + λ ∥ w ∥ 2 2 ​ X + λ I ) − 1 X ⊤ y ✗ shrinks only correlated features; close to or above ; pure prediction Lasso + λ ∥ w ∥ 1 ​ no closed form — coordinate descent + soft-thresholding ✓ exact zeros feature selection; believe few features matter Elastic Net + λ ( α ∥ w ∥ 1 ​ + ( 1 − α ) ∥ w ∥ 2 2 ​ ) coordinate descent ✓ + grouping correlated features AND want sparsity Figure 3 — Coefficient paths vs : ridge shrinks smoothly, lasso zeroes one by one Facts to volunteer in an interview: is chosen by cross-validation ; recovers OLS; kills all coefficients (intercept survives — never penalized). Standardize features first — both penalties are unit-sensitive. Ridge keeps correlated twins together with similar weights; lasso picks one twin ~arbitrarily and zeroes the other → unstable feature selection story; Elastic Net fixes this (grouping effect). : OLS is undefined ( X singular); ridge still works; lasso selects at most features. Bayesian one-liner: ridge = Gaussian prior, lasso = Laplace prior, MAP estimation (see Maximum Likelihood Estimation ). Degrees of freedom: ridge's effective dof ​ d i 2 ​ + λ d i 2 ​ ​ p ( ​ = singular values of ) — shrinkage spends fewer parameters than it has. # Polynomial regression Analogy. A polynomial degree is a bendiness dial on a ruler. Degree 1: rigid ruler. Degree 3: gentle flex that traces the trend. Degree 15: cooked spaghetti that passes through every point — including the noise — and flails wildly at the edges. The key conceptual trick: Polynomial regression IS linear regression — on expanded features: ​ = w 0 ​ + w 1 ​ x + w 2 ​ x 2 + ⋯ + w d ​ x d . Linear in linear model means linear in the parameters , not in . Same OLS solver, same normal equations, same everything. Figure 4 — Degree is the bias–variance dial: underfit / right / overfit What to know: Degree ⇒ bias , variance — the cleanest concrete instance of the bias–variance tradeoff ( Bias-Variance Tradeoff ). Train error always falls with degree; test error is U-shaped. Pick degree by CV. High-degree pathologies: wild oscillation near the data edges (Runge phenomenon), and explosive extrapolation outside the range. , x 3 are strongly correlated → multicollinearity → standardize, use orthogonal polynomial bases, and regularize (poly features + ridge is a strong combo). Better-behaved alternative: splines — piecewise low-degree polynomials joined smoothly at knots → local flexibility without global oscillation. Feature count explodes with interactions: full degree- expansion of features p + d ​ ) terms → regularization becomes mandatory. # Scoring: R² and adjusted R² Analogy. answers: how much better is your model than the laziest possible one? The lazy baseline predicts the mean ​ for everyone. = the fraction of the baseline's error your model eliminated. Definitions: ​ = ∑ i ​ ( y i ​ − y ^ ​ i ​ ) 2 (your model's leftover error); ​ = ∑ i ​ ( y i ​ − y ˉ ​ ) 2 (baseline's error). = 1 − SS tot ​ SS res ​ ​ (fraction of variance explained) 2 ​ = 1 − ( 1 − R 2 ) ⋅ n − p − 1 n − 1 ​ (pays a price per feature) The facts interviewers actually probe: Claim Truth ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] ? Only in-sample with an intercept. On test data can be negative — worse than predicting the mean. Adding any feature changes ? In-sample never decreases when you add a feature, even pure noise — that's why it can't do model selection. Adjusted fixes that? It penalizes , so it can fall when a feature adds nothing — better, but still in-sample; CV is the real judge. High = good model? No: leakage, overfitting, or just low-noise data. Low can still be valuable (finance lives at ≈ 0.01 ). for nonlinear models? The = squared correlation ​ ) identity holds only for linear-with-intercept OLS; report MSE/MAE for general models. Relationship to the metrics chapter: is a rescaled MSE — same ranking of models on the same data; it adds interpretability, not new information (see Model Evaluation Validation ). # Choosing features and going beyond a straight line Analogy. Feature selection is hiring for a small team: each new hire must justify a salary (complexity). Stepwise hiring by interviews alone (in-sample fit) hires charming frauds; you want references from outside the room (cross-validation, information criteria). Feature selection — three families: Family Idea Examples Cost / risk Filter rank features before modeling correlation, mutual information cheap; ignores interactions Wrapper search subsets by model performance forward/backward stepwise expensive; overfits the search; inference after selection is invalid Embedded selection happens inside training lasso , tree importances one shot; lasso = the principled stepwise Model-size criteria, one line each: AIC (prediction-oriented); BIC (heavier penalty, consistency-oriented; picks smaller models for large ). Beyond a straight line (staying in linear-model land): Transforms: , ​ , — fix skew and multiplicative effects. Log- means coefficients become % effects: ​ % per unit ​ . Interactions: add ​ ⋅ x 2 ​ when one feature's effect depends on another (price sensitivity differs by region). Polynomials / splines: splines = piecewise polynomials with smooth knots — flexible AND stable. GAMs: ​ f j ​ ( x j ​ ) — each feature gets its own smooth curve; still additive → still explainable feature by feature. When to leave linear land: heavy feature interactions you can't enumerate → gradient-boosted trees ( Classification Methods ); raw signal inputs (text/images) → deep learning. Production issues. Stepwise + p-values in prod reports: selection invalidates classic inference (the features were chosen because they looked significant — winner's curse). Use lasso for selection, then refit OLS on the chosen set ( relaxed lasso ) and validate out-of-sample. Target leakage via feature engineering: a days_since_last_payment feature computed with future knowledge gives = 0.99 offline, garbage online. Every feature must be computable at prediction time. Schema drift: a transform pipeline (log, interactions) trained against one feature scale silently breaks when an upstream team changes units. Version the preprocessing artifact with the model. # Which regression when — the recap # Decision table Situation Method One-line why Baseline, , want interpretation OLS BLUE under Gauss–Markov; exact CIs if errors are also normal Correlated features / unstable coefficients Ridge X + λ I ) − 1 always exists; variance Many features, few matter Lasso exact zeros = built-in selection Correlated features AND want sparsity Elastic Net L1 sparsity + L2 grouping Ridge / lasso / Elastic Net OLS undefined; lasso caps at features Curved relationship, one or few features Polynomial (low degree) or splines + CV linear in parameters; degree = bias–variance dial Outliers in Huber / quantile regression robust losses on a linear model Asymmetric cost / need intervals Quantile regression pinball loss; from cost ratio Counts Poisson regression (GLM) right noise model, log link Skewed positive target + OLS multiplicative errors; remember gives the median Nonlinear interactions everywhere Gradient-boosted trees leave linear land knowingly # 60-second interview answers Question Answer in one breath Derive OLS? Minimize ; set gradient ( y − X w ) = 0 → normal equations X w = X ⊤ y → = ( X ⊤ X ) − 1 X ⊤ y ; geometrically, project onto 's column space. Why can't you trust going up? In-sample rises with ANY added feature; use adjusted , AIC/BIC, or best: cross-validation. And test-set can be negative. Multicollinearity — symptoms and fix? Inflated coefficient variance, sign flips, big with no significant features; detect with 2 ​ ) ; fix with ridge, dropping/combining features, or PCA. Predictions are mostly fine; interpretation is not. Ridge vs lasso? Ridge: L2, closed form, shrinks, handles collinearity, never zeros. Lasso: L1, soft-thresholding, exact zeros, selection, unstable with correlated twins. Elastic Net blends. Is polynomial regression linear? Yes — linear in the parameters. It's OLS on expanded features; linear model never meant linear in . When is OLS BLUE? Gauss–Markov: zero-mean, homoscedastic, uncorrelated errors → best linear unbiased estimator. Normality NOT required (only for exact small-sample inference). Why does ridge beat OLS on test error? It trades a little bias for a big variance cut — minimizing test MSE bias² + variance + noise, not unbiasedness. # Common traps → fixes Trap Fix Judging models by in-sample adjusted at minimum; cross-validation for real Regularizing unstandardized features scale first, inside the CV pipeline Penalizing the intercept don't Interpreting coefficients under collinearity check VIF before telling a coefficient story p-values after stepwise selection invalid; use holdout validation or post-selection inference Trusting a linear model outside training range monitor input ranges; clamp; flag extrapolations log-transforming then exponentiating naively you get the median, not the mean (Jensen); add the smearing / /2 correction if you need the mean Fitting degree-15 polynomial because train error fell test error is U-shaped; pick degree by CV; prefer splines Connects backward: Loss Functions supplies the losses (MSE, Huber, quantile) and penalties (L1/L2). Connects forward: Classification Methods (logistic regression = this + sigmoid + CE), Model Evaluation Validation . # Related Regularization Bias-Variance Tradeoff Gradient Descent Classification Methods Decision Trees, Random Forests Gradient Boosting Data Preparation Feature Engineering

title: Classification Methods
heads: The Master Table — Every Classifier Side by Side
Naive Bayes — Fast and Great for Text
k-NN and SVM — Distance vs Margin
Trees, Forests, Boosting — Bagging vs Boosting
text: Classification — predicting a discrete label — is the single most common framing you'll be asked to reason about, and interviewers use it to probe whether you understand why one model beats another on a given dataset, not just how to call .fit() . We line every major classifier up side by side, split them into the two families that organize the whole field, then walk each one with its assumptions, strengths, and the questions it tends to attract. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Place any classifier in the generative vs discriminative split and say what it learns. Derive logistic regression from the log-odds and explain why it's the default baseline. Explain why Naive Bayes works despite a naive assumption that's almost always false . Contrast bagging vs boosting in one sentence and say which fights bias vs variance. Pick a classifier from the shape of the data: size, dimensionality, linearity, interpretability. # The Master Table — Every Classifier Side by Side Before any single method, hold the landscape in your head. The classifiers you'll be asked about differ along a few axes that actually predict their behavior: what they learn, whether the boundary is linear, how they scale, and how interpretable they are. Model Family Boundary Strengths Watch out for Logistic regression Discriminative Linear Usually well-calibrated probabilities, interpretable, fast Underfits nonlinear data Naive Bayes Generative Linear in log-space (multinomial/Bernoulli; Gaussian NB can be quadratic) Tiny data, text, very fast Independence assumption, poor calibration k-NN Discriminative (lazy) Nonlinear No training, simple Slow at predict, curse of dimensionality SVM Discriminative Linear or kernel Strong in high-dim, margin-based Slow on big data, no native probabilities Decision tree Discriminative Axis-aligned Interpretable, handles mixed types Overfits, unstable Random forest Discriminative (bagging) Nonlinear Robust, low tuning, strong default Larger, less interpretable Gradient boosting Discriminative (boosting) Nonlinear Often best on tabular Tuning-sensitive, slower to train Neural network Discriminative Arbitrary Crushes vision/text/audio Data-hungry, opaque, tuning Memory hook Two questions sort almost any classifier: does it model the data (generative) or just the boundary (discriminative)? and is the boundary a straight line or can it bend? Everything else is a footnote on cost and interpretability. Interview angle Walk me through which classifier you'd try. Don't recite — reason from the data. The senior move: name a fast linear baseline (logistic regression), then a strong nonlinear default (gradient-boosted trees for tabular, a neural net for perceptual data), and justify each by the data's structure. Jumping straight to XGBoost without a baseline reads as junior. # Two Families: Generative vs Discriminative This split organizes the entire chapter, so it's worth one clean restatement. A discriminative model learns the boundary directly — , or just where the line goes. A generative model learns how each class produces data — and — then flips it with Bayes' rule to classify. Discriminative Generative Learns — the boundary — the full story Classifies by Which side of the line? Which class most likely generated this ? Can sample / detect outliers? No Yes Data appetite Wants more data, hits lower error Works on small data if assumptions hold Examples Logistic regression, SVM, trees, NN Naive Bayes, GMM, LDA, HMM The practical takeaway is the Ng–Jordan result from Fundamentals : a generative model reaches its error floor with fewer samples but that floor is higher ; the matching discriminative model is slower to converge but ends up more accurate with enough data. So generative shines in the small-data regime, discriminative in the large-data regime. Memory hook Discriminative asks which side? Generative asks who made this? — it learns each class's recipe and picks the most plausible cook. # Logistic Regression — The Must-Know Baseline Despite the name, logistic regression is a classifier . It's the single most important model to be able to derive from scratch, because nearly every interview that touches classification touches it. The setup: a linear model produces a score x + b that lives anywhere on the real line, but a probability has to sit in . The sigmoid squashes it: 1 ​ . Read backwards, this says the model is linear in the log-odds : p ​ = w ⊤ x + b That single fact is the heart of the method — a one-unit change in a feature shifts the log-odds by its weight. It's trained by minimizing cross-entropy (log-loss), not squared error. The reason matters and gets asked: cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood under a Bernoulli model, it's convex in the weights (so any local optimum is global; with separable data the weights diverge unless regularized), and it punishes confident wrong predictions hard. Squared error on a sigmoid is non-convex and produces vanishing gradients when the model is confidently wrong — exactly when you most need a signal. Property Logistic regression Why it matters Output Usually well-calibrated probability Threshold it for any precision/recall tradeoff Boundary Linear in features Add interactions/polynomials for curves Loss Cross-entropy (convex) Global optimum, clean gradients Regularization L1 (sparse) or L2 (shrink) Controls overfitting, L1 selects features Memory hook Logistic regression is linear regression on the log-odds , then squashed by a sigmoid. Linear in log-odds, probability out. Interview angle Three near-certain questions: (1) Why sigmoid? — to map a real-valued score to and make it linear in log-odds. (2) Why cross-entropy not MSE? — convexity + non-vanishing gradients + it's the Bernoulli MLE. (3) Is it linear? — the boundary is linear in features, even though the sigmoid is nonlinear. Getting (3) right separates people who memorized from people who understand. Go deeper (optional) For multiclass, logistic regression generalizes to softmax (multinomial) regression: one weight vector per class, normalized to a distribution. Softmax + cross-entropy is exactly the output layer of most neural-net classifiers — so what's the last layer of a classifier net? is the same idea you already know. # Naive Bayes — Fast and Great for Text Naive Bayes is the canonical generative classifier and a perennial interview favorite because its central paradox is so clean: it rests on an assumption that is almost always false, and it works anyway. It applies Bayes' rule — — and makes the naive assumption that all features are conditionally independent given the class. That lets it factor into a product of per-feature terms, which is why it trains in a single pass and handles tens of thousands of features (every word in a vocabulary) effortlessly. The assumption is obviously wrong — in text, New and York are not independent. But Naive Bayes only needs the correct class to get the highest score , not accurate probabilities. The dependencies often distort all classes' scores in the same direction, so the argmax survives even when the probabilities themselves are badly miscalibrated. That's the resolution to the paradox, and the answer interviewers want. Variant Use on Models each feature as Multinomial NB Word counts (text) Count from a multinomial Bernoulli NB Binary presence/absence 0/1 per feature Gaussian NB Continuous features A normal distribution Two practical notes that come up: Laplace (add-one) smoothing is essential — without it, a single unseen word gives and zeroes out the whole product. And NB probabilities are poorly calibrated (pushed toward 0 or 1 by the independence assumption), so trust its ranking and labels, not its confidence numbers. Memory hook Naive Bayes assumes every feature votes independently. The assumption is a lie, but the winner of the vote is usually still right — good classification, bad probabilities. Interview angle Why does Naive Bayes work if the independence assumption is false? The crisp answer: it only needs the right class to win the argmax, not calibrated probabilities; the errors are often shared across classes and cancel at the decision. Bonus points for mentioning Laplace smoothing and that it's a strong, near-free baseline for text. # k-NN and SVM — Distance vs Margin These two are usually taught together because they represent two opposite instincts about what makes a good boundary: be like your neighbors versus stay as far from everyone as possible . k-Nearest Neighbors is the laziest model there is — it does no training, just stores the data.
