To classify a point, it finds the closest stored examples and takes a majority vote. Small means a jagged, low-bias/high-variance boundary; large smooths it out (higher bias, lower variance). Its weaknesses are exactly its design: prediction is slow (you compare against everything), it's memory-heavy, and it dies in high dimensions because distances become meaningless — the curse of dimensionality . It also demands feature scaling, since raw-scale features dominate the distance. Support Vector Machines take the opposite stance: among all lines that separate the classes, pick the one with the widest margin — the largest gap to the nearest points (the support vectors ). A wide margin is a built-in regularizer, which is why SVMs are strong in high-dimensional spaces like text. The kernel trick lets them draw nonlinear boundaries by implicitly mapping data to a higher-dimensional space without ever computing the coordinates — the RBF kernel is the common default. k-NN SVM Training None (lazy) Solve a convex optimization Idea Vote of nearest neighbors Maximize the margin Boundary Flexible, local Linear, or kernel for nonlinear Scales to big data? Predict is slow Training slow, predict fast Key knobs , distance metric, scaling (margin softness), kernel Memory hook k-NN: tell me who your neighbors are. SVM: draw the boundary down the widest empty street. One is lazy and local; the other is a global optimizer obsessed with the margin. Interview angle For k-NN expect what happens as grows? (bias up, variance down) and why does it fail in high dimensions? (distances concentrate, neighbors stop being meaningful). For SVM expect what's a support vector? (a point on or inside the margin that defines the boundary) and what does the kernel trick buy you? (nonlinear boundaries without explicit high-dimensional features). Go deeper (optional) The SVM parameter is the margin-softness knob: small = wide, soft margin tolerating misclassifications (more bias, less variance); large = narrow, hard margin fitting the training data tightly (less bias, more variance). It's the same bias-variance dial in margin clothing. # Trees, Forests, Boosting — Bagging vs Boosting Tree-based models dominate tabular data, and the progression from a single tree to forests to boosting is one of the most testable arcs in ML. A decision tree splits the feature space with a sequence of yes/no questions, choosing each split to most reduce impurity ( Gini or entropy for classification). It's wonderfully interpretable and handles mixed feature types with no scaling — but a single deep tree overfits badly and is unstable : change a few points and the whole tree can rearrange. That instability is the opening for ensembles. The two ways to combine many trees are the central contrast of this section. Bagging (Random Forest) Boosting (GBM / XGBoost) Trees are trained In parallel, independently Sequentially, each fixing the last Each tree sees A bootstrap sample (+ random feature subset at each split) The residual errors so far Primarily reduces Variance Bias Failure mode Slightly weaker than tuned boosting Overfits if over-trained / under-regularized Tuning burden Low (strong out of the box) Higher (learning rate, depth, rounds) Random forests grow many deep, decorrelated trees on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets, then average them. Averaging many high-variance, low-bias trees cancels the variance — a robust, low-maintenance default. Gradient boosting instead builds shallow trees one at a time, each trained on the previous ensemble's errors, steadily driving down bias. Tuned well (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), boosting is usually the top performer on heterogeneous tabular data. Memory hook Bagging = a committee voting in parallel to cancel each other's mistakes (kills variance). Boosting = a relay team , each runner covering the last one's shortfall (kills bias). Interview angle The bagging-vs-boosting contrast is asked constantly. Nail the one-liner: bagging trains independent trees in parallel to reduce variance; boosting trains dependent trees sequentially on residuals to reduce bias. Follow-ups: why are random-forest trees deep but boosting trees shallow? (deep = low-bias high-variance, perfect for averaging; shallow = weak learners boosting corrects gradually) and which overfits more easily? (boosting, since it keeps fitting residuals). # Ensembles in Full Zooming out, the ensembles above are three instances of one principle: combine many models so their errors cancel. Worth knowing all the named patterns. Method How it combines Mainly helps Bagging Parallel models on bootstrap samples, then average/vote Variance Boosting Sequential models on residuals Bias Stacking A meta-model learns to blend base models' predictions Both (if base models are diverse) Voting Hard (majority) or soft (average probabilities) Variance The condition for an ensemble to help is diversity : the base models must make different errors. Averaging ten copies of the same model gains nothing. This is why random forests inject randomness (bootstrap rows + random feature subsets) — to decorrelate the trees so their mistakes don't line up. Memory hook An ensemble only helps if its members are wrong in different ways . Diversity is the whole trick — identical experts add nothing; disagreeing experts cancel each other's blind spots. Go deeper (optional) Stacking/blending of diverse models wins many Kaggle competitions: train diverse base models (trees, linear, nets), then a meta-learner on their out-of-fold predictions. The subtlety is leakage — the meta-model must be trained on held-out base predictions, or it learns from data the base models already saw. # Which Classifier When The payoff of the chapter: matching a model to the data in front of you. This is the decision interviewers actually want to see you make. Situation Reach for Need a fast, interpretable baseline Logistic regression Text / very high-dimensional sparse data Naive Bayes or linear SVM Tabular data, want top accuracy Gradient boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM) Tabular data, want robust + low tuning Random forest Images, audio, language Neural network Small data, low dimensions, nonlinear k-NN or SVM (RBF) Need calibrated probabilities Logistic regression (usually well calibrated), or calibrate afterward Need to explain every prediction Single decision tree or logistic regression The meta-strategy: always start with a simple baseline (logistic regression or a shallow tree), measure it honestly, then escalate to a stronger model only if the baseline leaves accuracy on the table. The baseline also catches leakage — a too-good baseline score is a red flag, not a victory. Interview angle You have a tabular dataset with 50k rows and mixed feature types — what do you use? Strong answer: a logistic-regression baseline for a reference point and calibration, then gradient-boosted trees as the likely winner, justified by their fit to heterogeneous tabular data and their handling of nonlinearities and interactions without manual feature engineering. Then mention you'd validate the choice empirically — No Free Lunch. # Cross-Cutting Skills (Asked of Senior Candidates) Beyond naming models, senior interviews probe a few skills that cut across all classifiers. Handling class imbalance. When one class is rare (fraud, disease), accuracy is useless and most classifiers drift toward the majority. Levers: resample (SMOTE / oversample minority, undersample majority), reweight the loss to penalize minority errors more, and — most importantly — change the metric to precision/recall, F1, or PR-AUC instead of accuracy. Multiclass from binary models. Models like SVM are natively binary. One-vs-Rest trains one classifier per class against all others ( classifiers); One-vs-One trains one per pair ( classifiers, each on less data). Logistic regression and trees handle multiclass natively via softmax / multi-way splits. Calibration. A model can rank well but report dishonest probabilities (Naive Bayes, SVMs, deep nets often do). If you need the number 0.7 to mean 70% of the time, calibrate with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data (see Model Evaluation Validation ). Memory hook Three senior reflexes: imbalanced data → change the metric first, resampling/reweighting second. Binary-only model → wrap it in One-vs-Rest. Probabilities you'll act on → calibrate them. Rapid fire — Classification Two families: discriminative learns the boundary ; generative learns and can sample. Generative wins small-data, discriminative wins large-data. Logistic regression: linear in log-odds, sigmoid out, trained with convex cross-entropy. The boundary is linear; use it as the baseline. Naive Bayes: assumes conditional independence (false) but wins the argmax anyway; great for text; use Laplace smoothing; poorly calibrated. k-NN: lazy, local, dies in high dimensions, needs scaling. SVM: max-margin, strong in high-dim, kernel trick for nonlinearity. Trees overfit and are unstable. Bagging (random forest) = parallel trees killing variance; boosting (XGBoost) = sequential trees killing bias. Ensembles need diverse base models (wrong in different ways) to help. Pick by data: logistic baseline → boosting for tabular, NN for perceptual, NB/linear-SVM for text. Imbalance → change the metric (PR-AUC, F1) before resampling/reweighting. # One-Page Summary Concept The one thing to remember Two families Discriminative draws the boundary ; generative models and can sample. Logistic regression Linear in log-odds, sigmoid out, convex cross-entropy loss; the usually well-calibrated baseline. Why not MSE Cross-entropy is convex with non-vanishing gradients; it's the Bernoulli MLE. Naive Bayes Conditional-independence assumption is false but the argmax still wins; great, fast text baseline. k-NN Lazy, local, needs scaling, dies in high dimensions; trades bias for variance. SVM Maximize the margin; kernel trick for nonlinear boundaries; strong in high dimensions. Trees Interpretable but overfit and unstable — the reason ensembles exist. Bagging vs boosting Bagging = parallel trees, kills variance (random forest). Boosting = sequential trees on residuals, kills bias (XGBoost). Ensembles Only help when base models are wrong in different ways — diversity is the trick. Which when Logistic baseline → boosting for tabular, NN for perceptual, NB/linear-SVM for text. Imbalance Change the metric first (PR-AUC, F1), then resample/reweight. # Related Logistic Regression Generative vs Discriminative Bagging vs Boosting Precision Recall Regression Methods Decision Trees, Random Forests Gradient Boosting Naive Bayes k-Nearest Neighbors Support Vector Machines Class Imbalance Calibration

title: Decision Trees, Random Forests & Gradient Boosting
heads: How a Tree Chooses a Split
Stopping, Pruning, and Why Trees Are High-Variance
Random Forests: Bootstrap, Feature Bagging, OOB
Gradient Boosting as Functional Gradient Descent
When Trees Beat Neural Nets on Tabular Data
text: Tree models and their ensembles are the default answer for structured tabular data — if you can explain splits, bagging variance math, and boosting as gradient descent, you own the most-tested classical ML arc. A single decision tree is an axis-aligned partition of the feature space: a sequence of if/else questions that route each point to a leaf labeled by majority class or mean target. Alone it's interpretable but unstable; random forests and gradient boosting turn that instability into state-of-the-art tabular performance. This chapter goes past the survey in Classification Methods into split criteria with numbers, pruning, ensemble variance, functional gradient boosting, library-specific tricks, feature-importance traps, and when trees still beat deep nets. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Compute Gini / information gain (or variance reduction) for a candidate split and argue which feature wins. Explain cost-complexity pruning and why an unpruned tree is high-variance. Derive the random forest variance intuition + B ( 1 − ρ ) σ 2 ​ and what OOB error estimates. Describe gradient boosting as gradient descent in function space (pseudo-residuals, shrinkage, subsampling). State the XGBoost split gain with , , and histogram splits; contrast LightGBM and CatBoost headlines. Compare impurity vs permutation vs SHAP importance and name a sensible hyperparameter tuning order . Argue when GBDT beats neural nets on tabular data (and when it doesn't). # How a Tree Chooses a Split At each internal node the algorithm considers every feature and every allowable threshold, scores each candidate split, and keeps the best. Best means largest impurity reduction (classification) or largest variance reduction (regression). # Classification: Gini and entropy For node with class proportions ​ , Gini impurity is ∑ ​ p k 2 ​ Entropy is ​ p k ​ lo g 2 ​ p k ​ . A split into left ( ) and right ( ) children with weights ​ = n L ​ / n , ​ = n R ​ / n yields information gain ​ I ( L ) − w R ​ I ( R ) where is Gini or entropy. Splits maximize (equivalently minimize weighted child impurity). Gini and entropy usually agree; Gini skips logs and is the default in sklearn/CART. For multiclass , the same formulas use all classes; some libraries also support binary-only impurity (faster on many-class problems). # Regression: variance reduction For targets ​ in a node with mean ​ , node variance is 1 ​ ∑ ( y i ​ − y ˉ ​ ) 2 . A split is scored by how much weighted child variance drops — exactly the MSE improvement you'd get by assigning each point to the child whose mean is closer. Memory hook Gini = how often would a random label in this node be wrong if you guessed by the local class frequencies? High Gini = mixed labels = worth splitting. Interview angle Weak: we use Gini. Strong: we minimize impurity / maximize information gain; for regression that's within-node MSE. Splits are axis-aligned and greedy — no global optimum guarantee. # Worked numeric split example ID Feature Label 1 2 0 2 3 0 3 4 1 4 7 1 5 8 1 6 9 0 Root: 3 zeros, 3 ones → ​ = p 1 ​ = 0.5 , . Candidate split (points 1–4 left, 5–6 right): Left: two 0s, two 1s → Right: one 1, one 0 → Weighted Gini after split: 4 ​ ( 0.5 ) + 6 2 ​ ( 0.5 ) = 0.5 → (no gain) Candidate split (points 1–2 left, 3–6 right): Left: both 0 → Right: three 1s, one 0 → ​ = 1/4 , ​ = 3/4 , Weighted: 2 ​ ( 0 ) + 6 4 ​ ( 0.375 ) = 0.25 → Candidate split (points 1–5 left, 6 right): Left: two 0s, three 1s → Right: single 0 → Weighted: 5 ​ ( 0.48 ) + 6 1 ​ ( 0 ) = 0.4 → The tree takes first (largest impurity drop). This is greedy : later splits may not be globally optimal. flowchart TD R[ Root: G=0.5 ] -- | x ≤ 3.5 | L[ Left: all 0, G=0 ] R -- | x 3.5 | RR[ Right: G=0.375 ] This example is 1D and tiny. Real trees evaluate every feature and every mid-point threshold (or histogram bin boundary), which is per level for exact sorting — why histogram methods matter at scale. Rapid fire — Splits Classification: minimize weighted Gini or maximize information gain from entropy. Regression: maximize variance / MSE reduction. Splits are axis-aligned, greedy, local optima. Gini ≈ entropy in practice; Gini is cheaper. Multiclass uses the same formulas over all classes. # Stopping, Pruning, and Why Trees Are High-Variance # Growing and stopping criteria Trees grow until stopped by: Criterion Effect Max depth Hard cap on interactions Min samples per leaf Stops splitting tiny, pure-by-chance regions Min impurity decrease Ignores splits that barely help Max leaf nodes Budget on complexity Defaults that allow full growth (min samples = 1, no depth cap) memorize training noise — classic overfitting . # Cost-complexity pruning (CART) Post-pruning starts from a large tree ​ and trades fit against size. Define cost-complexity ​ ( T ) = R ( T ) + α ∣ T ∣ where is misclassification rate (or node MSE), is leaf count, and penalizes size. As increases, subtrees with small impurity gains get pruned first. Cross-validation on a grid of picks the subtree that generalizes best — the honest alternative to hand-tuning max depth. Memory hook Pruning = pay a tax per leaf so the tree can't buy tiny purity wins that don't survive validation. # High variance without ensembles Property Consequence Low bias (deep trees) Can fit complex interactions High variance Small label noise / subsample changes flip early splits → a completely different tree Discontinuous boundary Step functions; no smooth extrapolation Greedy splits Early mistakes propagate This is exactly why bias-variance interviews pair deep tree with variance , and why bagging targets variance while boosting targets bias. See Decision Trees for the card-level summary. Interview angle Why not one deep tree? → near-zero training error but unstable test performance; averaging or sequential correction fixes the pathology the inductive bias creates. Rapid fire — Pruning variance Stop with depth, min samples, min gain, or leaf budget. Cost-complexity ​ = R + α ∣ T ∣ ; CV on selects subtree. Single deep trees: low bias, high variance, unstable. Regression leaves predict constants — no extrapolation. # Random Forests: Bootstrap, Feature Bagging, OOB Random forests are bagging over deep CART trees with an extra randomization: at each split, consider only a random subset of features (often ​ for classification, for regression). # The two sources of randomness Bootstrap samples: each tree trains on points drawn with replacement (~63% unique rows per tree). Feature subsampling at splits: decorrelates trees that would otherwise all chase the same dominant feature. Goal: keep individual trees low-bias (deep) but make them diverse so averaging reduces variance. # OOB error Each point is left out of roughly 1/3 of trees (not in their bootstrap bag). Out-of-bag (OOB) predictions aggregate only those trees and give a free validation estimate without a holdout set — useful for monitoring, though you still want a proper cross-validation split for model selection. # Variance of the ensemble average Let trees each predict ​ ( x ) with variance and pairwise correlation between tree predictions. The forest prediction is ( x ) = B 1 ​ ∑ b ​ T b ​ ( x ) . Then ) = ρ σ 2 + B 1 − ρ ​ σ 2 Intuition: correlated trees contribute that doesn't shrink with ; only the uncorrelated fraction dies as . Feature subsampling exists to lower . Adding more trees can't fix fully correlated errors — diversity is the lever. Memory hook Forest variance = correlation floor plus a diversity bonus that vanishes as . Interview angle Trap: forests can't overfit if you add trees. Partially true for training loss, but test error plateaus — remains. Overfitting still happens via depth, leaf size, and overfitting to a fixed feature set. Rapid fire — Random forests Bootstrap rows + random features per split. OOB ≈ built-in validation; still use proper CV for selection. ) = ρ σ 2 + ( 1 − ρ ) σ 2 / B — correlation limits gains. Deep trees, low tuning, strong tabular default — see Bagging vs Boosting . # Gradient Boosting as Functional Gradient Descent Boosting builds an additive model ​ ( x ) = ∑ m = 1 M ​ η h m ​ ( x ) where each ​ is a weak learner (typically a shallow tree). # Pseudo-residuals Given loss , gradient boosting (Friedman) sets ​ ( x ) = F m − 1 ​ ( x ) + η h m ​ ( x ) and fits ​ to the negative gradient of the loss w.r.t. ​ : ​ = − ∂ F ∂ ℓ ( y i ​ , F ( x i ​ )) ​ ​ F = F m − 1 ​ ​ For squared loss , ​ = y i ​ − F m − 1 ​ ( x i ​ ) — ordinary residuals. For log-loss , residuals look like (classification pseudo-responses). This is gradient descent in function space , not weight space — see Gradient Descent . # Shrinkage and subsampling Learning rate (shrinkage): smaller steps need more trees but usually generalize better — tune and together (low , more estimators). Subsampling (stochastic boosting): each round fits on a random fraction of rows (and sometimes columns), injecting noise like bagging and reducing overfitting. Shallow trees (depth 3–8) keep each ​ a weak learner ; depth sets max interaction order ( leaves). Memory hook Boosting = steepest descent where each step is a small tree fit to the loss gradient — not relabeling mistakes only (that's AdaBoost's story), but the same fix what's wrong spirit. Rapid fire — Gradient boosting core Additive model; each tree fits negative loss gradient (pseudo-residuals). Squared loss → residual targets; log-loss → -style targets. shrinks steps; row subsampling regularizes. Shallow trees, many rounds — bias↓, watch overfitting. # XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost Libraries differ in how they find splits, grow trees, and handle categoricals — the gain formula and growth strategy are fair game in senior interviews. # XGBoost: second-order Taylor + regularized splits XGBoost approximates the loss with a second-order Taylor expansion at current predictions ​ : ​ + f ) ≈ ℓ ( y , F m − 1 ​ ) + g f + 2 1 ​ h f 2 with ​ ℓ and 2 ​ ℓ (gradient and Hessian ). For squared loss, ; for log-loss, . Summing over instances in a leaf with score , the optimal leaf weight solves = − H + λ G ​ where ​ , ​ , and is L2 on leaf weights. The split gain for a partition into and is 1 ​ [ H L ​ + λ G L 2 ​ ​ + H R ​ + λ G R 2 ​ ​ − H L ​ + H R ​ + λ ( G L ​ + G R ​ ) 2 ​ ] − γ is a minimum gain threshold (complexity penalty per split); shrinks leaf scores. Splits with negative gain are pruned. Histogram splits: bin continuous features once, then search split candidates on bin boundaries — per node instead of sorting all . Column blocks and cache-aware design explain much of its speed. Interview angle Write the gain without forgetting and the in every denominator . Weak: XGBoost is fast. Strong: second-order approximation, regularized leaf weights, histogram-based candidate splits. # LightGBM: leaf-wise growth, GOSS, EFB Leaf-wise (best-first) growth: split the leaf with largest loss reduction — deeper asymmetric trees for fixed leaf budget vs level-wise sklearn GBM. Risk: overfits if num_leaves is too large without min_data_in_leaf . GOSS (Gradient-based One-Side Sampling): keep large-gradient instances, random sample small-gradient ones — speeds training with minimal accuracy loss when gradients carry the signal. EFB (Exclusive Feature Bundling): merges sparse mutually exclusive one-hot columns to reduce dimensionality. # CatBoost: ordered boosting and categoricals Ordered boosting: computes gradients with permutation-based statistics so target leakage across boosting iterations is reduced (important when residuals reuse labels). Target statistics for categoricals: smooth counts like n k ​ + α p ​ with priors instead of naive one-hot explosion — strong on high-cardinality categoricals without manual encoding. Library Signature trick Watch XGBoost 2nd-order gain + , ; histogram More knobs; level-wise default in some APIs LightGBM Leaf-wise, GOSS, EFB num_leaves can overfit CatBoost Ordered boosting + native categoricals Slower on tiny data; GPU helps Rapid fire — GBDT libraries XGBoost gain uses , , , subtract per split. Histogram binning for speed at scale. LightGBM: leaf-wise, GOSS, EFB. CatBoost: ordered stats, ordered boosting for categoricals. # Feature Importance: Impurity, Permutation, SHAP Method What it measures Pitfall Impurity decrease (MDI) How much a feature reduced Gini/MSE in the forest Biased toward high-cardinality / continuous features with many split points Permutation importance Drop in validation metric when feature values are shuffled Needs held-out data; correlated features share importance SHAP (tree explainer) Consistent additive attributions from cooperative game theory Costly; still reflects training distribution Senior habit: use impurity for rough screening, permutation on a validation set for honest global ranking, SHAP for local explanations and debugging individual predictions — tie back to Model Evaluation Validation and Data Leakage (importance on leaky features lies). Importance ≠ causality. A feature can rank high because it's a proxy for the label or because of leakage , not because intervening on it would change outcomes. # Hyperparameter Tuning Order A practical sequence for GBDT (adapt for forests by dropping / tradeoffs): learning_rate + n_estimators — fix a modest (0.03–0.1), use early stopping on validation to set rounds. max_depth / num_leaves — interaction capacity; shallow first, then increase if underfitting. min_child_weight / min_data_in_leaf — smooth leaves, reduce noise fits. subsample + colsample_bytree — regularization once structure is right. reg_lambda , reg_alpha , gamma — fine-grain split/leaf penalties. Class weights or scale_pos_weight for class imbalance before chasing exotic losses. Random forests: tune max_depth , min_samples_leaf , max_features , then n_estimators until OOB/validation plateaus. Use Cross-Validation on the same preprocessing you'd ship — see Data Preparation Feature Engineering . Interview angle How do you tune XGBoost? → early stopping on learning rate and rounds first, then tree complexity, then stochastic fractions, then regularization — never tune 15 knobs randomly. # When Trees Beat Neural Nets on Tabular Data Gradient-boosted trees often win when: Moderate (thousands to millions), heterogeneous column types (numeric + categorical + missing). Low signal-to-noise where inductive bias toward axis-aligned splits helps. Need fast CPU training , interpretable partial dependence, little GPU ops burden. Irregular interactions without spatial structure (unlike images/text). Neural nets tend to win when: Massive data, rich perception (vision, audio, language) or sequences. End-to-end representation learning beats hand features. Homogeneous tensor data with translation/equivariance structure (CNNs). Recent benchmarks (e.g. TabTransformer-era studies) still show strong GBDT on many business tabular sets unless you invest heavily in embeddings and regularized deep architectures — see Training Neural Networks for the flip side. Rapid fire — Trees vs nets Tabular heterogeneous data → GBDT default; NN needs careful embeddings/regularization. Trees handle missing indicators natively in many libs; NNs need explicit handling. Trees: fast on CPU, partial dependence; NNs: scale on GPU for perceptual/modal data. Always benchmark — No Free Lunch. # Interview Angles and Traps Question Strong move Gini vs entropy Nearly identical splits; Gini cheaper; neither fixes imbalance alone Forest vs boosting Parallel variance reduction vs sequential bias reduction; RF deep, GBM shallow Can forests overfit? Yes — floor; depth and min leaf still matter Boosting learning rate Coupled with ; use early stopping XGBoost gain 2nd-order with , , , minus Feature importance MDI biased; prefer permutation + domain sense Tree extrapolation No on regression — constant leaves Go deeper (optional) Mondrian forests , quantile GBM , and monotonic constraints (XGBoost/LightGBM) encode domain shape priors — useful when scores must be monotone in risk factors. Rapid fire — Interview traps More forest trees always help test AUC — only until dominates. Boosting can't overfit — it can; monitor validation, use shrinkage/subsampling. Highest MDI feature is causal — not without experiments. Confusing AdaBoost reweighting story with gradient boosting gradient story — related ensemble idea, different mechanics. # One-Page Summary Concept The one thing to remember Split criteria Maximize impurity drop (Gini/entropy) or variance drop (MSE); greedy, axis-aligned Pruning ​ ( T ) = R ( T ) + α ∣ T ∣ ; CV on Single tree Low bias, high variance , unstable Random forest Bootstrap + random features; ) = ρ σ 2 + ( 1 − ρ ) σ 2 / B ; OOB estimate Gradient boosting Fit trees to negative loss gradients ; + subsampling regularize XGBoost gain 1 ​ [ H L ​ + λ G L 2 ​ ​ + H R ​ + λ G R 2 ​ ​ − H L ​ + H R ​ + λ ( G L ​ + G R ​ ) 2 ​ ] − γ LightGBM / CatBoost Leaf-wise + GOSS/EFB vs ordered boosting + target stats for categoricals Importance MDI biased; permutation on validation; SHAP for locals Tuning order rounds → depth/leaves → min leaf → subsample → Tabular winner GBDT default; NNs for perception/scale/representation # Related Decision Trees Gradient Boosting Bagging vs Boosting Classification Methods Bias-Variance Tradeoff Regression Methods Loss Functions Gradient Descent Cross-Validation Data Preparation Feature Engineering Class Imbalance Training Neural Networks

title: Clustering, Dimensionality Reduction & Anomaly Detection
heads: k-Means: Lloyd's Algorithm and Choosing k
text: Unsupervised learning is structure-finding without labels — clusters, low-dimensional views, and rare events — and interviews test whether you know when each method's geometry matches the data. With only inputs and no , algorithms hunt groupings , compressions , or outliers . This chapter covers clustering from k-means through density and hierarchy, dimensionality reduction beyond the PCA treatment in Eigenvectors, PCA SVD , honest reading of t-SNE/UMAP plots, anomaly detection without labels, and evaluation with and without ground truth. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Run Lloyd's k-means , state its objective, and initialize with k-means++ ; name failure modes and how to pick . Walk EM for a GMM and explain k-means as a hard, equal-variance limit. Contrast hierarchical , DBSCAN/HDBSCAN , and spectral clustering when blobs aren't spherical. Place kernel PCA, t-SNE, UMAP , and autoencoders relative to PCA and state what 2D embeddings can and cannot prove. Compare isolation forest, one-class SVM, LOF , reconstruction error, and simple z-score/IQR baselines. Evaluate clusters with silhouette / Davies–Bouldin and, when labels exist, ARI/NMI ; discuss anomaly metrics without labels . # k-Means: Lloyd's Algorithm and Choosing k # Objective and algorithm k-means seeks centroids ​ } and hard assignments minimizing ∑ k ​ x ∈ C j ​ ∑ ​ ∥ x − μ j ​ ∥ 2 2 ​ Lloyd's algorithm alternates: Assign: each point to nearest centroid. Update: ​ = mean of points in cluster . Each step lowers or leaves it unchanged; convergence is to a local minimum — run multiple restarts. k-means++ initialization picks centroids with probability proportional to squared distance to existing centers, spreading seeds and cutting worst-case iteration counts versus uniform random starts. Memory hook k-means = Voronoi diagram whose cell centers chase their means until they stop moving. # Choosing Heuristic Idea Caveat Elbow Plot vs ; bend suggests Subjective; inertia always decreases Silhouette Mean cohesion vs separation in Favors convex, separated blobs Domain Business segments, capacity Often beats blind metrics With external labels (rare in pure unsupervised, common in evaluation), use Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) or Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) — see §5. # Failure modes Wrong : splits or merges natural groups. Non-spherical / varying density: k-means assumes spherical, similar-variance clusters (see GMM/DBSCAN). Outliers: pull centroids; winsorize, robust clustering, or density methods. Scale: Euclidean distance dominated by large features — standardize continuous columns ( Data Preparation Feature Engineering ). Interview angle When does k-means fail? → elongated/manifold clusters, unequal sizes/densities, wrong , unscaled features. Offer DBSCAN, GMM, or spectral alternatives by geometry. See also k-Means Clustering . # Mini example: two clusters in 1D Points , . Initialization ​ = 1 , ​ = 9 : Assign: ​ , ​ . Update: ​ = 2 , ​ = 8 — converged (assignments unchanged). On data this clean almost any start converges to the same answer. Bad starts bite with more clusters: drop two initial centroids inside one true blob and none in another, and Lloyd converges with one blob split in two and two blobs merged into one cluster. Each step only moves centroids locally, so it never escapes that local optimum. That's why k-means++ and multiple restarts are defaults, not optional polish. Rapid fire — k-means Minimize within-cluster sum of squares; Lloyd assign/update. Local optima → multiple restarts; k-means++ for init. Elbow + silhouette + domain for ; scale features. Spherical-blob assumption; use GMM/DBSCAN when geometry differs. # GMMs and EM: Soft Assignment A Gaussian Mixture Model models data as a weighted sum of Gaussians: ∑ k ​ π j ​ N ( x ∣ μ j ​ , Σ j ​ ) EM algorithm: E-step: posterior responsibility ​ = P ( z = j ∣ x i ​ ) from current parameters. M-step: update ​ , ​ , ​ as weighted MLE with weights ​ . Output: soft cluster membership (probability per component), elliptical clusters when ​ are full. k-means limit: equal ​ = σ 2 I , responsibilities → hard 0/1, M-step → centroids as means — k-means is EM with a very stiff GMM. k-means GMM Assignment Hard Soft Shape Spherical Elliptical (covariance) Optimization Lloyd EM (local optimum) Memory hook k-means is a hard GMM wearing a spherical straightjacket. BIC for choosing : penalizes parameter count (each extra component adds means, covariances, weights). Pick with lowest BIC on a validation likelihood or full-data score — more principled than elbow when clusters overlap. Interview angle k-means vs GMM? → hard vs soft assignment; spherical vs elliptical covariances; Lloyd vs EM. Use GMM when blobs have different shapes/scales and you want uncertainty. Rapid fire — GMM / EM E-step: responsibilities; M-step: weighted means/covariances. Soft memberships; BIC/AIC often used to pick component count . k-means ≈ equal spherical covariances + hard assignments. # Hierarchical, DBSCAN, and Spectral Clustering # Hierarchical clustering Build a dendrogram by iteratively merging (agglomerative) or splitting (divisive) clusters. Linkage chooses merge distance: Linkage Merges when Behavior Single Nearest pair across clusters Chaining, elongated clusters Complete Farthest pair Compact clusters Average Mean pairwise distance Balanced Ward Smallest increase in within-cluster variance k-means-like, popular Cut the dendrogram at a height to get clusters — no need to specify upfront, but choice of cut remains. # DBSCAN and HDBSCAN DBSCAN defines clusters as dense regions separated by sparse gaps: neighborhood radius, min_samples core threshold. Core points have min_samples neighbors within ; border points attach to cores; noise labeled . Strengths: arbitrary shape, automatic noise, no fixed . Weaknesses: sensitive to in varying density — HDBSCAN builds a hierarchy over and extracts stable clusters. Interview angle DBSCAN vs k-means? → density-defined arbitrary shapes + explicit noise vs centroid/spherical assumption. # Spectral clustering (brief) When clusters are non-convex but separable on a graph , build a similarity matrix ​ = exp ( − ∥ x i ​ − x j ​ ∥ 2 /2 σ 2 ) , take the bottom eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian, and k-means in that embedded space. This is the same eigenvector instinct as PCA ( Eigenvectors, PCA SVD ) but on affinities , not raw covariance structure. flowchart LR KM[ k-means ] -- | spherical blobs | OK1[ Works ] DB[ DBSCAN ] -- | varying density arcs | OK2[ Works ] KM -- | two moons | BAD1[ Fails ] SC[ Spectral ] -- | two moons | OK3[ Works ] Rapid fire — Beyond k-means Hierarchical: dendrogram + linkage; Ward ≈ variance-minimizing merges. DBSCAN/HDBSCAN: density + noise; tuning matters. Spectral: graph eigenvectors for non-convex clusters. # Dimensionality Reduction Beyond PCA PCA (in Eigenvectors, PCA SVD ) finds orthogonal directions of max variance — linear, global, invertible (in the retained subspace). Several methods answer different questions. # Kernel PCA Maps implicitly via kernel ) and runs PCA in feature space — nonlinear structure without explicit coordinates. Cost scales with – ; choose kernel like an SVM ( Support Vector Machines ). # t-SNE Optimizes Student-t distribution in 2D/3D to match pairwise similarities in high dimensions (heavy tails avoid crowding). Great for visualizing local neighborhoods; not for: Distances between distant clusters (global layout unreliable). Downstream features — new points need out-of-sample extensions (e.g. parametric t-SNE) or refit. Cluster size faithfully represented (exaggerates local density). # UMAP Builds a fuzzy topological representation of high-D data and optimizes a low-D layout — often faster than t-SNE, can preserve more global structure, still primarily a visualization tool. Hyperparameters ( n_neighbors , min_dist ) control local vs global tradeoff. # Autoencoders Neural encoder and decoder = h ( z ) trained to minimize reconstruction loss. The bottleneck is a learned nonlinear embedding — useful for anomaly scores (reconstruction error) and as input to downstream models; needs more data and tuning than PCA. Method Linear? Global structure Typical use PCA Yes Yes Features, denoise, visualize PCs Kernel PCA No (kernel) Moderate Nonlinear visualization t-SNE No Local 2D exploration only UMAP No Local + some global 2D exploration, sometimes features Autoencoder No Learned Compression, anomalies, pretrain What t-SNE/UMAP cannot tell you Cluster count is not identifiable from a pretty 2D plot. Distance between blobs is not a rigorous inter-cluster metric. Always validate with quantitative metrics (silhouette on original space, stability across seeds, or labeled ARI/NMI if available). Practical workflow: PCA or UMAP for EDA → pick clustering in original (or PCA-reduced) space → only then color clusters on a 2D embedding for storytelling. Never cluster on 2D t-SNE coordinates alone — the projection distortion becomes your loss function. When pipelines need fixed-dimension features for downstream supervised models, prefer PCA , supervised reduced targets, or autoencoder embeddings with reconstruction monitored on validation. t-SNE/UMAP coordinates are not stable across refits unless you use parametric extensions. Memory hook PCA preserves variance; t-SNE/UMAP preserve neighborhoods for your eyes — not your production feature pipeline by default. Rapid fire — Dimensionality reduction PCA: linear, variance, see dedicated chapter. Kernel PCA: nonlinear via kernels; costly in . t-SNE/UMAP: visualization-first; local structure; global distances suspect. Autoencoders: learned bottleneck; need data; reconstruction for anomalies. # Anomaly Detection Without Labels Point anomalies are rare observations unlike the bulk of training data. Without labels, evaluation is hard — lean on domain review , stability , and proxy labels when you can. # Classical baselines z-score: flag per feature — assumes univariate normality; breaks in multivariate tails. IQR rule: outside — robust univariate fences. Good first screens; combine dimensions with multivariate methods below. # Isolation Forest Random trees isolate points by random splits; anomalies need fewer splits (short average path length). decision_function ~ inverse path length. Scales well; weak on very high-D without informative features. # One-Class SVM Finds a boundary around training data in feature (or kernel) space — points outside are anomalies. controls expected fraction of outliers. Sensitive to scaling and kernel choice; training cost grows with . # Local Outlier Factor (LOF) Compares local density of a point to its neighbors' densities — flags points much sparser than neighbors (local anomalies). Can miss global rare points in uniformly sparse regions. # Autoencoder reconstruction error High ∥ on validation/production points suggests the model never learned that region — watch domain shift ( Fundamentals on i.i.d.) masquerading as anomalies. # Evaluating without labels Approach What you get Injected synthetic anomalies PR on held-out injected points Historical incidents Partial precision if logged Human audit top- Operational precision proxy Stability across seeds Consistent flags are more trustworthy With sparse labels, report PR-AUC at low false-positive rates — see Precision Recall and ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC . Interview angle How do you validate anomaly detection with no labels? → inject controlled outliers, audit top scores with SMEs, track alert stability, and if any incidents exist treat them as weak positives — never trust unsupervised scores as precision without measurement. Rapid fire — Anomalies z-score/IQR: fast univariate screens. Isolation Forest: path length isolation; scalable. One-class SVM: boundary in kernel space; tune , scale features. LOF: local density contrast. Autoencoder: reconstruction error; mind domain shift. No labels → inject, audit, stability; PR at low FPR if any positives. # Cluster and Embedding Evaluation # Internal metrics (no labels) Silhouette (per point): where is mean intra-cluster distance, is mean distance to nearest other cluster — average over points. Davies–Bouldin: average worst ratio of within-cluster scatter to inter-centroid distance — lower is better; favors compact, separated clusters. Both assume convex, separated geometry like k-means — misleading on manifolds. # External metrics (labels available) ARI: chance-adjusted agreement between partitions (1 = perfect, 0 = chance). NMI: mutual information normalized — measures label information shared with clusters. Use when you have partial labels (e.g. evaluating customer segments against known tiers). Cluster stability: resample rows (bootstrap), re-cluster, and measure Adjusted Rand Index between runs or Jaccard overlap of pairs co-clustered. Stable structure survives noise; fragile partitions are interview red flags for we found segments claims without business validation. Memory hook Silhouette asks am I closer to my cluster than to the neighbor's? ; ARI asks do clusters match labels better than chance? Rapid fire — Evaluation Silhouette ↑ better; Davies–Bouldin ↓ better — both favor blobby k-means geometry. ARI/NMI when labels exist; chance adjustment matters for ARI. t-SNE plots are not evaluation — run metrics in input space or with labels. Bootstrap stability checks whether clusters are signal or seed noise. # Unsupervised in Production and Interviews Production unsupervised work is rarely run k-means and ship. Typical patterns: Use case Method sketch Pitfall Customer segments k-means/GMM on RFM + scale Segments drift — re-fit on a schedule Fraud / abuse Isolation Forest + rules Alert flood without PR at low FPR Embeddings for search Autoencoder or pretrain Train/serve skew — see [[data-leakage Catalog dedup HDBSCAN on embeddings Threshold tuning per category Interview angle How many clusters? → refuse a magic number — combine silhouette/BIC , stability across seeds , business interpretability , and downstream uplift (does a campaign per cluster beat one blast?). Metrics guide; owners decide. Rapid fire — Production interviews Re-fit on drift; monitor cluster sizes and centroids over time. Anomaly alerts need human review loops and explicit FPR budgets. Cluster in input space; visualize in 2D; don't invert that order. Partial labels + ARI beat eyeballing t-SNE. # One-Page Summary Concept The one thing to remember k-means Minimize within-cluster SSE; Lloyd + k-means++; local optima; scale features Choose Elbow, silhouette, domain; ARI/NMI if labels exist GMM / EM Soft elliptical clusters; k-means = hard spherical limit Hierarchical Dendrogram + linkage; Ward ≈ variance merges DBSCAN Density + noise; + min_samples; HDBSCAN for varying density Spectral Graph Laplacian eigenvectors for non-convex clusters Beyond PCA Kernel PCA (nonlinear), t-SNE/UMAP (viz), autoencoders (learned) t-SNE/UMAP limits Local structure only; don't infer or global distances Anomalies IF, OC-SVM, LOF, AE error; validate by inject/audit Metrics Silhouette/DB internal; ARI/NMI external # Related k-Means Clustering Eigenvectors, PCA SVD Fundamentals Classification Methods Support Vector Machines Data Preparation Feature Engineering Model Evaluation Validation Precision Recall ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC Embeddings Vector Search Recommender Systems

title: Logistic Regression
text: Say it in 30s: A linear classifier that outputs a probability. It puts a linear combination of features through a sigmoid to get P(y=1), and is trained by minimizing cross-entropy (= maximum likelihood under a Bernoulli model). Despite the name, it's classification. Why it's the must-know baseline Outputs probabilities (usually reasonably well calibrated, unless heavily regularized, reweighted/resampled or misspecified), not just labels. Interpretable : a weight is the change in log-odds per unit feature; exp(weight) is an odds ratio. Convex loss → any local minimum is global, fast to train. Unique if L2-regularized (or full-rank, non-separable data). On linearly separable data with no regularization there is no finite minimizer: weights grow without bound. The discriminative counterpart to Naive Bayes. Key points Decision boundary is linear; use feature engineering or kernels for nonlinearity. Regularize with L1 (sparse) or L2 (stable) — same penalties as linear regression. Multiclass via softmax (a.k.a. multinomial logistic regression). The math Sigmoid on logit x + b : 1 ​ , ln 1 − p p ​ = z (log-odds linear in ). Bernoulli NLL (one example): Dataset: 1 ​ ∑ i ​ L i ​ — convex in . Gradient: with , , ​ L = n 1 ​ X ⊤ ( σ ( X w ) − y ) . Odds ratio: ​ ) multiplies odds per unit increase in ​ . Decision boundary: x + b = 0 ( 1 ​ ). Separable data with no penalty → (likelihood unbounded); fix with . Trap: it can't separate XOR-like data without nonlinear features. Underfits genuinely nonlinear boundaries. See depth: Classification Methods (§3), TensorGym Study Notes . Related: Cross-Entropy Loss , Generative vs Discriminative , Gradient Descent , Precision Recall , Calibration .

title: Generative vs Discriminative
text: Say it in 30s: Discriminative models learn the boundary directly — P(y | x) — they only answer which class. Generative models learn each class's shape — P(x | y) and P(y) — then use Bayes' rule to derive P(y | x), so they can also generate new x. The canonical pair Logistic Regression (discriminative) vs Naive Bayes (generative). Discriminative usually wins with ample data (optimizes the thing you care about). Generative wins with little data or when you need to sample, detect outliers, or handle missing features. Examples Discriminative: logistic regression, SVMs, most neural net classifiers, random forests. Generative: Naive Bayes, GMMs, HMMs, and modern generative models (VAEs, diffusion, LLMs). The math Bayes rule: p ( x ∣ y ) p ( y ) ​ ∝ p ( x ∣ y ) p ( y ) . Discriminative models estimate (or a score/decision boundary) directly — no explicit . Generative / joint: ​ = ar g y max ​ p ( y ∣ x ) = ar g y max ​ p ( x ∣ y ) p ( y ) . Shared-covariance Gaussians (LDA): ​ , Σ ) with common . Log-posterior ratio for classes : p ( y = k ∣ x ) ​ = w ⊤ x + b because the quadratic Σ − 1 x cancels in the ratio — log-odds linear in , same functional form as logistic regression. Trap: generative in the classic sense (models P(x,y)) is a superset idea that also covers today's generative AI — be ready to bridge both meanings. See depth: Classification Methods (§2), Fundamentals (§1). Related: Logistic Regression , Maximum Likelihood Estimation , Naive Bayes .

title: Naive Bayes
text: Say it in 30s: Naive Bayes is a generative classifier: apply Bayes' rule with the naive assumption that features are conditionally independent given the class, so factors into a product of per-feature likelihoods. The independence assumption is almost always false, yet the argmax class often survives because errors distort all classes similarly; it's blazing fast, thrives on high-dimensional sparse text, and needs Laplace smoothing for unseen features. Key points Multinomial NB: word counts (text); Bernoulli NB: binary presence; Gaussian NB: continuous features as normals per class. Trains in one pass — counts and priors — scales to huge vocabularies. Probabilities are usually poorly calibrated (pushed toward 0/1); trust ranking/labels, not raw scores — see Calibration . Strong small-data baseline when assumptions are directionally right. The math Naive factorization (features conditionally independent given ): ∏ d ​ p ( x j ​ ∣ y ) . Log form (stable products): ∑ ​ lo g p ( x j ​ ∣ y ) − lo g p ( x ) . Argmax over needs only the first two terms. Laplace smoothing (categorical feature , value , class ): count ​ , class count ​ , vocabulary size ​ : ​ ( x j ​ = v ∣ y = c ) = N c ​ + α V j ​ N j c v ​ + α ​ . Tiny spam toy: , , → vs ham → predict spam . Common follow-ups / traps Why does it work if independence is false? → only needs the correct class to win, not accurate ; shared distortion across classes preserves the argmax. See Generative vs Discriminative . Zero probability problem? → Laplace (add-one) smoothing on counts. NB vs logistic regression? → generative vs discriminative; NB can win with very little data; logistic usually wins with enough data. See depth: Classification Methods (§4). Related: Logistic Regression , Maximum Likelihood Estimation , Cross-Entropy Loss .

title: k-Nearest Neighbors
text: Say it in 30s: k-NN is a lazy discriminative classifier (or regressor): store all training points, and at prediction time find the closest examples under a distance metric, then majority-vote (classification) or average (regression). There is no explicit training phase — capacity is controlled entirely by and the metric. Small = flexible, high-variance boundaries; large = smoother, higher bias. It needs feature scaling , suffers the curse of dimensionality , and prediction cost grows with . Key points trades bias vs variance: memorizes noise; large underfits local structure. Distances: Euclidean (default), Manhattan, cosine for sparse text; weighted k-NN down-weights distant neighbors. No native handling of mixed types without encoding; no built-in feature importance. Curse of dimensionality: in high , distances concentrate and nearest stops being meaningful. The math Predict: classification = majority label among nearest neighbors; regression = mean target (optionally distance-weighted: vote weight ​ = 1/ d j 2 ​ ). Metrics: Euclidean ​ , Manhattan ​ − y j ​ ∣ , cosine x ⊤ y ​ (common for sparse text). Curse of dimensionality: capturing fraction of mass in a -cube needs edge length — for , , edge (most of the unit hypercube), so local neighborhoods are hollow. Cover–Hart (asymptotic, , two classes): as , the 1-NN error satisfies ≤ R ≤ 2 R ∗ ( 1 − R ∗ ) ≤ 2 R ∗ , where is the Bayes error — consistent, but up to twice as bad. Common follow-ups / traps Train vs predict cost? → O(1) fit (just store), O(nd) per query unless you use approximate NN indices (see Embeddings Vector Search ). Regression? → average (or weighted average) of neighbor targets — cannot extrapolate beyond training range. Imbalanced classes? → distance ties and majority vote favor the common class; use weighted voting or a different model. See depth: Classification Methods (§5). Related: Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Data Preparation Feature Engineering , Support Vector Machines .

title: Support Vector Machines
text: Say it in 30s: An SVM finds the decision boundary that separates the classes with the widest possible margin — the hyperplane as far as possible from the nearest points of each class. Those nearest points are the support vectors and are the only ones that define the boundary. The kernel trick lets it draw nonlinear boundaries by computing dot products in a higher-dimensional space without ever building that space. Key points Boundary is a hyperplane w·x + b = 0 ; classify with sign(w·x + b) , labels coded y ∈ {+1, −1} . Fix the scale so on-margin support vectors satisfy y(w·x + b) = 1 (in the soft margin, violators have y(w·x + b) 1 ); then the half-margin is 1/||w|| , full margin 2/||w|| . Hard margin: minimize ½||w||² s.t. yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1 . Minimizing ||w|| = maximizing the margin. Soft margin (real data): minimize ½||w||² + C·Σξᵢ s.t. yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1 − ξᵢ , ξᵢ ≥ 0 . Slack ξ allows violations. C is the bias-variance knob: large C → punish violations hard (narrow margin, overfit risk); small C → tolerate violations (wider margin, more regularized). Kernel trick: the dual depends on the data only through dot products xᵢ·xⱼ , so replace them with a kernel K(xᵢ, xⱼ) to get a nonlinear boundary cheaply. Common kernels: RBF (Gaussian), polynomial, linear. The math Hard margin ( ​ ∈ { ± 1 } ): min ​ 2 1 ​ ∥ w ∥ 2 s.t. y i ​ ( w ⊤ x i ​ + b ) ≥ 1. On-margin points have ​ ( w ⊤ x i ​ + b ) = 1 ; margin width . Soft margin (slacks ​ ≥ 0 , trade-off ): min ​ 2 1 ​ ∥ w ∥ 2 + C i ∑ ​ ξ i ​ s.t. y i ​ ( w ⊤ x i ​ + b ) ≥ 1 − ξ i ​ . Equivalent hinge on score x + b : . Dual (kernelized): ​ ∑ i ​ α i ​ − 2 1 ​ ∑ i , j ​ α i ​ α j ​ y i ​ y j ​ K ( x i ​ , x j ​ ) with ​ ≤ C . Prediction ​ α i ​ y i ​ K ( x i ​ , x ) + b . RBF kernel: ) = exp ( − γ ∥ x − x ′ ∥ 2 ) — implicit high-dimensional feature map. Common follow-ups / traps What's the margin? → distance from the boundary to the nearest points ( 1/||w|| ; full margin width 2/||w|| ); SVM maximizes it. Which points matter? → only the support vectors; far-away points don't move the boundary. Why does the kernel trick work? → optimization needs only pairwise dot products, never the explicit high-dimensional features. What does C do? → trades margin width against training violations; it's the regularization parameter. Don't say SVM just draws a boundary — the defining idea is the maximum-margin boundary. See depth: Classification Methods . Related: Logistic Regression , Regularization , Bias-Variance Tradeoff .

title: Decision Trees
text: Say it in 30s: A decision tree partitions the feature space with a sequence of axis-aligned splits, greedily choosing each split to maximize impurity reduction (Gini or entropy for classification, variance reduction for regression). It's interpretable and handles mixed feature types with no scaling, but a deep tree overfits badly and is unstable — small data changes can reshuffle the whole structure. Key points Classification splits: minimize weighted Gini ​ p k 2 ​ or maximize information gain from entropy ​ p k ​ lo g p k ​ . Regression splits: minimize within-node variance (equivalent to minimizing MSE). Stopping: max depth, min samples per leaf, min impurity decrease; pruning via cost-complexity ​ ( T ) = R ( T ) + α ∣ T ∣ . High capacity → low bias, high variance on a single tree (why ensembles exist). The math Classification impurity at node with class fractions ​ : Gini ​ p k 2 ​ , entropy ​ p k ​ lo g 2 ​ p k ​ . A split into left/right with child weights ​ = n L ​ / n , ​ = n R ​ / n scores information gain ​ I ( L ) − w R ​ I ( R ) (maximize ). Regression: child means minimize within-node MSE, so maximize variance reduction ​ Var ( L ) − w R ​ Var ( R ) . Pruning: ​ ( T ) = R ( T ) + α ∣ T ∣ — is node misclassification or MSE, is leaf count, trades fit vs complexity. Check (6-point toy, §split in Trees chapter ): balanced root ​ = p 1 ​ = 0.5 ⇒ G = 0.5 ; split gives weighted child Gini . Common follow-ups / traps Why is a single tree high variance? → greedy splits amplify noise; the boundary is discontinuous and sensitive to which points land in which bootstrap-like subsets. Gini vs entropy? → usually very similar splits; Gini is faster (no log); neither handles class imbalance in the split criterion itself — use sample weights or a better metric. Can trees extrapolate? → No for regression: predictions are leaf means/constants only within training ranges. See depth: Decision Trees, Random Forests Gradient Boosting (§1–2). Related: Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Bagging vs Boosting , Classification Methods .

title: Bagging vs Boosting
text: Say it in 30s: Both are ensembles of many models, but they attack different errors. Bagging trains many strong, high-variance models (e.g. deep trees) in parallel on bootstrap samples and averages them — it reduces variance . Boosting trains weak, high-bias models (e.g. shallow trees) sequentially, each correcting the previous one's mistakes — it mainly reduces bias (and some variance). Bagging (e.g. Random Forest) Independent trees on resampled data; predictions averaged/voted. Random Forest adds feature subsampling to decorrelate trees. Robust, parallelizable, hard to overfit by adding trees. Boosting (e.g. AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost/LightGBM) Each learner focuses on the residuals/errors of the ensemble so far. Often the strongest tabular performers, but more tuning and can overfit if over-trained. Sequential → less parallelizable. One-liner: bagging = many independent opinions averaged (variance↓); boosting = a relay team fixing each other's mistakes (bias↓). The math Bagging: forest prediction = B 1 ​ ∑ b = 1 B ​ T b ​ . If each tree has variance and pairwise correlation , ) = B 2 1 ​ ( B σ 2 + B ( B − 1 ) ρ σ 2 ) = ρ σ 2 + B ( 1 − ρ ) σ 2 ​ . The variances and pairwise covariances are all there is. Diversity lowers (bootstrap + feature subsampling in RF); averaging shrinks only the part — you cannot average away fully correlated errors. Boosting: additive model ​ = F m − 1 ​ + ν h m ​ ( = learning rate). AdaBoost sets learner weight ​ = 2 1 ​ ln ( err m ​ 1 − err m ​ ​ ) from weighted error ​ , then reweights ​ ← w i ​ exp ( − α m ​ y i ​ h m ​ ( x i ​ )) (with ​ ∈ { ± 1 } ) and renormalizes, so misclassified points gain mass. Gradient boosting (card: Gradient Boosting ) fits ​ to loss gradients instead — same “fix residuals” idea, different mechanics. See depth: Classification Methods (§6–7). Related: Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Overfitting Underfitting , Decision Trees, Random Forests Gradient Boosting , Gradient Boosting .

title: Gradient Boosting
text: Say it in 30s: Gradient boosting fits an additive ensemble of weak learners (usually shallow trees) by functional gradient descent on the loss: each new tree is trained on the negative gradient (pseudo-residuals) of the loss with respect to the current predictions, then scaled by a learning rate (shrinkage). It mainly reduces bias , can overfit if you add too many rounds without regularization, and tuned implementations (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) often dominate heterogeneous tabular data. Key points Update: ​ ( x ) = F m − 1 ​ ( x ) + η h m ​ ( x ) with the learning rate (shrinkage). Tree ​ fits targets ∂ ℓ ( y , F m − 1 ​ ( x )) ​ — for squared loss, that's ordinary residuals ​ . Subsampling (stochastic boosting): each round trains on a random row fraction — adds regularization like bagging. Use shallow trees (depth 3–8); depth controls interaction order. Deep trees + many rounds → overfitting. The math Fit ​ to the pseudo-residual (negative loss gradient at current ​ ): ​ = − ∂ F ∂ ℓ ( y i ​ , F ) ​ ​ F = F m − 1 ​ ( x i ​ ) ​ , F m ​ = F m − 1 ​ + η h m ​ . Squared loss 1 ​ ( y − F ) 2 : ​ = y i ​ − F m − 1 ​ ( x i ​ ) . Logistic log-loss with as log-odds and : , so ​ = y i ​ − p i ​ exactly. XGBoost (2nd-order): leaf weight = − G / ( H + λ ) , ​ g i ​ , ​ h i ​ ; split gain 1 ​ [ H L ​ + λ G L 2 ​ ​ + H R ​ + λ G R 2 ​ ​ − H L ​ + H R ​ + λ ( G L ​ + G R ​ ) 2 ​ ] − γ . Splits with negative gain are pruned — same form as Trees chapter §XGBoost. Common follow-ups / traps Bagging vs boosting? → bagging averages independent high-variance trees (variance↓); boosting sequences weak learners on residuals (bias↓). See Bagging vs Boosting . Why learning rate? → smaller needs more trees but generalizes better — the classic learning rate vs n_estimators tradeoff. Best loss for classification? → log-loss / cross-entropy; don't use misclassification rate directly (non-differentiable). See depth: Decision Trees, Random Forests Gradient Boosting (§4–6). Related: Gradient Descent , Loss Functions , Cross-Entropy Loss .

title: k-Means Clustering
text: Say it in 30s: k-means partitions points into clusters by alternating assignment to nearest centroids and updating centroids to cluster means ( Lloyd's algorithm ). It minimizes within-cluster sum of squared distances — a non-convex objective, so initialization matters; k-means++ spreads initial centers and is the default fix. It assumes roughly spherical, equal-variance clusters and needs feature scaling; pick with elbow/silhouette and validate on the business question, not the plot alone. Key points Objective: ​ } min ​ j = 1 ∑ k ​ x ∈ C j ​ ∑ ​ ∥ x − μ j ​ ∥ 2 2 ​ . Hard assignment only; for soft clusters use a GMM + EM (k-means ≈ GMM with equal spherical covariances in the limit). Failure modes: wrong , non-convex blobs, varying cluster sizes/densities, outliers pulling centroids — DBSCAN/HDBSCAN or GMM may fit better. Always scale continuous features; Euclidean distance is scale-sensitive. The math Objective: K ​ ∑ x ∈ C k ​ ​ ∥ x − μ k ​ ∥ 2 2 ​ with ​ = ∣ C k ​ ∣ 1 ​ ∑ x ∈ C k ​ ​ x . Setting ​ = 0 gives ​ as the cluster mean — Lloyd’s update never increases . k-means++ init: sample centers with , where is distance to the nearest chosen center — spreads seeds, -approx guarantee in expectation. Silhouette for point : b − a ​ ( = mean intra-cluster distance, = mean distance to nearest other cluster). Cost: for points, clusters, dims, Lloyd iterations (assignment dominates). Common follow-ups / traps How choose ? → elbow on inertia (with caveats), silhouette (cohesion vs separation), domain knowledge; with labels, ARI/NMI on held-out structure. Guaranteed optimum? → No — Lloyd's only finds local minima; run multiple restarts. k-means on categoricals? → not without encoding; consider k-modes or model-based clustering. See depth: Clustering, Dimensionality Reduction Anomaly Detection (§1). Related: Eigenvectors, PCA SVD , Bias-Variance Tradeoff .
