title: Model Evaluation & Validation
heads: Ranking Metrics: NDCG vs MAP vs MRR
text: Building a model is half the job; knowing whether it’s any good is the other half, and it’s where most candidates are thinnest. This chapter is about measuring honestly. We start from the confusion matrix that every classification metric is built on, untangle precision from recall and the threshold that trades them, separate ROC-AUC from PR-AUC, cover calibration and ranking metrics, then turn to regression metrics and — crucially — how to split data so your estimate isn’t a lie. The recurring theme: the metric is a modeling decision , and choosing the wrong one is how good models get shipped to do the wrong thing. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Read a confusion matrix and derive precision, recall, and F1 from it cold. Explain the precision–recall tradeoff and how the threshold moves it. Say exactly when PR-AUC beats ROC-AUC (hint: heavy imbalance). Define calibration and why a well-ranked model can still be dishonest. Choose a cross-validation scheme that respects time and groups — no leakage. # The Confusion Matrix Every classification metric is an arithmetic combination of four counts, so the confusion matrix is the foundation you build everything else on. For a binary problem it cross-tabulates what actually happened against what the model predicted. Four cells, and every classification metric is just a ratio of them. Predicted Positive Predicted Negative Actually Positive True Positive (TP) False Negative (FN) — a miss Actually Negative False Positive (FP) — a false alarm True Negative (TN) The two error types are not interchangeable, and naming them correctly matters. A False Positive (Type I error) is a false alarm — you flagged something that was fine. A False Negative (Type II error) is a miss — you let something real slip through. Which one hurts more is entirely domain-dependent, and that asymmetry is what drives every metric choice in this chapter. Memory hook False Positive = “crying wolf” (Type I). False Negative = “missing the wolf” (Type II). Spam filter: a False Positive eats your real email; a False Negative just lets spam through — so you tune toward avoiding False Positives. Cancer screen: a False Negative is deadly — so you tune toward avoiding those. The cost asymmetry picks the metric. Interview angle Always ask, or state, which error is worse here . Candidates who optimize a model without distinguishing the cost of a miss from the cost of a false alarm signal they’ve never shipped anything. Tie it to the business: “in fraud, a missed fraud costs us the transaction; a false alarm costs a customer’s goodwill — those aren’t equal.” # Classification Metrics From those four cells come the metrics you’ll quote constantly. The danger metric is accuracy — (TP+TN)/total — because it collapses under imbalance: on a dataset that’s 99% negative, “always predict negative” scores 99% and is worthless. Precision and recall are the honest pair. Metric Formula Reads as Use when Accuracy T P + T N ​ Overall correctness Classes are balanced Precision T P ​ Of those I flagged, how many were right? False alarms are costly Recall (TPR) T P ​ Of the real positives, how many did I catch? Misses are costly F1 2 P R ​ Harmonic mean of P and R Imbalance, want one number Specificity (TNR) T N ​ Of the real negatives, how many did I clear? Care about the negative class Precision answers “when I say positive, am I right?” — it’s hurt by false alarms. Recall answers “did I find all the positives?” — it’s hurt by misses. F1 is their harmonic mean, not the arithmetic mean, deliberately: the harmonic mean stays low unless both are high, so a model can’t game F1 by maxing one and tanking the other. Memory hook Precision = “of my alarms, how many were real?” Recall = “of the real ones, how many did I sound an alarm for?” Precision polices false alarms; recall polices misses. F1 is the harmonic mean — it refuses to be fooled by one good number. Interview angle Expect “precision or recall for X?” Cancer screening → recall (never miss a case; false alarms get a follow-up test). Spam → precision (never trash a real email). Search results → precision (the top results must be relevant). Say the cost of each error type out loud and the answer falls out. # Threshold: Precision vs Recall Here’s the idea that ties the last section together: most classifiers output a probability , and you turn it into a label by picking a threshold (default 0.5, but that’s just a default). Precision and recall are not fixed properties of the model — they move as you slide the threshold , and they move in opposite directions. Slide the threshold high for precision, low for recall — you can’t max both at once. Raise the threshold and you only flag the cases you’re most sure about: precision climbs, recall falls (you miss the borderline positives). Lower it and you flag aggressively: recall climbs, precision falls (more false alarms). This is the precision–recall tradeoff , and the right threshold is a business decision , not a default — set it by the relative cost of a miss versus a false alarm. Memory hook The threshold is a dial, not a constant. Crank it up → cautious → high precision, low recall. Crank it down → trigger-happy → high recall, low precision. 0.5 is a default, not a law — set it by what an error costs. Interview angle “Your model’s recall is too low — what do you do?” First, cheap: lower the threshold (no retraining needed) and accept the precision hit. Then: resample/reweight for imbalance, add features, or change the model. Reaching for “lower the threshold” first shows you understand that precision and recall are threshold-dependent, not intrinsic. # ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC To judge a model across all thresholds at once, you use an area-under-curve summary. There are two, and knowing when each one lies is a classic senior question. The ROC curve plots True Positive Rate (recall) against False Positive Rate as the threshold sweeps. ROC-AUC is the area under it, interpretable as the probability the model ranks a random positive above a random negative. 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect. The PR curve plots Precision against Recall over the same sweep, and PR-AUC is its area. ROC can look great on imbalanced data; PR tells the truth because precision feels the flood of negatives. ROC-AUC PR-AUC Axes TPR vs FPR Precision vs Recall Baseline (random) 0.5 always The positive class prevalence Sensitive to imbalance? No — can look misleadingly good Yes — reflects rare-class difficulty Use when Classes roughly balanced; care about both classes Positive class is rare and is what you care about The key insight: FPR has the huge negative count in its denominator , so on imbalanced data a flood of false positives barely moves it — ROC-AUC stays optimistically high. Precision has the false positives in its denominator without the true negatives , so it feels every false alarm. When positives are rare and they’re what you care about (fraud, disease, click prediction), PR-AUC is the honest summary . Memory hook On a needle-in-a-haystack problem, ROC-AUC flatters and PR-AUC tells the truth. ROC dilutes false positives in a sea of true negatives; precision doesn’t get to hide them. Rare positive class → trust PR-AUC. Interview angle “You have 1% fraud and ROC-AUC is 0.95 — are you happy?” The trap is yes. Strong answer: ROC-AUC is inflated by the 99% negatives; check PR-AUC and the precision/recall at your operating threshold before celebrating. This single distinction is one of the most reliable senior-vs-junior separators in evaluation. # Calibration Ranking well and being honest about probabilities are different things, and the gap is calibration. A model is calibrated if, among all the times it says “0.7,” the event really happens about 70% of the time. AUC only cares about order ; calibration cares about whether the number means what it says . A calibrated model’s confidence matches reality; the diagonal is perfect. This matters whenever you act on the probability itself — expected-value decisions, pricing, risk thresholds, or feeding the score into downstream math. A model can have great AUC and terrible calibration: it ranks cases correctly but is systematically over- or under-confident. You diagnose it with a reliability diagram (predicted probability vs observed frequency) and fix it on held-out data with Platt scaling (fit a sigmoid) or isotonic regression (a flexible monotonic fit). Model Calibration out of the box Note Logistic regression Usually good Trained on log-loss; can drift if heavily regularized, reweighted or misspecified Naive Bayes Poor Independence assumption pushes probs to 0/1 SVM Uncalibrated scores (no probabilities) Needs Platt scaling Deep nets / boosted trees Deep nets: often overconfident; boosted trees/RF: often distorted (sigmoid-shaped, underconfident) Check a reliability diagram; calibrate if you act on the number Memory hook Calibration is honesty, not accuracy. “When I say 70%, does it happen 70% of the time?” AUC grades the ranking ; calibration grades the number . A model can ace one and flunk the other. Go deeper (optional) Don’t conflate calibration with discrimination (AUC). You can have perfect ranking and awful calibration (just squash all scores toward 0.5) or perfect calibration and poor ranking. If you only need to threshold or rank , calibration may not matter; if you multiply the probability into a decision , it’s essential. # Ranking Metrics: NDCG vs MAP vs MRR When the output is an ordered list — search, recommendations, retrieval — accuracy and AUC miss the point: what matters is whether the good items are near the top . Three metrics dominate, differing in what they reward. Metric Rewards Use when MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) The rank of the first relevant item One right answer (Q A, “I’m feeling lucky”) MAP (Mean Average Precision) Precision across all relevant items, binary relevance Multiple relevant items, relevant-or-not NDCG (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain) Graded relevance, discounted by position Items have degrees of relevance (star ratings) All three share the position-discount instinct: a relevant result at rank 1 is worth more than the same result at rank 10. NDCG is the most general because it handles graded relevance (a 5-star match beats a 3-star match) and normalizes against the ideal ordering, so scores are comparable across queries. MRR is the simplest — just 1/(rank of the first hit) — and fits “single correct answer” tasks. Memory hook MRR cares only about the first good hit. MAP cares about all the good hits, present-or-absent. NDCG cares about all of them and how good each is , discounted by position. Increasing sophistication: first → all → all-and-graded. Interview angle “How would you evaluate a recommender?” Don’t say accuracy. Say a ranking metric and justify it: NDCG if you have graded feedback (ratings, watch time), MAP for binary relevance with several right answers, MRR if there’s essentially one. Then mention that offline ranking metrics are a proxy — the real test is an online A/B on engagement (see ML System Design Interview Prep ). # Regression Metrics For continuous targets the question shifts to how far off, on average , and the choice among metrics is mostly about how you want to treat large errors and whether you want a unit-free score. Metric Behavior Use when MAE Mean absolute error; robust to outliers Outliers shouldn’t dominate; want error in original units MSE Mean squared error; punishes large errors hard Big misses are especially bad RMSE √MSE; same units as the target, still outlier-sensitive Want MSE’s penalty but readable units R² Fraction of variance explained (1 = perfect, 0 = mean-baseline) Want a unit-free “how much better than guessing the mean” The core tradeoff is MAE vs MSE/RMSE : squaring makes MSE punish big errors disproportionately, so it’s the right choice when a single large miss is unacceptable — but that same squaring makes it sensitive to outliers , which MAE shrugs off. R² rescales error against a “predict the mean” baseline, giving a unit-free score, but it can be misleadingly high on a strong trend and even go negative when the model is worse than the mean. (Adjusted , which penalizes adding useless features, is covered in Regression Methods .) Memory hook MAE treats all errors fairly (robust). MSE/RMSE square the error, so it obsesses over the big misses (outlier-sensitive). R² answers “how much better than just guessing the average?” — unit-free, but can flatter you. Interview angle “MAE or RMSE?” Answer with the outlier story: RMSE if large errors are disproportionately costly and the data is clean; MAE if outliers exist and you don’t want a few of them to dictate the model. If asked why a model has R² of 0.0 — it’s no better than predicting the mean; negative R² means worse than the mean. # Cross-Validation: How to Split Data A single train/test split gives a noisy estimate — you got lucky or unlucky with which points landed in test. Cross-validation averages over several splits for a stabler estimate, but the way you split must respect the structure of your data, or you leak the future into the past and your metric becomes a fantasy. k-fold rotates the test fold; but time and groups demand special splits. Scheme How it works Use when k-fold Split into k folds; each takes a turn as test Standard i.i.d. tabular data Stratified k-fold k-fold preserving class proportions in each fold Classification, especially imbalanced Leave-One-Out k = n; each point is its own test fold Tiny datasets (expensive) Time-series split Always train on past, test on future Temporal data — never shuffle Group k-fold Keep each entity entirely in one fold Repeated users/patients/docs The two splits that prevent leakage are the ones interviewers probe. Time-series CV never shuffles — you train on the past and test on the future, because random shuffling would let the model “see tomorrow” to predict today. Group CV keeps all rows of one entity (a patient, a user) together, so the model can’t memorize an individual in training and get credit for “predicting” them in test. And the golden rule from Fundamentals still binds: fit every preprocessing step (scaling, imputation) inside the training fold only , then apply it to the validation fold. Memory hook k-fold for ordinary data. Stratify when classes are imbalanced. Split by time for time series (never peek at the future). Split by group when the same entity repeats (never let it sit on both sides). The wrong split = silent leakage = a beautiful, lying score. Interview angle “How would you cross-validate a model that predicts next month’s sales?” The trap is plain k-fold. Right answer: a time-based split — train on earlier periods, validate on later ones, never shuffle — because shuffling leaks future information and inflates the score. Mention that preprocessing stats must be fit on the training fold only. Rapid Fire — Evaluation Validation Confusion matrix: TP/FP/FN/TN. False Positive = Type I (false alarm); False Negative = Type II (miss). Cost asymmetry picks the metric. - Accuracy lies under imbalance. Precision = of my alarms how many were real; Recall = of the real ones how many I caught; F1 = harmonic mean. - Threshold slides precision vs recall in opposite directions; 0.5 is a default, set it by error costs. - ROC-AUC flatters on imbalanced data (FPR hides false positives in true negatives); PR-AUC is honest when positives are rare. - Calibration = “when I say 70% it happens 70%.” AUC grades ranking, calibration grades the number; fix with Platt/isotonic. - Ranking: MRR (first hit) → MAP (all hits, binary) → NDCG (graded + position-discounted). - Regression: MAE robust; MSE/RMSE punish big errors and feel outliers; R² = variance explained vs the mean. - Cross-validation: stratify for imbalance, split by time for temporal data, split by group for repeated entities; fit preprocessing on the train fold only. # Which Metric When The chapter in one table — match the metric to the problem, because the metric is the objective you’re really optimizing. Problem Metric Balanced classification Accuracy (or AUC) Imbalanced classification PR-AUC, F1, precision/recall at threshold Cost of a miss ≫ false alarm Optimize recall Cost of a false alarm ≫ miss Optimize precision Acting on the probability value Calibration (reliability diagram + Platt/isotonic) Ranking / search / recommendation NDCG, MAP, or MRR Regression, clean data, punish big errors RMSE Regression with outliers MAE “How much better than the mean?” R² The closing principle ties the chapter to Fundamentals : separate the offline ML metric (what you compute on held-out data) from the online business metric (what you A/B test in production). A model that wins on offline AUC can still lose on revenue or engagement — so the metric you optimize must be a faithful proxy for the value you actually care about. Interview angle The unifying senior insight: choosing the metric is a modeling decision, made before you train. For any “how would you evaluate X?” answer in two layers — the offline metric tied to the error costs, and the online metric (A/B test on the business outcome) that’s the real arbiter. Saying “I’d pick the metric from what an error costs the business” is the line that lands. # One-Page Summary Concept The one thing to remember Confusion matrix TP/FP/FN/TN; FP = Type I (false alarm), FN = Type II (miss). Accuracy trap Useless under imbalance — “always negative” scores high and is worthless. Precision vs recall Precision = of my alarms how many real; recall = of the real ones how many caught. F1 Harmonic mean of precision and recall — both must be high. Threshold A dial that trades precision against recall; 0.5 is a default, set it by error cost. ROC vs PR AUC ROC-AUC flatters on imbalance; PR-AUC is honest when positives are rare. Calibration “When I say 70% it happens 70%” — AUC grades ranking, calibration grades the number. Ranking metrics MRR (first hit) → MAP (all hits) → NDCG (graded, position-discounted). Regression metrics MAE robust; RMSE punishes big errors / feels outliers; R² = variance explained. Cross-validation Stratify for imbalance, split by time for temporal, by group for repeats; fit preprocessing on train fold only. Which metric Match it to error costs; separate the offline metric from the online business metric. # Related Precision Recall ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC Cross-Validation Bias-Variance Tradeoff Calibration Ranking Metrics: NDCG, MAP MRR A/B Testing Online Experimentation Data Leakage Time-Series Validation Backtesting

title: A/B Testing & Online Experimentation
heads: Why offline metrics are not enough
Which test: z, t, Mann–Whitney, bootstrap
Ratio metrics and the delta method
text: Offline metrics tell you what might happen; online experiments tell you what did. A model can ace cross-validation and still fail in production — users react to latency, UX changes, and social influence in ways no holdout set captures. Online experimentation randomizes real traffic between control and treatment, estimates causal lift on business metrics, and is the gold standard for launch decisions in search, ads, and product ML. This chapter covers test design, hypothesis testing, sample size, variance reduction, ratio metrics, the pitfalls that inflate false positives, ranking-specific interleaving , and when multi-armed bandits complement fixed A/B tests. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Explain why offline evaluation is necessary but not sufficient for shipping. Design an A/B test: hypothesis, unit of randomization , primary, guardrail, and north-star metrics. State what a p-value is (and is not), Type I/II errors, and power , and compute sample size for a two-arm test. Choose among z-test, t-test, Mann–Whitney, and bootstrap; apply the delta method to ratio metrics. Name pitfalls: peeking, multiple comparisons, sample ratio mismatch , interference, and Simpson's paradox . Contrast interleaving and bandits with classic A/B for ranking and explore/exploit. # Why offline metrics are not enough Offline evaluation assumes a frozen dataset and a fixed scoring rule. Production breaks both assumptions: the data distribution drifts ( data drift ), user behavior is strategic (they adapt to the product), and the full system — latency, ranking blend, guardrails — changes the experience. A recommender with higher offline NDCG can lose online if it surfaces niche items users ignore, or if inference slows scroll speed. Offline metrics remain essential: they cheaply screen bad ideas, tune hyperparameters, and catch leakage before you burn traffic. The senior pattern is two gates : offline sanity (ranking metrics, calibration — see Calibration , Ranking Metrics ) then a powered online test on metrics users and the business actually care about. Neither gate alone is enough. # What offline still does well Use offline evaluation to reject broken rankers (NDCG collapse), compare feature sets under cross-validation , and validate calibration before a risky pricing model goes live. Use online tests to measure system-level effects: ranking policy + UI + latency + exploration. Training-serving skew ( ML in production ) shows up only online — features computed differently in the batch scorer than the live path look great offline and die in prod. # A/A tests and variance baselines Before trusting any B result, run an A/A test : two identical experiences, split randomly. You should see no significant lifts on the primary metric if instrumentation is honest. A/A estimates empirical variance of your metric under null — useful for sanity-checking precomputed sample sizes. Repeated A/A failures mean broken bucketing, cookie churn, or metric bugs — fix those before burning a real test. Memory hook Offline = does the model learn the past? Online = does the product win the future? Interview angle Weak: we'll A/B test after training. Strong: name what offline cannot see (network effects, UX, latency, long-term retention) and which metric you'll randomize on, with guardrails for revenue and safety. # Designing a test # Hypothesis and randomization unit Write a crisp null hypothesis ​ : no difference between control and treatment on the primary metric . The alternative ​ is a directional or two-sided lift you care about (e.g. conversion increases by at least ). Pre-register ​ , the primary metric, , minimum detectable effect (MDE) , and planned duration before traffic arrives. The unit of randomization must match how independence holds: Unit Use when Pitfall if wrong User Logged-in experience, one treatment per person Same user in both arms via cookies/devices Session Anonymous traffic, short-lived experiments Same user gets inconsistent UX across visits Request / page view Ultra-high volume, no stable user id Correlated requests from one user violate i.i.d. Cluster (market, school) Interference between neighbors Underpowered if clusters are huge Switchback (time blocks) Network effects, marketplace two-sided Seasonality and day-of-week confounds Getting the unit wrong is not a detail — it invalidates standard errors and p-values. # Primary, guardrail, and north-star metrics Primary metric : the one whose lift decides ship/no-ship (conversion, revenue per user, dwell time). One primary; everything else is secondary. Guardrail metrics : things that must not regress — crash rate, latency p99, spam reports, unsubscribe rate. A win on primary with a guardrail breach is a no-launch. North-star / OEC (Overall Evaluation Criterion) : long-horizon company health (retained revenue, LTV proxy). Often too noisy for a single test; use as context, not always as the test's only gate. Align metrics with precision vs recall thinking: optimizing clicks (recall of engagement) may tank precision of satisfaction — guardrails encode that trade-off. Rapid fire — Test design Pre-register hypothesis, primary metric, , MDE, and . Randomization unit = where independence lives. One primary metric; guardrails catch collateral damage. Offline screens; online proves causality. Wrong unit → wrong inference. # Hypothesis testing refresher Under ​ (no effect), the test statistic (difference in means, difference in proportions) has a known or estimable null distribution. The p-value is: ​ true ) It is not ​ true ) , not the false-positive rate, and not probability the lift is real. A small means: if there were truly no effect, data this extreme would be rare — evidence against ​ , not proof. Error Name Rate Meaning Reject true ​ Type I (e.g. 0.05) False launch — noise looked like signal Fail to reject false ​ Type II Missed a real win Reject false ​ Power (often 0.8) Detect a real effect of size Confidence intervals on the lift complement p-values: report lift = 0.3% (95% CI: 0.1%–0.5%) instead of only . See also p-Values Statistical Power and Math (§Statistics). The golden misread Never say there's a 95% chance the variant is better. Say under the null, this result would occur about 5% of the time or give a CI for the effect size. Interview angle If asked p = 0.03, what does that mean? — conditional probability under ​ , full stop. Bonus: mention you'd still check practical significance ( vs CI), guardrails, and whether you peeked. # Sample size and power For a two-sample test with equal allocation and a difference in means (or proportions with ≈ p ( 1 − p ) ), each arm needs approximately: 2 ( z 1 − α /2 ​ + z 1 − β ​ ) 2 σ 2 ​ where is the MDE (absolute), is per-unit variance under the null (or pooled estimate), is two-sided Type I rate, and power is . # Worked example (conversion rate) Control conversion ​ = 0.10 ; you want to detect absolute lift to (relative +10%). Use = p 0 ​ ( 1 − p 0 ​ ) = 0.09 . Take (two-sided, ​ = 1.96 ) and power ( ​ = 0.84 ): 2 × ( 1.96 + 0.84 ) 2 × 0.09 ​ = 0.0001 2 × 7.84 × 0.09 ​ ≈ 14 , 112 per arm ~28k users total for a simple binary metric. Rare events need more ; variance reduction (below) buys runway back. For unequal allocation (90% control / 10% treatment to limit risk), effective drops on the smaller arm — adjust formulas or use software; don't naively plug 10% into a 50/50 calculator. Continuous metrics (session length): plug sample variance from pilot data for . Pilot an A/A week to estimate variance when historical buckets lie. Interview angle Hand-waving two weeks is enough fails. Walk the formula: state , power, MDE, plug or , round up, mention CUPED if they use pre-period covariates. Memory hook Bigger , smaller . Noisier metric (larger ), bigger . Higher power, bigger . # Which test: z, t, Mann–Whitney, bootstrap Situation Test Why Large , mean or proportion Two-sample z-test CLT → normal statistic; use pooled SE for proportions Small , roughly normal metric Welch's t-test Unequal variances; uses t distribution Heavy tails, ordinal, outliers Mann–Whitney U Ranks only; tests stochastic dominance, not mean Weird shape, complex estimators Bootstrap on the statistic Resample users, rebuild , empirical CI For proportions , z-tests on ​ are standard at product scale. For revenue per user , means are skewed — consider trimming, log transform, or bootstrap CIs. Multiple arms → ANOVA or pairwise with multiplicity control. Rapid fire — Tests z for big- proportions/means; Welch t for small- means; Mann–Whitney when ranks beat means; bootstrap when the estimator is ugly. Always cluster at the randomization unit when resampling. # Ratio metrics and the delta method Many product metrics are ratios : = X ˉ / Y ˉ (clicks per impressions, revenue per session). The ratio of two sample means is not Gaussian with a simple SE. The delta method linearizes around ​ , μ Y ​ ) : / Y ˉ ) ≈ μ Y 2 ​ 1 ​ Var ( X ˉ ) + μ Y 4 ​ μ X 2 ​ ​ Var ( Y ˉ ) − μ Y 3 ​ 2 μ X ​ ​ Cov ( X ˉ , Y ˉ ) Plug sample estimates, get a z-statistic on the lift in . Alternatively, bootstrap at user level with ​ , Y i ​ ) pairs — often more robust in practice. Linearization (CUPED-style) on user-level ratios is another production trick. Interview angle How do you test revenue per visit? — never treat per-visit rows as i.i.d. if randomization is per user; aggregate to user numerators/denominators, then delta method or bootstrap. # Variance reduction: CUPED CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data) subtracts a baseline covariate correlated with the outcome. For user-level metric and pre-period covariate (pre-experiment engagement): Cov ( Y , X ) ​ , Y ′ = Y − θ ( X − E [ X ]) Analyze instead of . If is strongly predictive, ) ≪ Var ( Y ) , so the same MDE needs fewer users. is fit on pre-experiment data only (or control-only during the test) so you don't inject treatment into the variance reduction. Memory hook CUPED = remove the part of the metric you already knew from before the test. # Pitfalls and failure modes # Peeking and sequential testing Checking significance daily and stopping when inflates Type I error badly — you're multiple-testing over time. Fixes: fixed-horizon analysis at precomputed ; or valid sequential rules (e.g. O'Brien–Fleming, always-valid p-values, Bayesian monitoring with calibrated priors). Never stop when it looks good without a plan. # Multiple comparisons K secondary metrics or K variants → chance of a false positive grows. Bonferroni : use per test — conservative. Benjamini–Hochberg (FDR) : sort p-values ​ ≤ ⋯ ≤ p ( m ) ​ ; find largest with ​ ≤ m k ​ α ; reject hypotheses . BH controls false discovery rate — among rejected nulls, the expected fraction of false rejections is bounded by . Worked BH example ( secondary metrics, ): sorted p-values . Compare to k ​ α : — ✓; — ✗; — ✗; — ✗. The largest passing is 1, so reject only hypothesis 1. BH is step-up : check every , not just until the first failure — had ​ been , hypotheses 1–3 would all be rejected even though ​ failed its own threshold. Pre-specify families of hypotheses (engagement vs revenue) so post-hoc storytelling does not masquerade as discovery. # Sample ratio mismatch (SRM) If you intended 50/50 split but observed 52/48, assignment may be broken (bucketing bug, bot traffic, eligibility filters). Check with a chi-square goodness-of-fit test on assignment counts; an SRM invalidates the experiment — debug before interpreting lifts. # Novelty, primacy, and learning effects Novelty : users click new UI because it's new. Primacy : power users hate change. Run longer or segment new vs returning. Interference / network effects : one user's treatment affects another (rideshare pricing, social feeds). Use cluster randomization, geo holdouts, or switchback designs alternating treatment by time window — with care for diurnal patterns. # Simpson's paradox A treatment can win within every segment but lose aggregated (or the reverse) when segment sizes differ. Classic illustration: a new ranker wins on mobile and desktop separately but loses overall because treatment traffic shifted toward a lower-converting segment. Always slice by platform, country, or cohort when interpreting; pre-specify segments to avoid fishing. # Switchback and cluster designs (sketch) Cluster randomization : assign whole markets or schools to treatment — correlation within cluster inflates variance; use cluster-robust SEs or cluster-based sample size calculators. Switchback : alternate treatment and control by time window (e.g. hour blocks) so both sides see mixed conditions — reduces marketplace interference at the cost of autocorrelation in the time series. Analyze with time-aware models or paired contrasts across adjacent windows; watch day-of-week confounds. Launch on paradoxical aggregates If overall lift is negative but every country is positive, you may be overweighting a shrinking segment — fix weighting, don't blindly ship. Rapid fire — Pitfalls No peeking without sequential methods. Many metrics → FDR or Bonferroni. SRM chi-square → stop and debug. Novelty/primacy need time. Network effects need clusters or switchbacks. Simpson's paradox breaks naive aggregates. # Interleaving for ranking systems Classic A/B assigns users to always control or always treatment ranker — high variance for noisy click metrics. Interleaving merges ranked lists so one result page shows a blend of both systems' orderings (e.g. team-draft interleaving). Clicks on interleaved slots attribute preference directly between rankers with less traffic than full A/B. Offline NDCG/MAP/MRR still pre-screens; interleaving is a sensitive online pairwise comparison before a full deployment. Pair with recommender systems thinking. The DCG formula behind offline NDCG discounts position: ∑ k ​ lo g 2 ​ ( i + 1 ) 2 r e l i ​ − 1 ​ , NDCG@k = IDCG@k DCG@k ​ Online interleaving does not replace this — it answers a different question: which ranker earns the click on a blended page? Full A/B still validates business metrics (revenue, retention) after a ranker wins an interleaving duel. Rapid fire — Interleaving High sensitivity, low traffic for ranker A vs B. Team-draft builds fair merged lists. Offline NDCG uses graded relevance + log discount. Interleaving ≠ full product test — run both. # Multi-armed bandits vs fixed A/B A/B is pure explore-then-exploit : fixed allocation until , then pick a winner — best for clean causal estimates and stakeholder trust. Bandits adapt allocation toward better arms during the test ( Thompson sampling : for each arm maintain a posterior on conversion rate ​ + successes , β 0 ​ + failures ) ; each step sample ​ from each posterior and allocate traffic to the highest draw). Higher short-term reward (lower cumulative regret) but biased estimates if you need an unbiased lift for a launch memo — the final arm allocation is not 50/50. Explore/exploit framing: A/B explores then exploits at the end; bandits explore continuously. Use bandits when regret during the test is costly (ad creative, headlines); use fixed A/B when inference rigor, parallel guardrails, and clean causal reporting matter. Interview angle Bandit or A/B? — If the question is what's the causal lift with a reportable p-value? → A/B. If maximize reward while learning? → Thompson sampling or ε-greedy, with awareness that inference is harder. # Reading results and launch decisions A disciplined read: Primary metric : CI on lift, practical significance vs MDE, with correct interpretation. Guardrails : any regression beyond noise? Slices : stable across segments or Simpson warning? Quality checks : SRM, duration vs novelty window, AA tests passed earlier. Ship decision : launch, iterate, or kill — document opportunity cost of not shipping. If offline and online disagree, post-mortem distribution shift, metric definition mismatch, and interference before retraining alone. # Practical vs statistical significance A metric can be statistically significant (tiny p-value) but practically irrelevant — a 0.02% conversion lift at massive may not pay for engineering cost. Conversely, an underpowered test may fail to reject when the true lift is worthwhile. Report confidence intervals on business units (revenue per user per week) and compare the lower bound to a pre-defined minimum launch bar . Bias-variance thinking applies: noisy metrics need longer runs; overly precise peeking creates false certainty. # Bootstrap procedure (user-level) For skewed revenue: for each bootstrap replicate, resample users with replacement , compute mean revenue in control and treatment arms, store the difference; repeat times (e.g. ). The 2.5%–97.5% quantiles of differences form an approximate 95% CI. This respects user clustering and avoids normality assumptions. Same logic applies to bootstrap percentile tests on any smooth statistic — ratio metrics benefit from paired user resampling when users appear in both arms is impossible (only one arm per user). Go deeper (optional) CUPAC combines covariate adjustment with post-stratification; difference-in-differences handles geo rollouts when a full randomized experiment is politically impossible — know the identifying assumptions before citing them in an interview. Rapid fire — Launch Primary + CI + practical . Guardrails green. Segments consistent. No SRM, no peeking sin. Document kill/ship and monitor post-launch ( ML in production ). # One-page summary Concept The one thing to remember Offline vs online Offline cheap-screens; online proves causal product impact. Randomization unit Where independence holds — usually user, not pageview. Primary / guardrail One decision metric; guardrails block harmful wins. p-value ​ ) — not P(null true). Sample size ​ + z 1 − β ​ ) 2 σ 2 / δ 2 per arm. Ratio metrics Delta method or user-level bootstrap — not ratio of two tests. CUPED = Y − θ ( X − X ˉ ) , . Peeking / multiplicity Fixed horizon or sequential rules; BH/Bonferroni for many metrics. SRM Chi-square on split counts — broken bucketing invalidates the test. Interleaving / bandits Interleaving for ranker duels; bandits for regret, A/B for causal rigor. # Related p-Values Statistical Power Model Evaluation Validation Calibration Ranking Metrics: NDCG, MAP MRR Cross-Validation Math Recommender Systems ML in Production Data Drift

title: Causal Inference for ML Engineers
heads: Confounding, selection bias, and why correlation fails
Worked example: IPW on a small synthetic dataset
Evaluating uplift: Qini and uplift curves
Observational study or experiment: a decision table
text: A predictive model answers what will happen? ; a causal model answers what happens if we do this? The two questions need different tools. Most production ML is trained to predict: click, churn, default, purchase. Many business decisions, though, are interventions: send the coupon, show the ranking, change the price. A model that predicts well under the current policy can be useless, or harmful, for choosing the action, because the correlations it exploits were produced by the old policy and by hidden drivers of both action and outcome. This chapter covers the vocabulary (potential outcomes), why naive comparisons fail, and the toolbox for estimating effects when a randomized experiment is possible, partially possible, or not possible at all. For the mechanics of designing and analysing randomized tests, see A/B Testing Online Experimentation ; this chapter starts where randomization stops being available. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Define potential outcomes and distinguish ATE, ATT, and CATE, and explain the fundamental problem of causal inference. Explain why correlation fails (confounding, selection bias) and why randomization fixes it. Estimate an effect with propensity scores (matching, IPW, doubly robust) and state the assumptions that make it valid. Choose between difference-in-differences, synthetic control, instrumental variables, and regression discontinuity for a given setup. Build and evaluate an uplift model, including Qini curves, and name the S/T/X-learner trade-offs. Read a causal DAG and tell a confounder from a mediator from a collider. # Potential outcomes and the estimands For each unit and a binary treatment ​ ∈ { 0 , 1 } , define two potential outcomes : ​ ( 1 ) , the outcome if treated, and ​ ( 0 ) , the outcome if not. The individual causal effect is ​ ( 1 ) − Y i ​ ( 0 ) . Only one of the two is ever observed: ​ = T i ​ Y i ​ ( 1 ) + ( 1 − T i ​ ) Y i ​ ( 0 ) This is the fundamental problem of causal inference : the counterfactual is missing for every unit, so individual effects are never directly observed. Everything that follows is a strategy for replacing the missing counterfactual with something credible, usually a comparison group. Three common targets, which differ in whom they average over: Estimand Definition Question it answers ATE Effect if we treated everyone vs no one ATT Effect on those who actually got treated CATE Effect for units with covariates (heterogeneity) ATE and ATT coincide in a randomized trial with full compliance, but differ in observational data whenever the treated are unlike the population. CATE is the quantity that uplift models try to estimate, because targeting needs per-segment effects. Two standing assumptions underlie most methods: SUTVA (no interference, consistent treatment): one unit's outcome does not depend on others' treatment, and treated means one well-defined thing. Marketplaces, social networks, and shared-capacity systems violate the first part; see the switchback and cluster designs in the A/B chapter . Consistency: the observed outcome of a treated unit equals its . Memory hook Potential outcomes: two lives per unit, only one lived. Causal inference is the art of borrowing the other life from someone similar. # Confounding, selection bias, and why correlation fails Suppose a retention-email campaign was sent mostly to already-engaged users. Treated users retain more, but they would have retained more anyway. A confounder is a variable that affects both treatment assignment and outcome, creating association that is not causal. The naive difference in means decomposes as: E [ Y ∣ T = 1 ] − E [ Y ∣ T = 0 ] ​ ​ = ATT E [ Y ( 1 ) − Y ( 0 ) ∣ T = 1 ] ​ ​ + selection bias E [ Y ( 0 ) ∣ T = 1 ] − E [ Y ( 0 ) ∣ T = 0 ] ​ ​ The last term says: had nobody been treated, would the two groups still differ? If the treated would have done better anyway, the bias is positive and the naive gap overstates the effect. Selection bias is zero when treatment is independent of potential outcomes, which is exactly what randomization delivers. Why a high-AUC model does not fix this. Adding engagement as a feature to a predictor of retention improves AUC, but the coefficient on received email is then an association adjusted for observed features only. Unobserved drivers (intent, hidden targeting rules, who the campaign manager chose) remain, and even with all confounders observed, a feature attribution or coefficient is not by itself a causal effect without an explicit causal design. A related ML-specific trap: training on logged data from a previous policy teaches the model that the previous policy's choices were good, which is selection bias in disguise. See also Data Leakage for the cousin problem of features that encode the outcome. Common mistake Controlling for everything available. Conditioning on a mediator removes part of the effect; conditioning on a collider creates bias out of nothing (see the DAG section). The adjustment set should come from a causal story, not from all columns . # Randomization If is assigned by a coin flip, then , so the treated and control groups are exchangeable and the difference in means is unbiased for the ATE. Randomization balances observed and unobserved covariates in expectation, which is why it is the gold standard. It does not guarantee balance in any single small sample, which is why stratified randomization and regression adjustment (including CUPED, covered in the A/B chapter) are used to reduce variance. Randomization can still fail in practice: Non-compliance: assigned is not the same as received. Analyse by assignment (intent-to-treat) and, if needed, use assignment as an instrument for receipt (see IV below). Differential attrition: if dropout depends on treatment and outcome, balance is broken after the fact. Interference: spillovers contaminate control. When randomization is unavailable because of ethics, cost, or product constraints, the remaining sections are the fallback, each trading a stronger assumption for feasibility. # Propensity scores The propensity score is . It rests on two assumptions: Unconfoundedness (ignorability): . Given the observed covariates, treatment is as good as random. This is untestable. Overlap (positivity): for all in the support. Every kind of user has some chance of both arms. Rosenbaum and Rubin showed that conditioning on the scalar is enough to balance all of , which reduces a high-dimensional matching problem to one dimension. In practice is estimated with a classifier such as logistic regression or gradient boosting. Unlike a normal classifier, the goal is covariate balance, not accuracy, so check balance (standardized mean differences after weighting) rather than AUC. # Matching and stratification Matching pairs each treated unit with one or more control units that have similar propensity (or covariates) and compares outcomes within pairs. It estimates the ATT naturally and makes the comparison transparent, but discards unmatched units and needs care with caliper width. Stratification groups units into propensity bins (often five) and averages within-bin effects; it is coarse but easy to audit. # Inverse propensity weighting (IPW) IPW reweights each unit by the inverse of the probability of the arm it landed in, creating a pseudo-population in which treatment is independent of : IPW ​ = n 1 ​ i = 1 ∑ n ​ [ e ( X i ​ ) T i ​ Y i ​ ​ − 1 − e ( X i ​ ) ( 1 − T i ​ ) Y i ​ ​ ] Here ​ ) is the propensity score, ​ the treatment indicator, and ​ the observed outcome. A treated unit with was unlikely to be treated, so it stands in for units of its type. The formula targets the ATE (weights ); to target the ATT, use weights , which keep treated units at weight 1 and reweight controls to look like the treated. # Worked example: IPW on a small synthetic dataset A campaign targets 1,000 users in two engagement segments. Treatment was not random: high-engagement users were treated more often. Segment Users Treated Mean , treated Mean , control High engagement 600 480 0.8 0.50 0.40 Low engagement 400 80 0.2 0.20 0.10 Naive comparison over all users: treated mean ; control mean ; naive difference . Within each segment, the true lift is in both, but the treated group is weighted toward the high-engagement segment, so the naive gap is inflated by a factor of nearly three. Apply IPW: Treated term: 1 ​ [ 480 × 0.50/0.8 + 80 × 0.20/0.2 ] = 1000 300 + 80 ​ = 0.38 . Control term: 1 ​ [ 120 × 0.40/0.2 + 320 × 0.10/0.8 ] = 1000 240 + 40 ​ = 0.28 . IPW ​ = 0.38 − 0.28 = 0.10 . IPW recovers the within-segment lift of 0.10 (these numbers were checked with a short NumPy script). The example works because the single covariate fully explains assignment, which is precisely the unconfoundedness assumption. Go deeper (optional) IPW variance blows up when is near 0 or 1: one unit with carries weight 100. Practitioners truncate or clip propensities (for example to ), use stabilized or normalized weights (Hajek estimator), or restrict to the region of overlap, accepting that the estimand then changes to a trimmed population. # Doubly robust estimation (AIPW) Outcome regression fits ​ ( x ) = E [ Y ∣ T = t , X = x ] and averages ​ 1 ​ − μ ^ ​ 0 ​ . IPW models the assignment. The augmented IPW estimator combines them: DR ​ = n 1 ​ i ∑ ​ [ μ ^ ​ 1 ​ ( X i ​ ) − μ ^ ​ 0 ​ ( X i ​ ) + e ( X i ​ ) T i ​ ( Y i ​ − μ ^ ​ 1 ​ ( X i ​ )) ​ − 1 − e ( X i ​ ) ( 1 − T i ​ ) ( Y i ​ − μ ^ ​ 0 ​ ( X i ​ )) ​ ] It is consistent if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correctly specified, hence doubly robust . With cross-fitting (estimate nuisances on held-out folds), it also tolerates flexible ML nuisance models, which is the idea behind double machine learning. Doubly robust does not rescue you from unmeasured confounding or lack of overlap. Interview angle Weak: Match on features until the groups look similar. Strong: Propensity methods assume no unmeasured confounding and overlap; check overlap with propensity histograms per arm, check balance after weighting, trim extreme weights, and run a sensitivity analysis for how strong an unobserved confounder would need to be to erase the effect. Rapid fire: propensity methods Propensity score ; its job is balance, not prediction accuracy. Unconfoundedness is untestable; overlap is checkable with histograms. IPW reweights to a pseudo-population where . Extreme weights inflate variance; clip, normalize, or trim. AIPW is consistent if either the outcome or propensity model is right. Matching targets ATT naturally; IPW targets ATE by default. Sensitivity analysis (for example E-values or Rosenbaum bounds) quantifies how fragile the result is to hidden confounding. # Difference-in-differences When a policy hits one group at a known time and you observe both groups before and after, difference-in-differences (DiD) compares the change in the treated group with the change in a control group. The control group's change stands in for what would have happened to the treated group without the intervention. Under the parallel trends assumption, absent treatment the treated and control groups' outcomes would have moved by the same amount: DiD ​ = ( Y ˉ treat,post ​ − Y ˉ treat,pre ​ ) − ( Y ˉ ctrl,post ​ − Y ˉ ctrl,pre ​ ) Level differences between groups are allowed and are differenced out; only differing trends break the estimate. # Worked example: a 2x2 DiD A feature launches in one region. Weekly conversion rate (percent): Group Before After Change Treated region 10.0 14.0 +4.0 Control region 9.0 11.0 +2.0 A naive before/after on the treated region says points, but the control region also rose points for reasons unrelated to the feature (seasonality, a market-wide promotion). DiD points. Equivalently, the post-period gap (3.0) minus the pre-period gap (1.0) is 2.0. Checking and strengthening the assumption. Parallel trends is about the counterfactual, so it cannot be tested directly, but pre-period data help: plot several pre-periods and check the lines move together, and run an event-study regression with leads and lags (leads should be near zero). Pitfalls: Anticipation effects (behavior changes before launch) contaminate the pre-period. Regression to the mean if the treated group was chosen for an unusual recent value (Ashenfelter's dip). Staggered rollouts with heterogeneous effects can bias the classic two-way fixed effects estimator; modern estimators handle this, and a careful answer mentions it. Standard errors should be clustered at the level of treatment assignment, or inference is overconfident. # Synthetic control When there is one treated unit (a country, a city, a single large customer) and many potential controls, DiD with one hand-picked control is fragile. Synthetic control builds a weighted combination of control units, with non-negative weights summing to one, that matches the treated unit's pre-period trajectory as closely as possible. The post-period gap between the treated unit and its synthetic twin is the estimated effect. = ar g w ≥ 0 , ∑ j ​ w j ​ = 1 min ​ t ≤ T 0 ​ ∑ ​ ( Y 1 t ​ − j ∑ ​ w j ​ Y j t ​ ) 2 Here ​ is the treated unit's outcome at time , ​ the donor units', and ​ the intervention time. Good pre-treatment fit is the credibility check: if the synthetic unit cannot track the treated unit before the launch, the post gap means little. Inference typically uses placebo tests , which re-run the method pretending each donor was treated and ask whether the real gap is unusually large. Limits: needs a long pre-period, donors must be unaffected by the intervention, and the treated unit must lie inside the convex hull of donors. It is the standard answer to we launched in one market only and want the effect . # Instrumental variables When unmeasured confounding rules out adjustment, an instrument can still identify an effect. must satisfy: Relevance: affects treatment . Exclusion: affects the outcome only through . Independence: is as good as randomly assigned (unrelated to confounders). Monotonicity (needed to interpret the estimate as a LATE): no defiers, i.e. nobody takes treatment less because of the instrument. With a binary instrument, the Wald estimator is the ratio of two effects: IV ​ = E [ T ∣ Z = 1 ] − E [ T ∣ Z = 0 ] E [ Y ∣ Z = 1 ] − E [ Y ∣ Z = 0 ] ​ The numerator is the effect of the instrument on the outcome (reduced form); the denominator is its effect on treatment uptake (first stage). Dividing rescales the intent-to-treat effect by the compliance rate. Two-stage least squares generalizes this to covariates and continuous instruments. The classic ML-product instance is a randomized encouragement : users are randomly nudged to adopt a feature, but adoption is voluntary. Random assignment is the instrument, adoption is the treatment. Under monotonicity the estimate is a local average treatment effect (LATE) : the effect for compliers, those whose behavior the instrument changes, not necessarily for always-takers or never-takers. Common mistake Weak instruments. If the first stage is small, the ratio is unstable and biased toward the confounded estimate. Report the first-stage F-statistic; values below roughly 10 are a conventional warning sign. The exclusion restriction is also untestable, so the argument for it has to be made on domain grounds. # Regression discontinuity When treatment is assigned by a threshold on a continuous running variable (credit score above 650 gets the offer, age above a cutoff gets a service), units just above and just below the cutoff are nearly identical except for treatment. The jump in outcome at the cutoff estimates the local effect: ​ = x ↓ c lim ​ E [ Y ∣ X = x ] − x ↑ c lim ​ E [ Y ∣ X = x ] where is the cutoff. In practice, fit local linear regressions on each side within a bandwidth and compare the intercepts at . Key checks: no manipulation of the running variable (a density test for bunching just on one side), smoothness of covariates at the cutoff, and robustness to bandwidth. The estimate is local to the cutoff and may not extrapolate. Many ML systems create accidental discontinuities (a score threshold for manual review, a rank cutoff for a carousel slot), which makes RD a useful tool for evaluating deployed decision rules without an experiment. # DAGs: confounder, mediator, collider A causal directed acyclic graph (DAG) encodes assumptions about what causes what. Three basic structures decide whether to adjust for a variable when studying : flowchart LR subgraph Confounder C1[Z] -- T1[T] C1 -- Y1[Y] T1 -- Y1 end subgraph Mediator T2[T] -- M2[Z] M2 -- Y2[Y] end subgraph Collider T3[T] -- K3[Z] Y3[Y] -- K3 end Structure Path Adjust for ? Why Confounder (fork) Yes Opens a non-causal backdoor path; conditioning closes it Mediator (chain) Not for the total effect Conditioning blocks part of the causal effect; adjust only to study the direct effect, which needs further assumptions (no unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding) Collider No The path is closed by default; conditioning on opens it and induces spurious association Collider bias in ML terms: if a dataset only includes users who were approved (approval depends on both applicant quality and an unobserved trait), analysing within the approved set creates a correlation between the two causes. Selecting on the outcome or a consequence of it is a collider-type error and also underlies several selection-bias failures in offline evaluation of ranking systems (compare leakage , a different problem). The backdoor criterion gives the recipe: find a set of variables that blocks every non-causal path from to without containing descendants of , and adjust for it. The DAG is an assumption, not a result; two analysts with different DAGs can reach different adjustment sets from identical data. Memory hook Fork: adjust. Chain: leave it alone (for the total effect). Collider: do not touch. Rapid fire: quasi-experiments DiD needs parallel trends; check pre-trends and cluster standard errors. Synthetic control needs good pre-period fit and unaffected donors; infer with placebo tests. IV needs relevance, exclusion, independence, and (for a LATE) monotonicity; the estimate is for compliers. Weak first stage means a fragile IV estimate. RD compares units at a threshold; it is local and needs no manipulation of the running variable. A DAG is an assumption set; the adjustment set follows from it. # Uplift modelling A churn model ranks users by risk; an uplift model ranks them by incremental benefit from treatment, the CATE . The distinction matters because targeting the highest-risk users wastes money on sure things (would convert anyway) and lost causes (will not convert regardless), and may irritate sleeping dogs (treatment reduces conversion). Value lies in the persuadables . Uplift needs randomized (or well-adjusted) data with treatment and control labels; without them, the model learns the old targeting policy, not the effect. # Meta-learners at a glance Learner Idea Strength Weakness Two-model (T-learner) Fit ​ 1 ​ on treated, ​ 0 ​ on control; = μ ^ ​ 1 ​ − μ ^ ​ 0 ​ Simple, flexible Errors in two models do not cancel; noisy when arms are imbalanced Single-model (S-learner) One model with as a feature; = μ ^ ​ ( x , 1 ) − μ ^ ​ ( x , 0 ) Pools data Regularization can shrink the treatment feature to zero, hiding effects X-learner Impute individual effects using the other arm's model, fit CATE models on them, blend by propensity Strong when one arm is much smaller More moving parts Class transformation Create target and train one classifier; with balanced arms ( 1 ​ ), Single standard classifier Needs balanced arms or a reweighting correction; less data-efficient Other families include causal forests (trees that split on effect heterogeneity), R-learner and double ML (orthogonalize with propensity and outcome models), and direct uplift trees. The practical default is a T-learner or X-learner baseline with the same base model family as the prod

title: Precision & Recall
text: Say it in 30s: Precision = of the things I flagged positive, how many were right (TP / (TP+FP)) — punishes false alarms. Recall = of the actual positives, how many did I catch (TP / (TP+FN)) — punishes misses. They trade off as you move the decision threshold. When to favor which Recall when missing a positive is costly: cancer screening, fraud, safety. Precision when a false alarm is costly: spam filters, recommending an expensive action. F1 = harmonic mean of the two, for a single number when you care about both. The threshold link Lower threshold → more positives → higher recall, lower precision. Raise it → the reverse. This is why you report the PR curve , not a single point, on imbalanced problems. The math From the confusion matrix (TP, FP, FN, TN): T P ​ , R = T P + F N T P ​ = TPR = precision (of predicted positives, how many are correct); = recall (of actual positives, how many you caught). Both move when you change the score threshold. ​ = P + R 2 P R ​ , F β ​ = β 2 P + R ( 1 + β 2 ) P R ​ ​ is ​ with (harmonic mean); weights recall over precision. Worked counts: TP , FP , FN → , ​ = 0.8 . Prevalence ties rates to precision (Bayes): TPR ⋅ π ​ T P ​ , F P ​ . With , , : precision — decent ranking can still look awful on precision when positives are rare. Traps Accuracy is misleading under class imbalance (99% negatives → predict all-negative scores 99%). Precision/recall ignore true negatives by design — that's the point. See depth: Model Evaluation Validation (§2–3). title: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC
text: Say it in 30s: Both summarize a classifier across all thresholds. ROC plots TPR vs FPR; its AUC is the probability a random positive is ranked above a random negative. PR plots precision vs recall. On imbalanced data, prefer PR-AUC — ROC-AUC looks deceptively good because the huge negative class makes FPR tiny. Key points ROC-AUC = 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect; threshold-independent and class-balance-insensitive (which is both a feature and a bug). PR-AUC baseline is the positive class prevalence, so it honestly reflects rarity. Use ROC-AUC to compare rankers in general; switch to PR-AUC when positives are rare and false positives matter (fraud, retrieval, medical). The math At threshold (predict positive if score ): T P ​ , FPR = F P + T N F P ​ ROC plots as sweeps. ROC-AUC ​ s − ​ ) + 2 1 ​ P ( tie ) — the probability a random positive scores above a random negative (Mann–Whitney ​ n − ​ ) ). Pair count: positive scores , negative → of pairs favor the positive → (random baseline 0.5 ). PR-AUC is average precision : ∑ ​ ( R n ​ − R n − 1 ​ ) P n ​ ​ , P n ​ = recall and precision at the -th cut on the ranked list; ​ = R n ​ − R n − 1 ​ weights each precision by new recall mass. Baselines: ROC-AUC for an uninformative ranker is 0.5 regardless of prevalence; PR-AUC baseline is prevalence — predicting everything/nothing at the true positive rate yields . Trap: quoting a 0.95 ROC-AUC on a 1%-positive problem can hide poor precision at the operating point — show PR-AUC too. See depth: Model Evaluation Validation (§4). Related: Precision Recall , Logistic Regression , Class Imbalance , Calibration .

title: Calibration
text: Say it in 30s: A model is calibrated if predicted probabilities match reality — among cases scored 0.7, the event happens about 70% of the time. AUC and ranking metrics only care about order ; calibration cares whether the number means what it says. Fix miscalibration on held-out data with Platt scaling or isotonic regression; always check a reliability diagram before shipping scores into pricing or risk decisions. Key points Reliability diagram : bin predictions, plot mean predicted vs observed frequency; perfect calibration hugs the diagonal. Expected Calibration Error (ECE) : weighted average gap between predicted and observed rates across bins — a single scalar summary. Common pattern: boosted trees and deep nets often overconfident ; naive Bayes pushes to 0/1; logistic regression is usually reasonable out of the box when trained on log-loss. The math Calibration: among predictions with ​ = p , the empirical frequency is : ​ = p ) = p ECE bins predictions into ​ } , : ∑ M ​ n ∣ B m ​ ∣ ​ ​ acc ( B m ​ ) − conf ( B m ​ ) ​ ​ ) = label mean, ​ ) = mean ​ in bin . Example: , two equal bins with and → . Brier score (proper scoring rule): 1 ​ ∑ i ​ ( p ^ ​ i ​ − y i ​ ) 2 — penalizes both calibration and sharpness. Post-hoc fixes (fit on validation): Platt scaling ​ = σ ( a s + b ) on scores ; temperature scaling for -class logits . Proper rules (log-loss, Brier) reward honest probabilities on hold-out data. Common follow-ups / traps Great AUC — are we done? → Not if you threshold on the probability or multiply it into EV math; check calibration. Can I calibrate on the test set? → No — fit the calibrator on validation only, then report on test once. See depth: Model Evaluation Validation (§Calibration). title: Ranking Metrics: NDCG, MAP & MRR
text: Say it in 30s: Search and recommenders care about order , not a single label. MRR rewards the rank of the first relevant hit. MAP averages precision over all relevant items (binary relevance). NDCG handles graded relevance with position discount: k ​ l o g 2 ​ ( i + 1 ) 2 r e l i ​ − 1 ​ , then . Pick the metric to match the feedback type and how many “right answers” each query has. Key points Position discount: relevance at rank 1 counts more than at rank 10 — all three metrics bake that in. MRR = mean of — one gold answer (entity lookup, “I’m feeling lucky”). MAP = mean of average precision per query — several relevant docs, yes/no labels. NDCG normalizes against the ideal ranking so scores are comparable across queries. The math Position-discounted gain (same convention as A/B Testing ): ∑ k ​ lo g 2 ​ ( i + 1 ) 2 r e l i ​ − 1 ​ , NDCG@ k = IDCG@ k DCG@ k ​ ​ = relevance at rank (1-based); = for the best possible ordering. MRR 1 ​ ∑ q ∈ Q ​ r q ​ 1 ​ , ​ = rank of the first relevant item (0 if none). MAP averages precision-at-relevant-cut across queries (binary relevance). AP (one query) ​ ( R n ​ − R n − 1 ​ ) P n ​ ; Recall@ . Worked query (top 3): ranked relevances → ; ideal → → NDCG@3 . Three queries with first relevant at ranks → MRR 1 ​ ( 2 1 ​ + 1 + 3 1 ​ ) ≈ 0.61 . Common follow-ups / traps Why not accuracy on the top item? → Ignores the list structure and graded quality of lower ranks. Offline NDCG is a proxy — confirm lifts with online interleaving or A/B tests on engagement ( A/B Testing ). See depth: Model Evaluation Validation (§Ranking). Related: Recommender Systems , ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC , ML in Production .

title: Cross-Validation
text: Say it in 30s: A way to estimate generalization without wasting data on a fixed validation set. k-fold CV splits the data into k parts, trains on k−1 and validates on the held-out fold, rotates k times, and averages. You get a more stable performance estimate and a sense of its variance. Variants k-fold (k=5 or 10 typical): the default. Stratified k-fold : preserve class ratios per fold — use for imbalanced classification. Leave-one-out : k = n, low bias, high variance, expensive. Group k-fold : keep correlated rows (same user/patient) together to avoid leakage. Time-series split : train on past, validate on future — never shuffle time. Random k-fold leaks the future. The math -fold estimate and spread over fold scores ​ , : ​ CV ​ = k 1 ​ j = 1 ∑ k ​ s j ​ , SE ( μ ^ ​ CV ​ ) ≈ k ( k − 1 ) 1 ​ j = 1 ∑ k ​ ( s j ​ − μ ^ ​ CV ​ ) 2 ​ Bias–variance in : small (e.g. 5) trains each model on only of the data, so the score is slightly pessimistic, but the folds overlap less and the average is stabler. LOOCV ( ) trains on points — nearly unbiased — but the scores are almost the same model, so the estimate has high variance and costs fits. LOOCV (linear regression): leave-one-out predictions use PRESS residuals ​ − y ^ ​ i ​ ) / ( 1 − h ii ​ ) with hat diagonal ​ ; LOOCV MSE 1 ​ ∑ i ​ ( ( y i ​ − y ^ ​ i ​ ) / ( 1 − h ii ​ ) ) 2 . Nested CV: outer fold reports out ​ after tuning hyperparameters by inner CV on its train split only; $ ​ outer ​ = k out ​ 1 ​ ∑ j = 1 k out ​ ​ s j out ​ $ estimates generalization for the whole tuning protocol (not biased by picking hyperparams on the same folds you score). Example: five folds with accuracy → ​ CV ​ = 0.80 , . Traps Do all preprocessing (scaling, feature selection) inside the fold, or you leak. CV tunes hyperparameters; still keep a final untouched test set. See depth: Model Evaluation Validation (§8), Time Series Stationarity (§9). title: p-Values & Statistical Power
text: Say it in 30s: The p-value is ​ true ) — how surprising the result is if there is no effect. It is not ​ true ) , not the false-positive rate, and not “probability the lift is real.” Power is the chance to reject ​ when a true effect of size exists. Underpowered tests miss real wins; overpowered tests chase trivial deltas — pre-register , , and before you peek. Key points Type I ( ): false alarm — launch when there is no effect. Type II ( ): miss — fail to launch a real win. Per-arm sample size (two-sample mean or proportion, equal ): 2 ( z 1 − α /2 ​ + z 1 − β ​ ) 2 σ 2 ​ .
