title: Training Neural Networks
heads: Learning-rate schedules and the LR range test
Batch size and the linear scaling rule
Debugging: when loss won't go down
text: From affine stacks to stable training: activations, backprop, optimizers, normalization, and what to do when loss won't move. A neural network is not magic—it is repeated affine maps separated by nonlinearities , trained by gradient descent on a scalar loss . This chapter is the interview-depth tour: how universal approximation motivates depth, how backpropagation computes gradients, why gradients vanish or explode, how modern optimizers and learning-rate schedules behave (including Adam's bias correction and BatchNorm vs LayerNorm ), and a practical checklist when training stalls. For hands-on PyTorch loops and init basics, lean on PyTorch and TensorGym study notes rather than re-deriving them here. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Describe an MLP as stacked plus activations, and cite universal approximation in one breath. Write derivatives and deployment roles for ReLU, GELU, softmax, and when saturating activations hurt depth. Explain reverse-mode autodiff and walk a tiny two-layer backprop with tensor shapes. Prescribe fixes for vanishing/exploding gradients: He/Xavier variance, residuals, norm layers, clipping. Recite SGD, momentum, Adam (with bias correction), and why AdamW decouples weight decay from L2-under-Adam. Contrast BatchNorm train vs eval, LayerNorm/RMSNorm, dropout scaling, batch-size scaling, and mixed precision. Run a disciplined loss not decreasing debug pass starting with overfitting one batch. # MLPs and universal approximation Most feedforward training interviews start here: not a CNN 's locality, not a RNN 's recurrence—just fully connected layers. That simplicity makes MLPs the cleanest place to explain gradient descent , backprop , and gradient pathology before specializing architecture. A multilayer perceptron (MLP) alternates affine transforms and elementwise nonlinearities: = σ ( W ( l ) h ( l − 1 ) + b ( l ) ) , h ( 0 ) = x . Stacked linear layers without collapse to one linear map—why activations are non-negotiable for expressivity. The classical universal approximation result (Cybenko, Hornik) says that a feedforward net with a single hidden layer of sufficient width and a non-polynomial activation can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain arbitrarily well— width can buy expressivity. In practice we prefer depth because many functions need far fewer parameters when composed through layers than when crammed into one wide slab. Depth trades parameters for hierarchical structure (edges → parts → objects), which is why CNNs and transformers stack blocks instead of one giant layer. Memory hook Linear–nonlinear–linear–nonlinear: remove the bends and you're back to one straight line. Interview angle Weak: neural nets can learn anything. Strong: one hidden layer is enough in theory (width), but depth + composition is what we actually train because sample and compute efficiency matter; the hypothesis space is huge, so regularization and data still decide generalization. Rapid fire — MLPs MLP affine activation, repeated. No activation one linear layer. Universal approximation: one wide hidden layer suffices in theory. Depth composes features with fewer params than extreme width. Expressivity = generalization— overfitting still happens. # Activation functions Activations introduce curvature between affine blocks. Know the formula, the derivative, and the when . # Sigmoid and tanh Sigmoid: 1 ​ , derivative ( x ) = σ ( x ) ( 1 − σ ( x )) ≤ 4 1 ​ . Tanh: + e − x e x − e − x ​ , derivative ( x ) = 1 − tanh 2 ( x ) . Both saturate at large : gradients near zero → vanishing gradients in deep stacks. Still used where bounded outputs help (gates in LSTM / GRU , historical binary heads). For hidden layers in deep feedforward nets, prefer ReLU family activations. # ReLU family ReLU: , derivative if else . Leaky ReLU: with small (e.g. )—reduces dying ReLU. GELU: (Gaussian CDF)—smooth, used in BERT/GPT-style transformers . SiLU (Swish): —self-gated, similar role to GELU in modern vision and language models. ReLU's constant derivative on the positive branch helps gradient flow versus sigmoid; the trade-off is dead neurons (always off) and non-smoothness at zero—usually acceptable. Choosing in practice: CNN/MLP hidden layers ReLU or Leaky ReLU + He init. Transformer FFN and attention-adjacent blocks GELU or SiLU. Bounded gates in LSTM sigmoid/tanh by design. Output layer: linear + MSE for regression; linear + softmax/CE for classification; multi-label often uses per-logit sigmoid + BCE instead of softmax. # Softmax (output, not hidden) For logits : ​ = ∑ j = 1 K ​ e z j ​ e z i ​ ​ . Use at the output for mutually exclusive classes with cross-entropy on logits ( CrossEntropyLoss in PyTorch combines log-softmax + NLL for numerical stability). Not used between hidden layers—softmax would collapse representation diversity across units. Common mistake Applying softmax manually then MSE on probabilities for classification. Pair logits + cross-entropy instead; the log-softmax gradient is cleaner and well-conditioned. # Typical classifier head — loss expects raw logits logits = model(x) # (batch, num_classes) loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, y) Rapid fire — Activations Sigmoid/tanh saturate → vanishing grads in depth. ReLU default for MLP/CNN hidden layers; init with He. GELU/SiLU common in transformers. Softmax at multi-class output with cross-entropy on logits. See card: Activation Functions . # Backpropagation as reverse-mode autodiff Training needs ​ L for all parameters . Forward mode autodiff computes ∂ ( ⋅ ) ​ by chaining Jacobians along inputs—cheap when there are few inputs, expensive when there are millions of weights. Reverse mode (backprop) fixes one scalar loss and computes ∂ L ​ for every node in one backward sweep—cost for typical nets, which is why it's universal in deep learning. Mechanism: build a computational graph in the forward pass; in backward, apply the chain rule from toward inputs. If and , then ∂ L ​ = ∂ y ∂ L ​ ∂ u ∂ y ​ ∂ x ∂ u ​ . Memory hook Forward stores values; backward multiplies sensitivity along arrows pointing backward. # Worked two-layer example (shapes) Batch size , input dim ​ , hidden ​ , output ​ , scalar loss summed over batch. Stage Tensor Shape Input ​ ) Hidden pre-act ​ = X W 1 ​ + b 1 ​ ​ ) Hidden act ​ = ReLU ( Z 1 ​ ) ​ ) Logits ​ = H 1 ​ W 2 ​ + b 2 ​ ​ ) Loss 1 ​ ∑ ℓ ( Z 2 ​ , y ) scalar Backward (sketch): ​ ∂ L ​ from loss (e.g. softmax-CE: ​ − one_hot for hard labels). ​ ∂ L ​ = H 1 ⊤ ​ ∂ Z 2 ​ ∂ L ​ , ​ ∂ L ​ = ∂ Z 2 ​ ∂ L ​ W 2 ⊤ ​ . ​ ∂ L ​ = ∂ H 1 ​ ∂ L ​ ⊙ 1 Z 1 ​ 0 ​ (ReLU mask). ​ ∂ L ​ = X ⊤ ∂ Z 1 ​ ∂ L ​ . Frameworks implement this graph implicitly. See PyTorch ( loss.backward() , clip_grad_norm_ ). Deeper card: Backpropagation . Interview angle Strong answer names reverse mode , one backward pass for all parameters , and chain rule on the graph —not the loss goes backward magically. Rapid fire — Backprop Backprop reverse-mode autodiff on the forward graph. Scalar loss one cheap backward pass. Chain rule multiplies local Jacobians. Shared weights sum grads from all paths. Frameworks hide the graph; you still own numerical issues (NaNs, vanishing). # Vanishing and exploding gradients When ∂ h ( L ) ​ is a product of many layer Jacobians, spectral norms shrink gradients (early layers learn slowly); inflate them (overflow, NaNs). Saturating activations and poor initialization worsen this in deep MLPs and RNNs . Fixes (use several, not one): Initialization matched to activation (see below). Residual connections: = h ( l ) + F ( h ( l ) ) —gradient highway through identity (ResNet, transformer blocks). Normalization: BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm keep activations in a stable range. Gradient clipping: cap global norm before the optimizer step. loss.backward() torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm= 1.0 ) optimizer.step() # Xavier/Glorot vs He/Kaiming Let ​ , ​ be fan-in, fan-out. Goal: keep variance of activations (and often gradients) stable across layers. Xavier (Glorot), for sigmoid/tanh: ​ + n out ​ 2 ​ . He (Kaiming), for ReLU (accounts for halving variance through ReLU): ​ 2 ​ . Uniform draws use bounds ​ ; Gaussian uses . Default nn.Linear in PyTorch uses Kaiming-uniform—fine for ReLU; switch for tanh stacks. Memory hook He is 2 over fan-in —ReLU kills half the signal on average; He compensates. Rapid fire — Vanishing/exploding Deep products of Jacobians shrink or blow up grads. Sigmoid/tanh saturate. He for ReLU, Xavier for tanh/sigmoid. Residuals + norm + sensible LR. Clip norms in RNNs/LLMs. Card: Vanishing Exploding Gradients . # Optimizers and learning rates Stochastic mini-batch gradient: ​ = ∇ θ ​ ∣ B t ​ ∣ 1 ​ ( x , y ) ∈ B t ​ ∑ ​ ℓ ( f θ ​ ( x ) , y ) . # SGD, momentum, Nesterov SGD: ​ = θ t ​ − η t ​ g t ​ . Momentum: ​ = β v t ​ + g t ​ , ​ = θ t ​ − η v t + 1 ​ (typical ). Nesterov: evaluate gradient at lookahead ​ − η β v t ​ —curvature-aware, often smoother convergence. # AdaGrad, RMSProp AdaGrad: per-parameter accumulator ​ = G t − 1 ​ + g t 2 ​ ; update ​ / ( G t ​ ​ + ϵ ) . Sparse features (e.g. embedding lookups) get large effective steps early; dense deep nets see learning rates monotonically shrink to zero —training stalls. Historic, mostly superseded except where sparsity is extreme. RMSProp: exponential moving average of squared gradients: ​ = ρ v t − 1 ​ + ( 1 − ρ ) g t 2 ​ , θ t + 1 ​ = θ t ​ − η v t ​ ​ + ϵ g t ​ ​ . Same per-parameter scaling idea as AdaGrad, but ​ forgets old squared gradients—does not die automatically. Hinton's staple before Adam; still useful to mention because Adam is momentum + RMSProp-like denominator. # Adam (with bias correction) ​ = β 1 ​ m t − 1 ​ + ( 1 − β 1 ​ ) g t ​ , v t ​ = β 2 ​ v t − 1 ​ + ( 1 − β 2 ​ ) g t 2 ​ . Early steps bias ​ , v t ​ toward zero. Bias correction: t ​ = 1 − β 1 t ​ m t ​ ​ , v ^ t ​ = 1 − β 2 t ​ v t ​ ​ . Update: ​ = θ t ​ − η v ^ t ​ ​ + ϵ m ^ t ​ ​ . Defaults ​ = 0.9 , ​ = 0.999 , —standard for transformers and prototyping. # AdamW (decoupled weight decay) Classical Adam + L2 often implements weight decay through the gradient , so adaptive scaling changes effective decay per parameter. AdamW applies decay after the Adam step: ​ = θ t ​ − η v ^ t ​ ​ + ϵ m ^ t ​ ​ − η λ θ t ​ . Decoupled decay matches the intent of ​ regularization under adaptive methods—default for modern language-model pretraining. Interview angle If asked Adam vs AdamW, mention where weight decay enters the update—not just AdamW is better. Card detail: Optimizers . # Learning-rate schedules and the LR range test The PyTorch loop— zero_grad , forward, backward , step —is unchanged across optimizers; what moves is ​ and sometimes per-parameter scaling. Fixed rarely optimal long-term. Common schedules: Step decay: multiply by every epochs—simple CV baseline. Cosine decay: ​ = η m i n ​ + 2 1 ​ ( η m a x ​ − η m i n ​ ) ( 1 + cos ( π t / T )) —smooth anneal, popular with large-batch SGD. Warmup: linearly ramp from 0 (or small) to target over first steps—stabilizes Adam/transformers when , v ^ are immature; avoids giant early steps. One-cycle (Smith): ramp up to max LR then cosine down—sometimes trains faster with careful max LR. LR range test (Smith): start from a tiny , increase exponentially each mini-batch for one short epoch, plot loss vs . Choose just below where loss diverges or spikes—cheap guardrail before multi-day runs. Pair with weight decay sweeps separately; conflating both knobs obscures which one failed. Go deeper (optional) Cyclical LR and cosine with restarts explore multiple basins; useful in research, less often in production LLM recipes where warmup + single cosine is the template. Rapid fire — Optimizers LR SGD+momentum: vision after tuning. Adam/AdamW: transformers, defaults. Bias correction matters early. Warmup tames Adam at step 0. Cosine + weight decay common in LLMs. LR range test finds scale. One-cycle needs a known good max LR. # Batch size and the linear scaling rule Mini-batch SGD estimates the full-data gradient with noise that scales roughly like ​ . Larger batch lower gradient variance each step is a more faithful descent direction, but you take fewer steps per epoch. To keep a similar optimization trajectory when you scale , you often need a larger learning rate and/or more epochs . Linear scaling rule (Goyal et al.): if you multiply batch size by , try multiplying base learning rate by (especially after a short warmup ). Intuition: gradient magnitude grows roughly linearly with while noise shrinks as ​ ; linear LR scaling partially restores the signal-to-noise ratio of each update that small-batch SGD enjoyed. It works well for many ImageNet-scale CNN runs; it is a heuristic , not a theorem—always verify on your validation curve. Caveats interviewers like: Generalization gap: very large batches can converge to sharper minima unless you add regularization , train longer, or use tricks like ghost batch norm. Small batches: implicit gradient noise can help explore; mandatory when GPU memory caps —use gradient accumulation (sum grads over micro-batches, step once) to simulate large without raising memory. BatchNorm interaction: statistics from a batch of 2 are meaningless; sync BN or switch norm type when is tiny. Memory hook Double the batch? Often try double the LR (with warmup)—then verify on a val curve, not by faith. Interview angle Mention gradient accumulation when someone says I can't fit batch 512. That signals you've trained real models, not just read the scaling paper. # Normalization layers # BatchNorm Per feature (per channel in CNNs), normalize across batch: b , i ​ = σ i 2 ​ + ϵ ​ x b , i ​ − μ i ​ ​ , y b , i ​ = γ i ​ x ^ b , i ​ + β i ​ , with batch stats ​ , σ i 2 ​ . Training: compute from current mini-batch; update running_mean , running_var (EMA). Eval: freeze learned and use running —not batch stats. model.train() # BN uses batch stats, updates running buffers model. eval () # BN uses running_mean / running_var Small batches: high-variance hurt; consider GroupNorm or LayerNorm. # LayerNorm, RMSNorm, GroupNorm LayerNorm: normalize features within each example (across hidden dim / token)—no batch dependence; default in self-attention blocks. RMSNorm: scale by RMS without centering—faster, used in many LLMs. GroupNorm: normalize channel groups per spatial location—CV with small . # Pre-LN vs Post-LN Post-LN (original transformer): sublayer then norm—deeper models need careful warmup. Pre-LN: norm before attention/FFN, residual around sublayer output— more stable deep stacks; dominant in recent LLMs. Card: BatchNorm vs LayerNorm . Rapid fire — Normalization BN: across batch at train, running stats at eval—always train() vs eval() . LN/RMSNorm: per token, no batch stat. GN: small-batch CNNs. Pre-LN stabilizes deep transformers. Norm is not a substitute for good data. # Regularization for neural nets Neural nets interpolate easily; regularization and data discipline control variance . Dropout: Bernoulli mask on activations with rate ; inverted training scaling on survivors so eval needs no scale. train() on, eval() off. See Dropout . Weight decay: ​ penalty; with Adam use AdamW decoupling. Data augmentation: label-preserving transforms (vision: flip/crop; NLP: dropout on tokens)—effective capacity reduction. Early stopping: halt when validation metric stalls—cheap, strong. Label smoothing: replace one-hot with —calibration and less overconfident logits. Interview angle Tie regularization to variance reduction , not buzzwords. Mention train/eval behavior for dropout and BatchNorm in the same breath. # Mixed precision training Modern accelerators are fastest in 16-bit math; training still needs numerical care. Dtype Mantissa / exponent Typical use FP32 reference training master weights, loss accumulation FP16 less range CNN/vision AMP on NVIDIA bfloat16 wide exponent [[llm-training-and-alignment FP16 halves activation memory and unlocks Tensor Cores; bfloat16 trades mantissa bits for exponent headroom like FP32—often the default for billion-parameter stacks. Gradients in fp16 can underflow to zero; loss scaling multiplies the scalar loss by before backward() , then divides accumulated grads by before optimizer.step() . If infs appear, the scaler backs off . scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler() with torch.cuda.amp.autocast(dtype=torch.bfloat16): # or float16 loss = criterion(model(x), y) scaler.scale(loss).backward() scaler.step(optimizer) scaler.update() Keep sensitive reductions (large sums, loss aggregation) in FP32 when possible. Mixed precision is not fp16 weights only —it's a disciplined split of which ops run in which dtype. Rapid fire — Regularization precision Dropout train scaling. AdamW for decay with Adam. Augment + early stop + label smooth. AMP: autocast + loss scaling; bf16 often friendlier than fp16. # Debugging: when loss won't go down Work the list in order—don't random-tweak. Overfit one batch: train on a handful of examples until loss . If you can't, bug in model, loss, or labels—not need more data. Learning rate: too high (diverge/NaN) or too low (flat forever). LR range test or try $\times$3 and $\div$3. Data pipeline: shuffle, wrong labels , normalization mismatch train/val, leakage. Visualize a batch. NaNs/Infs: log max grad norm; clip; check for log(0), div by zero, bad init. Train/eval modes: dropout on at eval, BatchNorm using wrong stats—inflates or deflates metrics. Capacity: if train loss stays high, add width/depth; if train low / val high, regularize (see overfitting ). Loss pairing: logits + cross-entropy; regression + MSE; check reduction ( mean vs sum affects effective LR). Optimizer state: did you zero grad each step ( set_to_none=True saves memory)? Loading only weights but not Adam moments effectively cold-starts adaptation. Baselines: compare to a linear model or logistic regression on the same features—if the shallow model wins, your deep net may be misconfigured, not underpowered. for x, y in loader: # one batch optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none= True ) with torch.cuda.amp.autocast(enabled=use_amp): loss = criterion(model(x), y) scaler.scale(loss).backward() scaler.unscale_(optimizer) torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0 ) scaler.step(optimizer) scaler.update() Common mistake Tuning architecture for weeks while the model can't memorize 10 points—always overfit one batch first. Rapid fire — Debugging One-batch overfit proves the stack works. Then LR, data, NaNs, train/eval, capacity, loss pairing. Log grad norms. Clip before blaming the architecture. # One-page summary Concept The one thing to remember MLP Affine + nonlinear stack; depth composes features; universal approx with width in theory. Activations ReLU + He init in MLPs; GELU/SiLU in transformers; softmax + CE at class head. Backprop Reverse-mode autodiff; one backward pass for all params; chain rule on the graph. Vanishing/exploding Product of Jacobians; He/Xavier, residuals, norm, clipping. Optimizers SGD+momentum (vision); Adam bias correction; AdamW decouples weight decay. LR schedules Warmup for Adam/transformers; cosine/step/one-cycle per recipe. Batch size Linear LR scaling heuristic with warmup; small hurts BatchNorm. Normalization BN: batch train / running eval; LN/RMSNorm per token; Pre-LN for depth. Regularization Inverted dropout; AdamW; augment; early stop; label smoothing. Mixed precision autocast + loss scaling; bf16 when available. Debug checklist Overfit one batch → LR → data → NaNs → train/eval → capacity → loss match. # Related Backpropagation , Activation Functions , Optimizers , BatchNorm vs LayerNorm , Dropout , Vanishing Exploding Gradients PyTorch , TensorGym Study Notes , Gradient Descent , Cross-Entropy Loss Convolutional Neural Networks , Recurrent Neural Networks , Transformers and Attention Regularization , Overfitting Underfitting , Loss Functions

heads: Weights & bias are linear; activations are nonlinear
Backprop & weight update — order and timing (deep dive)
Is the update layer-by-layer or all at once?
Does layer ttt's update account for layer t+1t+1t+1's update?
Practical details that trip people up
text: ML + PyTorch study notes: weights, activations, and how backprop actually updates a network. # Weight initialization Initial weights are random and small (bias often 0, though nn.Linear draws it randomly too). Random, not zero — if all weights start equal, every neuron computes the same thing and gets the same update forever (the symmetry problem ). Randomness lets neurons specialize. Small, not huge — too big → signal/gradients explode (NaN); too small → they vanish (learns slowly). Principled inits scale randomness by layer fan: Xavier/Glorot (fan_in + fan_out; sigmoid/tanh) or He/Kaiming (fan_in; ReLU). nn.Linear defaults to kaiming_uniform_ with ​ : weights for ) fan_in ) ​ , which equals ​ when ​ ; bias uses ​ , 1/ fan_in ​ ) . Call nn.init.xavier_* or kaiming_* explicitly when the activation differs. Set torch.manual_seed(42) for reproducible runs. # Weights bias are linear; activations are nonlinear A neuron has two parts: Shapes: one example , batch , , → via batched matmul (same rule as X @ W in NumPy when rows are examples). Weights and bias do plain linear math ( ). Both are learned, both updated by gradient descent. The activation function is what's nonlinear (and it's fixed, not learned). Why needed: stacking linear layers with no activation collapses to one linear equation. Activations let the network model curves/complex patterns. Mental model: linear step → bend → linear step → bend → … # How weights are updated (gradient descent) One formula: ​ = w old ​ − ( η × gradient ) Gradient = direction steepness of how loss changes with the weight. positive → increasing the weight raises loss → decrease it. negative → increasing the weight lowers loss → increase it. Either way you move opposite the gradient → hence the minus sign ( descent ). Learning rate = step size. too big → overshoot, bounce around, diverge. too small → painfully slow. Hill analogy: gradient points steepest uphill; you step downhill (opposite) repeatedly until you reach the valley (low loss). Optimizers: plain SGD uses the formula directly; Adam adapts the step size per weight, but the core move opposite the gradient logic is the same. # How gradients are calculated (backpropagation) Backprop = the chain rule applied backwards through the network. In words: if A affects B and B affects C, then A's effect on C (A→B) (B→C). Just multiply the links. # Worked single-neuron example Setup: , , , . Chain for ​ : ​ → z → p → Loss . ​ ∂ L ​ = ∂ p ∂ L ​ ⋅ ∂ z ∂ p ​ ⋅ ∂ w 1 ​ ∂ z ​ = p ( 1 − p ) p − y ​ ⋅ p ( 1 − p ) ⋅ x 1 ​ = ( p − y ) x 1 ​ The cancels. Plugging in: ​ ∂ L ​ = ( 0.924 − 0 ) ⋅ 1 = 0.924 , ∂ w 2 ​ ∂ L ​ = ( 0.924 ) ⋅ 4 = 3.70 , ∂ b ∂ L ​ = 0.924 # Why the gradient is per-weight Every weight shares the same error term but is multiplied by its own input ​ . Different input → different gradient. ( ​ 's input was 4, so its gradient is 4× ​ 's.) # General per-weight formula Same error × input shape at every layer, however deep. Logits + CE (serving math). Stable softmax: ​ = exp ( z i ​ − m ) / ∑ j ​ exp ( z j ​ − m ) with ​ z j ​ . PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss = log-softmax + NLL in one; for logits and class index , ​ . # Multi-layer: why back For an earlier-layer weight the chain is longer (more links multiplied). The front part of that product is shared by all weights feeding a neuron, so backprop computes it once at the output and passes it backward as an error signal . Working right-to-left avoids recomputing shared pieces — that's the efficiency trick. # Division of labor in PyTorch forward pass → compute prediction, autograd records every operation. loss.backward() → chain-rule backwards, store one gradient per weight in weight.grad . opt.step() → use the gradients to nudge every weight simultaneously. # Backprop weight update — order and timing (deep dive) # Is the update layer-by-layer or all at once? All at once, at the end. No weight changes during backprop. 1. forward pass - compute predictions using CURRENT weights 2. backward pass - compute the GRADIENT for every weight in every layer (last layer - first layer, but ONLY computing numbers) 3. opt.step() - NOW update every weight in every layer SIMULTANEOUSLY The weights are frozen during the entire forward + backward pass. Backprop going right-to-left is only about computing gradients efficiently, not about updating in stages. # Does layer 's update account for layer 's update? No. Every gradient is computed w.r.t. the current (old) weights , assuming all other weights stay fixed. Each gradient answers: If I nudge this one weight a tiny bit and everything else stays put, how does the loss change? Then opt.step() nudges every weight at once — each under the assumption the others didn't move. # Doesn't that overcorrect? It can — and the learning rate is what keeps it safe. A gradient is only exactly true for an infinitesimally small step (it's a local linear approximation). The interaction between two layers' updates is a higher-order effect: → negligible when steps are small. So a small learning rate keeps the everyone else held fixed assumption valid. Any mismatch this round is re-measured and corrected next round. This is partly why too large a learning rate diverges : big steps make the layers interfere strongly, the assumption breaks, the overcorrection actually happens, and loss bounces/explodes. # Mental model One iteration = a single synchronized step where every layer moves as if the others didn't. Deliberately wrong but self-correcting: many small approximate steps, re-measuring all gradients each time, beats one big perfect jump. Over many iterations the whole network converges together. (Fancier optimizers, batch-norm, second-order methods exist partly to handle these inter-layer interactions better — plain gradient descent just relies on small steps + repeat. ) # Practical details that trip people up Tensor layout (NCHW vs NHWC). PyTorch image tensors default to : batch, channels, height, width. Many image libraries (PIL, NumPy, OpenCV) and some other frameworks use , so a conversion such as x.permute(0, 3, 1, 2) is often needed before a Conv2d . A silent shape bug here is common: the code may still run if the dimensions happen to be compatible, but the values are wrong. channels_last memory format keeps the logical NCHW shape while storing data NHWC-style, which some GPUs process faster. model.eval() vs torch.no_grad() do different jobs. eval() switches layer behaviour: dropout is disabled and batch norm uses running statistics instead of batch statistics. no_grad() (or inference_mode() ) stops autograd from recording operations, saving memory and time. It does not change dropout or batch norm. Validation and inference typically use both; using only no_grad() leaves dropout active, and using only eval() still builds a graph. Automatic mixed precision (AMP). torch.autocast runs selected ops (matmuls, convolutions) in half precision while keeping numerically sensitive ones (reductions, softmax, losses) in fp32. With fp16 , small gradients can underflow to zero, so GradScaler ( torch.amp.GradScaler( cuda ) ; the older torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler spelling is deprecated) multiplies the loss by a scale factor before backward() , then unscales the gradients before opt.step() and skips steps that contain inf/NaN. bf16 keeps fp32's exponent range with fewer mantissa bits, so it usually trains without a scaler on hardware that supports it, at the cost of lower precision per value. scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler( cuda ) # not needed for bf16 opt.zero_grad(set_to_none= True ) with torch.autocast( cuda , dtype=torch.float16): loss = loss_fn(model(x), y) scaler.scale(loss).backward() scaler.step(opt); scaler.update() # Quick reference: the whole picture 1. Get data (pandas) - preprocess (fit on train only) - convert to tensors 2. Init weights randomly (small) 3. For each epoch: forward: guess = activation(X·W + b) loss: measure wrongness backward: chain-rule back - gradient per weight (error × input) step: new = old − lr × gradient (every weight at once) 4. Loss curve slides down = learning 5. Evaluate on validation (eval mode, no_grad) # Related Gradient Descent Cross-Entropy Loss Logistic Regression TensorGym Study Notes Training Neural Networks Backpropagation Optimizers: SGD, Momentum Adam

heads: dim — which axis the operation runs along
keepdim=True — preserve the collapsed axis as size 1
squeeze / unsqueeze — remove / add a size-1 dimension
argmax — index of the max, not the value
torch.cat — join tensors along an axis
Softmax (turns logits into a probability distribution)
text: A cheat-sheet of the concepts covered while working through the TensorGym exercises ( Colab notebook ). # Tensors axes # dim — which axis the operation runs along The number you pass to sum , mean , max , softmax , etc. is the axis that gets collapsed. For a 2D tensor of shape [rows, cols] : dim=0 → travel down the rows → one result per column dim=1 → travel across the columns → one result per row x = torch.tensor([[ 1. , 2 , 3 ], [ 4 , 5 , 6 ]]) # shape [2, 3] torch. sum (x, dim= 0 ) # [5, 7, 9] (per column) torch. sum (x, dim= 1 ) # [6, 15] (per row) Rule of thumb: if the answer should have one number per column, use dim=0 ; per row, dim=1 . # keepdim=True — preserve the collapsed axis as size 1 Keeps shape [2, 1] instead of [2] so it broadcasts back against the original. m = torch. max (x, dim= 1 , keepdim= True ).values # shape [2, 1] x - m # works element-wise per row thanks to broadcasting # squeeze / unsqueeze — remove / add a size-1 dimension v = torch.tensor([ 1 , 2 , 3 ]) # [3] v.unsqueeze( 1 ) # [[1],[2],[3]] shape [3, 1] (column vector) v.unsqueeze( 0 ) # [[1, 2, 3]] shape [1, 3] (row vector) y = torch.tensor([[ 1 ],[ 2 ],[ 3 ]]) # [3, 1] y.squeeze() # [1, 2, 3] shape [3] squeeze only removes dimensions of size 1. keepdim=True is like a built-in unsqueeze . # argmax — index of the max, not the value a = torch.tensor([ 10 , 50 , 30 ]) torch. max (a) # 50 (the value) torch.argmax(a) # 1 (the position). Ties - first occurrence. Same in NumPy. With a dim / axis it returns the argmax along that axis. # torch.cat — join tensors along an axis torch.cat((A[:, :i], A[:, i+ 1 :]), dim= 1 ) # drop column i (join left right blocks) dim=1 joins side-by-side (columns); dim=0 stacks vertically (rows). @ is shorthand for torch.matmul . # dtype gotcha Integer literals make int tensors. mean / var error on int tensors, and mixed-dtype matmul fails. Cast with x = x.float() up front when inputs come from integer lists. # Math foundations # Variance: population ( ) vs unbiased ( ) torch.var(x) # default: / (N-1) unbiased (Bessel s correction) torch.var(x, unbiased= False ) # / N population Manual: 1 ​ ∑ ( x − x ˉ ) 2 (population) or divide by (unbiased). Use population when your data is the whole set (batch norm, standardize); when estimating from a sample. # Z-score standardization (per feature/column) ​ = σ 2 + ϵ ​ x − μ ​ mean = x.mean(dim= 0 , keepdim= True ) var = x.var(dim= 0 , unbiased= False , keepdim= True ) x_std = (x - mean) / torch.sqrt(var + 1e-8 ) # 1e-8 for numerical safety # Neural-network building blocks # Softmax (turns logits into a probability distribution) A logit = raw, unbounded model score before normalization. On paper, ​ = ∑ j ​ e z j ​ e z i ​ ​ = ∑ j ​ e z j ​ − m e z i ​ − m ​ with ​ z j ​ ( log-sum-exp trick ; same probabilities, no overflow). Broadcasting: trailing dimensions align right; size-1 axes stretch. Hence keepdim=True after max / mean so [B,1] subtracts from [B,C] . Batched matmul: [B,n,m] @ [B,m,p] → [B,n,p] . m = logits. max (dim= 1 , keepdim= True ).values # subtract max for numerical stability e = torch.exp(logits - m) probs = e / e. sum (dim= 1 , keepdim= True ) # each row sums to 1 The max-subtraction does not change the result (softmax is shift-invariant) — it just prevents exp overflow. Cross-entropy from logits: ​ = − z y ​ + m + lo g ∑ j ​ e z j ​ − m ; F.cross_entropy(logits, y) fuses this (don't softmax then log ). # Sigmoid logistic regression 1 ​ squashes any real to ; a logit of 0 → probability 0.5. logits = X @ w + b probs = torch.sigmoid(logits) # 1 / (1 + e^-z) preds = (probs = 0.5 ). float () # threshold for class labels # Normalization layers (normalize activations, not weights) All re-center/re-scale the values flowing between layers; they differ in what they average over: Method Averages over Batch-size dependent? Batch norm the batch, per feature ( dim=0 ) Yes — noisy for tiny batches Layer norm all features of one example No — used in transformers Group norm feature groups, per example No Batch norm (across the batch / rows): mean = data.mean(dim= 0 ) var = data.var(dim= 0 , unbiased= False ) # BN uses the biased (N) variance out = (data - mean) / torch.sqrt(var + epsilon) The mean/var are statistics computed from data each pass — not learned. Only the weights and the norm's learnable (scale) / (shift) are updated by gradient descent. text: A CNN slides small learnable pattern detectors ( filters / kernels ) across an image. Early layers find edges, deeper layers find textures, parts, then whole objects. Convolution is just sliding-window pattern matching with learned weights. The whole game is: spatial size shrinks, channel depth grows , then a head maps features to classes. # Image as a tensor An image is a tensor of shape (height, width, channels). Grayscale , RGB . After the first layer, channels stop being colors and become feature maps (one per filter). # The convolution operation A filter is a small weight grid (e.g. ) that spans all input channels. A filter over a 3-channel input is weights bias. Slide it; at each position multiply weights by the covered pixels, sum, add bias → one pixel of one output feature map. ​ ∑ ​ d j ​ ∑ ​ c ∑ ​ in ( i + d i ​ , j + d j ​ , c ) ⋅ w ( d i ​ , d j ​ , c ) Two properties make this cheap and powerful: Parameter sharing — the same weights are reused at every location. One edge detector works everywhere; you store it once. Local connectivity — each output depends only on a small patch (its receptive field ). One filter → one feature map. Use many filters (say 64) → 64 output channels. # The four knobs Stride — how many pixels the filter jumps each step. keeps size; roughly halves each spatial dim (downsampling). Padding — a border (usually zeros) added so the output size is controllable and border pixels are treated fairly. valid : , output shrinks. same : pad so output size input size (at ). For odd kernel : K − 1 ​ → , . Kernel size — the window edge length. Number of filters — sets the output depth (channels). # Output-size formula (memorize) W − K + 2 P ​ ⌋ + 1 Applied independently to height and width. Spatial size comes from this formula; depth comes from the number of filters . title: Computer Vision Beyond CNN Basics
heads: Average precision and mAP, defined precisely
Focal loss and the class-imbalance link
CLIP: dual encoders, text as supervision
text: From classify one image to find every object, label every pixel, and learn from images without labels — the architectures and losses an interviewer expects after the CNN basics. The CNN chapter covers filters, shapes, and the classification head. Real vision systems add four things on top: deeper backbones that still train (ResNets), tasks with structured outputs (detection and segmentation), a different backbone family (Vision Transformers), and pretraining that needs few or no labels (contrastive learning, CLIP). Each comes with one loss or metric that interviewers like to probe: IoU and mAP, focal loss, Dice, InfoNCE. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Explain why plain deep CNNs degrade and how a skip connection fixes it, and compute the parameter saving of a bottleneck block. Contrast two-stage and one-stage detectors, anchors and anchor-free heads, and say what IoU, NMS, and mAP compute, with a worked example. Distinguish semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation, and say why U-Net uses skip connections and why Dice loss helps with small foregrounds. Describe how a ViT turns an image into tokens, and give a hedged answer to ViT or CNN? Write the InfoNCE loss, and explain how CLIP does zero-shot classification. Pick a transfer-learning recipe and an augmentation policy for a given data size. # ResNets and skip connections # The degradation problem Stacking more layers should not hurt in principle: a deeper network could copy a shallower one and set the extra layers to identity. In practice, plain (non-residual) networks beyond a few dozen layers showed higher training error than shallower ones. This is called degradation . It is not overfitting, since the training error itself rises. It is an optimization problem: learning an identity mapping with a stack of nonlinear layers is hard for SGD, and gradients through many layers are poorly conditioned (see Vanishing Exploding Gradients ; normalization layers fixed much of the raw vanishing problem, but degradation persisted). # The fix: learn the residual A residual block computes where is a small stack (conv, norm, ReLU, conv, norm) and is carried around it by an identity skip connection . If the best thing a block can do is nothing, it only needs to push , which is easy (weight decay and small initializations push that way). The block learns a correction to its input rather than a whole new representation. The gradient view is the sharper argument. Differentiating : ∂ y ​ = ∂ x ∂ F ​ + I Across blocks, the product of Jacobians expands into a sum of paths, and one of those paths is pure identity from the loss straight to early layers. The gradient therefore has a route that does not pass through any weight matrix or nonlinearity, which greatly reduces (though does not eliminate) vanishing gradients as depth grows. A useful reading is that a ResNet behaves like an ensemble of many paths of different depths. Memory hook A plain layer must rewrite its input; a residual layer only has to edit it. The + x is a gradient highway. # Shape rules and projection shortcuts The sum requires and to have the same shape. When a stage downsamples (stride 2) or changes channel count, the shortcut uses a conv (with the same stride) to match, called a projection shortcut . Everywhere else it is a parameter-free identity. # Basic block vs bottleneck block ResNet-18/34 use the basic block : two convs. Deeper variants (50/101/152) use the bottleneck block : a conv that squeezes channels, a conv at the narrow width, and a conv that expands back. The expensive operates on a quarter of the channels. flowchart LR X[ x br/ 256 ch ]:::data A[ 1x1 conv br/ 256 to 64 ]:::conv B[ 3x3 conv br/ 64 to 64 ]:::conv C[ 1x1 conv br/ 64 to 256 ]:::conv S(( + )):::add Y[ out br/ 256 ch ]:::data X -- A -- B -- C -- S -- Y X -. identity skip .- S classDef data fill:#F1EFE8,stroke:#5F5E5A,color:#2C2C2A classDef conv fill:#E6F1FB,stroke:#185FA5,color:#042C53 classDef add fill:#FAEEDA,stroke:#854F0B,color:#412402 Parameter comparison at 256 channels (weights only, biases and norm parameters ignored): Block Layers Weights Basic two , 256 to 256 Bottleneck (256 to 64), (64 to 64), (64 to 256) The bottleneck is about 17 times cheaper than the basic block at the same external width, which is what lets ResNet-50 be deeper than ResNet-34 with a comparable cost. FLOPs scale the same way, since a conv's multiply-accumulates are its weights times the output spatial positions. For reference, one conv from 64 to 64 channels on a map costs M multiply-accumulates. Two practical refinements show up in later variants: pre-activation ordering (norm and ReLU before the conv, which keeps the skip path completely clean), and zero-initializing the last norm scale in each block so every block starts as an exact identity. Interview angle Weak answer: skip connections help gradients. Strong answer: degradation is a training-error problem, not overfitting; the block reparameterizes the target as a residual so identity is the easy default; and the term in the Jacobian gives gradients a path that does not depend on depth. Bonus: DenseNets concatenate rather than add, and Transformers use the same residual structure around attention and MLP blocks (see Transformers Attention ). Rapid fire — ResNets Degradation: deeper plain nets have higher training error; it is optimization, not overfitting. ; the Jacobian contains an identity term. Shape mismatch is handled by a projection shortcut. Bottleneck = squeeze, , expand; far fewer weights than two at full width. Batch norm follows each conv; global average pooling plus a linear layer is the head. Residual connections reappear in nearly every modern architecture, including Transformers. # Efficiency ideas at a glance # Depthwise separable convolutions A standard conv mixes space and channels in one step. A depthwise separable conv splits it: a depthwise conv applies one filter per input channel (spatial mixing only), then a pointwise conv mixes channels. K 2 C in ​ C o u t ​ ​ ​ vs depthwise separable K 2 C in ​ + C in ​ C o u t ​ ​ ​ For and ​ = C o u t ​ = 128 : standard weights, separable , about 8.4 times fewer. The ratio approaches for wide layers. MobileNet-style networks are built from these, usually with an inverted bottleneck (expand, depthwise, project). The trade-off: fewer FLOPs does not always mean lower latency, because depthwise convs have low arithmetic intensity and can be memory-bound on accelerators. # Compound scaling (EfficientNet) A network can be scaled in depth (layers), width (channels), and input resolution. Scaling only one saturates quickly. Compound scaling grows all three together with a single coefficient : , width ∝ β ϕ , resolution ∝ γ ϕ , α β 2 γ 2 ≈ 2 The constraint exists because FLOPs scale roughly linearly with depth and quadratically with width and resolution, so each increment of about doubles the compute. The constants are found by a small grid search on a base network, then is turned up to get the B0 to B7 family. The takeaway for interviews: scale dimensions jointly , and when tuning a backbone for a fixed budget, resolution matters as much as depth. Rapid fire — efficiency Depthwise separable: spatial and channel mixing done separately; about times cheaper for wide layers. Inverted bottleneck: expand with , depthwise , project back; skip connects the narrow ends. Compound scaling: depth, width, and resolution scaled together by one knob . FLOPs are a proxy; measure latency on the target hardware. Squeeze-and-excitation style channel attention is a cheap add-on in several efficient families. # Object detection Classification outputs one label per image. Detection outputs a set of (box, class, score) triples, with a variable number of objects. That raises three problems: how to propose locations, how to match predictions to ground truth, and how to remove duplicates. # IoU: the overlap measure Intersection over Union between two boxes and : ∣ A ∩ B ∣ ​ = ∣ A ∣ + ∣ B ∣ − ∣ A ∩ B ∣ ∣ A ∩ B ∣ ​ Worked example: and in ​ , y 1 ​ , x 2 ​ , y 2 ​ ) form. The intersection is the square from to , area . Each box has area , so the union is and IoU . IoU is 1 for identical boxes and 0 for disjoint ones. Training uses IoU thresholds to assign anchors as positive or negative (commonly around 0.5 to 0.7 for positive, below about 0.3 to 0.4 for negative, with variations by method), and evaluation uses a threshold to call a detection correct. Boxes are usually regressed as offsets relative to an anchor or grid cell, and IoU-based losses (GIoU, DIoU, CIoU) give gradients even when boxes do not overlap, which plain IoU cannot. # Two-stage detectors: the R-CNN family R-CNN : run a classical region proposer (about 2,000 boxes), crop and warp each, run a CNN on every crop. Accurate for its time, very slow. Fast R-CNN : run the CNN once on the whole image, then pool a fixed-size feature (RoI pooling) for each proposal. Proposals are still external. Faster R-CNN : replace the external proposer with a learned Region Proposal Network (RPN) that shares the backbone. Stage one proposes class-agnostic regions ( objectness plus box refinement); stage two classifies each region and refines the box. Mask R-CNN : adds a mask head per region for instance segmentation, and replaces RoI pooling with RoIAlign to avoid quantization error. Strength: strong localization and accuracy, especially for small objects and with feature pyramids. Cost: two sequential stages, so higher latency. # One-stage detectors: YOLO and RetinaNet One-stage detectors skip proposals and predict boxes and classes directly at every location of one or more feature maps, in a single pass. YOLO divides the image into a grid and each cell predicts boxes, an objectness score, and class probabilities; later versions use multi-scale feature maps and more refined heads. SSD predicts from several feature-map scales. RetinaNet is a one-stage detector with a feature pyramid and a focal loss (below), designed to close the accuracy gap with two-stage methods. The typical trade-off is speed for some accuracy, though the gap has narrowed a lot with modern designs. Choose by latency budget and object size distribution, not by family name. # Anchors vs anchor-free An anchor is a predefined box (a set of scales and aspect ratios at each location). The network predicts whether each anchor contains an object and a small offset to fix its shape. Anchors give a good starting guess, but they add hyperparameters (sizes, ratios, matching thresholds) and create a huge number of mostly-negative candidates, which is where the class imbalance below comes from. Anchor-free detectors drop the template boxes. Two common styles are keypoint-based (predict object centers, then regress width and height from that point) and per-location (every location predicts distances to the four box sides, plus a centerness or quality score). Transformer-based detectors (DETR) go further: they predict a fixed-size set of boxes and use bipartite (Hungarian) matching to the ground truth during training, which removes NMS at inference at the cost of slower convergence in the original formulation. # Non-maximum suppression (NMS) Dense predictors fire multiple times on the same object. Greedy NMS keeps the best box and discards its near-duplicates: Sort boxes by score. Keep the top box; remove every remaining box of the same class with IoU above a threshold with it. Repeat on what remains. Worked example with . Boxes (score): ​ = ( 0 , 0 , 10 , 10 ) (0.9), ​ = ( 1 , 1 , 11 , 11 ) (0.8), ​ = ( 20 , 20 , 30 , 30 ) (0.7), ​ = ( 0 , 0 , 10 , 12 ) (0.6). Pairwise IoUs: ​ vs ​ = 0.681 , ​ vs ​ = 0.833 , ​ vs ​ = 0.692 , and ​ overlaps nothing (IoU 0). Keep ​ . ​ (0.681) and ​ (0.833) both exceed 0.5, so both are suppressed. Next remaining is ​ ; nothing left overlaps it. Keep it. Result: ​ , b 2 ​ } . The failure mode: in crowded scenes, a true neighbor of the same class with high overlap gets suppressed. Soft-NMS decays neighbors' scores rather than deleting them, and trades duplicates against missed crowded objects. # Average precision and mAP, defined precisely Detection is scored per class, then averaged. For one class at IoU threshold : Sort all detections across the dataset by confidence, descending. Walk down the list. A detection is a true positive (TP) if its IoU with an unmatched ground-truth box of that class is at least (each ground-truth box can be matched once); otherwise it is a false positive (FP) . Duplicates of an already-matched object are FPs. At each rank compute cumulative and , where is the number of ground-truth boxes. AP is the area under the precision-recall curve, after making precision monotone non-increasing (each point takes the maximum precision at any recall at or beyond it). mAP is AP averaged over classes. Variants differ in how they handle IoU: one benchmark reports AP at a single threshold of 0.5, another averages AP over thresholds , which rewards tight localization. State which one is meant, because the numbers differ substantially. Worked example, one class, ground-truth boxes, five detections sorted by score with outcomes TP, TP, FP, TP, FP: Rank Outcome Cum. TP Cum. FP Precision Recall 1 TP 1 0 1.000 0.25 2 TP 2 0 1.000 0.50 3 FP 2 1 0.667 0.50 4 TP 3 1 0.750 0.75 5 FP 3 2 0.600 0.75 Monotone precision envelope: . Recall increases only at ranks 1, 2, and 4, each by 0.25. The last ground-truth box is not found, so recall stops at 0.75. Area , so . (Some benchmarks use fixed recall-point interpolation instead of the exact area; the number changes slightly.) This is the same precision-recall machinery described in Precision Recall and ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC , applied with a geometric matching rule. # Focal loss and the class-imbalance link A dense detector evaluates tens of thousands of candidate locations per image, and nearly all are background. Plain cross-entropy (see Cross-Entropy Loss ) sums over all of them, so thousands of easy negatives, each with a tiny loss, collectively dominate the gradient. Focal loss down-weights well-classified examples: ​ ) = − α t ​ ( 1 − p t ​ ) γ lo g p t ​ where ​ is the model's probability for the true class, is the focusing parameter (a typical value is 2), and ​ is an optional class-balancing weight. At it reduces to (weighted) cross-entropy. Numbers with and ​ = 1 : an easy example with ​ = 0.9 has CE and FL ⋅ 0.105 = 0.0011 , a roughly 100-fold reduction; a hard example with ​ = 0.1 has CE and FL ⋅ 2.303 = 1.865 , barely touched. The easy majority is effectively muted and the hard examples drive training. See Loss Functions for where this sits among other losses and Class Imbalance for alternatives such as resampling and hard-negative mining (the approach two-stage detectors and SSD-style methods take instead). Common mistake Quoting mAP without the IoU threshold, or computing AP by counting every detection above 0.5 IoU as a TP. Duplicate detections of one object must be FPs; that is exactly why NMS and the one-match rule matter. Interview angle Why did one-stage detectors lag two-stage ones at first? Extreme foreground-background imbalance: a proposal stage filters most background before classification, while a one-stage head sees it all. Focal loss (or hard-negative mining) is the fix. A strong answer then names the remaining trade-off: latency versus localization quality. Rapid fire — detection Output: set of (box, class, score); variable size. IoU = intersection area over union area; used for matching, NMS, and evaluation. Two-stage: propose then classify (Faster R-CNN); one-stage: dense direct prediction (YOLO, SSD, RetinaNet). Anchors: predefined box templates; anchor-free: predict center and extents directly. NMS removes same-class duplicates above an IoU threshold; Soft-NMS decays instead of deleting. AP = area under the monotone precision-recall curve for one class; mAP averages classes (and sometimes IoU thresholds). Focal loss multiplies CE by ​ ) γ to mute easy negatives. DETR-style set prediction with Hungarian matching avoids NMS. # Segmentation Segmentation labels pixels, not boxes. Task Output Distinguishes instances? Example question Semantic One class label per pixel No (all car pixels share a label) Which pixels are road? Instance A mask per object, with class Yes, countable things only Outline each person Panoptic Every pixel gets a class, and things also get an instance id Yes for things; stuff (sky, road) is not split Full scene parsing # U-Net U-Net is an encoder-decoder with skip connections. The encoder is a CNN that repeatedly downsamples, building context. The decoder upsamples (transposed convolutions or interpolation plus convolution) back to input resolution. At each decoder level, the feature map from the encoder level of the same resolution is concatenated , giving the decoder both what (deep, coarse semantics) and where (shallow, fine spatial detail). flowchart LR I[ Image ]:::data -- E1[ Enc 1 br/ full res ]:::conv -- E2[ Enc 2 br/ 1/2 ]:::conv -- E3[ Enc 3 br/ 1/4 ]:::conv -- B[ Bottleneck br/ 1/8 ]:::pool B -- D3[ Dec 3 br/ 1/4 ]:::head -- D2[ Dec 2 br/ 1/2 ]:::head -- D1[ Dec 1 br/ full res ]:::head -- M[ Per-pixel br/ class map ]:::data E3 -. concat .- D3 E2 -. concat .- D2 E1 -. concat .- D1 classDef data fill:#F1EFE8,stroke:#5F5E5A,color:#2C2C2A classDef conv fill:#E6F1FB,stroke:#185FA5,color:#042C53 classDef pool fill:#E1F5EE,stroke:#0F6E56,color:#04342C classDef head fill:#EEEDFE,stroke:#534AB7,color:#26215C Why it works with few labeled images: skip connections preserve boundaries that pooling would blur, and the model is fully convolutional, so any input size works. It is a common default in medical imaging and also appears as the denoising network in diffusion models. Other segmentation heads include dilated (atrous) convolutions, feature-pyramid decoders, and, for instances, Mask R-CNN's per-region mask branch. # Dice loss and imbalance In many tasks the target is a small fraction of pixels (a lesion, a thin road). Per-pixel cross-entropy can be satisfied by predicting background everywhere. The Dice coefficient measures overlap of prediction and target directly: 2 ∣ P ∩ G ∣ ​ , L Dice ​ = 1 − ∑ i ​ p i ​ + ∑ i ​ g i ​ + ϵ 2 ∑ i ​ p i ​ g i ​ + ϵ ​ Here ​ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] is the predicted foreground probability at pixel (soft, so the loss is differentiable), ​ ∈ { 0 , 1 } the label, and a small smoothing constant. Example: prediction covers 4 pixels, target covers 5, overlap 3 gives Dice . Dice relates to IoU by . Because both numerator and denominator scale with foreground size, a tiny object still contributes a meaningful loss. Caveats: the gradients can be noisy on very small or empty targets, so Dice is commonly combined with cross-entropy (or focal loss), and the metric (mean IoU or Dice) should be tracked per class rather than only pixel-wise accuracy, which is dominated by background. Rapid fire — segmentation Semantic: class per pixel; instance: mask per object; panoptic: both, covering every pixel. U-Net = encoder-decoder with same-resolution concatenation skips. Dice ; Dice loss is soft Dice. Pixel accuracy is misleading under imbalance; report mean IoU or per-class Dice. Dice plus cross-entropy is a common combined loss. # Vision Transformers # From image to tokens A Vision Transformer (ViT) treats an image like a sentence of patches.
