title: Recurrent Neural Networks
text: An RNN reads a sequence one item at a time, keeping a memory (hidden state) that summarizes everything seen so far. It predicts the next item from that memory. The whole game: one cell, one set of weights, reused at every step , with the memory passed forward and rewritten each step. Its fatal flaw is forgetting — the trace of early items fades, so it can't learn long-range dependencies. LSTMs and GRUs fix exactly that. # The core computation (one step) At each step the cell takes the new input ​ and the previous memory ​ , and produces the new memory: ​ = tanh ( W x h ​ x t ​ + W hh ​ h t − 1 ​ + b ) ​ t ​ = softmax ( W h y ​ h t ​ ) Read it as two streams meeting: the input's contribution ( ​ x t ​ ) plus the memory's contribution ( ​ h t − 1 ​ ), added together, then squashed by into . The squash is a pressure valve — it stops the memory from exploding over a long sequence and adds the non-linearity that makes the net expressive. There are a few distinct weight matrices, each with its own job: ​ — maps the input into memory space. ​ — maps old memory to new memory (the recurrence). ​ — maps memory to an output prediction. Parameter count (one vanilla RNN layer, input dim , hidden , with bias): ​ is , ​ is , bias is → with a single shared bias. PyTorch's nn.RNN stores separate input and recurrent biases, so it is . Add ​ separately if you count the readout. The same split applies to the gated cells: LSTM is and GRU is this count. Notation key = sigmoid, squashes any number to (a dial ); = squashes to (signed content). = elementwise multiply (two vectors, slot by slot) — distinct from matrix-vector multiply like ​ h t − 1 ​ . ​ , x t ​ ] = concatenation (glue the two vectors into one). Subscripts are timestep indices. Caution: in ( z i ​ ) the ​ is the pre-activation (the stuff inside the tanh), unrelated to the GRU update gate ​ . # Weight sharing (the defining feature) The same ​ , W hh ​ , W h y ​ are reused at every time step. Same matrices across layers means across time — step 2 does not get fresh weights, it reuses step 1's. Consequences: The model handles sequences of any length without adding parameters. It's one cell that loops , not a stack of distinct layers. The nodes in a drawing are the same cell at different times. # One evolving memory, not many There is one memory that takes a new value each step. ​ , h 2 ​ , h 3 ​ are not separate memories — they are snapshots of the same memory over time, like frames of a video. Each step reads the memory it was handed, computes a fresh updated version, and passes it forward . A node does not keep a private memory; the memory flows through each node, getting rewritten as it goes (note-passing down a row of people). # Stacking layers Don't confuse unrolling over time (the same one cell reused at each step) with stacking layers (genuinely different cells with their own weights, piled on top of each other). You can do both at once: stack layers, and unroll the whole stack over time. The hidden-state sequence from layer 1 becomes the input sequence to layer 2. Two flows that don't mix: each layer carries its own hidden state sideways through time, and at each timestep a layer's output feeds up as the next layer's input. Only the top layer's outputs are read for predictions. Note that stacking does not fix forgetting — without gates, each layer's sideways memory still fades, which is the whole reason LSTM / GRU exist. # Loss Next-item prediction uses cross-entropy , summed over the sequence: ∑ T ​ L t ​ , L t ​ = − lo g y ^ ​ t ​ [ correct item ] The pipeline is softmax then cross-entropy : softmax ( ​ = e z i ​ / ∑ j ​ e z j ​ ) turns raw scores into probabilities; cross-entropy ( ​ ) measures how little probability you gave the right answer. They are two consecutive operations, easy to conflate — the divide by the sum lives in softmax, the log lives in cross-entropy. # Training: Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) BPTT is ordinary backprop — applied to the RNN. The full cycle for one batch: Forward — run all steps, save ​ … h T ​ , compute the loss. (memory changes here; weights frozen) Unroll — lay the loop out as a chain of repeated cells, one box per step, so it looks like a normal deep network. Backward — walk from the loss back through the chain, computing a gradient contribution at each step. (memory frozen; gradients computed here) Update — the optimizer ( SGD/Adam ) nudges the weights once , using the summed gradient. (weights change here) Unrolling = stretching the loop memory → [cell] → memory → [cell] → ... into a row [step1] → [step2] → [step3] so the chain rule applies like in any feedforward net. The one thing BPTT adds over plain backprop: because the weights are shared across steps, each step gives a gradient contribution for the same , so you sum them across time , then update once. (You can't update mid-walk — step 3's gradient assumed the old .) Compute vs. update Gradients are computed at every node; the weights are updated only once, after summing all the per-step contributions. BPTT computes gradients, the optimizer spends them. # Why long-range learning fails (vanishing gradients) To send the gradient from a late step back to an early step , it must pass through every step in between, multiplying a Jacobian at each hop: ​ ∂ h t ​ ​ = i = k + 1 ∏ t ​ diag ( tanh ′ ( z i ​ ) ) W hh ​ This product of terms is the killer: ≤ 1 always (near 0 when saturated) → multiplying many sub-1 numbers drives the result toward 0 ( vanishing ). ​ raised to the power scales like its largest singular value : (with ≤ 1 ) vanish; is necessary (not sufficient) for the gradient to explode . So early steps contribute almost nothing to the summed gradient — they're heard but they whisper. The loss function (cross-entropy) is fine; the problem is purely getting the signal back through a long multiplicative chain. Truncated BPTT (only unroll the last steps) is the common practical workaround, at the cost of not learning very long dependencies. Gradient clipping when the global norm exceeds threshold : — caps explosion without changing direction if already small. Teacher forcing: at training time feed the true previous token (or label) as the next input instead of the model's own prediction, so the network learns on clean contexts. At inference you only have model outputs — exposure bias. Scheduled sampling mixes the two. # 30-second answer An RNN is one cell with shared weights and a single evolving memory; it blends the new input with the carried-over memory and squashes with at each step. Trained with BPTT (backprop on the unrolled, weight-shared chain, summing the shared weights' gradients across time). It fails on long sequences because the backward signal is a product of many Jacobians that vanishes (or explodes) — which is the whole motivation for LSTM / GRU gated memory. # See also Cross-Entropy Loss — the output loss (Objectives Losses) Gradient Descent — the optimizer that applies BPTT's gradients (Math) Convolutional Neural Networks — the other core architecture; uses ReLU, RNNs use tanh/sigmoid Next: LSTM GRU — gated fixes for vanishing gradients Vanishing Exploding Gradients Transformers Attention — what replaced RNNs for most sequence tasks

title: Long Short-Term Memory
text: An LSTM is an RNN cell that fixes vanishing gradients by adding a second memory line — the cell state — that information rides along with only gentle edits (keep + add) instead of being fully overwritten every step. Learned gates (sigmoid dials, 0→1) decide what to erase, what to write, and what to read. The name says it: it makes short-term memory able to act long-term. # The two memories Cell state — the long-term memory. A conveyor belt running across all steps. It mostly gets multiplied (forget) and added to (input), never fully rewritten. That additive path is why information and gradients survive long gaps. Hidden state — the short-term memory / working output. What the cell exposes right now to predict and pass forward. A vanilla RNN has only (hence it forgets). The LSTM's innovation is the added line. # What a gate is A gate is a tiny layer that outputs a number between 0 and 1 via sigmoid — a dial. 0 = block, 1 = let through. You multiply the dial against some information. The network learns to set the dial from context (it sees the new input ​ and previous output ​ ). # The three gates Forget gate ( ) — multiplies the belt to decide what to erase . Near 1 = keep the memory; near 0 = wipe it. (New subject in the sentence → drop the old one.) Input gate ( paired with a candidate) — decides what new content to add to the belt. The proposes candidate content; the sigmoid decides how much of it to write. Output gate ( ) — decides how much of the belt to read out as the hidden state ​ . One step in words: look at ​ and ​ → forget some of the belt → add new content to the belt → read a filtered view as the output. # Forward math (defined bottom-up) Symbols: squashes to (a dial), to (signed content), = elementwise multiply, ​ , x t ​ ] = concatenation, each = a learned matrix. = cell-state belt, = hidden state. Define the four pieces first — each just reads ​ , x t ​ ] : Forget dial ​ = σ ( W f ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much of the old belt to keep Input dial ​ = σ ( W i ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much new content to write Candidate ​ = tanh ( W g ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — the proposed new content (signed → tanh) Output dial ​ = σ ( W o ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much of the belt to expose Then assemble — update the belt (keep some old, add some new), then read it out: ​ = f t ​ ⊙ c t − 1 ​ + i t ​ ⊙ g t ​ ​ = o t ​ ⊙ tanh ( c t ​ ) Gradient highway: because the belt update is additive , ​ ∂ c t ​ ​ ≈ diag ( f t ​ ) — just the forget gate, not a W matrix. Chained across time it's ​ diag ( f i ​ ) ; if the net learns ​ ≈ 1 the gradient survives undimmed (the constant error carousel ). Params (one layer): four linear maps ​ , W i ​ , W g ​ , W o ​ each applied to ​ , x t ​ ] ∈ R h + d → outputs → with one bias per gate. PyTorch's nn.LSTM keeps separate input and recurrent biases, so count . # Why it fixes vanishing gradients In a plain RNN the backward chain multiplied ⋅ W at every hop and collapsed to ~0. In an LSTM the cell-state's backward term is roughly just the forget-gate value . If the network learns to hold that gate near 1, the gradient flows back across many steps almost undimmed. The gates create a near-multiplication-free highway for the gradient. # Stacking layers Stack LSTMs by feeding one layer's hidden-state sequence as the input sequence to the layer above. The wrinkle vs. a plain RNN stack: each layer carries two lines sideways through time — the cell state and the hidden state — but only is passed upward to the next layer. The belt is private to its layer and never leaves it. So depth and time stay orthogonal: and flow left-to-right within a layer; only flows bottom-to-top across layers. Top layer's is read for predictions. num_layers in PyTorch's nn.LSTM builds this for you. # 30-second answer An LSTM adds a long-term cell-state belt alongside the short-term hidden state, and three sigmoid gates (forget = erase, input = write, output = read). The belt carries memory by keep-and-add rather than overwrite, so both information and gradients survive long sequences. It does not change the loss ( cross-entropy stays the same) — only the memory-update machinery. # See also Recurrent Neural Networks — the base cell LSTM upgrades Gated Recurrent Unit — the leaner cousin (1 memory, 2 gates) Cross-Entropy Loss · Gradient Descent Transformers Attention — what replaced RNNs for most sequence tasks

title: Gated Recurrent Unit
text: A GRU is a streamlined LSTM : same core trick (gated, mostly-additive memory so gradients survive), but with one memory line instead of two and two gates instead of three. Fewer parameters → trains faster, needs less data, often just as good. # The setup No separate cell state — just one memory vector — and two sigmoid gates. # The two gates Update gate ( ) — the main one. A single slider doing the forget and input jobs together: toward 1 = keep old memory, ignore new; toward 0 = drop old memory, take in new. Keeping is the opposite of adding (if you keep 70%, you take 30% new). Holding it near 1 across steps is what preserves long-range memory and the gradient. Reset gate ( ) — decides how much of the past to ignore when drafting the new candidate memory. Lets the cell start fresh when the current input begins something new and old context would be noise. One step in words: reset gate decides how much past to fold into a candidate new memory → update gate decides how much of that candidate to swap in versus how much old memory to keep. # Forward math (defined bottom-up) Symbols: squashes to (a dial), to (signed content), = elementwise multiply, ​ , x t ​ ] = concatenation, each = a learned matrix. is the single memory state. Define the two dials and the candidate first — each reads ​ , x t ​ ] : Update dial ​ = σ ( W z ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much old memory to keep Reset dial ​ = σ ( W r ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much past to use when drafting Candidate t ​ = tanh ( W h ​ [ r t ​ ⊙ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ] ) — note the past is filtered by ​ before drafting Then blend old memory and candidate with the single update dial: ​ = z t ​ ⊙ h t − 1 ​ + ( 1 − z t ​ ) ⊙ h ~ t ​ (PyTorch convention: near 1 keeps the old memory.) Gradient: the leading term is ​ ∂ h t ​ ​ ≈ diag ( z t ​ ) , so holding ​ ≈ 1 keeps the gradient highway open — same additive trick as the LSTM, with one dial instead of separate forget/input gates. Params (one layer, PyTorch-style): three gates/candidate linear layers on concatenated → with one bias each. PyTorch's nn.GRU keeps separate input and recurrent biases, so count . # Inside one GRU cell Inputs ​ and ​ feed both gates and the candidate. The reset gate filters the past before the candidate is drafted; the update gate blends candidate vs. old memory at the very end. Convention here matches the note and PyTorch: z near 1 keeps the old memory , so the candidate gets weight . Some textbooks flip this; the math is identical, only the label on the dial moves. (Caveat: the candidate above is the original Cho form ; PyTorch applies the reset gate after the hidden matmul: ​ x + b in ​ + r ⊙ ( W hn ​ h + b hn ​ )) .) # The step, as a sequence # Stacking GRUs Real models rarely use one layer. You stack them: the hidden-state sequence from layer 1 becomes the input sequence to layer 2, and so on. Two directions of information flow, and they don't mix: Sideways (through time): each layer keeps its own hidden state and passes it to its future self at the next timestep. Layer 1 and layer 2 each have a separate memory line. Upward (through depth): at each timestep, a layer's output is fed as the input to the layer above it. Lower layers tend to pick up short, local patterns; higher layers compose them into longer-range structure. Only the top layer's outputs are usually read for predictions. More layers add representational depth but cost compute and can overfit on small data — same tradeoff as stacking anything. num_layers in PyTorch's nn.GRU does exactly this stacking for you. # LSTM vs GRU LSTM GRU Memories 2 (cell + hidden) 1 (merged) Gates 3 (forget, input, output) 2 (update, reset) Params more fewer Strength slight edge on very long / complex sequences faster, leaner, less data Neither changes the loss ( cross-entropy ). In practice: try both, pick by validation. GRU is a sensible default for speed or limited data; LSTM when sequences are long and complex. # 30-second answer A GRU merges the LSTM's two memories into one and uses two gates: an update gate (keep-old vs take-new in a single dial) and a reset gate (how much past to use when forming the candidate). Same gradient-saving idea as the LSTM, with less machinery. # See also Long Short-Term Memory — the fuller version Recurrent Neural Networks — the base cell both upgrade Cross-Entropy Loss · Gradient Descent Transformers Attention — what replaced RNNs for most sequence tasks

title: Graph Neural Networks
text: A GNN learns from data that lives on a graph — entities (nodes) wired together by relations (edges) — instead of a grid (images, CNNs ) or a sequence (text, RNNs ). The core trick is message passing : each node repeatedly updates its own vector by mixing in its neighbors' vectors. Stack rounds and a node sees everything within hops. # The setup A graph is nodes plus edges. Every node starts with a feature vector ​ (its raw attributes). The model learns from the features and the wiring — that's the whole reason to reach for a graph model rather than a plain MLP over the features alone. Three things a GNN can predict, depending on where you read out: node level — a label per node (fraud user, spam page) edge level — does a link exist / what kind (recommendation, knowledge graph) graph level — one label for the whole graph (molecule property) # Message passing — the engine Let ( k ) ​ be node 's vector after layer , with ( 0 ) ​ = x v ​ . One layer is three functions: Message — for each neighbor , build a message ​ = MSG ( h u ​ , h v ​ , e uv ​ ) , where ​ is an optional edge feature. Aggregate — collapse all neighbor messages into one vector with a permutation-invariant operator (sum, mean, or max — the result can't depend on neighbor order): ​ = AGG ({ m u → v ​ : u ∈ N ( v )}) . Update — fold the aggregate back into the node: ( k ) ​ = UPDATE ( h v ( k − 1 ) ​ , a v ​ ) . Every architecture below is just a different choice of these three functions. # GCN — the equation worth memorizing = σ ( D ~ − 1/2 A ~ D ~ − 1/2 H ( k − 1 ) W ( k ) ) = A + I — adjacency with self-loops (so a node includes itself). — diagonal degree matrix of . — the only learned parameter in the layer; — a nonlinearity (ReLU). Per node: ( k ) ​ = σ ( u ∈ N ( v ) ∪ { v } ∑ ​ d ~ v ​ d ~ u ​ ​ 1 ​ W ( k ) h u ( k − 1 ) ​ ) So GCN's message weight is pure geometry ( v ​ d ~ u ​ ​ ) — no learned per-edge importance, which is its main weakness. The symmetric normalization down-weights high-degree hub neighbors and keeps the operator's eigenvalues real and bounded (which both stabilizes training and, as below, causes oversmoothing). # GAT — learn the weights Replace the fixed coefficient with a learned attention weight ​ : ( k ) ​ = σ ( u ∑ ​ α v u ​ W h u ( k − 1 ) ​ ) , α v u ​ = ∑ w ​ exp ( e v w ​ ) exp ( e v u ​ ) ​ , e v u ​ = LeakyReLU ( a ⊤ [ W h v ​ ∥ W h u ​ ] ) Now the weight depends on the content of the two nodes, not just structure. Essentially transformer -style attention where the adjacency matrix is the attention mask. Usually multi-head. # GraphSAGE — the scalable template ( k ) ​ = σ ( W ⋅ [ h v ( k − 1 ) ​ ∥ AGG ({ h u ( k − 1 ) ​ }) ] ) It concatenates self with the neighbor aggregate (keeps node identity), and samples a fixed number of neighbors instead of using all — that's what makes it run on billion-edge graphs and work inductively on unseen nodes. # GIN — maximally expressive ( k ) ​ = MLP ( k ) ( ( 1 + ϵ ) h v ( k − 1 ) ​ + u ∈ N ( v ) ∑ ​ h u ( k − 1 ) ​ ) Uses sum , not mean or max, on purpose: mean can't tell from , max can't tell from . Only sum is injective over a multiset (preserves counts). This is the link to the Weisfeiler-Lehman test — GIN hits the 1-WL expressiveness ceiling. Sum is needed to reach the 1-WL ceiling; mean or max fall below it. # The three side by side A spectrum: structure decides everything (GCN) → content decides (GAT) → preserve maximum structural info (GIN). Cost: GCN ≈ GIN GAT; expressiveness order is GCN GAT/GraphSAGE GIN (for structure). None dominates: GAT often wins on feature-rich graphs, GIN on molecules, GCN is a shockingly hard baseline for the compute. # Depth, outputs, and oversmoothing One layer = see direct neighbors; two layers = neighbors of neighbors. Depth = reach. Then pool the final embeddings into the right readout head. Oversmoothing (the reason GNNs stay shallow, 2–4 layers): strip weights/nonlinearity and a layer is repeated multiplication by = D ~ − 1/2 A ~ D ~ − 1/2 , so layers k H . The eigenvalues of live in with the leading one at exactly , so every other component is shrunk by → 0 . All node embeddings collapse toward the dominant eigenvector — they become indistinguishable. This is why just add layers (which works for CNNs/transformers) actively hurts here. Residual connections, normalization, and jumping-knowledge layers fight this. Oversquashing — a related failure: a node's exponentially growing receptive field gets crammed into a fixed-size vector, so long-range dependencies get lost. # Training: losses, activations, batching There is no special GNN loss . The GNN produces embeddings; a readout head turns them into predictions, and the loss follows the head and task level (see Cross-Entropy Loss ). Node / graph classification — cross-entropy (softmax + CE for multi-class, sigmoid + BCE for binary/multi-label). In the transductive setting, compute the loss only over labeled training nodes even though message passing uses the whole graph. Regression (molecule property, ETA) — MSE or MAE / Huber. Link prediction — the one with a GNN-specific flavor. Score a candidate edge from the two embeddings (dot product ⊤ ​ h v ​ or an MLP on ​ ∥ h v ​ ] ), then train with negative sampling + BCE or a margin/ranking loss (BPR, max-margin). # Negative sampling Link prediction has possible pairs but only a few million real edges, so almost everything is a non-edge . You can't compute the loss over all negatives (intractable + hopelessly imbalanced — predict no edge everywhere and score 99.9999%). Instead, for each positive edge sample a handful of negatives (typically 1:1 to 1:5 ), usually by fixing and drawing a random it isn't linked to. Train the scorer to output high for real edges, low for sampled fakes . Same trick appears in word2vec (avoids a full-vocab softmax), recommendations/retrieval, and contrastive learning. The detail interviewers probe: Hard negative mining — sample negatives the model currently scores high (plausible fakes) for a stronger gradient than uniform-random easy negatives. Frequency/degree-based sampling (word2vec used freq ) to avoid over-sampling popular nodes. False-negative noise — a sampled negative may be a true-but-missing link; usually tolerated because it's rare. One-liner: negative sampling approximates an impossibly large negative set with a small representative (or deliberately hard) sample, turning all-vs-all into positive-vs-few-negatives. # Activations Nothing exotic. ReLU is the default between layers. LeakyReLU is a fixed architectural choice inside GAT's attention scoring ; ELU is a common GAT alternative. At the head: softmax (multi-class), sigmoid (binary / multi-label / link probability), linear (regression). The aggregator (sum/mean/max) is the pooling operator, not an activation, and must stay permutation-invariant. # The engineering gotchas Normalization — vanilla BatchNorm is awkward (batch = variable-size set of nodes/graphs); use LayerNorm , GraphNorm , or PairNorm (PairNorm is designed to fight oversmoothing ). Deeper GNNs = normalization + residuals + jumping-knowledge. Self-loops — = A + I so a node keeps its own features in the aggregation. Pooling for graph-level tasks — sum vs mean has the same expressiveness tradeoff as AGG (sum keeps size/count, mean normalizes it away); GIN recommends sum. Mini-batching is not row-slicing — either neighbor sampling (GraphSAGE) or subgraph batching (Cluster-GCN, GraphSAINT) for graphs too big for memory. Edge features — plain GCN/GAT use node features only; thread ​ through the message function (general MPNN ), or use R-GCN for typed edges in knowledge graphs (one weight matrix per relation). Optimizer — just Adam, nothing GNN-specific. # Heterogeneous and temporal graphs Heterogeneous graphs have several node and edge types (users, items, shops; clicks, purchases). A single shared weight matrix treats them all alike, so models give each type its own parameters: R-GCN uses one matrix per relation, and heterogeneous attention variants add type-specific projections and attention (HGT does this per node and edge type; HAN aggregates along hand-chosen meta-paths, i.e. typed paths such as user-item-user). The cost is more parameters per rare type, so sparse relations may need weight sharing or basis decomposition. Temporal / dynamic graphs have edges and nodes that appear over time. Two common framings: a sequence of snapshots (a static GNN per snapshot plus a recurrent or attention layer across time), or a continuous-time event stream (TGN-style models keep a per-node memory updated on each event, with time encodings). The main pitfall is leakage: train/validation/test splits must be chronological, and neighbors sampled for a prediction at time may only use edges before . # Use cases production Recommendations — Pinterest PinSage (GraphSAGE on the pin–board graph) is the classic deployed example; Uber Eats, Alibaba similar. Fraud / abuse — fraud rings are graph structure; isolated features miss them. Payments, marketplaces. Molecules / drug discovery — graph-level property prediction on molecular graphs. Maps / logistics — Google used a GNN for ETA prediction over the road graph. Knowledge graphs — link prediction, entity resolution (R-GCN handles typed edges). # Where they fail Oversmoothing / oversquashing — limits depth and long-range reach (above). Scalability — neighbor explosion: a -hop neighborhood can be most of the graph. Sampling helps but adds variance. Dynamic graphs — most GNNs assume a static graph; real graphs change constantly, and serving fresh embeddings is a real eng problem. Often don't beat simpler baselines — a tuned MLP + hand-engineered graph features frequently matches published GNN wins. If the signal is in node features, not topology, a GNN is overkill. Always benchmark a non-graph baseline first. # Metrics Depends on the task level (see Precision Recall , ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC ): Node / graph classification — accuracy, F1, AUC-ROC, AUC-PR (use PR for fraud — heavy class imbalance). Link prediction — AUC plus ranking metrics: Hits@k, MRR (mean reciprocal rank), MAP. Recommendation — Recall@k, NDCG@k, MRR. Regression (molecules, ETA) — MAE, RMSE. # One-line recall A GNN layer only chooses how to weight a neighbor (MSG), how to combine weighted neighbors (AGG), and how to fold that into the node (UPDATE). GCN fixes weights by degree, GAT learns them by content, GraphSAGE samples + concatenates, GIN sums and proves that's maximal. Everything else is plumbing. # See also Convolutional Neural Networks — convolution on a grid; GNN generalizes it to arbitrary graphs Transformers Attention — GAT is attention masked by the adjacency matrix Gradient Descent — how the weights are trained ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC · Precision Recall — the classification metrics above Cross-Entropy Loss — the usual node/graph classification loss Recommender Systems Home

title: Activation Functions
text: Say it in 30s: Without nonlinear activations, stacked linear layers collapse to one linear map. Activations bend the representation between affine layers so MLPs can approximate complex functions. ReLU ( ) is the default for hidden layers in feedforward nets; GELU/SiLU dominate transformers; softmax turns logits into a probability simplex at the output. Pick init to match the activation (He for ReLU, Xavier for tanh). Key points Sigmoid ) : = σ ( 1 − σ ) ; output gates, binary logits historically; vanishes in deep stacks. Tanh: zero-centered sigmoid; still saturates; occasional RNN gates. ReLU: if else ; derivative 0 or 1; fast; watch dying ReLU. Leaky ReLU / GELU / SiLU: non-zero or smooth negative slope; GELU in transformers. Softmax ​ = e z i ​ / ∑ j ​ e z j ​ : multi-class head; pair with cross-entropy . The math ( x ) Sigmoid ) − 1 ( x ) = σ ( 1 − σ ) ≤ 0.25 x ReLU if , else Leaky ReLU if , else slope GELU , often computed as ​ ( x + 0.044715 x 3 )) ) SiLU Softmax ​ = e z i ​ / ∑ j ​ e z j ​ : Jacobian ​ / ∂ z j ​ = p i ​ ( δ ij ​ − p j ​ ) (off-diagonal negatives — why CE on logits is stable). Nonlinear activations prevent depth from collapsing to one affine map. Common follow-ups / traps Why not linear activations? → ​ ( W 1 ​ x + b 1 ​ ) + b 2 ​ is still one affine map—no added capacity. Softmax + MSE for classification? → Wrong pairing; use cross-entropy on logits for stable gradients. See depth: Training Neural Networks (§Activation functions). Related: PyTorch , Logistic Regression .

title: Backpropagation
text: Say it in 30s: Backpropagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation on the network's computational graph: you evaluate the forward pass once, then apply the chain rule backward from the scalar loss to every parameter. For an -layer net with one output loss, reverse mode costs forward + backward passes versus for naive forward-mode per parameter—so it's the standard way to train deep nets. Key points Each node stores values from the forward pass; backward messages are ∂ L ​ multiplied along edges (chain rule). Shared weights (e.g. tied embeddings) sum gradients from all uses. Frameworks ( PyTorch ) build the graph implicitly; loss.backward() triggers reverse mode. See TensorGym notes for tensors + autograd. Vanishing/exploding gradients are a depth problem of backprop, not a bug in the algorithm—see Vanishing Exploding Gradients . Common follow-ups / traps Why not compute ∂ L ​ by finite differences? → Works in tiny nets; forward passes, unusable at scale. Is backprop the same as gradient descent? → No: backprop computes ; the optimizer uses it to update weights. See depth: Training Neural Networks (§Backpropagation). Related: Activation Functions , Loss Functions , Cross-Entropy Loss .

title: Vanishing & Exploding Gradients
text: Say it in 30s: Deep nets multiply Jacobians layer by layer. If typical singular values are below 1, gradients shrink exponentially in depth (vanishing—early layers don't learn); above 1, they explode (NaNs, unstable training). Saturating activations (sigmoid/tanh) vanish; ReLU helps but dead neurons and poor init still hurt. Fixes: He/Xavier init, residuals, normalization, gradient clipping, and shallower paths for signal. Key points Backprop through depth roughly scales like L ​ ∂ h ( l − 1 ) ∂ h ( l ) ​ —spectral norm of per-layer Jacobians matters. Vanishing: sigmoid derivative ; tanh saturates with derivative at large ; deep MLPs with either stall. Exploding: large weights + deep chain → overflow. He (ReLU): ​ ; Xavier (tanh/sigmoid): ​ + n out ​ ) . Residual: = h ( l ) + F ( h ( l ) ) gives a gradient highway through identity. clip_grad_norm_(params, max_norm) caps global norm before the optimizer step—standard in RNNs and LLM training. Common follow-ups / traps Is ReLU enough? → Helps a lot but doesn't remove vanishing entirely (dead ReLUs, very deep nets still need residuals + norm). Clip by value vs by norm? → Norm clipping preserves direction; value clipping can distort the update vector. See depth: Training Neural Networks (§Vanishing and exploding gradients). Related: Activation Functions , Backpropagation , LSTM .

title: Optimizers: SGD, Momentum & Adam
text: Say it in 30s: SGD takes steps (often on mini-batch gradients). Momentum accumulates velocity for smoother descent; Nesterov looks ahead before measuring the gradient. Adam adaptively scales each parameter's step using running estimates of gradient mean and variance, with bias correction early in training. AdamW fixes a subtle bug: decoupled weight decay shrinks weights directly instead of adding an L2 term into Adam's adaptive denominator. Key points SGD: ​ = w t ​ − η t ​ g t ​ , where ​ = ∇ L B t ​ ​ . Momentum: ​ = β v t ​ + g t ​ , ​ = w t ​ − η v t + 1 ​ . Nesterov: evaluate at ​ − η β v t ​ . Adam: ​ = β 1 ​ m t − 1 ​ + ( 1 − β 1 ​ ) g t ​ , ​ = β 2 ​ v t − 1 ​ + ( 1 − β 2 ​ ) g t 2 ​ ; t ​ = m t ​ / ( 1 − β 1 t ​ ) , t ​ = v t ​ / ( 1 − β 2 t ​ ) ; update t ​ / ( v ^ t ​ ​ + ϵ ) . AdamW: same Adam update, then (weight decay not folded into ). Default starting points: SGD+momentum for CV CNNs after tuning; Adam/AdamW for transformers and fast prototyping. Common follow-ups / traps Why warmup with Adam? → Early , v ^ are noisy; small avoids huge steps before EMAs stabilize—critical on transformers . Adam vs SGD generalization? → Adam often trains faster; well-tuned SGD+momentum sometimes generalizes better on vision—don't treat Adam as universally optimal. See depth: Training Neural Networks (§Optimizers). Related: Gradient Descent , Vanishing Exploding Gradients , PyTorch .

title: BatchNorm vs LayerNorm
text: Say it in 30s: BatchNorm normalizes each feature across the batch (per channel in CNNs), then applies learned scale/shift . It speeds training and acts like mild regularization, but batch statistics make train and eval differ—you must switch modes. LayerNorm normalizes across features within each example, so it works for batch size 1 and sequence models. Transformers mostly use LayerNorm or RMSNorm; GroupNorm is the CV fix when batches are tiny. Key points BatchNorm (train): = ( x − μ B ​ ) / σ B 2 ​ + ϵ ​ , + β , with ​ , σ B ​ from the current mini-batch. BatchNorm (eval): use running EMA accumulated during training— not the current batch. model.eval() enables this. LayerNorm: normalize over the hidden dimension for each token/sample independently—no cross-example dependence. RMSNorm: like LayerNorm without mean centering: divide by RMS only; common in LLMs for speed. Small batches: BatchNorm stats are noisy; prefer GroupNorm (normalize channel groups per spatial location) or LayerNorm. The math BatchNorm (per channel ): = ( x − μ B ​ ) / σ B 2 ​ + ϵ ​ , + β ; ​ , σ B ​ are mean/variance over batch axis (and spatial for ). Eval: replace ​ , σ B ​ ) with EMA running stats. LayerNorm on : reduce over hidden dim (per token). RMSNorm: ) + ϵ ​ (no mean centering). GroupNorm: split the channels into groups and, per sample (never across the batch), normalize over the group's channels plus . Axes cheat sheet (CNN ): BN reduces over ; GN over inside each sample; transformers : LN/RMSNorm reduce over . Common follow-ups / traps Why does my BN model degrade at inference? → Forgot eval() , or train/eval mismatch; running stats not updated if you never called train() during fit. Pre-LN vs Post-LN? → Pre-LN (norm before sublayer) stabilizes deep transformers ; Post-LN is original but harder to train without warmup. See depth: Training Neural Networks (§Normalization). Related: Vanishing Exploding Gradients , Self-Attention .

title: Dropout
text: Say it in 30s: Dropout randomly zeroes activations during training with probability , which prevents co-adaptation of neurons—like training an ensemble of thinned nets that share weights. Use inverted dropout : keep each unit with prob and multiply survivors by so the expected activation matches eval. At test time, dropout is off and you use the full network without scaling. Key points Training mask ; activation = h ⊙ m / ( 1 − p ) (inverted form). Typical : 0.2–0.5 on hidden layers; often lower or none on input/output. model.train() applies dropout; model.eval() disables it—same discipline as BatchNorm. Complements weight decay and data augmentation; less common in modern transformers (replaced partly by stochastic depth, LayerNorm, and huge data). The math Inverted dropout: mask , = m ⊙ h / ( 1 − p ) . Per unit, j ​ ] = h j ​ because ​ ] = 1 − p . Conditional on ​ , j ​ ) = 1 − p p ​ h j 2 ​ — extra noise during training. On a linear model, dropout on inputs is related to a data-dependent ridge-like penalty (not identical to fixed ​ ). MC dropout: keep random masks at test time and average predictions to approximate Bayesian model averaging. Common follow-ups / traps Do you scale at test time by ? → No if you used inverted dropout during training (PyTorch default in nn.Dropout ). Can dropout hurt a small dataset? → Yes—can underfit; reduce or drop dropout on the last layers. See depth: Training Neural Networks (§Regularization). Related: Overfitting Underfitting , Regularization .

text: Transformers, how LLMs are trained and aligned, how they are served, how RAG grounds them, and how to evaluate them. # Chapters Transformers Attention — the architecture LLM Training: Pretraining, Fine-Tuning Alignment — how the weights get made LLM Inference: Decoding, KV Cache Serving — how tokens get generated cheaply Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) — grounding answers in your data LLM Evaluation — knowing whether any of it works # Concept cards (owned here) Self-Attention Tokenization: BPE, WordPiece SentencePiece Decoding Strategies KV Cache LoRA Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning RLHF vs DPO Embeddings Vector Search Hallucination # See also (from other areas) Precision Recall — retrieval quality in RAG (Evaluation) Ranking Metrics — recall@k, MRR, NDCG for the retriever (Evaluation) Training Neural Networks — Adam, warmup, LayerNorm, mixed precision (Deep Learning) Cross-Entropy Loss — the pretraining objective (Objectives Losses) # If asked how does an LLM work Tokenize → embed → stack of attention + FFN blocks with residuals and LayerNorm → next-token softmax, trained with cross-entropy on trillions of tokens, then SFT and preference tuning. At inference, prefill the prompt, then decode token by token reading a growing KV cache. # If asked how do you eval an LLM Split into reference-based (BLEU/ROUGE/exact match), reference-free (LLM-as-judge), RAG-specific (faithfulness, context relevance), and human evals. title: Transformers & Attention
heads: Embeddings, logits, and the output head
BERT and GPT pretraining in one glance
text: Attention is all you need — if you can explain what that actually means. The transformer replaced RNNs as the default sequence architecture because self-attention reads the whole context in parallel instead of compressing it through a bottleneck hidden state step by step. This chapter builds the mechanism from first principles: scaled dot-product attention and masks, multi-head blocks, the residual FFN stack, positional encodings, encoder vs decoder families, complexity and efficient variants, then a numeric toy and PyTorch snippet. By the end you should sound like someone who has implemented a layer, not just imported transformers . What you'll be able to say after this chapter Contrast the RNN bottleneck with attention’s direct path between any two positions — and name the ) price. Write scaled dot-product attention with tensor shapes and justify ​ ​ scaling. Explain multi-head attention , projection parameters per layer (biases aside), and what different heads buy you. Walk through a transformer block (residuals, Pre-LN vs Post-LN, 4× FFN, GELU/SwiGLU) and why position is not optional. Place BERT / GPT / T5 on the encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder map and state their pretraining objectives . Name FlashAttention , sparse/window attention, and MQA/GQA as answers to cost and KV memory. # Why attention instead of recurrence An RNN passes a fixed-size hidden state ​ down the sequence. Information from token 1 reaches token only by surviving matrix multiplies and nonlinearities — the vanishing-gradient story in the RNN chapter is exactly bottleneck + sequential depth . Transformers delete the recurrence: every position can look directly at every other position in one layer via a learned similarity. RNN (unidirectional) Self-attention Path length between positions and steps through in one layer (all pairs computed) Parallelism over sequence Poor — step needs ​ Strong — all positions in one matmul wave Memory per layer hidden state ) attention weights (scores), activations Inductive bias Order and locality via recurrence Permutation equivariant without position — you must inject order Training long contexts on GPUs favors attention’s matmul parallelism; serving favors anything that shrinks the term or KV footprint ( KV cache , GQA, FlashAttention) — topics in LLM inference . Memory hook RNN = one hallway, message whispered person-to-person. Attention = everyone in the room hears everyone at once — louder, costlier, but nothing gets whispered away. Interview angle Weak: Transformers use attention instead of LSTM. Strong: recurrence forces sequential depth for long-range credit assignment and caps parallelization; self-attention trades that for all-pairs connectivity at d ) compute and explicit memory of pairwise weights. Rapid fire — Why attention RNN: shared weights over time, hidden bottleneck, vanishing long-range signal. Attention: direct pairwise routes, full-sequence parallel matmuls. Cost moves from sequential steps to attention map. Without position, attention is permutation equivariant — order must be added ( tokenization still defines discrete units). Foundation for GPT (decoder), BERT (encoder), T5 (both). Hooks to LSTM / GRU as gated fixes RNN never fully solved at scale. # Scaled dot-product attention Given token representations packed as rows of ​ , learn linear maps to queries, keys, values: ​ , K = X W K ​ , V = X W V ​ with ​ , W K ​ , W V ​ ∈ R d model ​ × d k ​ (often ​ = d model ​ in single-head form). Shapes: is ​ ; are ​ ; is ​ (typically ​ = d k ​ ). Attention output: ​ ​ Q K ⊤ ​ + M ) V is : row scores how much position attends to each key. Softmax is row-wise; multiply by ( ​ ) → output ​ . # Why divide by ​ ​ If components of and are roughly independent with mean 0 and variance 1, each dot product k = ∑ j = 1 d k ​ ​ q j ​ k j ​ has variance ​ (sum of ​ unit-variance products). Large magnitude logits push softmax into extreme one-hot regions where gradients vanish. Scaling by ​ ​ re-normalizes logits to variance — the original Transformer paper’s argument; it is the standard interview derivation. # Masks Add ​ to logits before softmax (0 = keep, large negative = block): Mask type Purpose Typical pattern Causal (autoregressive) Position may not attend to Upper triangle Padding Ignore padded batch slots Mask keys where token = PAD Encoder-decoder Decoder queries attend to encoder keys PAD mask on encoder side Causal masking is what makes a decoder-only stack a legal density model over sequences ( MLE / next-token cross-entropy ). Shape trap is , not . Saying attention is is wrong — the quadratic term is the score matrix unless you use sparse/linear attention. Interview angle If asked to write attention on a whiteboard, write shapes under every symbol and mention the mask. Missing ​ ​ is a yellow flag; confusing ​ with ​ per head in multi-head setups is a red flag. Rapid fire — Dot-product attention from with learned projections. Scores , scale ​ ​ for stable softmax. Output = weights . Causal mask for GPT-style generation; padding mask for batches. Complexity d k ​ ) for scores + d v ​ ) for weighted sum. Cross-attention: from one stream, from another (T5 decoder). # Multi-head attention One head learns one similarity pattern. Multi-head attention (MHA) runs heads in parallel with smaller ​ = d v ​ = d model ​ / h , concatenates, and projects: ​ = Attention ( Q W Q ( i ) ​ , K W K ( i ) ​ , V W V ( i ) ​ ) , MHA ( X ) = Concat ( head 1 ​ , … , head h ​ ) W O ​ What heads buy you: different subspaces can specialize (syntax vs position-local vs rare-token lookup); empirically heads are interpretable but not guaranteed — some attend to delimiters, previous token, or coreference. # Parameter count With heads and ​ dimension, the four projection matrices ​ , W K ​ , W V ​ , W O ​ are each effectively ​ × d model ​ (implemented as one fused matmul). 2 ​ weights per attention sublayer, ignoring biases — the canonical interview number. (FFN below often dominates: 2 ​ for 4× expansion.) Variant KV heads Effect MHA Full quality, largest KV cache MQA 1 All Q heads share one — minimal cache GQA Groups of Q heads share one KV head — Llama-2/3 default compromise Memory hook 4d² for attention projections; 8d² for FFN (up + down). When someone asks where do the parameters live? , say FFN + attn, not LayerNorm. Rapid fire — Multi-head Split ​ across heads. Concat + ​ mixes heads. 2 ​ attn params (no bias). Heads = parallel relation types; not all interpretable. MQA/GQA shrink KV for inference , not training FLOPs for full attention during prefill. # The transformer block A standard layer (Pre-LN variant, common in GPT-2+): flowchart TB X[Input X] -- LN1[LayerNorm] LN1 -- MHA[Multi-Head Self-Attention] MHA -- ADD1[Residual +] X -- ADD1 ADD1 -- LN2[LayerNorm] LN2 -- FFN[FFN: up proj → activation → down proj] FFN -- ADD2[Residual +] ADD1 -- ADD2 ADD2 -- Y[Output] Sub-layer 1: ​ = X + MHA ( LN ( X )) (Pre-LN) or ​ = LN ( X + MHA ( X )) (Post-LN, original Transformer). Sub-layer 2: ​ = Y 1 ​ + FFN ( LN ( Y 1 ​ )) . FFN (per token, same weights everywhere): ​ ϕ ( W 1 ​ x + b 1 ​ ) + b 2 ​ ​ ∈ R d model ​ × d ff ​ , ​ ∈ R d ff ​ × d model ​ with ​ = 4 d model ​ classic. is GELU in GPT/BERT lineages; SwiGLU (gated linear unit with SiLU) in Llama/Mistral: ​ ) ⊙ SiLU ( x W 3 ​ ) with a third matrix — more params, strong quality. Pre-LN vs Post-LN: Pre-LN trains deeper stacks more stably (gradients skip around LN); Post-LN was the original paper default. Production decoders are mostly Pre-LN. See normalization layers . Interview angle What's in a block? Residual + (Pre-)LN + MHA + residual + (Pre-)LN + 2-layer FFN. Two residuals → two gradient highways. FFN is per-position MLP — no cross-token mixing; only attention mixes tokens. Rapid fire — Block MHA mixes tokens; FFN transforms each token. Residuals + LN (Pre-LN dominant). FFN width 4×, GELU or SwiGLU. layers stacked. Output head: linear to vocab for next-token CE. Ties to activations , training stability. # Positional information Self-attention on alone is permutation equivariant : shuffling rows of and shuffles outputs the same way — the model cannot know word order. Positions must be injected . Method Idea Used in Sinusoidal Fixed waves at dimension pairs Original Transformer, some encoders Learned Trainable position embedding table GPT-2, BERT RoPE Rotate by position-dependent angles in complex pairs Llama, Mistral, most modern LLMs ALiBi Add linear bias to attention logits Some long-context models RoPE bakes relative position into the dot product (attention between and depends on ), extrapolates better than absolute learned positions when extended context is finetuned. ALiBi needs no position embedding table — bias slopes per head. Memory hook Attention without position is a bag of tokens. Position = how you break permutation symmetry. Rapid fire — Position Equivariance → must add order. Absolute (sinusoidal, learned) vs relative (RoPE, ALiBi). RoPE = industry default for decoders. Extrapolated context length is a train + architecture question, not just bigger cache. # Encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder Architecture Attention pattern Pretraining objective Example Encoder-only Bidirectional (no causal mask) Masked LM — predict masked tokens BERT Decoder-only Causal self-attention Next-token prediction (CLM) GPT Encoder-decoder Encoder bidirectional; decoder causal + cross-attention to encoder Span corruption / denoising T5, BART BERT sees full context; good for classification/embedding, not native autoregressive generation without extra machinery. GPT is the standard generative LLM stack; scales with CLM + alignment . T5 frames everything as text-to-text; cross-attention lets decoder queries pull encoder memory ( RAG echoes this pattern). Interview angle Can we use BERT to generate? — not autoregressively as trained; you'd need a separate head or architecture. Why is GPT decoder-only? — CLM + causal mask = simple scaling recipe for open-ended generation. Rapid fire — Families Encoder = understand (bidirectional). Decoder = generate (causal). Enc-dec = conditional generation. Objectives: MLM, CLM, span denoise. Maps to embeddings (encoder) vs chat (decoder). # Complexity and efficient attention Naive attention: compute ( d k ​ ) and multiply by ( d v ​ ) → d ) time, ) memory for materialized scores (training often needs dropout on weights). Approach What it does Sparse / local window Each token attends to neighbors — Longformer, BigBird Linear attention Kernel trick or low-rank approximations — sub-quadratic, different inductive bias FlashAttention Exact attention, IO-aware tiling — fewer HBM round-trips, not an approximation MQA / GQA Fewer KV heads — saves [[kv-cache FlashAttention does not change the math; it changes how matmuls hit GPU memory hierarchy — critical for long-context training and prefill. Sliding-window attention (e.g. Mistral): each token attends to the previous tokens plus optional global tokens — compute. Quality depends on whether your task needs rare long-range jumps in one hop. Grouped-query attention recap: query heads, KV head groups; each group of queries shares one head. Shrinks KV by vs MHA — the serving win in inference , not a change to the attention formula on paper. When interviewers ask how do we get to 128K context? , the honest answer is stacked : RoPE/ALiBi extrapolation, window + global patterns, FlashAttention for tractable exact blocks on GPU, and sometimes sparse retrieval for the tail ( RAG ) — not a single trick. Rapid fire — Efficiency d ) is the villain for long . Sparse = inductive bias; Flash = systems win on exact attn; GQA/MQA = inference KV. Speculative/decode tricks live in inference chapter . # Embeddings, logits, and the output head Token ids index rows of an embedding matrix ​ . The stack of transformer blocks maps with ​ . For language modeling , the next-token distribution at position uses the same embedding matrix as output projection (weight tying): ​ = H t ​ E ⊤ (plus bias sometimes omitted). Shapes: ​ is ​ ; ​ is — the dominant memory term for huge vocabs at the last layer only. Training computes all positions in parallel with a causal mask, so position predicts token ​ . That is self-supervised CLM matching self-supervised pretraining in the foundations chapter. Fine-tuning for classification often swaps the head for a task-specific linear layer on a chosen token ([CLS] in BERT, last token in GPT-style). Go deeper (optional) Mixture-of-experts (MoE) FFNs replace dense ​ , W 2 ​ with routed experts — params scale up but active FLOPs per token stay closer to a dense layer. Interview mention when discussing how billion-parameter models can be cheap per token. Rapid fire — Embeddings in and (often) out. Causal LM head at each position. Tied weights save params. Tokenization defines . Cross-entropy over vocab at train; decoding at inference. # Cross-attention (encoder-decoder) In T5-style stacks, encoder outputs ∈ R n enc ​ × d ; decoder hidden states ∈ R n dec ​ × d build from the decoder and from the encoder: , H enc ) = softmax ( d k ​ ​ Q dec ( K enc ) ⊤ ​ + M pad ​ ) V enc Decoder self-attention stays causal; cross-attention is fully connected to non-pad encoder positions. Shapes: attention map is ​ × n enc ​ — linear in encoder length, not quadratic in decoder alone. This is the same primitive as retrieval-conditioned models: encoder (or retrieved chunks) supplies memory; decoder queries it ( RAG at inference often skips cross-attn and concatenates into the prompt instead). Interview angle What attention does T5's decoder use? — causal self-attention on the target, then cross-attention into encoder representations, then FFN — two attention sublayers per block in the original design. Rapid fire — Cross-attention from decoder, from encoder. Padding mask on encoder keys. Lets conditional generation without causal blur on the source. Analog to memory interface in seq2seq before transformers replaced RNN encoders. # Worked example (toy numbers) Two tokens, ​ = 2 . Suppose after projections: 0 ​ 0 1 ​ ] , K = [ 1 1 ​ 0 1 ​ ] , V = [ 1 3 ​ 2 4 ​ ] Scores / 2 ​ : Row 0: ​ = 1/ 2 ​ , ​ = 1/ 2 ​ → equal logits → softmax . Row 1: , → scaled ​ ] → softmax favors key 1. Weights mixes value rows per query position. With causal mask, row 0 could only use key 0 (mask position 1 to ), changing the mix. This is the entire mechanism — only scale and grow. # Stacking depth identical blocks compound mixing: after layers, each token's representation can depend on paths through attention graphs (with residuals, direct low-frequency paths persist too). Depth buys iterated re-routing of information; width ( ​ ) and heads buy parallel relation types. Interviewers sometimes ask why not one huge attention layer? — depth + residuals approximate iterative refinement; also historical trainability (Pre-LN depth). Connection to training neural networks : same SGD/Adam story, but attention layers lack the RNN's explicit time-unrolled Jacobian product — long-range gradient paths can be shorter through a single attention hop, which helped replace LSTMs at scale before LSTM -class inductive bias was fully abandoned. # BERT and GPT pretraining in one glance BERT (encoder-only): sample positions, replace with [MASK] (or later whole-word masking), predict original token from bidirectional context. Training signal is denoising; you do not factorize ​ ) as a causal product. Fine-tune with task heads. GPT (decoder-only): maximize n − 1 ​ lo g p ( x t + 1 ​ ∣ x ≤ t ​ ) with causal mask — pure CLM (same objective as predicting ​ from the hidden at position in §Embeddings). Scaling this objective with data and parameters is the GPT-3/4 story. Alignment (SFT, RLHF, DPO ) sits on top of a CLM base. T5: random span corruption — spans replaced with sentinel tokens; decoder predicts corrupted spans. Unifies NLU/NLG as text-to-text. Trap BERT is generative — it models ​ ∣ context ) but not a left-to-right joint without autoregressive finetuning. # PyTorch sketch import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def scaled_dot_product_attention ( Q, K, V, mask= None ): # Q, K: (batch, heads, seq, d_k); V: (batch, heads, seq, d_v) d_k = Q.size(- 1 ) scores = torch.matmul(Q, K.transpose(- 2 , - 1 )) / (d_k ** 0.5 ) if mask is not None : scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0 , float ( -inf )) weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=- 1 ) return torch.matmul(weights, V) Fused kernels (FlashAttention) replace this naive triplet in production; the math matches. Interview trap Forgetting .transpose(-2, -1) on , applying softmax over the wrong dimension, or using unscaled logits because softmax fixes it — softmax does not fix vanishing gradients when logits are huge. # Common interview traps Trap Correct response Attention replaces FFN Both needed: MHA mixes tokens, FFN processes each position Transformer is d ) per layer for standard attention BERT and GPT are the same stack Masking + objective + use case differ More heads always help Diminishing returns; GQA trims heads for serving Positional encoding is optional Without it, set semantics only Interview angle Strong candidates connect to RNNs (bottleneck), to PyTorch shapes, and to production (GQA, Flash, prefill vs decode ). Weak candidates recite Q K V with no scaling or mask story. # One-page summary Concept The one thing to remember vs RNN Parallel all-pairs routing; pay d ) instead of sequential bottleneck Attention / d k ​ ​ ) V ; causal + padding masks ​ ​ Dot-product variance ​ ; scale keeps softmax in gradient-friendly range Multi-head subspaces; proj params per attn layer Block Pre-LN → MHA → residual → Pre-LN → 4× FFN → residual Position Break permutation equivariance; RoPE dominant in modern LLMs BERT / GPT / T5 Encoder MLM / decoder CLM / enc-dec denoise Efficiency FlashAttention (exact, IO-aware); sparse/window; MQA/GQA for KV # Related Recurrent Neural Networks Self-Attention Tokenization KV Cache LLM Inference LLM Training Alignment Embeddings Vector Search Normalization Layers PyTorch Cross-Entropy Loss Maximum Likelihood Estimation

title: LLM Training: Pretraining, Fine-Tuning & Alignment
heads: After pretraining: SFT and instruction tuning
Preference data and the reward model (RLHF stage 1)
RLHF stage 2: PPO with a KL anchor
DPO: preferences without an explicit RM
Choosing: full fine-tune vs LoRA vs prompting vs RAG
text: From next-token prediction to models people actually want to talk to. Modern chat LLMs are not one training run—they are a pipeline : self-supervised pretraining on web-scale text, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on instructions and demonstrations, then alignment that reshapes behavior toward helpful, honest, harmless responses. This chapter walks the objectives, the scaling math interviewers quote, and the alignment stack (RLHF, DPO, and cousins). It also covers when to full fine-tune vs LoRA vs prompt vs RAG , plus the distributed-training and memory accounting you need to reason about billion-parameter runs. What you'll be able to say after this chapter State the pretraining objective, link perplexity to average cross-entropy , and name what the data pipeline must fix (dedup, filtering, mixture). Contrast Kaplan vs Chinchilla scaling and quote compute FLOPs and the ~ 20 tokens/param recipe. Order the post-pretrain stages: SFT → preference optimization (RLHF or DPO) and say what breaks at each step. Write the Bradley–Terry reward-model loss, the PPO + KL picture, and the DPO loss—and explain why DPO removes the explicit reward model. Compute LoRA parameter savings for a layer and choose among full FT, LoRA, prompting, and RAG . Estimate VRAM for training as ~ 16 bytes/param (mixed precision + Adam) and name data / tensor / pipeline parallelism and ZeRO/FSDP. # Pretraining: next-token prediction at scale Intuition. Pretraining teaches a transformer to compress language: given prior tokens, predict the next one. No human labels—every token is a label. That is self-supervised learning in the sense of Fundamentals : the supervision signal is manufactured from the text itself. The objective is standard causal language modeling. For tokens ​ , … , x T ​ , ​ = − T 1 ​ t = 1 ∑ T ​ lo g p θ ​ ( x t ​ ∣ x t ​ ) This is token-level cross-entropy against a one-hot target—the same MLE story as maximum-likelihood-estimation , summed over the vocabulary. Perplexity is the human-readable cousin: ​ ) If average cross-entropy is 2.0 nats, PPL : the model is as surprised as if it were choosing uniformly among equally likely tokens at each step. Lower is better; PPL only compares models that share the same tokenizer and eval corpus. Memory hook Perplexity = exp(cross-entropy). Say bits per token in interviews only if you converted to ​ . Interview angle Weak: GPT predicts the next word. Strong: causal LM is joint density factorization ​ p ( x t ​ ∣ x t ​ ) trained by token CE; perplexity is the held-out average surprise. Architecture details live in Transformers Attention and Self-Attention ; here we care about data , compute , and what capability actually emerges. # Data pipeline: dedup, filter, mix Raw web text is poisonous without surgery. Production pipelines typically: Crawl normalize — HTML stripping, language ID, boilerplate removal; Tokenization defines the unit of supervision. Deduplication — exact (hash) and fuzzy (MinHash/SimHash) dedup removes copy-paste and mirrors that otherwise dominate gradients. Quality filtering — heuristics (length, symbol ratio), classifier scores, perplexity-under-a-small-LM filters drop low-quality pages. Mixture design — blend web, books, code, Wikipedia, etc. with tuned sampling weights; the mixture shifts the personality of the base model. Bad dedup inflates benchmark scores without real capability; bad filtering leaves toxicity and PII that later alignment must sand down. Batching and curriculum (ops detail). Pretraining packs variable-length sequences into fixed contexts with padding or packing (concatenate short docs with attention masks). Packing improves GPU utilization. Some runs use curriculum (easy→hard) or stage mixtures (ramp code fraction)—effects are modest versus data volume and dedup. Optimizer is usually AdamW with warmup + cosine decay; stability matters more at 100B+ scale than the exact schedule name. Tokenizer coupling: the same bytes→tokens map defines both the loss target and the perplexity unit. Comparing PPL across tokenizers (BPE vs SentencePiece, different vocab sizes) is an apples-oranges error in interviews. Common mistake Treating pretraining corpora as more is always better without dedup. Kaplan-era runs sometimes under-trained huge models; Chinchilla reframed the tradeoff (next section). # Scaling laws: Kaplan vs Chinchilla Kaplan et al. (OpenAI, 2020): loss scales as a power law in model size , dataset size (tokens), and compute . With data held relatively fixed, bigger models win—if you can pay the FLOPs. Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., DeepMind, 2022): for a fixed compute budget , the compute-optimal frontier balances and . Rule of thumb: train on about tokens (order-of-magnitude; exact constant depends on architecture and loss). Many 70B models were historically under-trained relative to their parameter count; Chinchilla says shrink the model and feed it more tokens instead. Compute estimate. One training step over tokens on an -parameter model costs roughly The factor 6 counts forward + backward through the dense transformer (matmul-heavy); constants vary with activation checkpointing, MoE sparsity, and hardware utilization. Interview use: given and a FLOPs budget, back-solve ; given Chinchilla, check whether your token count is in the right ballpark. Lens Emphasis Practical takeaway Kaplan Scale with compute Big models need proportionally more data than early runs used Chinchilla ~20 tokens/param at iso-compute For a fixed training budget, a smaller model on more tokens beats a big under-trained one; production models deliberately go far past 20 tokens/param because inference cost scales with , not # Emergent abilities: caveat Plots of benchmark jumps at certain scales are seductive but controversial . Many emergent curves are metric artifacts (discrete accuracy on small test sets) or reflect evaluation noise. Smooth intrinsic losses improve gradually; capability thresholds depend on how you measure. In interviews: acknowledge scale helps, but don't claim mystic phase transitions as settled science. Rapid fire — Pretraining Objective: causal LM = average token cross-entropy. PPL . Data: dedup + filter + mixture. Kaplan: power laws in , , . Chinchilla: ~20 tokens/param at iso-compute. Training FLOPs . Emergent abilities: treat skeptically—metrics and smooth loss often disagree. Pretrain is self-supervised next-token MLE ( Fundamentals §self-supervised). # After pretraining: SFT and instruction tuning Base models complete text; users want models that follow instructions . Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) / instruction tuning finetunes on pairs—often thousands to millions of curated examples plus synthetic data from stronger teachers. Loss is the same token CE, but only on response tokens (prompt tokens masked in the loss). This teaches format, tool-use syntax, refusals, and tone. SFT is still supervised ERM ( Empirical Risk Minimization ) with a narrower distribution. SFT alone does not encode human preferences between two valid answers—that is the alignment stage. It also does not inject fresh factual knowledge reliably; for facts, see RAG or targeted fine-tune. Interview angle What's the difference between pretrain and SFT? — distribution shift : pretrain mimics the internet; SFT mimics user-assistant conversations. Same loss, different data mask and mixture.* Memory hook SFT = same CE, mask the prompt, train the assistant turn. # Alignment: RLHF, DPO, and alternatives Alignment optimizes preferences : which completion humans (or rubrics) like better, not just which completion exists in the dataset. # Preference data and the reward model (RLHF stage 1) Collect pairs ​ , y l ​ ) : prompt , chosen ​ , rejected ​ . Train a scalar reward model ​ ( x , y ) with the Bradley–Terry pairwise loss: ​ = − E ( x , y w ​ , y l ​ ) ​ [ lo g σ ( r ϕ ​ ( x , y w ​ ) − r ϕ ​ ( x , y l ​ ) ) ] This is logistic regression on the margin between scores—identical in spirit to pairwise ranking losses in Loss Functions . The RM is usually a pretrained LM with a value head; it must generalize to completions unlike its training pairs or the next stage collapses. # RLHF stage 2: PPO with a KL anchor Policy ​ is the language model. PPO (or similar policy-gradient methods) increases expected reward ​ ( x , y )] while penalizing drift from a frozen reference ​ (typically the SFT checkpoint): max ​ E y ∼ π θ ​ ​ [ r ϕ ​ ( x , y ) ] − β E y ∼ π θ ​ ​ [ lo g π ref ​ ( y ∣ x ) π θ ​ ( y ∣ x ) ​ ] The KL term is the practical fix for reward hacking : without it, policies exploit RM blind spots—overlong answers, sycophancy, formatting tricks, or degenerate text that still scores high. trades improvement vs staying on-distribution. Challenges: RM bias, PPO instability, expensive online rollouts, careful batching of generations. RLHF vs DPO card contrasts this with direct preference optimization. PPO in one paragraph (interview depth). Policy-gradient RL maximizes reward but has high variance. PPO clips the ratio ​ ( θ ) = π θ ​ ( a t ​ ∣ s t ​ ) / π old ​ ( a t ​ ∣ s t ​ ) so large policy updates that would wreck the KL budget get attenuated. In LLM RL, actions are tokens (or whole responses treated as macro-actions), states are prompts plus partial generations, and the value baseline reduces variance. Production stacks batch thousands of completions per step—generation dominates wall-clock. That is why simpler offline losses (DPO) gained traction when reward is purely preference-shaped. Reward hacking examples worth naming: endless bullet lists, agreeing with false premises, repeating the prompt, or exploiting RM's love of length and markdown. Mitigations: length penalties, diverse RM ensembles, held-out human spot checks, and KL—not optional decoration. # DPO: preferences without an explicit RM Direct Preference Optimization reparameterizes the optimal reward so the policy update becomes a binary classification on preference pairs. With hyperparameter (same role as KL strength), ​ = − E ( x , y w ​ , y l ​ ) ​ [ lo g σ ( β lo g π ref ​ ( y w ​ ∣ x ) π θ ​ ( y w ​ ∣ x ) ​ − β lo g π ref ​ ( y l ​ ∣ x ) π θ ​ ( y l ​ ∣ x ) ​ ) ] Why it matters: no separate RM training loop, no PPO rollout memory—just weighted log-likelihood ratios on chosen vs rejected. The implicit reward is ​ π θ ​ ​ . Failure modes: sensitivity to , mismatch between SFT and preference data, and offline bias (no on-policy exploration). Method Reward model? Optimization Pros / cons RLHF Explicit ​ PPO + KL Flexible rewards; fragile, costly DPO Implicit via ​ Preference CE Simple, stable; offline, less flexible IPO Implicit Squared margin on pref. Mitigates overfitting to noise KTO Implicit Unpaired good/bad labels Data cheaper than pairs ORPO — SFT + odds-ratio pref. Single-stage shortcut # RLAIF, constitutional AI, verifiable rewards RLAIF replaces human labels with AI judge labels—scale with model bias risk. Constitutional AI uses written principles to critique/revise outputs before preference learning. RL with verifiable rewards shines when correctness is checkable: unit tests for code ( HumanEval -style), math answer keys, tool outcomes. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) compares multiple sampled completions per prompt and updates relative to the group mean—useful when scalar RM is weak but pass/fail verifiers exist. # Alignment data hygiene Preference datasets are smaller than pretrain corpora but leakier : duplicate prompts, annotator skew, and positional bias (humans prefer first shown answer). Decontaminate against benchmarks, balance task types, and track inter-annotator agreement . For DPO, keep the reference ​ fixed to the SFT snapshot you intend to stay near—retraining SFT without re-collecting preferences desyncs the implicit KL target. Where SFT ends and alignment begins: SFT teaches existence of a good answer format; alignment teaches relative quality among plausible answers. Skipping SFT and jumping to DPO on a cold base model usually fails because ​ is not yet a competent assistant. Go deeper (optional) Process supervision (reward each reasoning step) and rejection sampling fine-tuning sit between SFT and full RL—worth mentioning if the interviewer cares about reasoning models. Rapid fire — Alignment Bradley–Terry RM: ​ − r l ​ ) . PPO: maximize reward minus KL to ​ . KL fights reward hacking. DPO: sigmoid on ​ ) ; no explicit RM. IPO/KTO/ORPO: unpaired or one-shot variants. RLAIF/constitutional: AI labels + principles. Verifiable rewards + GRPO when you can check answers. Evaluate with LLM Eval and human side-by-side prefs. # Parameter-efficient fine-tuning Full fine-tuning of a 70B model is often prohibitive. PEFT trains a small adapter while freezing most weights. # LoRA For a frozen weight ​ × d in ​ , LoRA adds a low-rank update: = W + r α ​ B A , B ∈ R d out ​ × r , A ∈ R r × d in ​ Train only and ; ​ , d out ​ ) . Scaling keeps effective step size stable as rank changes. Common targets: ​ , W K ​ , W V ​ , W O ​ in each attention block; sometimes FFN projections for hard domain adaptation. See LoRA Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning . Parameter count (worked). Per adapted matrix: ​ = r ( d in ​ + d out ​ ) vs full ​ = d in ​ d out ​ . Example: ​ = d out ​ = 4096 , : ​ = 16 × 8192 = 131 , 072 vs N full ​ = 16 , 777 , 216 Four attention matrices per layer: trainable parameters. A 32-layer stack: LoRA params vs if you trained all attention weights— ~0.8% of attention alone, and ≪0.3% of a 7B model. Savings multiply because optimizers touch only trainable tensors. # QLoRA, adapters, prompts QLoRA stores base weights in 4-bit (NF4) with LoRA adapters in fp16/bf16—fits large-model tuning on one consumer GPU. Adapters insert small bottleneck FFNs per layer. Prefix / prompt tuning learns soft prompt embeddings; zero weight delta, least expressive but cheapest. Interview angle Strong LoRA answer includes where (Q/K/V/O), rank , , and a numeric savings estimate—not just low-rank matrices. # Choosing: full fine-tune vs LoRA vs prompting vs RAG Need Lean toward Why New stable facts at scale [[retrieval-augmented-generation RAG]] or refresh pretrain Behavior / tone / format SFT, LoRA, or DPO Preference and instruction data Domain style (legal, medical) LoRA or full FT on domain corpus Representation shift; watch forgetting One-off task description Prompting / few-shot Zero train cost; context-limited Max quality on narrow task, plenty GPU Full fine-tune Highest capacity; catastrophic forgetting risk Catastrophic forgetting: aggressive FT erases general capabilities. Mitigate with small LR, early stopping, elastic weight consolidation, mixing general replay data, or LoRA that leaves base weights intact. Distillation: train a smaller student to match a larger teacher (soft labels or hidden states). Used for cost at inference after you have an aligned teacher—pairs with LLM Inference economics. Two common patterns: Response distillation — teacher generates targets; student minimizes CE to those tokens (plus optional KL to teacher logits for richness). Preference distillation — teacher ranks pairs; student trained with DPO-style loss using teacher as judge—cheap scale before human polish. Distillation is not alignment by itself: if the teacher hallucinates, the student learns fluent falsehood faster. # Continued pretraining and mid-training Between base pretrain and SFT, some recipes run continued pretraining on higher-quality mixtures (more books, code, math) without instruction formatting—sometimes called mid-training . Goal: lift reasoning and domain knowledge before spending instruction tokens. This is still causal LM, not RL. It competes with RAG for facts: mid-training bakes knowledge in but freezes at cutoff; RAG stays fresh. Interview angle How would you add new product docs? — index + RAG for daily updates; optional LoRA on support tone; full continued pretrain only if the domain is the product (e.g., medical base model). Rapid fire — PEFT choices LoRA: = W + ( α / r ) B A ; params ​ + d out ​ ) per matrix. QLoRA: 4-bit base + fp16 adapters. Adapters/prefix: even fewer params. RAG for facts; FT/DPO for behavior. Forgetting: mix replay or use LoRA. Distill for cheap deployment. # Distributed training and memory math Billion-parameter training never fits one GPU. Three orthogonal splits: Data parallelism — same weights, different micro-batches; all-reduce gradients (DDP). Tensor parallelism — split individual layers across devices (Megatron-style). Pipeline parallelism — split layers across stages; micro-batches fill the pipeline bubble. ZeRO / FSDP shard optimizer states, gradients, and weights across ranks so no single GPU holds full Adam state—critical for large models without tensor parallel. # Bytes per parameter (training) Mixed-precision AdamW commonly allocates, per trainable parameter: Component Typical storage Weight (fp16/bf16) 2 B Gradient (fp16) 2 B Adam , (fp32) 8 B Master weight (fp32, optional) 4 B Interview rule of thumb: bytes/param for fp16/bf16 weights + fp16 grads + fp32 Adam ( ); bytes/param when you also keep an fp32 master copy of weights (the usual mixed-precision recipe—matches × 16 ≈ 112 GB below). Activation memory adds separately (scales with batch, sequence length, layers; gradient checkpointing trades compute for activations). Example: 7B full FT × 16 ≈ 112 GB optimizer + weights + grads alone—why ZeRO-3 or LoRA is mandatory on 8×80GB. Worked Chinchilla sanity check. Suppose parameters and Chinchilla suggests tokens (~140B). Training FLOPs × 1.4 × 1 0 11 ≈ 5.9 × 1 0 21 FLOPs. A 7B model trained on only 30B tokens is badly under-trained for its size. Going the other way is common and deliberate: Llama 2 7B saw ~2T tokens (~290 tokens/param), over-training relative to Chinchilla because a smaller model that is cheaper to serve is worth extra training compute. Chinchilla answers best loss per training FLOP , not best model to deploy . Sequence parallelism checkpointing also matter for long contexts: activations scale with batch layers seq hidden; gradient checkpointing recomputes activations in backward pass to shave memory at ~20–30% extra compute. For inference serving memory see KV Cache —training and serving budgets differ. Optimizer details: Optimizers , Gradient Descent , Training Neural Networks , PyTorch . Memory hook Train memory ≈ 16× params (bytes) for Adam in mixed precision—before activations and KV for long seq. Rapid fire — Distributed memory Data parallel: shard batches, sync grads. Tensor parallel: shard layers. Pipeline: shard depth. ZeRO/FSDP: shard optimizer states. FLOPs . VRAM + activations. Checkpoint activations to save memory. Inference memory is different (see KV Cache ). # One-page summary Concept The one thing to remember Pretrain objective Causal LM = token CE; PPL Data Dedup + quality filter + curated mixture Kaplan vs Chinchilla Iso-compute: ~20 tokens/param; don't under-train giants Compute FLOPs for training throughput planning SFT CE on assistant tokens only; teaches format, not prefs RLHF RM Bradley–Terry: ​ − r l ​ ) RLHF policy Max reward KL vs ​ ; stops hacking DPO Sigmoid on ​ ) ; no explicit RM LoRA ; ​ + d out ​ ) params/matrix Fact vs behavior RAG/facts; FT/DPO/behavior Forgetting Replay, small LR, LoRA, or multi-task mix Distributed DP + TP + PP; ZeRO/FSDP shard optimizer Train memory ~16 bytes/param (mixed Adam) + activations # Related Transformers Attention Self-Attention Tokenization Cross-Entropy Loss Loss Functions RLHF vs DPO LoRA Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) LLM Eval LLM Inference Training Neural Networks Optimizers Gradient Descent Regularization Fundamentals

title: LLM Inference: Decoding, KV Cache & Serving
heads: Multi-turn, chat templates, and context growth
text: Training teaches the distribution; inference is how you sample from it under latency and dollar constraints. Autoregressive transformers generate one token at a time. The forward pass you studied for training is only half the story: serving adds scheduling , memory accounting , and a policy for choosing each token. That simple loop hides a systems problem: decoding policy (greedy vs nucleus), KV cache memory, prefill vs decode bottlenecks, batching, quantization, and speculative tricks. This chapter is what ML engineers need after the architecture chapter — enough to reason about vLLM, cost per 1K tokens, and why your 70B model feels fast on short prompts but crawls on long threads. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Describe the autoregressive loop and how it differs from teacher forcing in training. Pick greedy, beam, temperature, top- , top- for a scenario and name repetition penalties. Write the KV cache memory formula and explain GQA/MQA savings. Contrast prefill (compute-bound) vs decode (memory-bandwidth-bound) and TTFT vs ITL . Explain continuous batching , PagedAttention , weight-only INT4 , and speculative decoding at a high level. Name the cost/latency trade-off and mention constrained decoding briefly. # Autoregressive generation Training maximizes ​ lo g p θ ​ ( x t ​ ∣ x t ​ ) with teacher forcing — the model always sees gold prefixes. Inference feeds back its own samples: Encode prompt tokens ​ (may fill KV cache). Sample ​ from ​ ) . Append; repeat until EOS or budget. Each step is one forward pass producing logits ; decoding turns into a token id; the embedding of that id becomes the next input. The objective at train time is cross-entropy / MLE ; at serve time it is latency × quality × cost . Memory hook Training looks ahead with correct homework; inference writes the exam one word at a time and can't erase. Interview angle How does GPT generate? Not it predicts the next word — autoregressive factorization of joint , one conditional per step, with decoding policy and KV cache determining wall-clock. Rapid fire — Autoregressive Chain rule over tokens. One forward per new token at decode. Logits → decoding → append. Teacher forcing only in training. Vocab size sets final linear cost. Hooks: Tokenization , hallucination grows with loose sampling. # Decoding strategies Let ​ be logits for token . Common transforms: Strategy Rule When to use Greedy ​ = ar g max i ​ z i ​ Low-latency drafts, code with grammar hints Beam search Keep top partial sequences MT, summarization (metric-friendly, dull chat) Temperature Softmax on ; sharper Control randomness monotonically with Top- Sample among largest logits Fixed tail cap; still breaks on flat tails Top- (nucleus) Smallest set with cum. prob Chat, creative writing — adaptive width Repetition penalty Down-weight logits of tokens in recent context Reduce loops; can harm list-like facts Sampling vs search: beams optimize approximate joint likelihood of a finished string; i.i.d. sampling at each step does not sample from the sequence joint unless you temper and penalize carefully. For chat products, top- + temperature + repetition penalty is the usual stack; for benchmarks with references, greedy or beam . Trap Lower temperature always more factual — false. It anchors to the model's mode , which can still be wrong confidently ( hallucination ). Interview angle Strong answers pair a strategy with a product constraint : latency (greedy), diversity (nucleus), metric (beam), safety (constrained + low temperature on structured fields). # Beam search (sketch) At step , beam search keeps the top partial sequences by log-probability ​ lo g p ( x s ​ ∣ x s ​ ) . Each beam expands children; prune back to . Complexity scales with and vocab — rarely used in low-latency chat at large .
