Length normalization 1 ​ ∑ lo g p avoids bias toward shorter strings. # Logits processing pipeline (production) Typical order: (optional) repetition/frequency penalties on logits → divide by temperature → top- mask → top- mask → softmax sample or argmax. Penalties are heuristic; they are not in the training loss. See Decoding Strategies card for the 30s version. Rapid fire — Decoding Greedy = fast, repetitive. Beam = quality/latency trade for structured outputs. Temperature scales entropy. Top- adapts to peaked/flat distributions. Penalties fix loops not truth. Mismatch with training (exposure bias) is structural — mitigated by RLHF/ DPO , not decoding alone. # The KV cache For layer , attention needs , V ( ℓ ) for all past positions. Recomputing them each step is ) cumulative work over length . Caching stores past ; each decode step only computes for the new token and appends to cache. Per layer, stored tensors (per batch element): ​ × t × d head ​ Memory estimate (bytes): ​ × d head ​ × seq_len × batch × bytes Factor 2 = store both and . = transformer layers; ​ = KV heads ( in MHA, in MQA, in GQA). Often ​ × d head ​ = d model ​ (same total KV width as MHA). Example sanity check: , ​ = 8 , ​ = 128 , seq = 4096, batch = 1, FP16 (2 bytes): GB per sequence. With full multi-head attention ( ​ = 32 , as in Llama-2-7B) the same context costs GB — GQA's 4× saving, and the reason KV memory, not weights, caps batch size at long contexts. Memory hook 2LKVT — 2 tensors, L layers, KV heads (not Q), T tokens, times width and batch. Interview angle When asked why GQA? , don't say faster attention vaguely — decode is bandwidth-bound reading growing KV; sharing KV heads shrinks memory and bytes moved per token. # Stepping through one decode iteration For token at time (1-indexed after prompt): Embed ​ → run one transformer layer at a time. At layer : compute ( ℓ ) ​ from current hidden; ( ℓ ) ​ , v t ( ℓ ) ​ from current hidden; concatenate ​ , v t ​ along sequence dim to cached ​ , V 1 : t − 1 ​ . Attention for position uses queries at only, but keys/values for — complexity per layer per step → ) summed over generation (hence cache). Final hidden → logits → decode → ​ . Without cache, you'd re-run layers 1.. for all positions each step — L ) forward redundancy. Details: KV Cache card; architecture: Transformers Attention (MQA/GQA). Rapid fire — KV cache Cache only. Q recomputed each step. Memory linear in seq_len. Formula: ​ d head ​ T B × bytes. Quantized KV possible. Prefill fills cache once; decode appends. # Prefill vs decode Two phases in a request: Phase What runs Typical bottleneck Latency metric Prefill All prompt tokens in parallel (causal) Compute (matmul FLOPs on long prompt) Time to first token (TTFT) Decode One new token per forward Memory bandwidth (read full KV each layer) Inter-token latency (ITL) Long prompts: prefill dominates TTFT. Long generations : decode steps add up; each step touches the entire KV history — why context length hurts more at serve than a naive linear in tokens intuition suggests. Throughput (tokens/s) rises with batching multiple requests — until KV memory fills the GPU. Rapid fire — Prefill/decode Prefill = parallel prompt; decode = serial tokens. TTFT vs ITL. Compute-bound prefill, bandwidth-bound decode. FlashAttention helps prefill/training IO; GQA helps decode KV. Continuous batching mixes prefill+decode across users. # Hardware mapping (brief) One decode forward is mostly matrix multiplies + reading KV . Large models use tensor parallelism (split weight columns across GPUs; all-reduce activations) or pipeline parallelism (layer stages). Data parallel duplicates weights for independent batches — distinct from sharding a single 70B. The ML story ties to systems: if ITL is high, profile whether you are KV-bandwidth limited (long context, many users) or compute limited (huge vocab softmax, unquantized weights). PyTorch torch.compile and vendor kernels matter at the margin; KV and batching dominate SaaS economics. Rapid fire — Parallelism TP = split layers/weights across GPUs on one request. PP = stages. DP = replicate for throughput. EP for MoE experts. Pick based on model size vs batch size. # Continuous batching and PagedAttention (vLLM) Static batching waits for the slowest sequence — GPUs idle. Continuous batching (iteration-level scheduling) admits new requests and finishes others between decode steps without draining the whole batch. PagedAttention (vLLM): treat KV cache like virtual memory pages — non-contiguous fixed-size blocks, allocated on demand. Cuts fragmentation when sequences differ in length; enables higher batch utilization. Interview sound bite: KV is dynamic-length per request; paged blocks let the scheduler pack GPUs without reserving max-length rectangles for every slot. Interview angle How would you serve 1000 concurrent chats? — mention batching, max context, KV memory accounting, paged KV, separate prefill/decode queues, and autoscaling on TTFT SLOs. Rapid fire — Serving Continuous batching = dynamic req sets per step. PagedAttention = fragmented KV blocks. vLLM ecosystem standard for OSS serving. Tensor parallel for large models across GPUs. LoRA adapters add memory headroom constraints. # Quantization Type What is quantized Typical use INT8 weight + activation Both Throughput on supported kernels; needs calibration Weight-only INT4/INT8 in linear layers GPTQ, AWQ — shrink memory, matmul in FP16/BF16 accumulate FP8 Weights and/or activations H100-class hardware GPTQ / AWQ — post-training weight quantization with error compensation; AWQ protects salient weights. Trade-off: bandwidth and capacity vs perplexity regression; 4-bit often fine for 70B serve, eval on your tasks. Activation quantization is harder (dynamic ranges); weight-only is the default for LLM inference when people say INT4 model. AWQ vs GPTQ (interview): both are post-training 4-bit weight methods. GPTQ minimizes layer-wise squared error with approximate second-order info (Hessian). AWQ identifies salient weight channels (where activations are large) and protects them during quant — often better perplexity at same bit-width. Neither removes need for downstream eval on your tasks. KV cache quantization (FP8/INT8 KV) is emerging: halves KV bytes with task-dependent quality impact — separate from weight quant. Interview angle Why not train INT4 from scratch? — PTQ on a strong FP16/BF16 checkpoint is cheaper; QAT exists but is heavier. Production path: train bf16 → GPTQ/AWQ → serve with kernels that dequant on the fly. Rapid fire — Quantization Weight-only = smaller, faster load, less KV untouched. GPTQ/AWQ = PTQ recipes. INT4 ≈ 4× weight compression. Watch outliers in layers. Distillation (separate) transfers behavior to smaller dense models. # Speculative decoding and distillation Exposure bias reminder: the model was trained on gold prefixes but tested on its own samples — errors compound. Decoding tricks (nucleus, penalties) mitigate symptoms; RLHF / on-policy fine-tuning ( RLHF vs DPO ) addresses the train–test mismatch in distribution. Speculative decoding: a draft model (small, fast) proposes tokens; the target large model validates them in parallel (one batched forward). Accept tokens while draft agrees with target distribution; on mismatch, resample — exact same distribution as target decoding under standard schemes, lower latency when draft is accurate. Distillation: train a smaller student on teacher logits/outputs — not a runtime trick but a permanent cap-ex swap ( training chapter). Different question from speculative decode at serve time. Interview angle Don't conflate speculative decoding (same model quality, draft speedup) with quantization (approximate weights) or distillation (different model). Rapid fire — Speedups Speculative = draft + verify. Medusa/EAGLE variants learn draft heads. Distillation = offline shrink. RAG adds prefill tokens — hits TTFT and KV, not just param count. # Cost and latency trade-offs Rough mental model for cost per 1K tokens : GPU-hour price ​ Levers: Lever Latency Cost Quality risk Smaller model / quant ↓ ↓ ↑ GQA / shorter context ↓ ITL ↓ memory small Greedy vs nucleus ↓ samples same repetition vs diversity Bigger batch ↑ TTFT tail ↓ $/token none if scheduled well Speculative decode ↓ decode steps extra draft GPU low if draft good SLO framing: interactive chat optimizes TTFT + ITL ; offline batch optimizes $/token . Long input RAG pays prefill on retrieved + prompt tokens — budget context in product design. Rapid fire — Economics Decode steps × batch × model width = wall-clock. KV caps concurrent users. Quant and GQA buy seats on same GPU. Measure on your prompt length distribution, not marketing benchmarks. # Batching math: tokens per second If average output length is ​ and batch size is , sustained decode throughput tokens/s (one token per sequence per step). Prefill adds a one-time cost proportional to prompt length ​ per request. Total GPU-seconds per request scales roughly as: ​ L in ​ + c decode ​ L out ​ Constants absorb width, layers, and quant — exact profiling beats theory. Raising improves ​ amortization until KV fills memory. Memory hook Prefill once, decode many — long answers multiply ITL steps; long prompts hit TTFT once but inflate KV for the whole session. # Adapters at inference ( LoRA ) Low-rank adapters add to frozen weights. Serving implication: either merge LoRA into base weights offline (one graph) or run dual matmuls per layer (base + adapter). Multi-tenant hosts may load hundreds of adapter sets — memory and routing become product problems, not just forward-pass math. Rapid fire — LoRA serve Merge for speed; separate for hot-swapping adapters. Base model quantized once; adapter precision choice affects quality. # Structured output and constrained decoding When outputs must follow JSON, grammar, or tool call schemas, constrained decoding masks illegal logits at each step (finite-state machine, grammar compiler, or bitmask on vocab). Libraries (Outlines, guidance, XGrammar) compile constraints once per request. Brief: reduces post-hoc repair and hallucination -shaped formatting errors; adds CPU-side mask work; still needs a capable base model for semantics. Memory hook Constrained decoding = legal moves only on the logit chessboard each turn. Rapid fire — Structured Mask illegal tokens before softmax. JSON/tool APIs in production. Complements eval schema checks. Not a substitute for validation on side effects (tool execution). # Multi-turn, chat templates, and context growth Chat models wrap user/assistant turns in a template ( |user| , [INST] , etc.) defined at tokenization time. Each new user message re-prefills the full history (unless you cache prefix KV externally). Multi-turn sessions therefore: Grow KV linearly with total tokens in context. Re-run attention over all prior turns on every new user message at prefill — TTFT rises with thread length. Need truncation or summarization policies in product (keep last tokens, summarize middle). Prefix caching (same system prompt across users): if many requests share an identical long system block, some engines cache KV for that prefix and reuse — amortizes RAG-style static instructions. Interview angle Why did my chatbot slow down after 50 turns? — context length and prefill on full history, not model getting tired. Rapid fire — Multi-turn Templates define token pattern. KV stores full visible history. Truncate/slide window/product policy. Shared system prompt cache is a deployment optimization. # Production monitoring (what to chart) Offline perplexity does not predict serve health. Track TTFT p50/p99 , ITL p50/p99 , tokens/s/GPU , KV memory utilization , batch size , and preemption rate on queues. Quality: sample conversations + LLM eval / human review — latency SLOs and quality regressions decouple (quant can hurt one not the other). Rapid fire — Monitoring Separate latency SLOs from quality dashboards. Alert on OOM, queue depth, TTFT spikes. Log prompt/completion token counts per request for cost attribution. # Common interview traps Trap Fix KV cache saves FLOPs in training Training uses full-sequence parallel attention; cache is inference Beam is always better Wrong for open-ended chat; exposure to dull modes INT4 = 4× faster always Speedup = memory bandwidth + kernel support; model-dependent Confusing TTFT with total latency Long outputs: sum of ITLs dominates Forget batch in KV formula Linear in batch — saturation is memory-limited Interview angle System design prompts ( serve Llama 70B to 10k users ): start with KV memory per user × concurrency , then decoding, then quant/parallelism. ML-only answers miss the bottleneck. # One-page summary Concept The one thing to remember Autoregressive One token per forward; sample from ​ ∣ x t ​ ) Decoding Greedy/beam/temperature/top- /penalties — quality–diversity–latency KV cache Store per-layer ; ​ d head ​ T B × bytes GQA/MQA Fewer KV heads → less cache bandwidth Prefill vs decode Prompt parallel (TTFT); tokens serial (ITL, bandwidth) Serving Continuous batching + PagedAttention (vLLM) Quant Weight-only INT4/AWQ/GPTQ for capacity; watch task eval Speculative Draft model proposes, target verifies — same distribution Structured Mask illegal logits each step # Related Transformers Attention Decoding Strategies KV Cache Tokenization Self-Attention LLM Eval LLM Training Alignment Retrieval-Augmented Generation LoRA PEFT Hallucination PyTorch Gradient Descent

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
heads: Building the system: latency and cost
RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context
text: Ground the model in evidence you control instead of whatever it memorized in pretraining. Retrieval-augmented generation answers user questions by retrieving relevant documents, then generating conditioned on that context. It attacks the three production headaches of raw LLMs: knowledge cutoff , hallucination , and unverifiable claims . Done well, you get cite-able answers and cheaper updates than retraining—swap the index, not the weights. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Draw the RAG pipeline from ingestion to grounded answer and name where latency and quality trade off. Choose chunking , embedding training (bi-encoder + InfoNCE), and ANN vs sparse retrieval—and when to hybrid with BM25 and rerank with a cross-encoder. Split evaluation into retrieval (recall@k, MRR, NDCG) vs generation (faithfulness, relevance)—and point to LLM Eval for the full rubric. Diagnose failure modes (bad chunks, wrong docs, lost-in-the-middle) and pick fixes from a systems table. Contrast RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context for facts, freshness, and cost. # Why RAG exists Parametric knowledge in an LLM is implicit , static (training cutoff), and uncalibrated —the model sounds equally sure when wrong. RAG externalizes knowledge into a corpus you can version , audit, and delete. Product wins: Freshness — re-index docs hourly; no full retrain. Attribution — show sources; users trust and verify. Hallucination control — when retrieval is good, you can measure faithfulness to context (see Hallucination ). Cost — updating facts via FT or continued pretrain dwarfs embedding + index maintenance for many enterprise KBs. RAG does not replace alignment or instruction following; it feeds the evidence slot in a prompt assembled by your orchestration layer ( LLM Inference , Decoding Strategies ). Treat the retriever as a recall subsystem with its own SLIs—never as a black box bolted onto an otherwise unchanged chatbot. Memory hook Weights = fuzzy memory. Index = filing cabinet with page numbers. Interview angle Weak: RAG searches Google then GPT answers. Strong: bi-encoder retrieval over chunked embeddings, optional sparse hybrid + cross-encoder rerank, context assembly with faithfulness eval—FT only when behavior must change, not when a PDF updated. # Pipeline overview flowchart LR A[Documents] -- B[Ingest chunk] B -- C[Embed] C -- D[(Vector index)] Q[User query] -- E[Query rewrite / HyDE] E -- F[Retrieve top-k] D -- F F -- G[Rerank] G -- H[Assemble context] H -- I[LLM generate] I -- J[Answer + citations] F -- K[Sparse BM25] K -- L[Hybrid merge RRF] L -- G Stages map cleanly to ownership: data engineering (ingest/chunk), search (embed/index/retrieve), and LLM (prompt + decode). Latency budgets usually spend 30–60% on retrieval+rereank, 40–70% on generation for single-hop QA. # Production concerns beyond the diagram Versioned indexes — blue/green re-embed when the encoder changes; never mix incompatible vector spaces in one index. Access control — filter by tenant_id / ACL at retrieval time; the LLM must never see unauthorized chunks. Caching — embed frequent queries; cache reranker results for head traffic. Observability — log retrieved chunk IDs with each answer for replay when users flag wrong responses. Prompt injection — untrusted docs are attackers; delimit untrusted text, strip instructions, and optionally run a lightweight harmful-instruction detector on retrieved content. Rapid fire — Why shape RAG fixes cutoff, hallucination risk, and missing citations. Cheaper factual updates than FT. Pipeline: ingest → chunk → embed → index → retrieve → (rerank) → prompt → generate. Hybrid adds BM25 for lexical matches. Evaluate retrieval and generation separately ( LLM Eval ). # Ingestion and chunking Ingestion parses PDFs, HTML, tickets, slides into clean text—respect structure (headings, tables) where possible. Metadata (title, section, ACL, timestamp) travels with each chunk for filtering and citations. Chunking is the silent killer of recall. Tradeoffs: Strategy How When it helps Fixed token windows 256–512 tokens, overlap 10–20% Simple baseline; overlap reduces boundary cuts Structure-aware Split on headings / paragraphs Docs, policies, wikis Semantic Embed sentences; merge until similarity drops Variable-density notes Parent–child Small child chunks for search; parent for context Need precise hit + wide context Too small → fragments lose meaning. Too large → dilute embedding, waste context window, bury the answer ( lost-in-the-middle : models under-attend to middle chunks in long prompts). Rule of thumb: start 384–512 tokens with 50–80 token overlap on English prose; shrink for structured logs, grow for legal contracts where sentences chain across pages. Validate by sweeping chunk size on retrieval recall@k—optimum is rarely the first guess. Metadata for filtering — date, product SKU, geography, doc type—lets you run faceted retrieval ( only policies effective in 2024 ) before vector search, improving precision without touching the LLM. Common mistake Embedding entire 10-page PDFs as one vector—retrieval returns the right file but the generator still cannot find the sentence. Memory hook Chunk for the retriever's eye; parent doc for the generator's brain. # Embeddings and indexing # Bi-encoders vs cross-encoders A bi-encoder maps query and document independently: typically cosine after L2-normalization (dot product on unit vectors). Encode all documents offline , store in a vector database—query time is one embedding + ANN search. See Embeddings Vector Search and Two-Tower Retrieval . A cross-encoder jointly encodes through a transformer and outputs a scalar relevance score. Accurate for reranking tens of pairs, impossible for millions without a first stage. # Contrastive training (InfoNCE) Train so positives are close and negatives far. With temperature , ​ = − lo g ∑ k ​ e sim ( q , d k ​ ) / τ e sim ( q , d + ) / τ ​ In-batch negatives are cheap; add hard negatives (BM25 top misses that are wrong) to avoid collapse. Same family as ranking losses in Loss Functions (§embeddings). Domain mismatch (legal vs chat) needs finetune or adapters on your corpus. Embedding API choice: off-the-shelf models (E5, BGE, GTE, OpenAI embeddings) are fine to prototype; production on private jargon usually needs contrastive finetune on , d − ) triples mined from click logs or SME-labeled pairs. Evaluate with the same recall@k slice you will gate in CI. Two-tower symmetry: often (shared weights) for queries and docs; asymmetric towers help when queries are short questions and docs are long passages ( Two-Tower Retrieval ). # Score calibration and thresholds Raw cosine scores are not probabilities. For abstention ( I don't know ), fit a validation score threshold or small calibrator so precision on answered queries meets SLO. Hybrid RRF sidesteps calibration for merging ranks but you still need thresholds for whether to answer at all . # ANN indexes: HNSW, IVF, PQ Exact nearest neighbor does not scale. Approximate methods trade recall for speed: Index Idea Knobs Tradeoff HNSW Graph greedy search M , efConstruction , efSearch High recall, RAM-heavy IVF Cluster buckets, probe few nlist , nprobe Fast at scale; needs training PQ Compress vectors subquantizers Saves RAM; hurts recall Tune until recall@k on a labeled dev set plateaus within latency SLO. # Sparse BM25 and hybrid search BM25 scores lexical overlap—excellent for SKUs, error codes, names dense retrievers miss. Hybrid : run dense + sparse, merge with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) : ∑ ​ k + rank i ​ ( d ) 1 ​ with constant (often 60). No score calibration needed. Recommender Systems intuition: two weak experts, one rank list. # Reranking, query rewriting, HyDE Retrieve top 50–200, cross-encode down to 5–15. Query rewriting expands acronyms or decomposes multi-part questions. HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings): LLM drafts a fake answer, embed that to search—helps lexical mismatch when used cautiously (adds latency + hallucination risk in the draft). Rapid fire — Retrieval stack Bi-encoder: independent ; fast ANN. Cross-encoder: joint; rerank only. InfoNCE with in-batch + hard negs. ANN: HNSW/IVF/PQ recall–latency tradeoffs. BM25 + RRF hybrid. Rerank top-k'. HyDE/rewrite for query drift. # Context assembly and generation Pack reranked chunks into the prompt with clear delimiters , source titles, and (if possible) ordered by relevance with the best chunk near the start or end —not the middle—mitigating lost-in-the-middle. Instruct the model to cite chunk IDs and refuse when context is insufficient. Prompt template sketch (interview whiteboard): System: Answer only from CONTEXT. Cite [id] after each claim. Say insufficient context if needed. CONTEXT: [1] title: …\n text [2] … USER: question Variants add JSON output for downstream apps or force bullet + citation formatting for support macros. Keep system and user roles consistent with how the base model was SFT'd ( LLM Training ). Decoding choices matter: lower temperature for factual extracts; require quotes for high-stakes domains. Chain with tools ( LLM Inference ) when answers need arithmetic or live APIs in addition to RAG. # Open vs closed domain Setting Corpus Retrieval stance Closed Fixed approved KB High precision; abstain aggressively Open web Internet + crawls Hybrid + heavy safety filters Internal + web Blended indexes Namespace separation; never mix ACLs Closed-domain support bots should tune high precision@k even if recall suffers—wrong retrieved policy is worse than I don't know. # Data flywheel Production RAG improves when you log queries, retrieved IDs, clicks, and thumbs-down . Hard negatives for embedding finetune come from retrieved but user rejected. Golden sets grow from escalations. Without this loop, offline recall plateaus while user complaints climb. Rapid fire — Generation ops Delimit CONTEXT; cite IDs; abstain instruction. Best chunks at edges against lost-in-the-middle. Lower temperature for facts. Closed domain = precision over recall. Log retrieval for hard-negative mining. LoRA teaches cite-format, not the facts themselves. Interview angle If they probe context limits: retrieval quality dominates—stuffing 100k tokens of mediocre chunks loses to 8k of reranked gold. # Evaluation Split metrics—conflating them hides whether retrieval or generation failed. # Retrieval On queries with labeled relevant doc IDs: Recall@k — fraction of queries with a hit in top ( Precision Recall ). MRR — focuses on the rank of the first correct doc. NDCG@k — graded relevance; see Ranking Metrics . Improve recall before touching the LLM. Worked retrieval example (conceptual). Ten test queries; relevant doc appears in top-3 for seven queries → Recall@3 = 0.7. If the first relevant doc ranks 1,1,4,2,1,9,1,… positions, MRR averages . NDCG adds graded labels ( partially relevant vs perfect ). Report per-domain slices—support tickets often need higher than executive FAQs. # Generation Reference-free checks aligned with LLM Eval : Faithfulness / groundedness — answer entailed by provided context? Answer relevance — addresses the question? Context relevance — were retrieved chunks on-topic? Human side-by-side still gold for tone; LLM-as-judge scales regression tests. Pair with standard Model Evaluation Validation hygiene: fixed dev/test splits, no query leakage from train chunks, and regression gates in CI when you change embedders. Memory hook Retrieval metrics = did we fetch the right page? Generation metrics = did we read it honestly? # Building the system: latency and cost Typical single-hop Q A serving path (numbers are illustrative): Stage Latency share Cost driver Query embed 5–15 ms GPU batching ANN search 10–40 ms index RAM, efSearch BM25 (optional) 5–20 ms inverted index size Cross-encoder rerank 50–200 ms pairs × GPU LLM generation 0.5–3 s output tokens If reranking dominates, cap candidates (50 not 500) or distill to a smaller cross-encoder. If generation dominates, shorten context (fewer chunks) after you have verified recall— never cut retrieval budget first without metrics. Batch vs stream: retrieval can batch across users; generation often streams tokens. Separate autoscaling: search tier (CPU/GPU hybrid) vs LLM replica pool. # Failure modes and fixes Symptom Likely cause Fix Confident wrong answer Retrieval miss + no abstain Hybrid search, query rewrite, raise , reranker Answer ignores docs Prompt/format; middle placement Delimiters, move best chunk to edges, cite-or-abstain instruction Contradictory sources Stale/conflicting chunks Metadata filters, recency boost, de-dup index Right doc, wrong span Chunk too large Smaller chunks + parent summary Slow p95 Big , heavy cross-encoder Two-stage retrieve→rerank, cache embeddings, HNSW tuning Works in English only Monolingual embeddings Multilingual encoder or translate pipeline Privacy leak ACL not enforced at query Per-tenant filters, doc-level security metadata Rapid fire — Eval failures Recall@k, MRR, NDCG on retrieval. Faithfulness + relevance on generation ( LLM Eval ). Missed retrieval → hybrid + rerank. Ignored context → prompt + lost-in-the-middle placement. Stale index → versioning. ACL at retrieve time, not post-hoc. # Agentic, multi-hop, and GraphRAG Multi-hop RAG iterates: decompose question, retrieve subqueries, aggregate—agent loops tie to tool eval in LLM Eval . A classic pattern is ReAct -style: the model emits a search query, reads chunks, then decides the next hop. Risks: error compounding (wrong hop-1 doc poisons hop-2), cost explosions (each hop = retrieve + LLM), and eval difficulty (credit assignment per hop). Mitigations: max-hop limits, confidence gating ( stop if score threshold ), and logging intermediate queries for human review. GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph (entities, relations) over the corpus for global questions ( themes across 10k tickets ) where flat chunk search fails. Community summaries on graph clusters support questions like what are the recurring outage causes? without retrieving 50 random chunks. Heavier offline build (entity extraction, resolution, graph layout); wins on holistic synthesis over connected evidence, not factoid lookup. Briefly: default to single-hop RAG until benchmarks prove multi-hop; add graphs when queries are inherently relational or require aggregate themes across many documents. Interview angle Design enterprise RAG — narrate ACL-aware ingest, hybrid retrieval, rerank, cite-or-abstain prompt, split eval dashboards, and rollout via offline recall before online A/B—not we'll fine-tune GPT on all PDFs. # RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context Approach Best for Weakness RAG Fresh facts, citations, many docs Retrieval errors; latency; orchestration Fine-tune / LoRA Style, format, domain reasoning patterns Catastrophic forgetting; stale facts; cost ([[llm-training-and-alignment Long context Many docs already in prompt; simpler stack Quadratic attention cost; still attends poorly mid-context; no automatic cite Practical stacks combine : RAG for evidence, modest LoRA for tone, long context for conversation history—not for whole corpora. When long context displaces RAG: code assistants with open files in-repo, multi-turn legal review where the user pastes exhibits, or chat with this one PDF under ~100 pages. When the corpus is many documents, dynamic , or needs citations , RAG remains cheaper and more honest than stuffing context. Fine-tuning complementary role: LoRA on (instruction, grounded answer) pairs teaches citation format and abstention given retrieved text in the prompt—it does not replace the index. Full FT to memorize product specs goes stale the week pricing changes. Go deeper (optional) Compression retrievers (LLMLingua), late interaction models (ColBERT), and learnable sparse-dense hybrids blur the clean bi-encoder story—mention if the role is search ML, not just LLM glue. # ColBERT and multi-vector retrieval (sketch) Classic bi-encoders compress a whole passage into one vector—cheap but lossy. ColBERT keeps a vector per token and scores with a late interaction (MaxSim): match query tokens to document tokens, sum best hits, then aggregate. You store more vectors per doc but retrieve with two-stage pruning. Interview one-liner: ColBERT trades index size for finer overlap signals between query spans and doc spans—strong on keyword overlap inside long passages. # Security checklist for interviewed designs Untrusted content is input — retrieved text can say ignore previous instructions. Sanitize — XML/JSON delimiters; optional secondary classifier on chunks. Grounding eval in CI — faithfulness regression on adversarial chunks that tempt override. Least privilege — retrieval service credentials cannot exfiltrate unrelated tenants. Citation verification — post-check that cited IDs appear in the prompt and support the claim (lightweight string/NLI). These sit alongside model-level alignment ( LLM Training )—RAG security is systems security. Interview closure sentence: I'd ship single-hop hybrid RAG with rerank, cite-or-abstain prompting, split retrieval and faithfulness evals per LLM Eval , and only fine-tune adapters for tone—not for facts. That single sentence shows you understand the full stack end to end, from index freshness to grounded generation. Rapid fire — Advanced security ColBERT: multi-vector late interaction, better span overlap, bigger index. Prompt injection via corpus is real; delimit and test. Citation verify in post-processing. Closed ACL at retrieve. Flywheel: logged rejects → hard negatives. # One-page summary Concept The one thing to remember Purpose Ground answers in an updatable corpus with citations Chunking 256–512 tokens + overlap; structure-aware when possible Encode Bi-encoder + InfoNCE; domain-finetune if needed Search ANN (HNSW/IVF/PQ); tune recall@k vs latency Hybrid BM25 + dense, merge with RRF Rerank Cross-encoder on top 50–200 Context Delimiters; best chunks at edges; cite-or-abstain Eval Retrieval: recall/MRR/NDCG; gen: faithfulness ([[llm-eval vs FT RAG for facts/freshness; FT for behavior vs long ctx Context window ≠ reliable memory over huge paste # Related Embeddings Vector Search Hallucination LLM Eval LLM Training: Pretraining, Fine-Tuning Alignment Two-Tower Retrieval Loss Functions Ranking Metrics Precision Recall Recommender Systems Model Evaluation Validation LLM Inference Decoding Strategies Transformers Attention

title: LLM Evaluation
heads: Paired comparison on the same items
How would you evaluate X? (answer template)
text: Offline scores are cheap lies unless you know what they measure and what they miss. Language models do not output a single correct label; they output open-ended text under prompts you chose, decoded with knobs that inject randomness. LLM evaluation is the discipline of turning that mess into decisions: ship or hold, model A or B, safe enough for this surface. The interview version is not reciting benchmark names—it is naming a hierarchy of evals (cheap regression → benchmarks → judges → humans → online experiments), picking metrics that match the failure mode, and reporting uncertainty so a 0.5-point leaderboard twitch does not fool anyone. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Explain why n-gram scores, perplexity, and static benchmarks each break for instruction-tuned chat models. Design a versioned golden set from production logs without contaminating training or the test pool. Compute pass@k with the unbiased estimator and defend execution-based code eval. Run LLM-as-judge with rubrics, bias probes, and human agreement metrics (κ, Spearman, win-rate/Elo). Split RAG and agent evals into component vs end-to-end, with links to retrieval metrics and faithfulness. Size an offline comparison: confidence intervals on accuracy and ~1,200 paired items for a 2-point lift under McNemar. Close with online guardrails and point to A/B Testing Online Experimentation for causal launch decisions. # Why LLM evaluation is hard Classical model evaluation assumes a fixed label space and a loss you can average. LLMs violate every convenience: Difficulty What breaks Practical consequence Open-ended outputs Many strings are equally good Reference metrics need gold answers or rubrics Multiple valid answers Paraphrase, style, language Exact match punishes correct but differently worded replies Non-determinism Sampling ( temperature , top- ) Same prompt → different scores unless you fix the seed or use greedy decode Prompt sensitivity Small wording changes swing quality You must version prompts with datasets ([[decoding-strategies Distribution shift Prod queries ≠ academic benchmarks High MMLU, low user satisfaction Evaluation is therefore not one number—it is a stack of complementary checks, each trading cost, coverage, and fidelity. flowchart TB U[Unit tests / regression suite] -- B[Offline benchmarks] B -- J[LLM-as-judge] J -- H[Human evaluation] H -- O[Online A/B guardrails] Unit tests / regression suites are tiny, hand-written cases you run on every merge: JSON schema, citation format, refusal on a known jailbreak, “don’t call tool X without user confirm.” They are the CI of LLM products—fast, brittle if neglected, invaluable for catching regressions. Offline benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval, etc.) give broad coverage cheaply but saturate and leak (see below). LLM-as-judge scales subjective quality when humans are too slow—at the cost of judge biases you must measure. Human eval remains the reference for preference alignment ( RLHF vs DPO , LLM Training Alignment ). Online A/B measures what users and revenue actually do—see A/B Testing Online Experimentation . Memory hook Cheap tests catch regressions; benchmarks catch breadth; judges catch nuance; humans catch truth; A/B catches reality. Interview angle Weak: “We’d look at perplexity and BLEU.” Strong: regression suite on every deploy, task-specific golden set with versioning, LLM-judge with position-bias controls, human spot-check on disagreements, powered online test on downstream metric with safety/latency guardrails. Rapid fire — Why hierarchy Open outputs, many valid answers, sampling noise, prompt sensitivity. Eval stack: unit/regression → benchmarks → LLM judge → human → online A/B. No single metric is sufficient. Version prompts with datasets. Prod ≠ benchmark distribution. # Building an evaluation set Metrics are only as honest as the items you score. # Golden sets and production mining A golden set is a frozen collection of (prompt, optional context, reference or rubric) with expected behavior. Sources: Hand-authored — edge cases you know users hit (pricing policy, medical disclaimer). Production logs — sample real queries; stratify by intent, difficulty, language, and failure tags from support tickets. Adversarial buckets — jailbreaks, injection attempts, trick questions with known wrong answers. Turn logs into labels with human annotators or SME review; never auto-label with the model you are shipping. # Stratification and difficulty Report metrics per slice (easy/medium/hard, domain, tool-use vs chit-chat). Aggregate accuracy hides “great on head traffic, catastrophic on refunds.” Use explicit difficulty tags or model-based pre-labeling, then human audit of the hard bucket. # Versioning and contamination Treat prompt template , model checkpoint , judge model , and dataset version as a single artifact. When you fine-tune or distill, scrub training data for benchmark leakage and near-duplicates of your golden set ( data leakage ). Holding out a “private” eval that never touches training is the same golden rule as Fundamentals : test once, honestly. Contamination Public benchmarks appear in pretraining corpora. Leaderboard gains may be memorization, not capability. Prefer held-in-house sets and periodic refresh from fresh prod traffic. Go deeper (optional) For RAG, golden sets need retrieved contexts frozen per question—otherwise you are evaluating generation and retrieval drift in one number. See Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) . # Reference-based text metrics When you have a reference answer , overlap metrics are cheap baselines. They correlate with humans on narrow tasks (short QA, extraction) and fail on creative or long-form generation. Metric What it measures When it works When it lies Exact match (EM) Normalized string equality Single-span answers (e.g. SQuAD-style) Any paraphrase fails Token F1 Token overlap precision/recall vs gold QA with flexible phrasing Synonyms, word order, extra explanation BLEU Weighted n-gram precision vs reference; brevity penalty punishes short outputs MT with close references Rewards generic fluent text; poor on dialogue ROUGE-N N-gram recall vs reference Summarization (cover reference phrases) Ignores coherence and factuality ROUGE-L Longest common subsequence F1 Summary ordering Same factuality blind spot chrF Character n-gram F-score Morphologically rich languages Still reference-dependent BERTScore Cosine similarity of contextual embeddings (per token, matched) Paraphrase-tolerant QA Can score fluent wrong facts highly Interview angle If asked “BLEU vs ROUGE”: BLEU emphasizes precision (did you copy reference n-grams?); ROUGE emphasizes recall (did you cover reference content?). Neither checks truth—pair with execution, retrieval faithfulness, or human/LLM rubrics for hallucination . Detokenize before scoring ( tokenization ); otherwise token F1 is not comparable across models. Rapid fire — Reference metrics EM/F1 for short QA spans. BLEU = n-gram precision + brevity penalty (MT). ROUGE-N/L = n-gram/LCS recall (summaries). chrF = character F1. BERTScore = embedding similarity—better paraphrase, not better facts. All need gold references; weak on open-ended chat. # Code and math evaluation # pass@k and the unbiased estimator For code, draw completions per problem; the problem is solved if any of the first passes unit tests. If of samples pass, the unbiased pass@k estimator (when ) is: n ​ ) ( k n − c ​ ) ​ Worked example: independent samples, pass tests, : 20 ​ ) ( 1 15 ​ ) ​ = 1 − 20 15 ​ = 0.25 For , , : —most problems are solved if at least one of ten tries can succeed when 30% of single draws pass. HumanEval and MBPP report pass@1 with for stable estimates on hard tasks. # Execution sandboxes and extraction Run tests in an isolated sandbox (no network, time/memory caps)—latency and security are part of eval design ( LLM Inference ). Answer extraction matters: models wrap code in markdown or prose; brittle parsers create format sensitivity —measure with and without a canonical extractor. Math : sympy/numeric checks, or LLM graders on equivalence classes; beware LaTeX formatting games. Memory hook pass@k answers: “If my user gets tries, what fraction of tasks succeed at least once?” # Perplexity Perplexity is ) where is average token negative log-likelihood on a corpus—equivalently, the perplexity of a held-out text under the model ( cross-entropy loss ): 1 ​ t = 1 ∑ T ​ lo g p ( x t ​ ∣ x t ​ ) ) Lower perplexity means the model assigns higher probability to the actual next tokens— fluency under the training distribution . Do not compare perplexity across tokenizers —different BPE merges change and the partition of probability mass ( Tokenization ). After instruction tuning, perplexity on web text poorly tracks helpfulness, safety, or factuality ; use task evals instead. Perplexity remains useful for pretraining comparisons on the same tokenizer/vocab and for catching catastrophic corruption after quantization. Rapid fire — PPL PPL = exp(average token CE). Lower = better fit to eval text. Same tokenizer/vocab only. Weak proxy for chat quality post-alignment. Good for pretrain/quant sanity checks. # LLM-as-judge When references are missing or subjective, a stronger model (or ensemble) scores outputs against a rubric. # Modes Mode How Pros Cons Pointwise Rate one response 1–5 on dimensions Simple aggregation Absolute scores drift Pairwise Which of A or B is better? Stable for preferences Needs two samples Reference-guided Score against gold / retrieved context Grounds factuality Needs references Design rubrics with observable criteria (“ cites source,” “arithmetic correct,” “refuses policy violation”) not vague “quality.” Chain-of-thought judging (judge reasons before score) often improves consistency—hide reasoning from the user-facing model. # Known biases and mitigations Bias Symptom Mitigation Position First answer wins in pairwise Swap order , average; reject inconsistent judges Verbosity Longer = better Rubric cap on length; length-normalized pairwise; strip preambles Self-preference Judge favors own family Use third-party judge; blend judges; calibrate on gold Anchoring Early dimension skews later Separate calls per dimension or blind ordering Measure bias with position tests (same pair, swapped), length-matched pairs , and known-answer probes (one response clearly wrong). # Agreement with humans Cohen's κ for categorical ratings (chance-corrected agreement). Spearman / Kendall for rankings across models vs human panels. Win rates and Bradley–Terry / Elo from pairwise outcomes— Chatbot Arena style: update from expected vs actual wins. Disagreements flag items for human adjudication—do not silently average conflicting judges. Interview angle Strong judges answer: which mode (pairwise for prefs), rubric dimensions, swap-order protocol, third-party judge to fight self-preference, κ vs human on a 200-item anchor set, escalate ties to humans. Rapid fire — Judges Pointwise / pairwise / reference-guided. Concrete rubrics + optional CoT. Position → swap average. Verbosity → length controls. Self-preference → external judge mix. Validate with κ, Spearman, win rates, Elo. Disagreements → human. # Meta-evaluation of judges Treat the judge as a model with its own QA bar: Test–retest reliability — same item, same rubric, multiple draws; unstable judges get temperature cuts or structured JSON outputs. Inter-judge agreement — multiple LLM or human judges; low agreement surfaces hard items for adjudication. Adversarial probes — pairs where one response is clearly worse (injected factual error); judges should not tie. Stratified analysis — accuracy of the judge by difficulty, domain, and failure type , mirroring how you slice model metrics. # Human evaluation Humans remain the anchor when stakes are high or labels are subjective: Side-by-side preference — show two completions; pick better (foundation of RLHF preference data). Likert ratings — helpfulness, accuracy, tone on 1–5; use clear anchors (“3 = acceptable, not delightful”). Domain expert review — lawyers, clinicians, finance SMEs judge real workflows, not toy prompts. Red teaming — adversarial sessions probing safety (overlaps with safety evals below). Sample enough items per slice for powered comparisons; blind models when possible to avoid brand bias. Rapid fire — Human meta-eval Side-by-side for prefs; Likert with anchored rubrics; SMEs for domain truth. Judge QA: test–retest, inter-judge agreement, adversarial probes, stratified breakdown. Blinding reduces brand bias. # RAG and agent evaluation # RAG: component vs end-to-end RAG fails in two places— retrieval and generation —so split metrics: Layer What to measure Typical metrics Retriever Did relevant evidence appear in top- ? Recall@ , MRR, NDCG ([[ranking-metrics Generator Faithful to context? On-topic? Faithfulness / groundedness , answer relevance , context precision/recall End-to-end User question answered correctly Human or rubric on final output; cite entity match Faithfulness catches intrinsic hallucination (answer contradicts or adds beyond context); answer relevance catches answers that quote docs but ignore the question. Link generation faithfulness to Hallucination mitigation. # Agents: trajectory vs outcome Agents call tools over multiple steps ( Transformers Attention for long contexts, LLM Inference for latency budgets): Task success — did the user goal complete (ticket filed, chart rendered)? Tool-call validity — right tool, schema-valid args, no hallucinated APIs. Planning quality — sensible decomposition vs circular re-planning; often judged in trajectory eval. Trajectory eval — score each step (plan quality, recovery after error) vs outcome-only (cheap but misses unsafe paths). Step efficiency — solved in 3 steps vs 15 affects cost and user patience. Budgets — cap latency , token cost , and tool side effects as first-class metrics alongside success rate. Failure mode categorization — track rates for hallucination, retrieval miss, planning failure, tool misuse, policy violation—not one aggregate accuracy. Failure mode dashboards feed the next golden-set slice and regression tests. Rapid fire — RAG agents Split retrieval (recall/MRR/NDCG) from generation (faithfulness, relevance). End-to-end for product truth. Agents: success, valid tools, trajectory vs outcome, step count, cost/latency guardrails. # Safety evaluation Safety is not binary “refuse all”— over-refusal breaks product (refusing benign medical FAQs) while under-refusal risks harm. Red teaming — adversarial personas, multi-turn escalation, automated attack generators. Jailbreak / prompt-injection suites — static transcripts plus dynamic tests with untrusted retrieved content (RAG injection). Toxicity / bias — slice by demographic descriptors; measure rates and severity, not single scalar “toxicity score.” Refusal quality — correct refusals on policy violations; false refusal rate on in-scope help requests. Log incidents in prod as new regression cases. Pair offline suites with guardrail metrics online (reports per 1k sessions, escalation rate). Over-refusal Optimizing refusal rate alone teaches models to say “I can’t help” everywhere. Report conditional accuracy: helpfulness given safe queries, refusal given unsafe. # Benchmark literacy (and skepticism) Know the headline benchmarks—and why leaders distrust them alone: Benchmark What it tests Caveat MMLU Multi-subject multiple-choice knowledge Saturating; contamination sensitive HellaSwag Commonsense sentence completion Format hacks; less chat-relevant ARC (Easy/Challenge) Grade-school science MC Narrow reasoning style GSM8K Math word problems Parser/format sensitivity HumanEval / MBPP Code synthesis pass@k depends on ; sandbox discipline MT-Bench Multi-turn dialogue LLM-judge heavy; domain drift Static benchmarks saturate as models train on similar data; leaderboard overfitting chases points without user value. HELM-style reporting—many scenarios, metrics, and calibration slices—is the antidote: report accuracy, robustness, fairness, efficiency together, not one heroic number. Refresh public-facing numbers with private holdouts and prod-sampled evals. Rapid fire — Benchmarks MMLU/ARC/HellaSwag = knowledge/commonsense MC. GSM8K = math. HumanEval/MBPP = code (pass@k). MT-Bench = multi-turn chat. Saturate + leak → trust in-house refresh + multi-metric HELM mindset. # Statistics of evaluation A finite eval set gives a sample of accuracy ​ ; treat uncertainty explicitly ( p-values statistical power , Calibration for probability quality elsewhere). # Confidence intervals on accuracy If of items are correct, Wilson score 95% CI is tighter than naive ​ ± 1.96 p ^ ​ ( 1 − p ^ ​ ) / n ​ . Example: correct → ​ = 0.85 , Wilson interval approximately —about points at . Bootstrap resampling of items also works when metrics are non-smooth (e.g. custom rubric scores). # Paired comparison on the same items Compare models A and B on identical prompts —use McNemar on discordant pairs (B right/A wrong vs A right/B wrong), not two independent proportion tests. Worked sizing: Suppose A is 85% accurate, B is 87% on the same items, with 4% “only B correct” and 2% “only A correct” (discordant rates). For two-sided , 80% power: ​ − p 01 ​ ) 2 ( z α /2 ​ + z β ​ ) 2 ( p 01 ​ + p 10 ​ ) ​ ≈ 0.0 2 2 ( 1.96 + 0.84 ) 2 ⋅ 0.06 ​ ≈ 1 , 176 You need on the order of 1,200 labeled examples to reliably detect a 2 percentage point paired accuracy lift under those discordant rates. (If you evaluated arms on independent random halves of traffic, required per arm is far larger—roughly 4,700+ per model for similar gaps—another reason paired item design wins offline.) # Variance from sampling With , rerun stochastic evals with fixed seeds or report mean ± std over samples. For regression suites, prefer greedy decode ( ) for determinism unless the product is explicitly stochastic. Interview angle When someone cites “85.3% vs 85.1%”: ask , paired or not, CI width, and whether prompts matched . Reject point deltas smaller than the Wilson half-width. # Online evaluation Offline wins do not guarantee prod wins—latency, UX, and user adaptation matter. Complement offline stacks with: Signal What it tells you Thumbs up/down, regenerations Implicit preference; biased by UI placement Edits / copy rate User fixes model output—strong quality signal Downstream KPIs Conversion, resolution time, ticket reopen rate A/B tests Causal lift on primary metric—design in [[ab-testing-and-experimentation Guardrails Latency p99, cost per session, safety incidents, [[precision-and-recall Pre-register primary and guardrail metrics before launch. Offline evaluation screens; online proves value. Rapid fire — Online Implicit feedback is noisy but cheap. Edits = strong dissatisfaction signal. A/B for causality with guardrails. Monitor latency, cost, safety—not just quality thumbs. # How would you evaluate X? (answer template) Use this one-page skeleton in system-design and ML rounds: Objective surface — chat, RAG over KB, agent with tools, code assistant; failure cost (money, safety, brand). Success definition — task success rate, user resolution, cite-or-abstain policy, max latency/cost. Offline stack — regression CI → versioned golden set (sourced how, stratified how) → benchmarks only for screening. Metrics per modality — reference metrics if gold exists; execution for code; retrieval + faithfulness for RAG; tool validity for agents. Human / judge layer — when humans enter, rubric, pairwise vs pointwise, bias controls, κ on anchor set. Statistics — report ​ with CI; paired tests for model comparisons; needed for target MDE. Online — primary KPI, guardrails, experiment duration, rollback triggers. Ops — log prompts/retrieval IDs, refresh eval monthly, contamination hygiene. Memory hook I-O-M-G-H-S-O: Intent, Offline stack, Metrics, Judges, Humans, Statistics, Online. # One-page summary Concept The one thing to remember Why it's hard Open outputs, many valid answer

title: Self-Attention
text: Say it in 30s: Self-attention lets every token attend to every other token in one parallel step: each position builds query, key, and value vectors; scores are dot products scaled by ​ ​ , softmaxed into weights, and used to mix values. There is no hidden state carried forward in time — the memory of the sequence lives entirely in those pairwise weights. Key points Shapes: ; attention output is . Scaled dot-product: / d k ​ ​ ) V ; scaling keeps logits near unit variance as ​ grows. Causal mask (decoder): set future positions to before softmax so position only sees . Padding mask : zero out padded positions in keys so they are never attended to. Parameter cost per layer (single block): four projections → (biases optional in the count). Common follow-ups / traps Why divide by ​ ​ ? → dot products of ​ -dim random vectors have variance ​ ; scaling avoids softmax saturation. Self-attention vs cross-attention? → self: from same sequence; cross: from decoder, from encoder (e.g. Transformers Attention in encoder-decoder stacks). Complexity? → d ) in sequence length for the attention matrix. See depth: Transformers Attention (§Scaled dot-product attention). Related: Recurrent Neural Networks , KV Cache , Normalization Layers .

title: Tokenization: BPE, WordPiece & SentencePiece
text: Say it in 30s: LLMs do not read characters or words natively — a tokenizer maps text to a fixed vocabulary of subword IDs. BPE (GPT) and SentencePiece (T5, Llama) grow vocab by merging the most frequent pairs; WordPiece (BERT) picks merges that raise training likelihood. Rare words become several tokens, common fragments become one. Token count drives cost, context limits, and eval quirks. Key points BPE : start from bytes/chars, iteratively merge the most frequent pair; used in GPT-2/3/4 lineage. WordPiece : merge pairs that maximize likelihood of training data (greedy); ## prefix marks continuations in BERT. SentencePiece : treats the sentence as a raw byte stream with a special space marker ( ▁ ); no language-specific pre-tokenization — same code for Chinese and English. OOV handling : no unknown-token dead ends; anything is a composition of subwords (may be long for rare strings). Pitfalls : leading spaces, punctuation, and casing change tokenization; same word in prompts can split differently after fine-tuning. The math BPE: repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent symbol pair until vocab size . Example corpus aa , aa , ab : counts a|a ×2, a|b ×1 → merge aa ; repeat on aa , aa , ab until is met. WordPiece: merge pair with score (pointwise mutual-information style). Unigram LM: choose a vocab to maximize ​ lo g ∑ segmentations s ​ ∏ t ∈ s ​ p ( t ) over all segmentations of training strings. Trade-off: larger → shorter sequences (fewer tokens per doc) but more embedding rows and a larger softmax. Common follow-ups / traps Why subwords not words? → finite vocab, open vocabulary, morphology shared across words; trade-off is longer sequences for rare terms. Does tokenizer affect LLM eval ? → yes — BLEU/F1 on tokens vs detokenized strings; different models are not comparable token-for-token. Special tokens? → BOS, EOS, PAD, mask, chat template markers; they occupy vocab slots and affect attention masks. See depth: Transformers Attention (§Positional information). Related: Embeddings Vector Search , LLM Inference , Maximum Likelihood Estimation .

title: Decoding Strategies
text: Say it in 30s: After the model outputs logits for the next token, decoding is the policy that picks one ID. Greedy takes the argmax; temperature scales logits before softmax; top- and top- (nucleus) truncate the candidate set; beam search keeps multiple hypotheses for quality at higher cost. Training uses teacher forcing on ground truth; inference uses your decoding choice — mismatch is why greedy text can look dull and high-temperature text can hallucinate. Key points Greedy / argmax : fast, deterministic, often repetitive; good for code with constrained syntax when paired with penalties. Temperature : divide logits by ; sharpens, flattens — exploration vs faithfulness to the model. Top- : sample only from the largest logits; fixed width regardless of distribution shape. Top- (nucleus) : smallest set whose cumulative prob ; adapts to flat vs peaked distributions. Beam search : keep partial sequences; strong for translation/summarization, poor for open-ended chat creativity. Common follow-ups / traps When beam vs sample? → beam for reference-based generation metrics; sampling + nucleus for dialogue and creative writing. Repetition penalty? → down-weight logits of tokens already in the context; fixes loops but can hurt factual lists. Does decoding affect hallucination ? → high temperature and loose sampling increase drift; does not replace grounding ( RAG ). See depth: LLM Inference: Decoding, KV Cache Serving (§Decoding strategies). Related: Cross-Entropy Loss , KV Cache , LLM Eval .

title: KV Cache
text: Say it in 30s: Autoregressive decoding would recompute keys and values for all past tokens at every new step — wasteful. A KV cache stores, per layer, the and projections for tokens already processed; each decode step only runs the new token through the stack and appends to the cache. Memory grows linearly with context length; that footprint is often the serving bottleneck, which is why GQA/MQA share KV heads across query heads. Key points Cached tensors: for each layer, ​ . Memory (order of magnitude) : ​ × d head ​ × seq_len × batch × bytes (factor 2 = and ). Prefill computes cache for the prompt in one parallel pass; decode is one token at a time, mostly reading cache. Queries are not cached — only and are reused when attending from the new position. Quantized KV (INT8/FP8) trades accuracy for capacity; PagedAttention ( vLLM ) maps logical cache to non-contiguous GPU pages. Common follow-ups / traps Why not cache ? → each step's query is new; past keys/values are fixed given past hidden states. GQA vs MQA? → grouped-query attention: several Q heads share one KV head; multi-query: one KV head for all Q heads — bigger KV savings, some quality loss. Does cache change training? → no — training is parallel over full sequence; cache is an inference-only optimization. See depth: LLM Inference: Decoding, KV Cache Serving (§The KV cache). Related: Self-Attention , Decoding Strategies , LoRA PEFT .

title: LoRA & Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
text: Say it in 30s: Full fine-tuning updates every weight; PEFT updates a tiny side path instead. LoRA freezes the pretrained matrix and learns a low-rank update = W + r α ​ B A , with ​ × r , ​ —so you train ​ + d out ​ ) parameters per adapted layer instead of ​ d out ​ . Typical targets: attention ​ , W K ​ , W V ​ , W O ​ (sometimes FFN). QLoRA adds 4-bit quantized base weights plus LoRA adapters in higher precision. Key points Rank trades capacity for cost: – is common; scales the effective learning rate of the adapter (often or ). At , , one square matrix trains params instead of M (≈0.8%)—four attention matrices per layer ≈ trainable vs M frozen per layer. Alternatives: adapters (bottleneck FFN inside each block), prefix / prompt tuning (learn soft prompt vectors, zero change to weights). Merge adapters into at inference for zero latency overhead; keep separate for multi-task swapping. Common follow-ups / traps Why low-rank works? → instruction shifts often lie in a low-dimensional subspace; you're not re-learning the whole representation. LoRA vs full FT? → LoRA when data is modest and you must preserve base capabilities; full FT when the task rewires behavior heavily (watch catastrophic forgetting). Which matrices? → all four attention projections give the best quality/$; FFN LoRA helps on hard domain adaptation. See depth: LLM Training: Pretraining, Fine-Tuning Alignment (§Parameter-efficient fine-tuning). Related: RLHF vs DPO , Quantization , Training Neural Networks , Regularization .

title: RLHF vs DPO
text: Say it in 30s: Both turn human (or AI) preferences into a better chat model, but RLHF does it in two explicit stages—train a reward model on pairwise comparisons, then optimize the policy with PPO while penalizing KL drift from a frozen reference—whereas DPO folds the reward into a classification loss on preferences and skips the reward model and RL loop entirely. RLHF is more flexible (multi-objective rewards, verifiers); DPO is simpler, cheaper, and usually more stable to train. Key points RLHF reward model: Bradley–Terry loss ​ ) − r ( x , y l ​ )) on chosen ​ vs rejected ​ . RLHF policy: PPO maximizes expected reward minus ​ ∥ π ref ​ ) to curb reward hacking and collapse. DPO: directly increases ​ ( y w ​ ∣ x ) / π ref ​ ( y w ​ ∣ x ) relative to ​ via a sigmoid on log-likelihood ratios; plays the same role as the KL coefficient. Variants: IPO (regression on margins), KTO (unpaired labels), ORPO (SFT + preference in one stage). Common follow-ups / traps Why KL to the reference? → without it the policy exploits the reward model (verbosity, sycophancy, gibberish that scores high). When prefer RLHF? → need online feedback, tool-verified rewards, or a reward you can't write as a closed-form preference loss. DPO failure modes? → distribution mismatch if SFT and preference data disagree; too small → hack, too large → no movement. See depth: LLM Training: Pretraining, Fine-Tuning Alignment (§Alignment after SFT). Related: LLM Eval , Cross-Entropy Loss , Loss Functions , LoRA Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning .

title: Embeddings & Vector Search
text: Say it in 30s: An embedding maps text (or images, queries, items) into a fixed dense vector so that semantic similarity becomes cosine distance or dot product. Bi-encoders embed query and document separately—fast because you pre-index documents—while cross-encoders score query–document pairs jointly and are accurate but too slow for millions of docs. Training uses contrastive losses (InfoNCE): pull a positive pair together, push negatives apart in a batch. At scale you retrieve with ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF+PQ) that trade a little recall for sub-millisecond latency. Key points Pooling: mean/max over token vectors, or use the [CLS] / last token for sentence-level reps; L2-normalize if using cosine via dot product. InfoNCE: ​ e sim ( q , d k ​ ) / τ e sim ( q , d + ) / τ ​ —in-batch negatives are free but biased; hard negative mining fixes easy-batch collapse. Hybrid search: dense + BM25, merged with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)—sparse catches exact entities dense misses. ANN knobs: HNSW efConstruction / M (recall vs build time); IVF nlist / nprobe ; PQ compresses vectors at recall cost. The math Similarity: cosine a ⊤ b ​ ; for unit vectors, dot product equals cosine and 2 ​ = 2 − 2 cos θ . InfoNCE with temperature : ​ e sim ( q , d k ​ ) / τ e sim ( q , d + ) / τ ​ ( positive, others negatives). Eval: recall@ = fraction of queries whose true neighbor ranks in top of ANN. PQ memory: floats ( bytes) → byte codes if splits into subvectors with centroids each — e.g. , B B. HNSW graph search: expected hops vs brute . Common follow-ups / traps Bi- vs cross-encoder? → bi-encoder for candidate generation @ millions; cross-encoder to rerank top 50–200. Why normalize? → dot product on unit vectors equals cosine; stabilizes training and indexing. Metric at interview? → recall@k on retrieval, MRR when one right doc matters, NDCG when grades differ—see Ranking Metrics . See depth: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) (§Embeddings indexing). Related: Two-Tower Retrieval , Loss Functions , Recommender Systems , Precision Recall .

title: Hallucination
text: Say it in 30s: Hallucination is when a language model states confident, fluent facts or details that are wrong or unsupported. It is not random noise—it is the model doing what it was trained to do: predict plausible continuations. Mitigations ground the model in evidence ( RAG , citations), constrain decoding (lower temperature when facts matter), add verification loops (retrieval check, calculator, code exec), and measure faithfulness so you can regress fixes. Key points Root causes: parametric knowledge is incomplete/stale; MLE rewards fluency over truth; no built-in I don't know ; long contexts bury the needle ( lost-in-the-middle ). Types: intrinsic (contradicts provided context) vs extrinsic (invents facts with no support in context or world). Reduce rate: retrieve before generate; require citations; rerank for relevance; instruction-tune on abstain if unsure ; RLHF/DPO with factuality rewards. Eval: human review, NLI-based faithfulness, LLM-as-judge with entity-level checks—details in LLM Eval . The math LM training maximizes ​ p ( x t ​ ∣ x t ​ ) — plausibility , not calibrated truth; token probabilities need calibration for confidence. Faithfulness (given context ): fraction of answer claims entailed by under an NLI check. Self-consistency: sample completions } , aggregate by majority vote on extracted answers — reduces stochastic slips, not missing knowledge. Common follow-ups / traps Can you eliminate hallucinations? → not with prompting alone; combine grounding + eval + refusal policies. Hallucination vs creativity? → same mechanism; product choice is when grounding is mandatory vs when invention is desired. RAG fix everything? → no—bad retrieval + confident generation = grounded-sounding lies; fix retrieval and faithfulness together. See depth: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) (§Failure modes), LLM Eval . Related: Decoding Strategies , LLM Inference , Model Evaluation Validation .
