title: Time Series Stationarity
heads: The four components of a series
ACF and PACF — reading the order of a model
text: Time-series forecasting — the one corner of ML where the i.i.d. assumption is dead on arrival: order is the signal, and the past leaks into the future. After this chapter You can say why time series breaks ordinary ML; decompose a series and test it for stationarity; read ACF/PACF to pick model orders; write down the AR, MA, ARIMA, and exponential-smoothing equations; choose between classical and ML approaches; and validate with the right backtest and metric. # Why time series is different In standard supervised learning the examples are exchangeable — shuffle the rows and nothing changes. A time series is the opposite: each observation ​ is indexed by time, and order is the signal . Observations are autocorrelated ( ​ depends on its own past), so you can never shuffle or do random train/test splits — doing so trains on the future to predict the past, the most fatal leak in forecasting. And the process itself often changes over time, so the distribution is moving. The mindset: a forecast is a conditional expectation ​ t + h ​ = E [ y t + h ​ ∣ information up to t ] . # The four components of a series The classical lens decomposes a series into four parts; most models target one explicitly. Additive decomposition: the observed series is the sum of trend, seasonal, and residual parts. Component What it is Example Trend ( ) Long-run direction A product's user base growing over years Seasonality ( ) Fixed, known-period cycle Retail spiking every December; traffic by hour Cyclical ( ) Long swings, no fixed period Business cycles — harder to model Residual ( ) What's left after structure Irregular, ideally unpredictable The distinction interviewers like: seasonality has a fixed period (12 months, 7 days) while a cycle does not — that's why seasonality is easy to encode and cycles are not. # Additive vs multiplicative How the components combine is a modeling choice. The additive model assumes they add: ​ = T t ​ + S t ​ + R t ​ Use it when the seasonal swing is a roughly constant size regardless of level. The multiplicative model assumes they multiply: ​ = T t ​ × S t ​ × R t ​ Use it when the swing scales with the level (December is always +30%). A key trick: logs turn multiplicative into additive, since — which is why log-transforming is the standard first move when variance grows with the level. # Stationarity Most classical models assume the series is stationary : statistical properties don't change over time. Two definitions matter: Strict stationarity — the full joint distribution is time-invariant: ​ ​ , … , y t n ​ ​ ) and ​ + s ​ , … , y t n ​ + s ​ ) have the same distribution for every shift and every set of times. It constrains everything (all moments, tails, dependence), so it is rarely testable. Weak (covariance) stationarity — only the first two moments are constrained: constant mean ​ ] = μ , finite constant variance, and an autocovariance ​ , y t + k ​ ) that depends only on the lag , not absolute time. This is what ARMA theory and the ADF/KPSS tests refer to in practice. Strict stationarity with finite second moments implies weak stationarity; the converse fails in general (for example, a series whose variance is constant but whose higher moments change). For a Gaussian process the two coincide, because the mean and covariance determine the whole distribution. A stationary series has stable structure, so a fixed set of coefficients can capture it. Differencing turns a trending (non-stationary) series into one with a stable mean. The usual fix is differencing — model the change, ​ = y t ​ − y t − 1 ​ — which removes a linear trend; seasonal differencing ​ − y t − m ​ removes a season of length . The number of differences needed is the in ARIMA. Confirm with a unit-root test (Augmented Dickey–Fuller), whose null is non-stationary ; a small p-value means you can treat it as stationary. Use the minimum — over-differencing injects artificial autocorrelation. # ACF and PACF — reading the order of a model Two plots tell you which classical model to use. The ACF at lag is the correlation between ​ and ​ , including indirect effects through intermediate lags. The PACF at lag is the same correlation after removing all shorter lags — the direct effect only. AR(2) signature: the PACF cuts off at the AR order while the ACF decays. MA is the mirror image. Plot pattern Implies PACF cuts off after lag ; ACF tails off AR( ) — read from the PACF ACF cuts off after lag ; PACF tails off MA( ) — read from the ACF Both tail off gradually ARMA( ) — pick via AIC/BIC # Classical models: the ARIMA family ARIMA is built from two atoms. An autoregressive AR( ) model says today is a linear function of its own recent past plus noise: ​ = c + ϕ 1 ​ y t − 1 ​ + ϕ 2 ​ y t − 2 ​ + ⋯ + ϕ p ​ y t − p ​ + ε t ​ A moving-average MA( ) model says today is a function of recent shocks (past forecast errors): ​ = μ + ε t ​ + θ 1 ​ ε t − 1 ​ + θ 2 ​ ε t − 2 ​ + ⋯ + θ q ​ ε t − q ​ Combine them for ARMA( ) ; apply it to a series differenced times and you get ARIMA( ) — difference until stationary, then explain it with autoregressive and moving-average terms. SARIMA adds a seasonal set of terms at lag ; ARIMAX/SARIMAX add exogenous regressors (promotions, holidays, price). Orders come from ACF/PACF plus minimizing AIC/BIC; auto_arima automates the search. Interview cue Difference between AR and MA? AR regresses on past observed values; MA regresses on past errors/shocks. AR has long memory (a shock propagates through the recursion); a pure MA( ) remembers exactly steps. # Exponential smoothing (ETS) The other classical family forecasts with a weighted average of past observations whose weights decay exponentially — recent data matters most. Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES) tracks just the level: ​ = α y t ​ + ( 1 − α ) ℓ t − 1 ​ , y ^ ​ t + h ​ = ℓ t ​ sets how fast old data is forgotten. SES has no trend or seasonality, so it forecasts a flat line. Holt adds a trend equation (sloped forecast); Holt–Winters adds a seasonal one. Modern libraries frame these as the ETS (Error, Trend, Seasonal) state-space family with likelihood fitting and prediction intervals. Useful fact: SES ARIMA(0,1,1) and Holt ARIMA(0,2,2) — two languages for an overlapping set of processes. Model Captures Forecast shape SES Level only Flat Holt Level + trend Sloped line Holt–Winters Level + trend + seasonality Sloped line with repeating season # Modern / ML approaches With many related series, long histories, rich covariates, or nonlinearities, ML methods take over. Approach Idea Shines when Lags + gradient boosting Engineer lag/rolling/calendar features, fit XGBoost/LightGBM Tabular forecasting with strong covariates Prophet Trend + Fourier seasonality + holidays, fit Bayesian Business series, holidays, gaps; interpretable DeepAR Autoregressive RNN across many series, outputs a distribution Thousands of related series; needs uncertainty N-BEATS / N-HiTS Deep fully-connected basis expansion, no recurrence Strong pure-DL univariate accuracy Temporal Fusion Transformer Attention over mixed covariates; quantiles Multi-horizon with mixed covariate types Two ideas matter more than any architecture. The shift from local models (one ARIMA per series) to global models (one network across all series) lets a sparse series borrow strength from similar ones — a main reason global models (e.g. LightGBM in M5, the ES-RNN hybrid in M4) won recent M-competitions. And probabilistic forecasting — outputting quantiles or a full distribution — matters because inventory and staffing decisions live in the tails. Note that well-tuned classical models and gradient boosting remain hard to beat on a single short series; deep learning earns its keep at scale. # Validation done right You cannot use random K-fold — it leaks the future. The correct procedure respects time: train up to time , forecast the next steps, score, then roll the cutoff forward and repeat. Time-series cross-validation: train on the past, test on the next block, roll forward. An expanding window keeps all history; a sliding window keeps a fixed recent window (better under drift). Three details separate a correct backtest from a broken one: forecast at the same horizon you care about in production; insert a gap if features look ahead; and build every feature from information available at prediction time. Always compare against a naive baseline ( tomorrow = today, this December = last December ) — a model that can't beat the last value isn't worth shipping. # Forecasting metrics Metric Idea Watch out for MAE ​ ∣ Robust; same units; linear in error RMSE ​ ) 2 ​ Penalizes big misses; outlier-sensitive MAPE ​ ∣ / ∣ y ∣ Explodes near zero; asymmetric MASE Cleanest: beats naive; scale-free WAPE ​ ∣ / ∑ ∣ y ∣ Volume-weighted; popular in retail Pinball loss asymmetric per-quantile loss For probabilistic forecasts; pair with coverage Choose by the decision: RMSE when big misses are costly, MAE/WAPE when cost is linear, MASE for scale-free comparison across series, and pinball loss + coverage for distributions. Avoid MAPE for series that approach zero. Interview cue Why not MAPE? Undefined at zero, blows up for small actuals, and asymmetric — so it quietly rewards under-forecasting. Reach for MASE (scale-free, naive-anchored) or WAPE. # One-page summary Topic The one thing to remember Why it's different Order is the signal; data is autocorrelated; never shuffle or random-split. Components Trend + seasonality (fixed period) + cycle (no fixed period) + noise (in practice the cycle is folded into trend or residual). Additive vs multiplicative Constant swing → additive; swing scales with level → multiplicative (log makes it additive). Stationarity Constant mean/variance/autocovariance. Difference to remove trend; ADF to confirm; minimum . ACF / PACF PACF cuts at → AR( ); ACF cuts at → MA( ); both tail → ARMA. ARIMA family AR = past values; MA = past errors; I = differencing. SARIMA adds seasonality; X adds covariates. Exponential smoothing Exponentially decaying weights. SES (level) → Holt (+trend) → Holt–Winters (+season). Modern ML Lags + boosting; Prophet; DeepAR/TFT/N-BEATS. Global local at scale; forecast distributions. Validation Rolling/expanding backtest at the production horizon; beat a naive baseline. Metrics RMSE (big misses), MAE/WAPE (linear), MASE (scale-free), pinball+coverage (probabilistic). Avoid MAPE near zero. # Related Cross-Validation Stationarity ARIMA vs Exponential Smoothing Time-Series Validation Backtesting

title: Stationarity
text: Say it in 30s: A weakly stationary series has constant mean, constant variance, and autocovariance that depends only on lag , not calendar time. Most raw business series trend and season — so ARIMA starts with differencing ( ) until ADF (or KPSS) says you're stable enough to fit AR/MA terms. Over-differencing adds fake structure; under-differencing leaves unit roots and nonsense forecasts. Key points Trend → remove via differencing or detrending; seasonality → seasonal differencing ​ − y t − m ​ . ADF: null = unit root (non-stationary); small → reject unit root. KPSS: null = stationarity; small → reject stationarity (still needs differencing or detrending). Stationarity is the license for fixed ARMA coefficients; breaks under regime change → drift monitoring in production forecasts. The math Weak stationarity: ​ ] = μ constant, ​ ) = σ 2 finite and constant, and ​ , Y t − k ​ ) depends only on lag , not . Differencing removes polynomial trend: ​ = Y t ​ − Y t − 1 ​ ; seasonal ​ Y t ​ = Y t ​ − Y t − m ​ . Random walk ​ = Y t − 1 ​ + ε t ​ : ​ ) = t σ ε 2 ​ grows with → not stationary; first difference ​ = ε t ​ often is. ADF test regression: ​ = α + β t + γ Y t − 1 ​ + i = 1 ∑ p ​ δ i ​ Δ Y t − i ​ + ε t ​ ​ : γ = 0 (unit root, i.e. non-stationary). A small -value rejects ​ : the series you tested is stationary enough for ARMA. Failing to reject means difference it and test again — the opposite of KPSS, whose null is stationarity. Common follow-ups / traps Can I use random train/test split? → No — time order; see Time-Series Validation Backtesting . Is seasonality non-stationarity? → Seasonal strength can be stationary after seasonal differencing or Fourier terms (Prophet). See depth: Time Series Stationarity (§Stationarity). Related: ARIMA vs Exponential Smoothing , Cross-Validation .

title: ARIMA vs Exponential Smoothing
text: Say it in 30s: ARIMA models structure with autoregressive past values (AR), past shocks (MA), and integration (differencing, ). Exponential smoothing (ETS) forecasts with exponentially decaying weights on past observations — SES for level, Holt for trend, Holt–Winters for seasonality. They overlap: SES ≡ ARIMA(0,1,1), Holt ≡ ARIMA(0,2,2). Pick ARIMA when you read ACF/PACF; pick ETS when you want a simple state-space level/trend/season story with one smoothing knob per component. Key points ARIMA : difference times, then AR on and MA on . SARIMA adds seasonal ​ at period . ETS: ​ = α y t ​ + ( 1 − α ) ℓ t − 1 ​ (level); extends to trend/season states. Short univariate series: well-tuned ETS or auto-ARIMA; many series + covariates: lags + Gradient Boosting or TFT. Common follow-ups / traps AR vs MA? → AR = memory in observed ; MA = memory in shocks (PACF vs ACF cutoffs). When does deep learning win? → Many related series, long history, rich exogenous features — not one short line. See depth: Time Series Stationarity (§Classical models / §Exponential smoothing). Related: Stationarity , Time-Series Validation Backtesting .

title: Time-Series Validation & Backtesting
text: Say it in 30s: Never random K-fold on time series — it leaks the future. Use rolling-origin evaluation: train on data up to time , forecast horizon , score, advance , repeat. Choose expanding window (all history) or sliding window (recent window only) based on drift. Features must use only information available at prediction time; match production horizon in the backtest or metrics lie. Key points Expanding window: grows training set — stable if the process is stationary enough. Sliding window: fixed length — better when old regime is irrelevant. Add a gap (embargo) if features use long lags to prevent peeking. Always benchmark vs naive (last value, seasonal naive); report MASE or WAPE for scale-free comparison. The math Rolling-origin error: origins ​ , … , t T ​ , horizon , loss : = T 1 ​ j = 1 ∑ T ​ ℓ ( y t j ​ + 1 : t j ​ + h ​ , y ^ ​ t j ​ + 1 : t j ​ + h ​ ) Expanding train window: ( j ) ​ = { y 1 ​ , … , y t j ​ ​ } . Sliding: fixed length , ( j ) ​ = { y t j ​ − W + 1 ​ , … , y t j ​ ​ } . Horizon- error scores exactly the steps you ship; add embargo gap between train end and forecast start if features use lags . ​ MAE ​ , sMAPE = n 100% ​ t ∑ ​ ( ∣ y t ​ ∣ + ∣ y ^ ​ t ​ ∣ ) /2 ∣ y t ​ − y ^ ​ t ​ ∣ ​ MASE beats the naive benchmark; sMAPE is bounded but unstable near zero actuals (same caveat as MAPE). Common follow-ups / traps Can I use cross-validation? → Only time-series CV (purged, embargoed) — see Cross-Validation for generic pitfalls, not the default splitter. Why did offline beat naive but prod failed? → Wrong , leakage in features, or train/serve skew on live covariates. See depth: Time Series Stationarity (§Validation done right). title: ML System Design Interview Prep
text: # Stage 1: Business Objective Goal: Understand WHY this system exists before touching anything technical. Interviewers want to see you think before building. Questions to ask: What is the core business goal? (revenue, safety, engagement, retention?) What is the scale? (DAU, QPS, catalog size) What latency is acceptable? ( 100ms real-time, 1s near-real-time, batch OK?) What data freshness is needed? (model needs to reflect events from 5 min ago or 5 days ago?) Are there hard constraints? (regulatory, fairness, GDPR, COPPA, geographic) Which is worse: false positives or false negatives? Is there an existing system? What's broken about it? Business metrics to know: CTR, CVR (conversion rate), GMV DAU/MAU, retention, session length Map FP/FN cost to business: fraud FN = money lost, fraud FP = user friction # Stage 2: ML Objective Goal: Translate business goal → concrete ML problem. Task types: Binary classification — spam, fraud, click prediction Multi-class — intent detection, category tagging Ranking / LTR — search, feed, recommendations Regression — price, ETA, bid value Multi-task — predict CTR + CVR jointly Generative — query rewriting, summarization Business metric → ML proxy: Business Metric ML Proxy CTR AUC-ROC, log loss Revenue CVR, predicted value Relevance NDCG, MRR, MAP Safety Recall @ high precision Engagement Predicted watch time Loss functions: Problem Loss Binary classification Binary cross-entropy (log loss) Multi-class Categorical cross-entropy Imbalanced classification Focal loss Regression MSE / MAE / Huber Ranking (pairwise) BPR loss, hinge loss Ranking (listwise) LambdaRank, ApproxNDCG Embeddings / contrastive Triplet loss, NT-Xent (SimCLR) Distillation KL divergence + task loss Key framing decisions: Point-wise vs. pairwise vs. listwise ranking Single-task vs. multi-task (shared bottom, mixture of experts) Do you need calibrated probabilities or just a good ranking? # Stage 3: High-Level Design Goal: Sketch the end-to-end pipeline. Get the boxes and arrows right before going deep. Standard pipeline: Data sources → Feature engineering → Feature store ↓ Training pipeline → Model registry ↓ Serving layer → Prediction store / cache ↓ Logging → Feedback loop Common architecture patterns: Two-tower (retrieval) User tower + Item tower → dot product → ANN index Item embeddings precomputed offline Used by: YouTube, Pinterest, TikTok for candidate generation Cascade / Funnel (retrieval → ranking → re-ranking) Retrieval (ANN, BM25, CF) → Ranking (GBDT, DNN) → Re-ranking (business rules, diversity) Used in: search, feed ranking, ads Sequence model (temporal) LSTM / Transformer over user history → next-item prediction Used in: Netflix, Spotify, TikTok Real-time + batch hybrid Batch features (stable, cheap) + real-time features (fresh, expensive) merged at serving # Stage 4: Data Feature Engineering Goal: Where does data come from, how do you label it, what features do you extract. Data sources: User interaction logs (clicks, watches, purchases, skips, dwell time) Item/entity metadata (title, category, price, content embeddings) Context (time of day, device, location, session position) Social graph (follows, co-views, shares) External signals (weather, trending topics) Labeling strategies: Explicit: ratings, thumbs up/down — sparse, high quality Implicit: clicks, watches, purchases — dense, noisy (click ≠ satisfaction) Proxy labels: watched 50% of video as engagement positive Human annotation: content quality, safety, NLP tasks Label leakage gotchas: Features computed after the event (e.g., final view count when predicting CTR) Future data leaking into training window Feature types: User: demographics, long-term interests, embedding of ID Item: category, price, recency, popularity, content embedding User-item cross: past CTR on this category, historical spend Context: time, device, session position, query Feature engineering techniques: Normalization / standardization — for neural nets Log transform — heavy-tailed distributions (price, counts) Bucketization — continuous → categorical Target encoding — replace category with mean label (watch for leakage) Embeddings — for high-cardinality IDs (users, items, queries) Hashing trick — very high cardinality, reduces memory Feature crosses — jointly encode two features (A × B) Sequence aggregation — mean/sum/attention pooling over user history Feature store: Offline store: Hive, BigQuery, Spark — batch features, used in training Online store: Redis, DynamoDB (managed by Feast / Tecton) — low-latency features at serve time Point-in-time correctness: training features must reflect what was known AT prediction time Class imbalance: Downsample negatives (very common in click prediction — 1:100 or worse) Calibration correction after downsampling negatives at keep-rate : ​ / ( p s ​ + ( 1 − p s ​ ) / w ) , equivalent to adding to the logit (a negative shift, since ) Weighted loss Focal loss # Stage 5: Model Goal: Choose and justify your model. Know the tradeoffs. Model cheat sheet: Need Model Fast baseline Logistic regression Tabular data, ranking LightGBM / XGBoost Large-scale retrieval Two-tower + FAISS ANN Dense ranking DNN / DCN (Deep Cross Network) Sequential / session Transformer (SASRec, BERT4Rec) Social graph GNN (GraphSAGE, PinSage) Multimodal (text + image) CLIP-style dual encoder Model tradeoffs: Logistic Regression Pros: fast, interpretable, calibrated, easy to debug Cons: low capacity, needs manual feature engineering When: baseline, very high QPS, features already good GBDT (XGBoost, LightGBM) Pros: handles tabular data extremely well, no normalization needed, built-in feature importance Cons: doesn't handle embeddings, hard to do online learning When: ranking, fraud, structured tabular data DNN / MLP Pros: learns feature interactions, handles embeddings end-to-end Cons: more data needed, harder to debug, slower than GBDT When: ranking with many features, multi-task setups Two-Tower Pros: item tower precomputed offline → fast retrieval Cons: no user-item interaction at inference time (shallow) When: retrieval at massive scale Transformer Pros: captures sequential context, state of the art for NLP Cons: expensive to train and serve, needs lots of data When: session modeling, NLP tasks, query understanding GNN Pros: captures social / graph structure natively Cons: complex to build and serve When: social feed ranking, fraud on transaction graphs Training considerations: Learning rate schedule: warmup + cosine decay Regularization: L1/L2, dropout, early stopping Positional bias: items shown first get more clicks — debias during training Exposure bias: model only sees items that were previously shown # Stage 6: Inference Serving Goal: Get predictions to users at scale, efficiently. Batch vs. Real-time vs. Near-real-time: Mode Latency Freshness Use case Batch 0ms (precomputed) Stale (hours/days) Email recs, item embeddings Near-real-time Seconds/minutes Fresh Trending, fraud streaming Real-time 100ms Very fresh Feed ranking, search Serving architectures: Precomputed / lookup: store embeddings or scores in Redis, retrieve at serve time Online inference: feature retrieval → model scoring → post-processing in budget Cascade / multi-stage: cheap model for retrieval → expensive model on small candidate set Latency optimization: Quantization: FP32 → FP16 or INT8 (2-4x speedup, small accuracy loss) Distillation: train small student from large teacher Pruning: remove low-importance weights Caching: cache predictions for popular user/item pairs ANN for retrieval: FAISS, ScaNN, HNSW (millisecond-scale over billions of vectors) Batching: group requests on GPU to maximize throughput Scalability: Horizontal scaling: replica-based, load balanced GPU serving: large batches / transformers CPU serving: low-latency tabular / small models Feature lookup budget: Redis P99 ~1ms, DB can be 10-100ms — budget carefully Deployment strategies: Shadow mode: run new model in parallel, no user impact, compare offline Canary: 1-5% traffic, monitor metrics A/B test: randomized experiment, measure business metric Interleaving: blend two ranked lists, measure clicks — faster signal than A/B Multi-armed bandit: explore/exploit, useful when A/B is too slow # Stage 7: Deep Dives Improvements Goal: Show depth by proactively naming hard problems and how you'd solve them. Cold Start New user: popular items, context features (device, referral), demographic priors New item: content embeddings (image, text, metadata), zero-shot via pretrained model Exploration: epsilon-greedy, Thompson sampling, UCB Data Freshness / Training Latency How fast does the model react to new events? Options: real-time feature updates, online learning (SGD on stream), continuous training Tradeoff: freshness vs. stability Model Monitoring Drift Data drift: input distributions shift (COVID changed all user behavior overnight) Concept drift: feature-label relationship changes Detection: KL divergence, PSI (Population Stability Index), shadow scoring Response: automated retraining triggers, alerting Bias Fairness Selection bias: model trained on biased exposure (only seen items) Popularity bias: popular items get over-recommended, feedback loop amplifies Demographic fairness: disparate impact across groups Debiasing: inverse propensity scoring (IPS), adversarial debiasing, constrained optimization Feedback Loops / Echo Chambers Model recommends what it predicts users like → users only see those items → model gets reinforced Mitigations: exploration budgets, diversity constraints, counterfactual evaluation Multi-Objective Optimization Competing objectives: engagement vs. revenue vs. safety vs. diversity Approaches: weighted sum of losses, Pareto optimization, constrained (maximize revenue s.t. engagement ≥ threshold), mixture of experts per objective Reranking After ranking: diversity (no 3 consecutive same artist), freshness boost, sponsored insertion, safety filtering Privacy Differential privacy: calibrated noise on gradients or outputs Federated learning: train on-device, aggregate updates ID hashing = pseudonymization only; not a formal privacy guarantee # Quick Reference Cheat Sheets # Loss Functions Problem Loss Binary classification Binary cross-entropy Multi-class Categorical cross-entropy Imbalanced Focal loss Regression (large errors costly) MSE Regression (robust / outliers) MAE / Huber Ranking pairwise BPR, hinge Ranking listwise LambdaRank, ApproxNDCG Embeddings Triplet loss, NT-Xent Distillation KL divergence # Models Need Model Baseline Logistic regression Tabular / ranking LightGBM / XGBoost Retrieval at scale Two-tower + FAISS Dense ranking DNN / DCN Session / sequential SASRec / BERT4Rec Graph signals GNN (GraphSAGE, PinSage) Multimodal CLIP-style dual encoder # Inference Need Approach Sub-10ms Precomputed + Redis lookup ~100ms budget Online inference, light model Stale OK Batch + feature store Real-time events Kafka + Flink streaming Large model, throughput matters Quantization + GPU batching Billion-scale retrieval ANN (FAISS, ScaNN, HNSW) # Business Metric → ML Metric Business ML CTR AUC-ROC, log loss Revenue CVR, predicted bid value Relevance NDCG, MRR, MAP Safety Recall @ fixed high precision Engagement Predicted watch time # Related Recommender Systems ML in Production: Serving, Monitoring MLOps A/B Testing Online Experimentation Calibration

title: Recommender Systems
heads: Problem framing: what are we optimizing?
Implicit feedback: confidence weights (Hu / Koren / Volinsky)
Negative sampling, position, and exposure bias
Exploration as a first-class system component
Worked design sketch: short-video For You feed
text:
Recommendations are the canonical ranking problem: you only see feedback on what you showed, the catalog is enormous, and the metric you optimize is rarely the metric the business cares about. Every large consumer product eventually becomes a recommender. Search, feeds, ads, marketplaces, and similar items are the same skeleton with different labels: retrieve a tractable candidate set from a sea of items, rank them with rich cross-features, then re-rank for policy, diversity, and freshness. This chapter is the technical depth behind that funnel — explicit vs implicit feedback, matrix factorization and implicit ALS, two-tower retrieval with corrected sampled softmax, ranking model families, bias correction, cold start, and how offline ranking metrics relate to online engagement. Use ML System Design Framework for the design spine. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Frame recsys as retrieval + ranking with different latency budgets and label semantics (explicit vs implicit). Write down matrix factorization with L2 regularization and the Hu–Koren–Volinsky objective for implicit feedback. Explain the multistage funnel (billions → thousands → tens) and where two-tower ANN vs heavy rankers sit. Name in-batch negatives, sampled softmax, and log-frequency (logQ) correction for unbiased retrieval training. Diagnose exposure, position, and popularity bias — and cite IPW, exploration, and re-ranking as fixes. Connect recall@k, NDCG, and coverage offline to watch time / retention online without conflating them. # Problem framing: what are we optimizing? A recommender answers: given this user and context, which items should we show, in what order? That question hides three separate decisions interviewers expect you to unpack. Feedback type. Explicit feedback is a deliberate rating or vote (stars, thumbs). Labels are sparse but semantically clear. Implicit feedback is behavior: clicks, plays, dwell time, purchases, skips. It is abundant but ambiguous — a skip is not a hate, and silence is not disinterest if the item was never shown. Most production systems are implicit-first because coverage of the catalog matters more than calibrated star predictions. Relevance. Relevant is not universal. For search, relevance is query–document match. For a For You feed, it is often predicted engagement (watch time, completion rate) plus creator health guardrails. For e-commerce, it may be purchase probability × margin. Say out loud which objective you're proxying and what you sacrifice. Business objectives vs ML proxies. Optimizing click-through rate can inflate clickbait; optimizing watch time can favor long passive videos; optimizing GMV can ignore satisfaction. Strong answers name a north-star (e.g. D7 retention) and treat model heads as proxies tuned via A/B Testing Experimentation . Multi-task ranking (CTR + dwell + share) is the usual compromise — see Models Loss Functions Reference for MMoE and listwise losses, not duplicated here. Signal Pros Cons Explicit ratings Clear polarity Sparse, selection-biased reviewers Implicit clicks Dense Exposure-biased; position-biased Dwell / watch time Closer to satisfaction Noisy; background playback Purchases / GMV Revenue-aligned Extremely sparse; delayed Memory hook Implicit feedback answers what did they do when they saw it? — not what would they do if we showed everything. Interview angle Weak: We predict whether they'll like it. Strong: we predict expected watch time (or click) conditional on exposure, train on logged impressions with position debiasing, and validate online on session length with diversity guardrails. Rapid fire — Framing Explicit = sparse, clear; implicit = dense, ambiguous. Relevance is product-specific (match vs engagement vs revenue). Offline ranking metrics proxy online north-stars — never confuse them. Multi-task heads separate CTR from depth-of-engagement. Name exposure before you talk about negatives. # Content-based vs collaborative filtering Content-based filtering recommends items similar to what the user liked, using item features (tags, text embeddings, visual embeddings from a CNN/ViT). It works on day one for new items with metadata and does not need a crowd — but it struggles with taste nuance and serendipity ( users who liked A also liked B when A and B look unrelated). Collaborative filtering (CF) exploits interaction patterns : users who agreed in the past will agree again. User–user CF is rare at scale (sparse neighborhoods). Item–item CF ( customers who bought X also bought Y ) still appears in baskets. Matrix factorization and embedding retrieval are the scalable CF story: latent factors compress co-occurrence structure. Hybrid production systems almost always blend both: content embeddings for cold-start items , CF/two-tower for personalization, plus popularity/trending priors. Link: Embeddings Vector Search for ANN serving details. Neighborhood methods still appear in interviews: item–item cosine on co-purchase vectors is to precompute but cheap at serve for similar products. At billion scale you precompute top- neighbors offline and store in a key-value store. Interview angle When asked content vs CF, answer with a timeline : content dominates minute zero, CF dominates month three, hybrid forever. # Matrix factorization Model user and item with vectors ​ , q i ​ ∈ R d . For explicit ratings ​ , a standard objective is regularized squared error on observed entries : min ​ ( u , i ) ∈ O ∑ ​ ( r u i ​ − p u ⊤ ​ q i ​ ) 2 + λ u ∑ ​ ∥ p u ​ ∥ 2 + λ i ∑ ​ ∥ q i ​ ∥ 2 This is low-rank factorization of the partially observed rating matrix. Alternating Least Squares (ALS) fixes one side and solves linear least squares for the other — embarrassingly parallel, great on explicit data in Spark. SGD samples pairs and updates with a learning rate; flexible for extensions (side features, neural layers). # Implicit feedback: confidence weights (Hu / Koren / Volinsky) For implicit data, let ​ be raw interaction strength (e.g. play count), ​ = 1 [ x u i ​ 0 ] the preference indicator, and confidence weights ​ : ​ = 1 + α x u i ​ where scales how much you trust repeated consumption. The weighted ALS objective minimizes: min ​ u , i ∑ ​ c u i ​ ( p u i ​ − p u ⊤ ​ q i ​ ) 2 + λ u ∑ ​ ∥ p u ​ ∥ 2 + λ i ∑ ​ ∥ q i ​ ∥ 2 Intuition: observed clicks are strong positives; missing entries are negatives with low confidence — not definitely disliked. Modern stacks often replace pure MF with two-tower neural CF , but interviewers still expect you to write this objective and explain ALS vs SGD. Common mistake Treating every unclicked impression as a hard negative in implicit MF — that assumes uniform exposure and destroys tail-item recall. Memory hook Implicit MF: positives are confident; unobserved is maybe negative, weighted by ​ , not 0/1 dogma. Rapid fire — Matrix factorization Dot product of user/item embeddings = score. Explicit MF: squared error + L2 on . Implicit: ​ ∈ { 0 , 1 } with confidence ​ = 1 + α x u i ​ . ALS alternates closed-form blocks; SGD samples pairs. Neural MF adds features and nonlinearities → two-tower retrieval. # The multistage funnel You cannot score a billion videos with a 500-feature DCN at 50ms. Production recsys is a funnel : flowchart LR C[ Catalog
~10⁹ items ] -- R[ Retrieval
~10³–10⁴ candidates ] R -- K[ Ranking
~10²–10³ scored ] K -- RR[ Re-ranking
~10–50 shown ] Typical latency budgets (order-of-magnitude): retrieval 10–30ms (mostly ANN + light models), ranking 30–80ms (heavy GPU/CPU ensemble), re-rank blend 10ms (rules + MMR). Recall dominates retrieval (miss the right item and ranking never sees it); precision and calibration dominate ranking; diversity, freshness, policy dominate re-rank. Stage Catalog → out Primary metric Model class Candidate generation – → – Recall@k CF, two-tower + ANN, graph walk, BM25 Ranking thousands → hundreds NDCG / AUC GBDT, Wide Deep, DCN, DIN, MMoE Re-ranking hundreds → ~10–50 Diversity, policy MMR, rules, lightweight scorer Union multiple retrieval sources : personalized ANN, trending, subscriptions, exploration buckets, editorial. The ranker learns to merge evidence; retrieval diversity improves recall. Quantitative intuition. If each retrieval channel contributes 500 candidates and you dedupe, you might feed 1500–2500 unique IDs to the ranker. Truncate to top 200 by a cheap pre-score (dot product or heuristic) if the ranker budget is tight. Latency is often dominated by feature lookup and cross feature materialization , not the final MLP forward pass — cache hot user histories and precomputed item stats. For search-plus-feed products, query understanding (intent, language) feeds the user tower as context features; the same two-tower index serves browse and search with different tower inputs. Interview angle Draw the funnel before naming a model. Say approximate candidate counts and where ANN runs vs full cross-features. Rapid fire — Funnel Retrieve wide, rank deep, re-rank for product rules. ANN at billions; cross-features only on thousands. Multiple recall channels merged before rank. Latency budget forces decoupled item embeddings offline. # Two-tower retrieval Architecture. A user tower ​ ( user features ) → u ∈ R d and item tower ​ ( item features ) → v ∈ R d . Score v (sometimes cosine after L2 norm). Serving win: precompute all item vectors offline, build an ANN index (HNSW, ScaNN, FAISS); online, compute once, one ANN query → top- . No per-pair forward pass. Training with in-batch negatives. For a batch of (user, positive item) pairs, negatives are other items in the batch. Loss is often sampled softmax / InfoNCE: ) ∑ ​ ln exp ( u ⊤ v + / τ ) + ∑ j ∈ N ​ exp ( u ⊤ v j ​ / τ ) exp ( u ⊤ v + / τ ) ​ logQ correction. Popular items appear as negatives more often in in-batch sampling, biasing the partition function. Importance sampling correction subtracts log item frequency: ​ exp ( u ⊤ v k ​ − ln Q ( v k ​ )) exp ( u ⊤ v j ​ ) ​ where ​ ) ∝ item exposure frequency (estimated from logs). Without correction, retrieval over-promotes head items — a classic popularity bias amplifier. Hard negative mining (same category, rejected impressions) and curriculum learning appear in mature systems; start with in-batch + logQ in interviews. Memory hook Two-tower = dot product retrieval; items offline in ANN, users online once — decoupling is the scale trick. See also the card Two-Tower Retrieval . Rapid fire — Two-tower User tower once per request; item tower offline → ANN. In-batch negatives scale training. Sampled softmax with temperature . logQ debiases frequent negatives. BPR/triplet losses are pairwise alternatives — see Loss Functions . # Ranking models (brief catalog) After retrieval, you have budget for user×item crosses : match scores, co-occurrence, real-time context, sequence encodings. Family Idea When it shines GBDT ([[gradient-boosting Gradient Boosting]]) Binned dense + sparse features Wide Deep Linear crosses + DNN Memorize frequent rules + generalize DCN / DeepFM Explicit feature crossing High-cardinality categoricals DIN / DIEN Attention over user history Session-heavy feeds MMoE Shared trunk, gating per task CTR + watch time + share jointly Train on logged impressions with sampled negatives for classification, or listwise / pairwise objectives for pure ranking — details in Models Loss Functions Reference and Ranking Metrics . Calibration matters if scores feed auctions or multi-stage fusion: see Calibration . # Pointwise, pairwise, and listwise training Pointwise: each (user, item) row is a binary or regression label — click, watch seconds. Fast to engineer; ignores slate context. Pairwise: prefer over (BPR, hinge) — aligns with implicit feedback but ignores position among many positives. Listwise: optimize entire impression list (LambdaRank, softmax over slate, ApproxNDCG) — closest to NDCG but heavier and sensitive to exposure bias in logs. Production often trains pointwise multi-task heads for scale, then listwise fine-tuning on a smaller reranked set. Feature families at rank time (memorize the four buckets from ML System Design Framework ): Family Examples Role User age cohort, activity rate, embeddings of history Prior taste Item category, creator tier, content embedding Prior quality Cross match scores, co-watch counts, same-creator Personalization Context time of day, device, geo, position (train only) Situational Real-time crosses (last 5 clicks → attention over candidate categories) are why DIN-style sequence encoders beat static profiles on feeds. Go deeper (optional) Graph-based retrieval (PinSage, item graphs) propagates signal along co-engagement edges — strong when CF density is high but cold nodes need content side information. See Graph Neural Networks for message-passing intuition. Interview angle Don't recite every architecture. Pick GBDT baseline → justify deep ranker for sequence/cross features → mention multi-task if the product cares about more than clicks. # Negative sampling, position, and exposure bias Negative sampling for implicit CTR: sample items the user did not interact with, often stratified (uniform + hard negatives). Too-easy negatives inflate AUC but hurt retrieval recall; too-hard without debiasing confuses exposure with dislike. Position bias: higher slots get more clicks regardless of quality. Fixes: (1) train with position as a feature , zero it at serving ; (2) inverse propensity weighting (IPW) — weight each click by ​ ( click ∣ pos ) from a position model; (3) randomized exploration slots to estimate propensities. Exposure / selection bias: you only observe labels for recommended items — a feedback loop . Unbiased learning-to-rank and exploration (ε-greedy buckets, Thompson sampling on arms) prevent the model from only reinforcing past winners. Connect to Data Leakage : future engagement used as a label for past decisions must respect causality. Rapid fire — Bias Skip ≠ hate; missing ≠ negative without exposure model. Position feature trick at serve-time zero. IPW reweights clicks by slot propensity. Exploration breaks the filter bubble in training data. # Cold start, diversity, freshness, exploration User cold start: no history → onboarding tastes, demographics, popular/trending , or content-based from first clicks. Item cold start: metadata / content embedding at upload → immediately in ANN; CF signal accumulates with impressions. Card: Cold Start . Diversity: Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) and determinantal point processes (DPP) re-rank to reduce redundancy. Freshness: inject time-decayed or new creator slots in re-rank. Exploration: multi-armed bandits on item clusters or new uploads; balance regret vs learning — often 1–5% traffic. Memory hook Cold item = content vector day zero; cold user = prior + trending until history exists. # Feedback loops and popularity bias Positive feedback reinforces items already shown → rich get richer . Mitigations: debiased training (IPW, causal estimators), propensity-scored negatives, exploration traffic, and coverage metrics in offline eval. Monitor creator concentration (Gini on impressions) as a guardrail alongside engagement. # Exploration as a first-class system component Reserve 1–5% of impressions for uniform random, Thompson sampling on cluster arms, or new-item buckets . Exploration traffic is not wasted — it generates unbiased counterfactual data for propensity models and prevents retrieval collapse to yesterday's winners. Trade-off: short-term CTR dip vs long-tail recall. Mention regret qualitatively; you do not need full bandit proofs in system design rounds. Engineering requirements: log explore_flag , route explore slates through the same ranker with exploration-only features zeroed, and power A/B tests on explore rate separately from model changes. # Offline vs online metrics Offline What it measures Gap Recall@k Did the right item appear in top- ? Ignores position within slate NDCG@k Graded relevance with position discount Needs labels; still not causality Coverage Fraction of catalog recommended Anti-popularity-bias guardrail MAP / MRR Binary relevance ranking Search-style Online: session length, retention, revenue — via controlled experiments. Offline lifts in NDCG do not guarantee online wins if exploration policy or slate composition changed. Always pre-register guardrails (reports, diversity). Rapid fire — Metrics Recall@k for retrieval quality; NDCG for ranker; coverage for tail health. Offline optimizes logged policy; online tests new policy with A/B. Connect proxy to north-star explicitly. # Worked design sketch: short-video For You feed Scope. 200M DAU, short videos, ~100ms end-to-end, mostly implicit feedback. Objective. Multi-task ranker: , , ; online north-star = DAU-weighted watch time + retention guardrail. Data. Impression logs with position, dwell, user/item IDs; content embeddings at upload; point-in-time user history from ML in Production feature store patterns. Retrieval (~20ms). Two-tower ( ) + HNSW on item vectors; union trending + following + explore bucket; . Ranking (~70ms). MMoE over DCN crosses (user stats × video stats × match); train with position feature zeroed at serve; IPW on clicks. Re-rank (~10ms). MMR on creator/topic; freshness boost; policy filters (age, region). Eval. Offline: recall@1000 on held-out watches, NDCG@10 on impressions; online: A/B on watch time / D7 retention; monitor Data Drift vs Concept Drift weekly. Capacity planning (back-of-envelope). 200M DAU × ~50 requests/day ≈ rank calls/day. If retrieval returns 2000 and rank scores 200, heavy rank forward passes are full catalog — that is why the funnel exists. ANN index rebuild nightly on fresh item embeddings; incremental updates for new uploads every few minutes. Failure modes to volunteer: retrieval recall collapse after embedding drift; ranker overfitting to position; explore budget cut amplifying popularity bias; creator starvation without MMR. Pair with production practices in ML in Production . Interview angle End with monitoring + retrain cadence unprompted — that's the staff signal ML System Design Framework emphasizes. Rapid fire — Design sketch 10⁹ → 2k retrieve → rank 200 → show 20. Two-tower + unions. MMoE ranker with debiased clicks. MMR + freshness re-rank. NDCG offline, retention online, drift post-launch. # One-page summary Concept The one thing to remember Feedback Implicit is dense and exposure-biased; explicit is sparse and clear. CF vs content CF for taste; content for cold items; hybrid in production. Implicit MF ​ = 1 + α x u i ​ weights confidence; unobserved ≠ hard negative. Funnel Billions → ANN retrieve → cross-feature rank → policy re-rank. Two-tower Offline item ANN + online user vector; logQ fixes in-batch popularity bias. Bias Position feature at train/serve split; IPW; exploration for exposure. Cold start Content embedding for items; prior/trending for users. Metrics Recall@k retrieval, NDCG rank, coverage tail; online A/B on north-star. # Related ML System Design Framework ML System Design Interview Prep Models Loss Functions Reference Two-Tower Retrieval Cold Start Embeddings Vector Search Ranking Metrics A/B Testing Experimentation Loss Functions

title: Case Study: Search Ranking
text: Search is recommendation with an explicit query: the user tells the system what they want, so relevance is sharper, the latency budget is tighter, and the labels are more biased than almost anywhere else. This case study works one reference design end to end: a site search box over a large catalog of documents (products, articles, listings). The skeleton is the retrieve-then-rank funnel from Recommender Systems and the spine is the ML System Design Framework ; this note adds what is specific to queries: understanding the query, mixing lexical and dense retrieval, learning to rank from clicks that are biased by position, and measuring quality when relevant is a judgment call. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Scope a search ranking problem and state a defensible latency and capacity budget with arithmetic. Draw a four-stage pipeline (query understanding, hybrid retrieval, L1 and L2 ranking, re-ranking) and say what each stage optimizes. Explain why BM25 and dense retrieval are complementary and how their candidates are fused. Choose between pointwise, pairwise, and listwise learning to rank, and say why LambdaMART is a strong default. Describe position bias and how to correct it (position features, inverse propensity weighting, interleaving, randomization) and what counterfactual LTR does at a glance. Choose offline metrics (NDCG, MRR) and online metrics (CTR, abandonment, reformulation rate) and say how they can disagree. # Problem statement and clarifying questions Prompt. Design the ranking system behind a search box for a catalog of roughly 200 million documents. Users type short free-text queries; the system returns a ranked page of about 10 results. Questions worth asking before drawing anything, and the assumption taken here for each: Question Why it matters Assumption used What is a good result? Decides label source and metric Satisfied session: clicked a result and did not reformulate quickly Is intent navigational, informational, or transactional? Changes how much personalization helps Mixed; head queries mostly navigational or transactional Scale: users, queries per user, catalog size Capacity and index design 50M daily users, 8 queries each, 200M documents Latency budget Bounds model size and candidate counts 200 ms end to end at p99, 150 ms for the ranking path Freshness Index update path New or changed documents searchable within minutes Personalization allowed? Features and privacy Light personalization (locale, past engagement), no cross-user leakage Languages and typos Query understanding scope Several languages; typos common on mobile Human rating budget Label strategy A small rater pool for a few thousand judged queries per month The task is a learning-to-rank problem layered on retrieval : given a query, pick a candidate set that contains the relevant documents, then order it so the most useful appear first. The ranking quality is measured on the top handful of positions, because users rarely look past the first screen. # Requirements and back-of-envelope scale Functional requirements: return a ranked list, support filters and facets, handle typos and synonyms, expose a debug explanation for each result for internal tools. Non-functional requirements: p99 under 200 ms, availability that degrades gracefully (lexical-only results if the neural stages fail), and an index update path that does not require a full rebuild. Traffic. Daily queries are × 8 = 4 × 1 0 8 . Average load is /86 , 400 ≈ 4 , 630 QPS. With a peak factor of about 3 for daily and regional shape, plan for roughly QPS. Compute per query. Suppose the retrieval union returns 1,000 candidates, a light first-pass ranker (L1) costs 0.01 ms per candidate on one core, and a heavier second-pass ranker (L2) scores the top 200 at 0.05 ms per candidate: At peak the ranking CPU is cores, before headroom, feature fetch, and retrieval. Planning for two to three times that is reasonable, and a neural cross-encoder on a small final slice, if used, is better served from accelerators. Scoring all 200M documents with even the light model would cost × 0.01 ms = 2 , 000 core-seconds per query, which is the whole reason the funnel exists. Dense index memory. One 256-dimensional vector per document: Representation Size for 200M vectors float32, 256-d × 256 × 4 B ≈ 205 GB int8 (scalar or product quantization), 256-d float32, 768-d So a compact embedding with quantization and a sharded approximate nearest neighbor index is feasible, while full-width float vectors are costly. See Embeddings Vector Search for index trade-offs. Logging volume. Logging 10 impressions per query at about 300 bytes each gives × 10 × 300 B ≈ 1.2 TB/day of impression logs, which is why sampling and compact schemas matter for the training pipeline. # Architecture flowchart LR Q[ Query ] -- QU[ Query understanding br/ normalize, spell, intent, expand ] QU -- LEX[ Lexical retrieval br/ BM25 inverted index ] QU -- DEN[ Dense retrieval br/ query tower + ANN ] LEX -- FUS[ Fusion + dedupe br/ about 1000 candidates ] DEN -- FUS FUS -- L1[ L1 ranker br/ light GBDT, top 200 ] L1 -- L2[ L2 ranker br/ LambdaMART or neural, top 50 ] L2 -- RR[ Re-rank br/ diversity, business rules, freshness ] RR -- OUT[ Page of 10 + snippets ] FS[( Feature store br/ doc, query, user stats )] -- L1 FS -- L2 LOGS[( Impression + click logs )] -- TRAIN[ Offline training + evaluation ] OUT -- LOGS TRAIN -- L1 TRAIN -- L2 Typical latency allocation inside the 150 ms ranking path: query understanding 10 ms, retrieval 30 ms (lexical and dense in parallel), fusion and feature fetch 20 ms, L1 10 ms, L2 30 ms, re-rank and snippet generation 20 ms, leaving slack for network and tail variance. # Query understanding Retrieval can only return what the query representation allows, so the cheap stages in front matter. Normalization : lowercasing, Unicode normalization, tokenization appropriate to the language, stemming or lemmatization for the lexical side. Spelling correction : a noisy-channel or sequence model that proposes corrections, with a conservative threshold; auto-correct only when confidence is high, otherwise show did you mean . Intent classification : a small classifier predicts intent (navigational, transactional, informational) and category. Its output is both a feature and a router (for example, restricting retrieval to a vertical). Entity and attribute extraction : parse red running shoes size 9 into structured filters plus free text. Expansion and rewriting : synonyms and learned rewrites from session logs (query A frequently reformulated to B and then clicked). Rewrites trade recall for precision, so they are usually applied as soft additions with lower weight, not as replacements. Query-level signals worth caching: the rewritten query, intent distribution, and top results for head queries. A small fraction of distinct queries accounts for a large share of traffic, so a result cache keyed by normalized query and locale absorbs a meaningful fraction of load; the cache TTL is a freshness decision. Interview angle Weak answers start with train a ranking model . Strong answers first note that recall is capped by retrieval and query understanding, and that the ranker cannot recover a document that never entered the candidate set. # Retrieval: lexical, dense, and hybrid Lexical retrieval (BM25). An inverted index maps terms to postings lists; BM25 scores a document by term frequency saturation and inverse document frequency with length normalization: ∑ ​ IDF ( t ) f ( t , d ) + k 1 ​ ( 1 − b + b avgdl ∣ d ∣ ​ ) f ( t , d ) ( k 1 ​ + 1 ) ​ Here is the term count in , the document length, the corpus average, ​ controls saturation and controls length normalization. It is fast, interpretable, handles rare exact tokens (part numbers, names) well, and needs no training. It fails on vocabulary mismatch: cheap laptop will not match budget notebook . Dense retrieval. A two-tower encoder maps the query and each document into a shared vector space; relevance is an inner product, and an ANN index returns nearest neighbors. This bridges vocabulary gaps and handles paraphrase, but it can blur exact matches and rare identifiers, and it requires training data and an embedding refresh path. The training recipe (in-batch negatives, hard negatives mined from non-relevant lexical top results, corrections for sampling bias) is covered in Two-Tower Retrieval . Hybrid. The two retrievers fail differently, so combine them. Two common fusion options: Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) : score each document by ​ 1/ ( k + rank r ​ ( d )) over retrievers , with around 60. It needs no score calibration across retrievers, which is why it is a good first choice. Learned fusion : pass both scores and ranks as features into L1 and let the ranker decide. This usually wins once enough labeled data exists but requires the features to be present for documents retrieved by only one source (use a missing-value indicator, not zero). Retrieval aims at recall at a candidate budget: the fraction of judged-relevant documents that appear in the top 1,000 union. Optimize that, and track it per query segment, because head and tail queries behave very differently. Memory hook BM25 is a precise but literal reader; dense retrieval is a loose but forgiving one. Hybrid uses both because their misses do not overlap. # Ranking stages L1 (cheap, wide). Takes about 1,000 candidates and keeps 200. It uses features available without expensive joins: retrieval scores, document static quality, query-document text match features (BM25 per field), freshness, popularity, and basic user locale. A gradient boosted tree ( Gradient Boosting ) is a strong fit: fast inference, robust to feature scale, handles missing values. L2 (expensive, narrow). Takes the top 200 and orders the top 50. Richer features: personalization, historical click and conversion rates for the (query, document) pair or (query cluster, document), embedding similarity from a cross-attention model, and document quality models. Options: Model Strength Cost or risk LambdaMART (boosted trees with lambda gradients) Directly optimizes a rank-aware objective, strong with tabular features Limited use of raw text unless embeddings are features Deep ranker over features (DCN style) Learns crosses, multi-task heads More data and serving cost Cross-encoder (query and document jointly in a transformer) Best text relevance Latency; confined to the top 20 to 50 LLM-based reranker Strong on complex queries Highest latency and cost; use on a small slice or offline to produce labels A pragmatic design uses LambdaMART as L2 with a cross-encoder score as one input feature computed on the top slice only. Re-rank. Rules and light models apply diversity (avoid ten near-duplicates), freshness boosts for time-sensitive intents, business constraints (availability, region, safety filters), and de-duplication. Keep this layer thin and auditable. # Learning to rank Three formulations, in order of how much they use the list structure: Pointwise : predict a relevance grade or click probability per document with regression or classification. Simple, but optimizes a loss that is not rank-aware. Pairwise : for documents with ​ y j ​ for the same query, minimize a loss on the score difference, for example the RankNet form ​ = lo g ( 1 + e − σ ( s i ​ − s j ​ ) ) where ​ is the model score and a scale. Listwise : optimize a list-level objective directly or through a smooth surrogate (ListNet softmax cross-entropy over the list, or LambdaRank). LambdaRank and LambdaMART. Instead of differentiating a non-smooth metric, LambdaRank defines the gradient for each pair as the pairwise gradient scaled by how much swapping the pair would change the metric: ​ = 1 + e σ ( s i ​ − s j ​ ) − σ ​ ​ Δ NDCG ij ​ ​ Pairs that matter for the top of the list get larger gradients. LambdaMART plugs these lambdas into gradient boosted trees. It remains a strong default because tabular features dominate in many ranking stacks, the training is stable, and inference is fast. Click bias and position bias. Raw clicks are not relevance. A document at position 1 is clicked more because it is seen more, regardless of quality. Treat the click probability as the product of examination and relevance: where is the displayed position. If examination probability depends only on position, then training on raw clicks learns the old ranker's ordering back. Remedies: Position as a feature, zeroed or fixed at serving. Simple and common; works if the model can separate position effects from content effects. The risk is that the model leans on the position feature and under-fits content. Inverse propensity weighting (IPW). Weight each clicked example by . Propensities are estimated from randomization experiments (swap positions on a small share of traffic) or from EM-style estimation using result pairs shown at different positions. High weights inflate variance, so clip them. Randomization and exploration. A tiny shuffle bucket (for example a fraction of a percent of traffic, within one adjacent swap) gives unbiased signals at a measurable cost. Click models (cascade, dynamic Bayesian networks) that explain clicks as examination along the list. Trust bias and context bias (clicks on a result depend on neighbors, and users trust top results) are second-order but appear when propensities are poorly estimated. Counterfactual LTR at a glance. Counterfactual learning to rank treats logged clicks as outcomes of a logging policy and uses importance weighting to estimate how a new ranker would have performed, without deploying it. The estimator is unbiased only if the propensity model is right and every relevant document had nonzero exposure. In practice, it is used to select among candidate rankers offline before an A/B test and to weight training, with the clipping and variance caveats above. It does not replace online experiments; see A/B Testing Experimentation . Common mistake Training the next ranker on clicks produced by the current ranker without any bias correction. Offline metrics against those same clicks will look excellent, because the new model reproduces the old ordering. # Features Group features by what produces them so each can be given the right freshness and the right store ( ML in Production ): Family Examples Notes Query Length, intent distribution, language, historical click entropy, query frequency Batch plus cached Document Static quality, age, popularity, field lengths, authority, price or availability Batch, with streaming for availability Query-document BM25 per field, embedding cosine, term coverage, proximity, historical (query cluster, document) CTR Mixed; computed at request time or from joins User and context Locale, device, coarse engagement history, session so far Online store; privacy review Retrieval Source (lexical, dense, both), source scores and ranks Free, and strong Rules of thumb: prefer rate features with smoothing (for example Bayesian-smoothed CTR) over raw counts, bucket and clip heavy-tailed counts, keep a missing indicator for sparse features, and ensure the same transformation code runs in training and serving to avoid Training-Serving Skew . Historical click features computed over a window that includes the target impression are a classic source of Data Leakage : compute them as of the time before the query. # Labels: clicks versus human ratings Source Strength Weakness Clicks, dwell, conversions Abundant, reflects real use, fresh Position and presentation bias, noisy, favors clickbait Skips and reformulations Weak negative signal A skip may mean the snippet already answered the query Human relevance ratings (graded 0 to 4) Cleaner, consistent, can cover tail queries Expensive, slow, rater disagreement, may not match user intent LLM-produced judgments Cheap and scalable Needs calibration against humans; can share blind spots with the ranker A practical blend: train the main ranker on debiased click-derived labels (weighted by purchase or long-click rather than raw click), and keep a golden set of human-judged queries stratified by head, torso, and tail, used for evaluation, for sanity-checking offline metrics, and as an auxiliary training signal. Measure inter-rater agreement; if raters disagree with each other, the ceiling on any metric is low and metric differences below that noise are not meaningful. LLM-based judges can extend coverage but should be audited on a human sample and not used as the sole gate. Negatives: documents shown above a clicked document are more reliable negatives than those never shown; unshown documents are unlabeled, not negative. Hard negatives for dense retrieval training can be mined from lexical top results the user skipped. # Metrics Offline ranking quality. Definitions and derivations live in Ranking Metrics ; the essentials here: ∑ k ​ lo g 2 ​ ( i + 1 ) 2 r e l i ​ − 1 ​ , NDCG@k = IDCG@k DCG@k ​ Worked check: a page with graded relevance has ; the ideal order gives , so NDCG@4 is about . Moving the grade-3 document to position 3 would cost far more than moving the grade-1 document, which is why NDCG weights the top. MRR averages of the first relevant result and suits navigational queries with one right answer. With first-relevant ranks 2, 1, and 4 across three queries, . Also track: recall at the candidate budget for retrieval, a per-segment breakdown (head, torso, tail, language, category), zero-result rate, and calibration if scores feed another system ( Calibration ). Online. CTR on the first page, click position distribution, long-click or satisfaction rate, abandonment (no click and no reformulation soon after), reformulation rate , time to first click, and downstream conversion. CTR alone can be gamed by attractive but unhelpful results, and abandonment can rise even when the answer was in the snippet. Pre-register guardrails: latency, zero-result rate, share of traffic with errors, and diversity. When offline and online disagree. Reasons include a biased offline label set, a ranker that changes the exposure distribution (so logged labels no longer cover its outputs), a gain on tail queries masked by head traffic, and novelty effects. Use interleaving (blend two rankers' lists and attribute clicks) for sensitive, low-traffic comparisons, then a full A/B test for ship decisions ( A/B Testing Experimentation ). Interview angle Name both the offline metric and the reason it can mislead. NDCG improved but abandonment rose is a realistic scenario to discuss, with candidate causes and the next diagnostic cut by query segment. # Latency budget and capacity Stage Budget (p99) Levers Query understanding 10 ms Cache by normalized query; small models Retrieval (parallel lexical and dense) 30 ms Sharding, early termination, quantized ANN, tiered index Fusion + feature fetch 20 ms Batched feature reads, co-located store, precomputed doc features L1 10 ms Tree models, vectorized scoring L2 30 ms Candidate cap, distillation, accelerator batching Re-rank + snippets 20 ms Precomputed snippets for head docs Slack 30 ms Hedged requests, timeouts with fallbacks If a stage exceeds its deadline, serve the previous stage's order rather than failing: a degraded but valid ranking beats a timeout. Distillation of the heavy ranker into a lighter model, feature pruning by importance per millisecond, and caching of head-query pages all reduce cost; see the efficiency discussion in ML in Production . # Freshness and indexing Two paths: a batch path (full index and embedding refresh nightly or weekly) and a streaming path (new or updated documents indexed within minutes via an append-only delta index merged periodically). If 2 percent of the 200M documents change per day, that is about 4 million documents to re-embed and re-index daily, roughly 46 per second on average; small enough for a streaming path. Dense vectors for new documents come from the same encoder, so they are comparable to existing ones; when the encoder is retrai

title: Case Study: Fraud and Abuse Detection
heads: Layering: rules, model, graph, and humans
Thresholding by business cost and capacity
text: Fraud detection is a classification problem where positives are rare, labels arrive late and are partly missing, the adversary adapts to your model, and the right threshold is a business cost, not a statistic. This case study designs a real-time fraud and abuse system for a payments and marketplace platform: every transaction is scored before it is approved, and a smaller set of account-level events (signups, logins, payouts) are scored for abuse. The same architecture, with different features, serves other abuse problems such as fake accounts and promo exploitation. The core difficulties are the ones named in the framing line, and they interact: because the model blocks transactions, it also changes which labels it will ever see. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Scope a fraud problem with prevalence, volume, review capacity, and cost-of-error numbers, and verify the arithmetic. Explain why a layered design (rules, model, graph and review) beats a single model. Handle extreme class imbalance without breaking calibration, and handle delayed and selection-biased labels with time-based splits. Choose a decision threshold from costs and capacity, and report precision at a fixed review capacity. Describe graph features, adversarial adaptation, drift monitoring, and active learning for the review queue. Discuss explainability and the cost of false positives to legitimate customers. # Problem statement and clarifying questions Prompt. Design a system that detects fraudulent transactions on a platform processing around 200 million transactions per day, deciding in real time whether to approve, challenge, hold, or decline each one. Question Why it matters Assumption used What counts as fraud, and who confirms it? Defines labels Chargebacks, confirmed analyst decisions, and customer reports Prevalence? Drives metrics and sampling About 0.1 percent of transactions Latency budget at authorization time? Bounds model and feature complexity 100 ms p99 for the scoring call Cost of a missed fraud versus a wrongly blocked good transaction? Sets threshold Missed fraud about 80 currency units, false positive about 5 (friction, support, lost sale) Review capacity? Bounds the queue 400 analysts, about 100 cases each per day Label delay? Shapes training and evaluation Chargebacks arrive 30 to 60 days later Are there regulatory explanation duties? Model class and logging Yes: reason codes for declines Is the adversary adaptive? Retraining and rule agility Yes, organized rings probe and adapt # Requirements and back-of-envelope scale Traffic. /86 , 400 ≈ 2 , 315 transactions per second on average. With a peak factor of 4 (evening and event spikes), plan for about per second. Fraud volume. At 0.1 percent prevalence, × 0.001 = 200 , 000 fraudulent transactions per day. A classifier that approves everything is 99.9 percent accurate, which is why accuracy is useless here ( Class Imbalance ). Review capacity. cases per day, which is ) = 0.02% of transactions. If analysts were the only defense, even perfect precision would catch at most of fraud; at 60 percent precision, confirmed cases, or 12 percent of the day's fraud. The consequence is the central design principle: automation must handle the bulk, and humans are reserved for the ambiguous middle . Feature lookups. If each decision needs around 40 online features, peak lookups are reads per second, which dictates a low-latency key-value store with precomputed aggregates rather than on-the-fly warehouse queries. Training data size. Over a 90-day window there are positives and about negatives. Keeping all positives and 1 percent of negatives gives roughly rows, a size that trains comfortably on a cluster, at the price of a calibration correction (below). # Architecture flowchart LR EV[ Transaction / event ] -- FE[ Feature assembly br/ online store + request context ] FE -- RU[ Rules layer br/ hard blocks, allow lists, velocity caps ] RU -- MD[ Model layer br/ GBDT / NN score ] GR[( Graph store br/ accounts, devices, cards, addresses )] -- FE MD -- DEC{ Decision br/ by score band } DEC -- | low | AP[ Approve ] DEC -- | middle | CH[ Challenge or hold br/ step-up auth, review queue ] DEC -- | high | DL[ Decline ] CH -- RQ[ Review queue br/ prioritized, capacity-aware ] RQ -- LB[( Labels br/ analyst + chargebacks + reports )] AP -- LB LB -- TR[ Training + backtesting ] TR -- MD STR[ Streaming aggregates br/ velocity, counters ] -- FE MON[ Monitoring br/ drift, precision, capacity ] -- MD Decision bands. Scores are mapped to actions, not to a single approve or decline. Low scores are approved; high scores are declined or blocked; the middle band triggers step-up authentication (for example a one-time code), a hold, or review. Step-up is valuable because it converts a probabilistic decision into evidence, and it generates labels cheaply. # Layering: rules, model, graph, and humans A single model is rarely the right design. Each layer has a distinct job: Layer Role Strength Weakness Rules Hard policy (sanctions lists, known-bad devices, velocity caps) and fast emergency response Instant to deploy, transparent, no training lag Brittle, accumulate, hard to retire Model Learns interactions across hundreds of signals, produces a calibrated risk score Generalizes beyond known patterns Label lag, needs retraining, opaque Graph Detects rings through shared devices, cards, addresses, payout accounts Catches coordinated behavior invisible per-transaction Computation cost, risk of guilt by association Human review Resolves ambiguity, produces high-quality labels Judgment, context Scarce, slow, inconsistent Rules and models are complementary in time: when a new attack appears, a rule can be live in minutes, while the model needs fresh labeled examples. A good practice is to treat every rule as a hypothesis with a measured precision and an owner, retire rules the model has absorbed, and feed rule outputs in as model features (with care to avoid the model simply copying a rule). # Data and labels Labels are the hardest part of this problem, and they are flawed in four distinct ways. Delay. A chargeback may arrive 30 to 60 days after the transaction. Recent data is therefore right-censored : a transaction from last week labeled not fraud may simply not have matured. Training on it injects false negatives. The fix is a maturation window : train only on transactions old enough that most fraud has surfaced (for example 45 days), and use faster proxy labels (analyst decisions, customer reports, step-up failures) for recent weeks, with their different noise characteristics recorded. Selection bias. The system only observes outcomes for what it approved. A declined fraudulent transaction yields no chargeback, and a declined good one yields no complaint that gets recorded. A model trained only on approved traffic learns a distorted distribution, and the bias tends to grow as the model's decisions shape which transactions are ever observed. Mitigations: a small random-approve holdout (approve some borderline transactions despite a high score, bounded by cost), reject inference techniques with their assumptions stated, and using labels from step-up flows and review. Noise. Chargebacks include friendly fraud (a genuine customer disputes a legitimate purchase), and analysts disagree. Keep label provenance as a column and consider weighting or separate heads. Incomplete coverage. Fraud that is never detected is labeled negative. Estimates of true prevalence from audits of random samples give a sanity check on the labeled rate. Time-based splitting. Random splits leak: the same card, device, or ring appears in both train and test, and patterns from the future inform the past ( Data Leakage ). Split by time with a gap equal to the maturation window, and evaluate on the most recent matured period, as in Time Series Validation . For account-level abuse, also split by entity so a ring is entirely in train or entirely in test when measuring generalization to new rings. Point-in-time features. Velocity counters and aggregates must be computed as of the decision time, not from a later snapshot; see ML in Production on point-in-time joins and Training-Serving Skew . # Features Family Examples Transaction Amount, currency, merchant category, time of day, payment method, shipping versus billing mismatch Entity history Account age, historical spend mean and variance, past disputes, ratio of amount to account norm Velocity Count and sum of attempts per card, device, IP, account in the last 1 minute, 1 hour, 24 hours, 7 days Device and network Device fingerprint age, emulator or proxy signals, IP reputation, geolocation distance from last event Behavioral Session telemetry, typing and navigation patterns, time from signup to first high-value action Graph Degree and connected-component size of shared identifiers, fraction of neighbors flagged, embeddings from a graph model Context Merchant risk score, event or promotion periods Streaming aggregates are central: velocity features computed in a stream processor and written to the online store at second-level freshness. Ratios against the entity's own history (for example the amount as a multiple of the 30-day median) are usually more informative than raw values because they normalize between small and large spenders. Graph features. Fraud rings reuse infrastructure: several accounts share a device, a payout account, or a shipping address. Useful graph signals are connected-component size and age, the number of distinct accounts per device or card, the proportion of neighbors with confirmed fraud (label propagation), and learned node embeddings from a graph neural network ( Graph Neural Networks ). Two cautions: neighbor-label features leak if the neighbors' labels were determined after the decision time, so compute them point in time; and shared infrastructure can be innocent (a household, a university network), so guilt by association needs thresholds and secondary evidence. Heavy graph computation usually runs near-real-time on a graph store and publishes compact features to the online store rather than traversing the graph inside the 100 ms path. # Model choices Option Fit Trade-off Logistic regression Baseline, easy reason codes Limited interactions Gradient boosted trees Strong default on tabular, fast inference, handles missing values and mixed scale Needs feature engineering; interactions are tree-limited Deep models (sequence models over event history, entity embeddings) Learn from raw behavior sequences More data and serving cost, harder to explain Graph neural network Captures ring structure Heavier infrastructure, staleness Anomaly detection (isolation forest, autoencoder) Unsupervised signal for new attack types High false positive rate; best as a feature or alert, not the sole gate A reasonable stack: gradient boosted trees ( Gradient Boosting ) as the primary scorer, with graph-derived and sequence-derived features as inputs and an unsupervised anomaly score as an additional input. Multiple models can specialize by segment (card-present versus online, new versus established accounts) when the base rates and attack types differ, at the cost of more models to maintain. Imbalance handling. Options, in order of how often they are enough: (a) no resampling, with class weights or a metric suited to imbalance; (b) downsampling negatives , which cuts training cost but distorts probabilities; (c) oversampling or synthetic positives, which risks overfitting to duplicated points and is often unnecessary with boosted trees. If negatives are kept with probability , scores must be corrected to recover the true probability: ​ − p s ​ + 1 β p s ​ ​ where ​ is the model's output on the sampled data. With , a sampled score of corresponds to a true probability of , about 1 percent, not 50 percent. Skipping this step makes thresholds meaningless and breaks cost-based decisions; verify with a reliability check on an un-resampled validation window ( Calibration ). Common mistake Evaluating on a resampled, balanced validation set. Precision on a 50/50 set bears no relation to precision at 0.1 percent prevalence. # Thresholding by business cost and capacity Given a calibrated probability of fraud, declining a transaction is better than approving it when the expected loss from fraud exceeds the expected loss from friction: ​ ( 1 − p ) ⋅ C F P ​ ⟹ p C F P ​ + C F N ​ C F P ​ ​ With ​ = 5 and ​ = 80 , the threshold is . This is a statement about calibrated probabilities ; with a miscalibrated model, the same score threshold encodes a different risk. In practice the costs vary by amount (a missed 5,000-unit fraud is not an 80-unit loss), so the threshold is per-transaction, using the amount as a multiplier on ​ . Capacity constraint. The review queue limits how many borderline cases can be examined. Two operating modes: Cost-optimal : apply the formula, then check that the middle band fits capacity. Capacity-constrained : rank by expected value of review (risk times amount) and review the top per day. The metric is then precision at capacity (precision among the top 40,000 daily cases) together with recall of fraud value captured. Because the queue is small relative to the problem, scoring bands need an auto-resolve path (step-up authentication) to avoid sending everything uncertain to people.
