Thresholds are revisited whenever costs, fraud mix, or capacity change, and should be separable from model training so operations can adjust them quickly. # Real-time versus batch Path Latency Uses Examples Real-time scoring Under 100 ms Decide at authorization with online features Transaction approve, challenge, decline Near-real-time Seconds to minutes Stream aggregates, graph updates, account-level triggers Velocity counters, ring detection on new links Batch Hours to days Deep behavior models, full-graph analysis, backfills, retrospective review Nightly sweep of approved transactions, payout holds Batch detection catches fraud the real-time path missed, enabling actions such as delaying a payout, freezing an account, or recalling a shipment. It also serves as a second chance where the cost of waiting is low. Keep the feature definitions shared between paths to limit skew. Fail-open versus fail-closed behavior must be an explicit policy when the scoring service is unavailable (for example approve low-value transactions and hold high-value ones), with rules still applied as a safety net. # Adversarial adaptation and drift Fraudsters probe: they test small amounts, vary devices, and adapt to whatever gets blocked. This changes how the system must be run. Concept drift is the default. The relationship between features and fraud shifts as tactics change, not only the input distribution; see Data Drift vs Concept Drift . Retrain frequently (daily or weekly for fast-moving segments) on matured labels plus fresh proxy labels, and keep a champion-challenger setup. Avoid revealing the decision boundary. Generic decline messages, randomized step-up, and delayed decisions give attackers less information. Rate-limit probing. Feature robustness. Prefer signals that are costly to fake (account tenure, long-lived device history, payment instrument age) over easily spoofed ones. Monitor feature importance shifts as an attack indicator. Rapid response lane. Rules, deny lists, and per-segment threshold changes act within minutes while a retrained model takes longer. Red teaming. Periodically simulate attacks against the staging system to find weak features. Monitoring. Track score distribution, decline and challenge rates by segment, step-up pass rates, approval rate, chargeback rate by cohort once matured, and the precision of each rule. A sudden drop in the fraud rate may mean the attackers moved to a segment you do not measure, not that the problem is solved. # Review queues and active learning The review queue is both an operational process and the best source of high-quality labels. Design it deliberately: Prioritization. Rank cases by expected loss avoided, risk times amount, not by score alone; break ties by case age to meet service levels. Active learning. Reserve a portion of review capacity for uncertain cases (scores near the threshold) and for a random sample of lower scores. Uncertainty sampling improves the labels where the model is least certain, and the random sample gives unbiased performance estimates and covers blind spots. Mixing the two avoids a feedback loop where only the model's confident cases are ever examined. Analyst tooling. Show the model's reason codes, linked entities from the graph, and prior decisions to speed decisions and improve consistency. Quality control. Double-review a sample to measure analyst agreement, and track label turnaround so that fast labels can feed retraining. Capacity feedback. If the middle band overflows capacity, tighten the band or add automated step-up; if it underflows, widen the band to harvest more labels. # Evaluation Offline. Use PR-AUC and precision at a fixed recall or capacity , not accuracy or ROC-AUC alone; ROC-AUC can look excellent at extreme imbalance while precision is poor ( ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC , Precision and Recall ). At 0.1 percent prevalence a random scorer has precision 0.001, which is the baseline to compare against. Evaluate value-weighted metrics: fraud dollars caught, false-positive dollars, and net savings under the cost model, in addition to counts. Evaluate on a time-based hold-out with a maturation gap, reported per segment (new accounts, payment types, geographies). Check calibration by reliability curve and expected calibration error ( Calibration ), since thresholds depend on it. Run backtests : replay the last several weeks day by day with the deployed policy and the candidate policy, applying the capacity constraint, to estimate net savings and queue load. Online. A/B tests are possible but slow because the main outcome (chargebacks) is delayed and rare; use leading indicators (decline and challenge rates, step-up pass rate, analyst confirmed-fraud rate in review) for early read and the matured chargeback rate for the final read ( A/B Testing Experimentation ). Randomize at the entity level (account or card) where possible, since a ring touching both arms contaminates the comparison. Guardrails: approval rate, customer complaints, support contacts, conversion on challenged flows, and latency. Shadow mode for a new model: score without acting, compare with the incumbent and with later labels, then ramp. # Explainability and false-positive cost Declines have costs beyond the 5-unit placeholder: lost customer lifetime value, support load, and trust. Good customers who are wrongly declined may not return, so the cost can be skewed toward high-value, high-frequency customers. Design implications: Track false positive rate by customer segment , including a fairness check so that the model does not systematically burden certain regions or groups; see the fairness checks in ML in Production . Provide reason codes for each decision (top contributing features through SHAP-style attributions or a surrogate), logged for audit and shown to analysts. Tree models make this practical at serving cost. Reason codes shown to customers should be generic enough not to teach attackers. Prefer step-up over decline in the gray zone, since a customer who passes a challenge is retained and a fraudster often fails. Provide an appeal path and use appeals as labels. Keep a decision log (inputs, score, rule hits, model version, action) for audit and reproducibility. Interview angle Weak answers say use SMOTE and optimize F1 . Strong answers state the cost matrix, derive the threshold from calibrated probabilities, name the label delay and selection bias, and mention step-up authentication and review capacity as part of the decision policy. # Failure modes Failure Symptom Mitigation Label delay misread as improvement Recent fraud rate looks low Maturation win

title: Case Study: A RAG Question-Answering Assistant
text: A retrieval-augmented assistant is a search system whose last stage is a language model: quality is capped by what retrieval finds, safety is capped by what the prompt lets through, and cost is capped by how many tokens each answer drags along. This case study designs an internal knowledge assistant for a large organization: employees ask natural-language questions and receive grounded answers with citations drawn from documents they are allowed to see (policies, wikis, tickets, design docs, slide decks). The concepts behind the pieces are in Retrieval-Augmented Generation , Embeddings Vector Search , and LLM Evaluation ; this note assembles them into one system with numbers, trade-offs, and failure modes. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Scope a RAG assistant with corpus size, query load, token budget, and cost arithmetic. Describe the ingestion pipeline and justify chunking choices. Explain hybrid retrieval plus reranking and the difference between retrieval metrics and answer metrics. Construct a prompt that supports citations and handles missing evidence, and describe defenses against prompt injection. Enforce document permissions at retrieval time and keep the index fresh. Design an evaluation suite (recall@k, faithfulness, answer relevance, human review) and an observability loop. # Problem statement and clarifying questions Prompt. Design a question-answering assistant over an organization's internal documents. It should answer in natural language, cite its sources, respect access controls, and say so when the documents do not contain the answer. Question Why it matters Assumption used Who are the users and what do they ask? Query mix drives retrieval and eval design 100,000 employees; policy lookups, how-to, troubleshooting, summarization of specific documents Corpus size and formats Ingestion, chunking, index size 2 million documents; text, tables, slides, PDFs, some scanned Document sensitivity and permissions Retrieval filtering Per-document and per-folder ACLs that change daily Freshness Ingestion path Changes visible within about an hour Answer latency tolerance Streaming and model choice First token under 2 s, full answer within about 10 s Is a wrong answer costly? Guardrail strictness Moderate to high in HR, legal, security topics Languages Embedding model choice A few major languages Is the assistant allowed to take actions? Injection blast radius Read-only: no tools beyond retrieval The task is grounded generation : produce an answer whose claims are supported by retrieved passages, with the option to abstain. The success criteria are three-part: the right evidence was retrieved, the answer is faithful to it, and the answer addresses the question asked. # Requirements and back-of-envelope scale Corpus. With 2 million documents averaging 15 chunks each, the index holds × 15 = 30 × 1 0 6 chunks. Vector memory. For a 1,024-dimensional embedding: Representation Size for 30M vectors float32 × 1024 × 4 B ≈ 123 GB float16 int8 float16 at 768-d An ANN index adds graph overhead on top. Quantized or smaller embeddings, or a disk-backed index, keep memory manageable, with a small recall cost to be measured rather than assumed. Query load. users 5 questions/day questions per day, which is /86 , 400 ≈ 5.8 QPS on average and, with a peak factor of 4 for the working-day shape, about 23 QPS. That is small for retrieval; the cost and latency are dominated by the generator. Tokens per request. Six retrieved chunks of about 400 tokens each, plus a 300-token system prompt and a 200-token question and history: With a typical answer around 350 output tokens, daily volume is × 2 , 900 = 1.45 × 1 0 9 input tokens (1.45 billion) and output tokens. Illustrative cost. Using placeholder prices of 3 units per million input tokens and 15 units per million output tokens (substitute real prices): 3 ​ + 350 × 1 0 6 15 ​ ≈ 0.0087 + 0.00525 ≈ 0.014 per query or about units per day at queries. If a cache absorbs 30 percent of queries, daily cost drops to roughly units. Input tokens (context) are the lever you control most directly: fewer, better chunks reduce both cost and latency. Latency. A rough budget: query rewrite 150 ms, retrieval 80 ms, rerank 120 ms, prompt assembly 10 ms, generator time to first token 600 ms, then streaming decode. At about 60 tokens per second, 350 output tokens take roughly 5.8 s, so a full answer completes in about 6 to 7 s while the user sees text after under 1.5 s. Streaming is therefore part of the design, not polish; see LLM Inference and KV Cache for serving details. Ingestion load. If 2 percent of documents change per day, that is 40,000 documents or about 600,000 chunks to re-embed daily, around 7 chunks per second: a small, steady load. The initial backfill of 30 million chunks is the heavy job and is run as a batch. # Architecture flowchart TB subgraph Ingest[ Ingestion (async) ] SRC[ Sources: wiki, drive, tickets ] -- PARSE[ Parse + clean br/ layout, tables, OCR ] PARSE -- CHUNK[ Chunk + metadata br/ doc id, section, ACL, timestamps ] CHUNK -- EMB[ Embed ] EMB -- VIDX[( Vector index )] CHUNK -- LIDX[( Lexical index BM25 )] end subgraph Serve[ Query path ] U[ User question + identity ] -- RW[ Rewrite / contextualize ] RW -- RET[ Hybrid retrieval br/ dense + BM25, ACL filter ] VIDX -- RET LIDX -- RET RET -- RR[ Rerank br/ cross-encoder, top 6 ] RR -- PR[ Prompt builder br/ instructions, evidence, citations ] PR -- LLM[ Generator ] LLM -- GR[ Output checks br/ citation + groundedness + policy ] GR -- ANS[ Answer with citations ] end CACHE[( Semantic + exact cache )] -- RET ANS -- OBS[( Traces, feedback, eval sets )] OBS -- EVAL[ Offline eval + dashboards ] # Ingestion and chunking Parsing decides what the model can ever know. PDFs with multi-column layouts, tables, and scanned pages are common failure sources: a table flattened into text can become unreadable, and OCR errors become retrieval misses. Preserve structure (headings, list items, table rows) as metadata, extract tables into a text form that keeps row and column labels, and track a parse-quality signal per document so failures are visible. Chunking is the highest-leverage ingestion decision. Options: Strategy Pros Cons Fixed size with overlap (for example 400 tokens, 15 percent overlap) Simple, predictable Cuts across sentences and sections Structure-aware (split on headings and paragraphs, merge small pieces) Chunks match meaning units Variable size, needs reliable parsing Hierarchical (small chunks for retrieval, parent section for context) Precise retrieval with enough context for the generator More storage, extra logic Semantic or model-based boundaries Adaptive Cost, harder to debug A solid default is structure-aware chunks of a few hundred tokens with a heading breadcrumb prepended ( Policy Travel Reimbursement ) so that a chunk is interpretable on its own, plus a retrieve-small, expand-to-parent step for context. Too-small chunks lose the antecedent of pronouns and the conditions of rules; too-large chunks dilute the embedding and waste tokens. Tune chunk size by retrieval recall on a labeled question set rather than by intuition. Metadata to store with every chunk: document ID and URL, title, section path, author, created and modified timestamps, document type, language, ACL identifiers, and a content hash for deduplication and change detection. Deduplicate near-identical documents (copies, versions), or retrieval will return five copies of one policy. # Embeddings and hybrid retrieval Embedding model choice. Compare candidate models on your own question and passage set, not only on public leaderboards. Factors: quality in the corpus's domain and languages, dimension (index size and speed), maximum input length, inference cost, and whether queries and documents use different prefixes or instructions. Fine-tuning on in-domain pairs (questions with clicked or judged passages) can help when vocabulary is specialized, but start by measuring a strong off-the-shelf model. Why hybrid. Dense retrieval handles paraphrase; lexical retrieval (BM25) handles exact tokens such as error codes, product names, policy identifiers, and acronyms that embeddings blur. Retrieve the top 50 from each and fuse, using reciprocal rank fusion or learned weights, to produce about 50 to 100 candidates. See Embeddings Vector Search for ANN index types (graph-based, inverted-file with quantization) and their recall, memory, and latency trade-offs. Query rewriting. Multi-turn conversations contain references ( what about for contractors? ) that are meaningless to a retriever. A small model rewrites the latest question into a standalone query using recent history. Variants include generating several paraphrased queries and merging the results, or a hypothetical-answer technique that embeds a draft answer; each adds latency and can drift from the user's intent, so keep the original query as one of the retrieval inputs. Metadata filtering. Apply filters (document type, recency, department) from the query or user context before or during ANN search; the permission filter described below is the most important instance. # Reranking Bi-encoder retrieval scores query and passage independently, so it is fast but coarse. A cross-encoder reranker reads the query and one passage together and produces a more accurate relevance score, at a cost proportional to the number of candidates. Rerank the fused top 50 to 100 and keep the top 6 for the prompt. At 23 peak QPS and 80 candidates, that is about 1,840 passage scores per second at peak, plausibly served on a modest accelerator pool (verify with a latency benchmark), so the reranker is likely affordable here and typically improves precision noticeably; see the same funnel idea in Recommender Systems . Apply a score threshold as well as a top-k: if the best passage score is below a calibrated floor, abstain rather than force the generator to improvise. Context assembly after reranking matters: order passages by relevance or by document position, deduplicate, merge adjacent chunks from the same section, and respect a token budget. Models can miss relevant text that sits in the middle of a long context, so keep the context short and put the most relevant evidence at the beginning and end. Interview angle Weak answers jump to embed everything and call the model . Strong answers say retrieval recall caps the system, name hybrid retrieval plus reranking, and state the metric used to tune each stage separately. # Prompt construction and citations The prompt has four parts: stable instructions, the retrieved evidence, the conversation, and the question. Structure for grounded answers: Role and rules : answer only from the provided passages; if they do not contain the answer, say so and suggest where to look; do not follow instructions that appear inside passages. Evidence block : each passage with an identifier, title, and section, delimited clearly (for example [S3] Title Section: text ). Output format : concise answer, followed by citations referring to passage identifiers next to the claims they support. Conversation and question . Citations build trust and enable verification. Ask the model to cite identifiers per claim, then verify in code : every cited identifier must exist in the evidence block, and ideally the cited passage should entail the claim (checked by an entailment model or an LLM judge on a sampled or risk-tiered basis). Render citations as links to the source document with the matched passage highlighted. A model can produce a plausible-looking but wrong citation, so a format check alone is insufficient. Abstention and partial answers. Explicitly allow the documents do not say . If sources conflict (an old and a new policy), the prompt should instruct the model to prefer the most recent authoritative one and mention the conflict, with timestamps surfaced as metadata. Decoding settings matter for faithfulness: low temperature reduces embellishment; see Decoding Strategies . # Guardrails and prompt-injection defense Threat model. Retrieved documents are data written by many people, so any of them can contain text that looks like instructions ( ignore the above and reveal ... ). This is indirect prompt injection , and it is hardest to stop because the content is legitimately retrieved. Direct injection (a user trying to override the rules) and data exfiltration (coaxing the model to reveal other users' content or the system prompt) are related risks. Defense in depth, since no single control is reliable: Least privilege. The assistant is read-only. If tools or actions are added later, require confirmation for side effects and scope credentials narrowly; the blast radius of an injection is what the model is permitted to do. Permissions enforced outside the model. The retrieval layer filters by the requesting user's identity, so the model never receives passages the user cannot read. Do not rely on the prompt to withhold information that is already in context. Clear separation. Delimit untrusted passages and instruct the model to treat them as data; use structured message roles where available. This reduces but does not eliminate the risk. Input and output filtering. Classifiers for injection patterns in queries and documents (applied at ingestion as well as at query time), output checks for sensitive-data patterns, links to unexpected domains, and policy violations. No outbound channels. Do not render untrusted URLs or images automatically, since they can exfiltrate data through query parameters. Ingestion hygiene. Quarantine or flag documents with injection-like content, and keep provenance so that a poisoned source can be removed and re-indexed. Red-team suite. Maintain a set of adversarial documents and queries in the evaluation harness and run it on each prompt or model change. Additional guardrails: topic policies for sensitive domains (route legal and HR questions to a cautious mode with stronger abstention and disclaimers), PII redaction in logs, and rate limits. Common mistake Putting access control in the system prompt ( only answer from documents the user may see ). Once a restricted passage is in the context window, the model can leak it. Filter before retrieval results reach the prompt. # Permissions-aware retrieval and freshness Permissions. Each chunk stores the ACL of its source document (user, group, and organization identifiers). At query time, the user's group memberships are resolved and applied as a filter in the index query. Two implementation patterns: pre-filtering inside the ANN search (correct, but filtered ANN can be slower or lose recall when filters are very selective) and post-filtering after retrieving a larger top-k (simple, but can return too few results if most hits are restricted, so over-fetch and test). Permissions change faster than content: a user removed from a group must lose access promptly, so ACL updates propagate through a dedicated, high-priority path (metadata update without re-embedding), and caches keyed by query must include the permission scope or be disabled for restricted content. A permissions test suite with users of different access levels is part of the release checks. Freshness. Use change data capture or webhooks from sources to trigger incremental re-ingestion, with periodic full crawls as a safety net to catch missed events. Use content hashes to skip unchanged chunks, soft-delete removed documents immediately (a tombstone filter) rather than waiting for compaction, and track an index lag metric (time from source change to searchable). Versioned documents need a policy: keep only the current version, or keep history with an as of filter. When the embedding model changes, re-embed everything into a new index and switch over atomically; mixing embeddings from different models in one index makes similarity scores meaningless. # Caching, latency, and cost Technique What it saves Risk Exact-match response cache (normalized query and permission scope) Entire pipeline for repeated questions Stale answers; scope leakage if keys omit permissions Semantic cache (nearby query embeddings reuse an answer) Generation cost for paraphrases False hits on questions that differ in a key detail; tune similarity threshold conservatively Retrieval cache Retrieval and rerank for frequent queries Staleness after document updates Prompt prefix caching Repeated system prompt and shared prefix tokens Requires stable prompt prefix ordering Context trimming (rerank threshold, fewer chunks, compression) Input tokens Lower recall of needed evidence Model routing (smaller model for easy or high-confidence queries) Cost and latency Quality drop if routing misclassifies Streaming Perceived latency None significant Cost control starts with the arithmetic above: input tokens dominate, so six well-chosen chunks beat twelve mediocre ones. Track cost per answered question and cost per resolved question, which differ when users re-ask. Apply timeouts and a fallback path (return the top passages with links if the generator is unavailable). # Evaluation RAG has two failure sources, retrieval and generation, so evaluate them separately and then together. General principles of LLM evaluation, judge reliability, and contamination are in LLM Evaluation . Evaluation set. Build 300 to 1,000 questions covering the real mix (look up a fact, multi-step, multi-document, ambiguous, unanswerable, adversarial), each with reference passages and, where feasible, a reference answer. Sources: sampled production queries (with privacy review), subject-matter expert writing, and synthetic questions generated from documents then filtered by humans. Include a deliberate share of unanswerable questions to measure abstention. The set needs enough size to be informative: with 300 questions and a pass rate near 80 percent, the 95 percent confidence interval is about percentage points ( ​ ), so small differences between variants are noise. Retrieval metrics. Recall@k : fraction of questions for which at least one (or all) of the needed passages appear in the top . Track recall at the candidate stage (top 50 to 100) and after rerank (top 6). MRR and NDCG for ordering quality ( Ranking Metrics ). Context precision : fraction of the passages placed in the prompt that were actually useful, which affects cost and distraction. Generation metrics. Faithfulness (groundedness) : are all claims supported by the retrieved passages? Typically measured by decomposing the answer into claims and verifying each against the evidence with an entailment model or LLM judge. Unfaithful answers are the form of Hallucination that RAG is meant to prevent. Answer relevance : does the answer address the question asked? Answer correctness against the reference, when one exists. Citation accuracy : do citations point to passages that support the claim? Abstention quality : correct refusal on unanswerable questions, and low false-refusal rate on answerable ones. Why the decomposition matters. End-to-end success is roughly bounded by the product of stages. If the needed passage is in the candidate set 90 percent of the time, survives reranking 95 percent of the time, and the generator uses it correctly 90 percent of the time, success is about , and the per-stage numbers tell you where to invest. Judges and humans. LLM judges scale but have biases (favoring longer answers, their own style) and need calibration: score a sample with humans, measure agreement, and keep the judge prompt and model fixed while comparing variants. Human review stays essential for high-risk topics, for new failure categories, and for periodically auditing the judge. Report results with confidence intervals and per-category breakdowns. Online. Thumbs up and down, copy or click-through on citations, follow-up and rephrase rate (a rephrase soon after an answer often signals failure), escalation to a human or ticket creation, and task-level outcomes where measurable. Run A

title: Bandits & Reinforcement Learning Basics
heads: Choosing: Supervised vs Bandit vs RL in Products
text: Learning from the consequences of your own actions. Core vocabulary, the algorithms worth knowing by heart, and how to choose between bandit, RL and supervised formulations in a product. Supervised learning assumes labels are given. When a system chooses what to show, the data it later learns from depends on those choices, and there is a trade-off between using what is known and gathering information. Bandits and reinforcement learning formalize that setting. For the recommendation application see Recommender Systems ; for the broader interview structure see ML System Design Framework . What you'll be able to say after this chapter Define an MDP, the value functions, and the Bellman equation. Distinguish value-based from policy-based methods, and on-policy from off-policy. Write the Q-learning update and the policy gradient estimator at a glance. Implement epsilon-greedy, UCB and Thompson sampling and state their regret behavior under stated assumptions. Explain LinUCB for contextual bandits. Describe IPS and doubly robust off-policy evaluation, with their conditions. Decide among supervised learning, a bandit, and full RL for a product problem. # The Landscape Setting State Action affects future states? Feedback Example Supervised None (inputs given) No Correct label Spam classification Multi-armed bandit None No Reward of the chosen arm only Which headline variant to show Contextual bandit Context per round No Reward of the chosen action only Choose an article for this user now Reinforcement learning State evolves Yes Delayed reward Multi-step dialogue, inventory control, game play Bandit feedback is partial : you see the reward only for the action taken, never for the counterfactual alternatives. RL adds sequential dependence : actions change future states and rewards. # Markov Decision Processes Memory hook MDP = states, actions, transitions, reward, discount: the future depends on the present only. An MDP is a tuple : States , actions . Transition kernel ∣ s , a ) satisfying the Markov property : the next state depends on the history only through the current state and action. Reward (or ) ) and discount . A policy maps states to action distributions. The objective is to maximize expected discounted return ​ = ∑ k ≥ 0 ​ γ k r t + k ​ . The discount keeps the sum finite and expresses a preference for earlier rewards; near 1 gives a long horizon, and the effective horizon is about . # Value functions ( s ) = E π ​ [ G t ​ ∣ s t ​ = s ] , Q π ( s , a ) = E π ​ [ G t ​ ∣ s t ​ = s , a t ​ = a ] The Bellman expectation equation expresses value recursively: ( s , a ) = r ( s , a ) + γ E s ′ ∼ P ​ [ a ′ ∑ ​ π ( a ′ ∣ s ′ ) Q π ( s ′ , a ′ ) ] The Bellman optimality equation characterizes the best achievable value: ( s , a ) = r ( s , a ) + γ E s ′ ​ [ a ′ max ​ Q ∗ ( s ′ , a ′ ) ] , π ∗ ( s ) ∈ ar g a max ​ Q ∗ ( s , a ) The optimality operator is a -contraction in the max norm, so repeatedly applying it (value iteration) converges to when the model is known and the state-action space is finite. Interview angle The one-sentence difference between and : scores a state under a policy; scores a state-action pair and therefore lets you pick actions without a model of the environment, which is why model-free methods learn . # Value-Based vs Policy-Based Methods Value-based Policy-based Actor-critic Learns ; policy is greedy with respect to it ​ ( a ∣ s ) directly Both: policy (actor) and value (critic) Action space Discrete (max over actions must be tractable) Discrete or continuous Discrete or continuous Policy type Typically deterministic plus exploration noise Naturally stochastic Stochastic or deterministic Typical variance / bias Typically lower variance, can be unstable with function approximation Typically high variance, usually converges to a local optimum Variance reduced via baseline, bias from critic error Examples Q-learning, DQN REINFORCE A2C, PPO Other axes to name: Model-free vs model-based : whether a model of and is learned and used for planning. On-policy vs off-policy : on-policy methods learn about the policy that generates the data; off-policy methods can learn about one policy from data generated by another, which enables reuse of logs and replay buffers. # Q-Learning Q-learning is an off-policy temporal-difference method. After observing ) : max ​ Q ( s ′ , a ′ ) − Q ( s , a ) ] The bracketed term is the TD error : a bootstrapped target ​ Q ( s ′ , a ′ ) minus the current estimate. It is off-policy because the target uses the greedy action regardless of which action the behavior policy takes next (SARSA, in contrast, uses the action actually taken and is on-policy). In the tabular case, Q-learning converges to under standard conditions: every state-action pair is visited infinitely often and the step sizes satisfy the usual stochastic-approximation conditions. With neural networks (DQN-style) , the update becomes regression on the target ​ Q θ ˉ ​ ( s ′ , a ′ ) with two stabilizers: Experience replay : sample past transitions at random to decorrelate updates. Target network : is a slowly updated copy of , so the target does not chase itself. The combination of function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy data (the deadly triad ) can diverge; these tricks reduce, but do not eliminate, the risk. Taking the max over noisy estimates also causes overestimation bias , addressed by Double Q-learning (select the action with one network, evaluate it with another). # Policy Gradient at a Glance Parameterize ​ and ascend ​ ​ [ R ( τ )] . The policy gradient theorem gives ​ J = E π θ ​ ​ [ t ∑ ​ ∇ θ ​ lo g π θ ​ ( a t ​ ∣ s t ​ ) Ψ t ​ ] where ​ is a signal for how good the action was. The log-derivative trick is what makes this possible: the gradient passes through the sampling distribution without differentiating the environment. Choice of ​ Name Property Total return ​ REINFORCE Unbiased, high variance ​ − b ( s t ​ ) REINFORCE with baseline Still unbiased if does not depend on the action; lower variance ( s t ​ , a t ​ ) − V π ( s t ​ ) (advantage) Actor-critic Lower variance; bias depends on critic accuracy PPO limits how far each update moves the policy by clipping the probability ratio ​ = π θ ​ ( a t ​ ∣ s t ​ ) / π θ o l d ​ ​ ( a t ​ ∣ s t ​ ) : it maximizes ​ A t ​ , clip ( ρ t ​ , 1 − ϵ , 1 + ϵ ) A t ​ ) ] . This keeps updates inside a region where the old data is still a reasonable sample for the new policy. PPO is widely used, including in preference-based fine-tuning of language models (RLHF), where the environment is a learned reward model. Go deeper Stochastic policies make exploration automatic and permit continuous actions; the cost is sample inefficiency. Value-based methods reuse data more aggressively. Many practical systems combine them (actor-critic with a replay buffer), which brings back the stability issues of off-policy learning. # Exploration vs Exploitation Memory hook UCB is optimistic, Thompson sampling is random in proportion to belief, epsilon-greedy is random regardless of belief. Exploitation picks the action that currently looks best; exploration picks others to improve estimates. A system that never explores may lock onto a suboptimal action because its estimates for the others are never corrected. Formally, performance is measured by regret : the cumulative gap between the reward of the best fixed action and the reward obtained, − E [ t = 1 ∑ T ​ r t ​ ] Constant exploration gives linear regret; good algorithms achieve sublinear regret (logarithmic in for stochastic bandits with the right assumptions). # Multi-Armed Bandits arms, arm has unknown mean reward ​ . Each round pick an arm, observe a reward (assumed i.i.d. per arm for the stochastic bandit setting). Let ​ ( t ) be pulls of arm and ​ k ​ its sample mean. # Epsilon-greedy With probability pick a uniformly random arm; otherwise pick ​ μ ^ ​ k ​ . Simple, easy to implement, easy to explain. Wasteful: exploration is uniform, ignoring uncertainty, and a fixed yields linear regret. Decaying ​ ∝ 1/ t (with a suitable constant tied to the reward gaps) can recover logarithmic regret, but needs knowledge of those gaps to tune. # UCB (Upper Confidence Bound) Optimism in the face of uncertainty: pick the arm with the highest plausible mean. ​ = ar g k max ​ [ μ ^ ​ k ​ + N k ​ ( t ) 2 ln t ​ ​ ] (this is UCB1 for rewards in ). The bonus shrinks as an arm is pulled more, so under-sampled arms get tried, and clearly bad arms stop being pulled once their upper bound falls below the best arm's mean. UCB1 attains regret for stochastic bounded rewards. It is deterministic given the history, which can be inconvenient for delayed or batched feedback (all concurrent requests pick the same arm). # Thompson sampling Maintain a posterior over each arm's parameter; sample one value per arm from the posterior and play the arm with the largest sample. For Bernoulli rewards (click or no click) with a prior, after ​ successes and ​ failures: ​ ∼ Beta ( 1 + s k ​ , 1 + f k ​ ) , play ​ θ k ​ . Exploration is proportional to the probability an arm is best given current beliefs. Randomized, so it handles delayed and batched feedback gracefully. Often performs comparably to or better than UCB empirically, and has matching regret guarantees for several reward models. Requires a reasonable model of the reward and prior; with a misspecified model the guarantees do not hold. Algorithm Exploration mechanism Needs Notes Epsilon-greedy Random with probability Only ​ Baseline; tuning of matters UCB Optimism bonus ​ ​ Bounded or sub-Gaussian rewards Deterministic; strong theory Thompson Posterior sampling Posterior or conjugate model Randomized; strong empirical use Non-stationarity. If arm means drift (trends, seasonality, content freshness), use discounted or sliding-window estimates, or a floor on exploration, otherwise old data keeps estimates stale. Interview angle Asked A/B test vs bandit? Answer with the trade-off. A/B tests give clean, unbiased inference about effect sizes and long-horizon metrics for a fixed allocation. Bandits shift traffic toward better arms during the experiment (lower regret) but complicate statistical inference, are sensitive to non-stationarity and delayed rewards, and optimize one reward metric, so they fit short-lived, low-stakes, many-variant optimization such as creatives or ranking blends rather than long-term guardrail-heavy decisions. # Contextual Bandits In each round a context ​ is observed (user, time, device), the learner picks an action ​ , and sees reward ​ for that action only. The goal is a policy with high expected reward. The difference from RL is that actions do not influence future contexts; the difference from supervised learning is partial feedback. # LinUCB Assume expected reward is linear in features: ⊤ ​ x (the disjoint model; a shared-parameter version uses joint features ). Per action keep ​ = λ I + t : a t ​ = a ∑ ​ x t ​ x t ⊤ ​ , b a ​ = t : a t ​ = a ∑ ​ r t ​ x t ​ , θ ^ a ​ = A a − 1 ​ b a ​ (a ridge-regression estimate) and choose ​ = ar g a max ​ θ ^ a ⊤ ​ x t ​ + α x t ⊤ ​ A a − 1 ​ x t ​ ​ The second term is the width of a confidence interval for the prediction: large when the context ​ lies in directions where action has little data. controls exploration. Linear Thompson sampling is the randomized counterpart: sample a ​ ∼ N ( θ ^ a ​ , σ 2 A a − 1 ​ ) and act greedily on the sample. Considerations: The regret guarantees need the linear model to hold (or be approximately right). With neural reward models, practical variants use ensembles, dropout or last-layer Bayesian linear regression for uncertainty. Features should be normalized; ​ updates are rank-one, so the inverse can be maintained incrementally. Logging the probability of the chosen action is essential for later off-policy evaluation. # Off-Policy Evaluation (OPE) at a Glance Memory hook IPS reweights, DM models, DR does both and needs only one to be right. Goal: estimate the value of a new (target) policy from logs collected by a different logging policy , without deploying it. Logged data: ​ , a i ​ , r i ​ , μ ( a i ​ ∣ x i ​ )) . Direct method (DM) : fit a reward model ( x , a ) and compute D M ​ = n 1 ​ ∑ i ​ ∑ a ​ π ( a ∣ x i ​ ) r ^ ( x i ​ , a ) . Low variance; biased if the reward model is wrong. Inverse propensity scoring (IPS) : reweight logged rewards by how much more (or less) likely the target would have taken the logged action: I P S ​ = n 1 ​ i = 1 ∑ n ​ μ ( a i ​ ∣ x i ​ ) π ( a i ​ ∣ x i ​ ) ​ r i ​ Unbiased if (1) the logging propensities are known (or correctly estimated) and (2) overlap holds: wherever . Variance can be large when weights are large, so clipping or self-normalization is used (introducing some bias, in exchange for lower variance). Doubly robust (DR) : combine both, D R ​ = n 1 ​ i ∑ ​ [ a ∑ ​ π ( a ∣ x i ​ ) r ^ ( x i ​ , a ) + μ ( a i ​ ∣ x i ​ ) π ( a i ​ ∣ x i ​ ) ​ ( r i ​ − r ^ ( x i ​ , a i ​ ) ) ] It is consistent if either the reward model or the propensities are correct (hence doubly robust ), and typically has lower variance than IPS when is reasonable. Estimator Bias Variance Requires DM Depends on reward-model error Low Good reward model IPS Unbiased with correct propensities and overlap High Logged propensities DR Unbiased if propensities or model correct Medium Both available For sequences (full RL) the importance weights multiply over time steps, so variance can grow exponentially with horizon, which is why trajectory-level OPE is much harder than bandit OPE; per-decision weights, fitted-Q evaluation, and DR variants for RL are used. Practical conditions OPE fails silently when the logging policy never took the actions the new policy prefers (no overlap), when propensities were not logged, or when the environment changes between logging and deployment. Treat OPE as a filter that selects candidates for an online test, not a replacement for it. # Choosing: Supervised vs Bandit vs RL in Products Question If yes, lean toward Are correct labels available, independent of what the system does? Supervised learning Does the system choose an action, and you only observe the outcome of the chosen action? Contextual bandit (or supervised with IPS-weighted logs) Do current actions meaningfully change future states or future user behavior, and is long-term reward the target? RL (or a bandit with a carefully chosen proxy reward) Can you simulate or safely experiment at scale? RL becomes feasible; otherwise prefer offline or conservative methods Considerations: Most recommendation and ranking systems begin as supervised models trained on logged engagement, plus a small amount of exploration. Bandits layer on where freshness and uncertainty matter (new items, creative or layout selection, notification timing). RL fits when long-term effects dominate , for example optimizing session-level or retention outcomes, notification pacing, or sequential decision problems such as bidding with budgets. The costs: reward design (a wrong reward is optimized relentlessly), delayed and noisy credit assignment, off-policy evaluation difficulty, instability, and the engineering burden of simulators or safe exploration. A pragmatic intermediate step is to train a supervised model on proxies for long-term outcomes (for example predicted next-session return) and use it as a feature or objective term, before moving to full RL. Offline RL / batch RL learns from logged data without exploration, but suffers distribution shift: the learned policy may choose actions the logs never covered, and Q estimates for those are unreliable. Conservative methods penalize such actions. Guardrails apply to any learner that acts: constraints on harmful actions, fallback policies, gradual rollout, and monitoring of reward-hacking symptoms (the proxy rises while true satisfaction does not). Interview angle A strong framing: start from the simplest formulation that matches the data-generating process. If the decision is independent per request, it is a contextual bandit at most; escalate to RL only with a concrete argument that actions change future states in a way that matters, and say how reward, evaluation, and safe rollout will be handled. Rapid fire: bandits and RL Bandit feedback is partial: only the chosen action's reward is seen. RL adds sequential dependence: actions change future states. scores state-action pairs, so greedy action choice needs no model. Q-learning is off-policy because its target uses the greedy next action. A fixed epsilon gives linear regret; UCB and Thompson reach logarithmic regret under assumptions. Log the probability of every chosen action, since IPS needs it later. OPE needs overlap; treat it as a filter ahead of an online test. Start from the simplest formulation: supervised, then bandit, then RL. # One-page summary Concept The one thing to remember MDP ; Markov property; return ​ = ∑ γ k r t + k ​ Value functions , ; Bellman: ( s , a ) = r + γ E [ max a ′ ​ Q ∗ ( s ′ , a ′ )] Q-learning Off-policy TD: , ⋅ ) − Q ] ; DQN adds replay and target network; overestimation bias Policy gradient ; baseline or advantage reduces variance; PPO clips the ratio Value vs policy Value-based: discrete actions, sample-efficient; policy-based: continuous, stochastic, high variance; actor-critic blends Regret − E ∑ r t ​ ; fixed gives linear, UCB and Thompson give logarithmic (under assumptions) Bandit algorithms Epsilon-greedy (random), UCB (optimism), Thompson (posterior sampling) LinUCB Ridge estimate per arm plus bonus A − 1 x ​ OPE IPS (unbiased with overlap, high variance), DM (biased, low variance), DR (either correct) Product choice Supervised if labels independent of actions; bandit for per-request choice with partial feedback; RL when actions shape future states and long-term reward matters # Related Recommender Systems Cold Start : where exploration pays off most A/B Testing Online Experimentation : fixed-allocation experiments versus bandits RLHF vs DPO LLM Training: Pretraining, Fine-Tuning Alignment ML System Design Framework Training Neural Networks Cross-Entropy Loss Gradient Descent

title: Responsible ML: Fairness, Explainability & Privacy
heads: Worked example: metrics from confusion matrices
text: A model that scores well on aggregate metrics can still be unfair to a subgroup, impossible to explain, or leak the data it was trained on. These are engineering properties to specify, measure, and monitor. Responsible ML covers three overlapping concerns: fairness (does the system treat groups comparably?), explainability (can people understand why it produced an output?), and privacy (does training and serving expose individuals?). In interviews they appear as system design follow-ups ( how would you make sure this does not discriminate? , how would you explain a rejection? , can your model leak training data? ). Good answers define the metric, say where in the pipeline the problem enters, name the trade-off, and describe how it is monitored after launch. Regulatory and legal points here are stated only generally and are not legal advice; requirements differ by jurisdiction and domain, so a real system needs input from legal and compliance specialists. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Define demographic parity, equalized odds, equal opportunity, and calibration within groups, and compute them from a confusion matrix. State the fairness impossibility result with its conditions and explain what it implies for metric choice. Locate where bias enters (data, labels, features, objective, deployment) and pick pre-, in-, or post-processing mitigations with their costs. Explain permutation importance, PDP/ICE, SHAP, and LIME, including their assumptions and failure modes, and why attention is not automatically an explanation. Describe k-anonymity's limits, differential privacy with epsilon, federated learning, and membership inference. Outline model cards, fairness monitoring, and LLM-specific risks. # Fairness definitions Let be the model's decision, the true outcome, and a sensitive attribute (group membership). Different definitions encode different ideas of fairness; they are not interchangeable. Criterion Requirement Intuition Demographic (statistical) parity = 1 ∣ A = a ) = P ( Y ^ = 1 ∣ A = b ) Same selection rate across groups, regardless of true outcomes Equal opportunity = 1 ∣ Y = 1 , A = a ) = P ( Y ^ = 1 ∣ Y = 1 , A = b ) Qualified people are accepted at equal rates (equal true positive rate) Equalized odds Equal TPR and equal FPR across groups Equal error rates of both kinds Calibration within groups ​ = s , A = a ) = s for every group A score means the same thing in every group Predictive parity Equal precision (PPV) across groups A positive decision is equally reliable in every group Demographic parity ignores the label, so it can force acceptance of unqualified candidates in one group or reject qualified ones in another when true rates differ. It fits cases where the outcome label itself is suspect. Equal opportunity and equalized odds condition on the true label and so assume the label is a trustworthy measure of the outcome. Calibration within groups is natural for probabilistic scores (see Calibration ), since a risk score is only useful for decisions if it means the same thing for everyone. # Worked example: metrics from confusion matrices Two groups of 100 people each, with a binary decision: Group TP FP FN TN A 40 10 10 40 B 15 20 5 60 Computed values (checked with a short script): Metric Group A Group B Gap Base rate 0.50 0.20 0.30 Selection rate 0.50 0.35 0.15 TPR (recall) 0.80 0.75 0.05 FPR 0.20 0.25 0.05 PPV (precision) 0.80 0.43 0.37 Accuracy 0.80 0.75 0.05 Reading it: demographic parity is violated by 15 points; equal opportunity is off by 5 points; equalized odds is off by 5 points on each rate; and precision differs sharply (0.80 vs 0.43), so a positive decision is far less reliable for group B. The model's error rates are similar across groups, yet precision diverges. That gap is a mechanical consequence of different base rates, which leads to the impossibility result. Memory hook Parity looks at decisions, odds look at errors given the truth, calibration looks at the truth given the score. # The impossibility result Several results (Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan; Chouldechova) show that fairness criteria conflict. A precise statement for a binary classifier: when the base rates differ between groups, = P ( Y = 1 ∣ A = b ) , and the classifier is not perfect, it is not possible to have equal PPV (predictive parity) and equal FPR and equal FNR across groups simultaneously. The identity behind it, for group prevalence : p ​ ⋅ PPV 1 − PPV ​ ⋅ ( 1 − FNR ) If PPV and FNR are equal across groups but differs, FPR must differ. For group B above: 0.2 ​ × 0.429 0.571 ​ × 0.75 = 0.25 , matching the table. The score-based version (Kleinberg et al.) says that calibration within groups and balance for the positive and negative classes (equal average score among true positives, and among true negatives, across groups) cannot all hold unless base rates are equal or prediction is perfect. Conditions to state in an interview: the result needs unequal base rates and imperfect prediction. It does not say fairness is impossible in general, and it vanishes if base rates are equal or if the classifier is perfect. Its practical meaning is that choosing a fairness criterion is a value judgement about which error matters, to be made with domain, policy, and legal input, and then documented. For lending-style risk scores, calibration is often prioritized; for screening or access-to-opportunity settings, equal opportunity is common; when the label reflects historical discrimination, parity-style targets may be defended. Interview angle Weak: Make the model fair by removing the sensitive attribute. Strong: Dropping the attribute often leaves the signal in place because proxies (postal code, school, browsing patterns) carry it. Pick the metric tied to the harm, measure it across groups using held-out data with sensitive attributes, and discuss the trade-off, noting that with unequal base rates and an imperfect classifier calibration and equal error rates cannot hold together. # Where bias enters the pipeline Bias is not a single bug in the model; it can enter at each stage. Problem framing and target choice. A proxy label (arrests instead of offences, spend instead of need, clicks instead of satisfaction) carries the measurement process's bias. Data collection and sampling. Under-representation, convenience samples, and survivorship (only approved applicants have repayment labels) distort what the model sees. See Class Imbalance for the minority-group cousin. Labels. Human annotators and historical decisions encode prior judgement. Label noise can be group-dependent. Features. Proxies for protected attributes; features that are measured with different quality across groups (a sensor, a language, a lighting condition). Objective and metrics. Optimizing average accuracy lets the majority group dominate; a single threshold on a score with different distributions per group yields different error rates. Evaluation. Aggregate metrics hide subgroup failures; test sets that mirror the training distribution inherit its gaps. Deployment and feedback loops. Model decisions shape future data (who gets shown, who gets loans), reinforcing initial skews. See Data Drift for shifts that affect groups unevenly. Interface and human use. Automation bias, or users overriding the model differently by group. Common mistake Treating fairness as a post-training audit. Many causes sit upstream (labels, sampling, target definition) and cannot be repaired by threshold tweaks alone. # Mitigation: pre-, in-, and post-processing Stage Methods Strengths Costs and risks Pre-processing Re-sampling, re-weighting, relabelling, learning fair representations, collecting more data for under-served groups Model-agnostic; addresses data causes May discard signal; representations can still leak group information In-processing Fairness constraints or penalty terms in the loss, adversarial debiasing (a head tries to predict from representations), group-robust objectives (minimize worst-group loss) Directly optimizes the trade-off Training complexity; constraints may not generalize off the training distribution Post-processing Group-specific thresholds, score adjustment to equalize TPR/FPR Works on a fixed model; easy to audit Uses the sensitive attribute at decision time (may be restricted); can reduce accuracy; ties to the chosen metric Common trade-offs and caveats: Accuracy vs fairness. Constraints usually cost some aggregate accuracy, but the cost may be small, and when group data quality differs, improving data can improve both. Fairness through unawareness (removing ) tends to fail because of proxies, and prevents measurement of disparities. Group metrics are not individual fairness. Similar individuals should receive similar outcomes; group parity can still treat individuals inconsistently. Intersectionality. Fairness across gender and age separately does not guarantee fairness for each combination; sample sizes get small, so use confidence intervals. Feedback. A mitigation tested on historical data can shift behaviour after deployment, so re-measure in production. Rapid fire: fairness Demographic parity compares selection rates and ignores labels. Equal opportunity compares TPR; equalized odds compares TPR and FPR. Calibration within groups: the score means the same thing for every group. With unequal base rates and an imperfect classifier, calibration/predictive parity and equal FPR/FNR cannot all hold. Removing the sensitive attribute does not remove proxies and blocks auditing. Pre-processing fixes data, in-processing changes the loss, post-processing adjusts decisions. Report per-group metrics with confidence intervals; small groups give noisy estimates. The choice of fairness metric is a policy decision, not only a technical one. # Explainability Why explain. Debugging (finding leakage or spurious cues), trust and adoption, recourse for affected people, regulatory expectations about meaningful information on automated decisions (stated generally), and detecting fairness problems. Global vs local. A global explanation describes the model overall (which features matter on average, the shape of a relationship). A local explanation describes one prediction (why this applicant was declined). Intrinsically interpretable models (sparse linear models, small trees, generalized additive models) provide explanations by construction; post-hoc methods approximate explanations for black boxes. For high-stakes settings, a well-tuned interpretable model is often competitive and worth trying first. # Permutation importance Shuffle one feature's values on held-out data and measure the drop in the metric. A large drop means the model relies on that feature. It is model-agnostic and simple, but with correlated features the model can fall back on the correlated twin so importance is split or understated, and shuffling creates unrealistic rows. It measures reliance of the model, not causal importance in the world. Compute it on held-out data, since on training data it can reward overfit features. Compare with impurity-based importance of tree ensembles, which is biased toward high-cardinality features. # PDP and ICE A partial dependence plot averages the prediction over the data while sweeping one feature across its range: ​ ( x j ​ ) = E X − j ​ ​ [ f ^ ​ ( x j ​ , X − j ​ ) ] where ​ are the other features. An ICE (individual conditional expectation) plot draws one curve per instance. PDP assumes the swept feature is independent of the others; with correlation it evaluates the model on implausible combinations (for example age 20 with 30 years of tenure). Averaging can also hide heterogeneity, such as opposite slopes for two subgroups canceling to a flat line, which ICE reveals. Accumulated local effects (ALE) plots handle correlation better. # SHAP in depth SHAP assigns each feature a Shapley value from cooperative game theory: its average marginal contribution to the prediction over all orderings of feature arrival . For a prediction , with baseline ​ (the expected prediction) and features: ​ + j = 1 ∑ M ​ ϕ j ​ , ϕ j ​ = S ⊆ F ∖ { j } ∑ ​ M ! ∣ S ∣ ! ( M − ∣ S ∣ − 1 )! ​ [ v ( S ∪ { j }) − v ( S ) ] Here is the set of all features and is the model's expected output when only the features in are known. The sum over subsets is the weighting that makes the attribution satisfy efficiency (contributions add up to the prediction minus baseline), symmetry , dummy (a feature that never changes the output gets zero), and additivity . Exact computation is exponential, so implementations use TreeSHAP (polynomial-time for tree ensembles), KernelSHAP (a sampled weighted regression), and DeepSHAP-style approximations. Assumptions and failure modes to know: How missing is defined. requires marginalizing out features not in . The interventional (marginal) version samples absent features independently of present ones, which can create unrealistic inputs under correlation; the conditional version respects correlations but can attribute credit to features the model does not use, because they are informative about used ones. Neither is universally right; the choice should match the question. Background dataset matters. Attributions are relative to a baseline distribution; changing it changes the numbers. Not causal. SHAP explains the model, not the world. A high SHAP value says the model leans on a feature, not that changing it changes the outcome. Correlated features share credit in ways that can mislead feature selection. Additive local attributions can hide interactions; SHAP interaction values address pairs. Manipulability. Adversarially constructed models can behave fairly on the perturbed samples used by sampling-based explainers while remaining biased on real data. Cost and instability. KernelSHAP is expensive and sampling variance can reorder close features. Units. For classifiers, values for tree-ensemble classifiers are often in log-odds (raw margin) rather than probability; interpret accordingly. Global importance from SHAP is usually the mean absolute value 1 ​ ∑ i ​ ∣ ϕ j ( i ) ​ ∣ over a dataset; beeswarm plots add direction. # LIME in depth LIME explains one prediction by fitting a simple local surrogate (typically a sparse linear model) to the black box's behaviour in a neighbourhood of the instance. It samples perturbed points around , queries the model, weights samples by proximity, and fits: min ​ L ( f , g , π x ​ ) + Ω ( g ) where is the model, a simple interpretable model from family , ​ the proximity kernel around , and a complexity penalty (for example, number of non-zero weights). Failure modes: Instability. Results depend on random sampling; repeated runs can give different top features. Neighbourhood definition. The kernel width is a hyperparameter with no principled default; explanations can change substantially with it. Unrealistic perturbations. Perturbing tabular features independently, or masking words or superpixels, creates off-manifold inputs where the model's behaviour is not representative. Local linearity. If the decision boundary is strongly nonlinear in the neighbourhood, the surrogate is a poor fit; check its fidelity (local ). No consistency guarantees. Unlike SHAP, LIME has no efficiency or consistency axioms, and can be fooled like other perturbation-based methods. A practical stance: use SHAP for tree models where TreeSHAP is exact and fast; use LIME-style or KernelSHAP methods when only black-box access is available (gradient-based methods when gradients are accessible), and verify explanations with sanity checks (do they change when the model is retrained on randomized labels?). Go deeper (optional) Counterfactual explanations answer what is the smallest change that would flip the decision? , which is often more actionable for recourse than feature attributions. They require constraints on actionability (age cannot be reduced) and plausibility, and the set of valid counterfactuals is rarely unique. # Attention is not explanation In transformers , attention weights show where information is mixed, and are tempting to display as what the model looked at . Studies have shown that attention weights can be altered substantially without changing predictions, that different attention patterns can yield the same outputs, and that weights often correlate poorly with gradient-based importance. Reasons include: values are mixed after weighting (a high weight on a token with a near-zero value vector contributes little), many layers and heads combine in complex ways, and residual paths bypass attention. Attention can still be a useful diagnostic, but claiming it as a faithful explanation needs supporting evidence from perturbation or attribution methods. See Self-Attention for the mechanism. Interview angle A strong answer separates faithfulness (does the explanation reflect what the model actually computes?) from plausibility (does it look reasonable to a human?). A plausible but unfaithful explanation is worse than none, because it creates unearned trust. Rapid fire: explainability Global explains the model overall; local explains one prediction. Permutation importance: shuffle on held-out data; correlated features distort it. PDP averages over the others and assumes independence; ICE shows heterogeneity. SHAP: Shapley values, additive and efficient, relative to a background baseline. SHAP and LIME explain the model, not causal effects in the world. LIME is a local sparse surrogate; it is sensitive to the sampling kernel and to off-manifold perturbations. Attention weights are not guaranteed to be faithful explanations. Consider interpretable models first when the stakes are high. # Privacy # PII handling Practical measures include data minimization (collect and retain only what is needed), purpose limitation, access controls and audit logs, encryption in transit and at rest, retention limits with deletion workflows, separation of identifiers from features (tokenization, pseudonymization), and care with free-text fields, logs, and embeddings, which can contain personal data. Pseudonymization is not anonymization, since identifiers can often be re-linked with auxiliary data. Many privacy regimes include deletion or access rights, so the pipeline needs lineage: knowing which datasets and models used a given person's data. Whether and how a trained model must be changed after a deletion request is a legal and technical question; options range from periodic retraining to machine unlearning research methods. # k-anonymity and its limits A release is k-anonymous if every combination of quasi-identifiers (age band, postcode, gender) appears for at least records, so each person hides among at least others. Limits: Homogeneity. If all records in a group share the same sensitive value, it is revealed anyway; l-diversity and t-closeness add constraints on sensitive-value distribution. Background knowledge. An attacker who knows extra facts narrows the group. Composition. Several independently anonymized releases of overlapping data can be joined to re-identify people. High dimensionality. With many attributes, almost every record is unique, so generalization destroys utility. Well-known re-identification of anonymized datasets by linking with public records illustrates these limits. # Differential privacy Differential privacy (DP) bounds how much any single person's data can change the output distribution. A randomized mechanism is -differentially private if for all datasets differing in one person's record and all output sets : P [ M ( D ′ ) ∈ S ] + δ Intuition: an observer of the output cannot tell with confidence whether any particular person was in the dataset. Smaller means stronger privacy and more noise; near 0 is close to the output is independent of any individual , while large values (tens) give weak guarantees. is a small failure probability, set well below . Noise is calibrated to the sensitivity (the maximum effect of one record

title: ML in Production: Serving, Monitoring & MLOps
heads: Incident checklist: metrics dropped — what now?
Putting it together: ads click model slice
text: Training is a batch job; production is a streaming system with customers attached — skew, drift, and delayed labels are the default, not the exception. Shipping a model is the beginning. The interview version of MLOps is not a tool name-drop checklist — it is the ability to trace a user request through features, model version, business metric, and back to the training data snapshot that produced the weights, then say what you would check when any link in that chain weakens. The failure modes that dominate mature teams are not wrong architecture but training-serving skew , point-in-time violations in the feature store, silent drift , and metrics that look fine while revenue moves . This chapter covers inference modes, deployment patterns, registries and reproducibility, drift taxonomy and detection (including PSI), retraining strategy, latency/cost levers, fairness checks, and an incident playbook when live metrics drop. Pair with ML System Design Framework and Model Evaluation Validation . What you'll be able to say after this chapter Choose batch vs online vs streaming inference from latency and freshness requirements. Define point-in-time correctness and list three causes of training-serving skew. Compare shadow, canary, blue/green, and A/B deployment with rollback triggers. Separate covariate shift, prior shift, and concept drift — and name PSI, KS, and KL/JS as detectors. Explain delayed labels, proxy metrics, and when scheduled vs triggered retrain wins. Walk the incident checklist when production metrics drop without panicking. # Inference modes: batch, online, streaming Batch inference scores a large corpus on a schedule (nightly ad propensities, churn scores for CRM). Pros: cheap amortization, heavy models OK. Cons: scores stale until the next run — bad when events matter in minutes. Online (real-time) inference computes predictions per request with a latency SLO (p99 100ms common for ranking/ads). Needs feature serving from caches/stores, horizontal autoscaling, and often model distillation or smaller architectures. Streaming inference updates features and sometimes model state on an event stream (Kafka → Flink). Use when features are volatile (last-5-minute clicks) or when you fuse batch baselines with real-time deltas. Mode Freshness Cost profile Typical use Batch Hours–days Low $/prediction at scale Churn lists, catalog tags Online Sub-second Per-QPS infra + cache Search rank, fraud score Streaming Event-driven Pipeline ops + state Session features, counters Hybrid lambda/kappa patterns are the norm: batch user embeddings daily, stream session counters per request, merge at the ranker. Request path (mental model). Client → API gateway → feature fetch (parallel RPCs) → model server (batched GPU) → post-processing (calibration, business rules) → response. Each hop consumes budget; feature stores are often parallelized with a hard timeout — missing features fall back to defaults that must match training sentinels. SLO example: p99 80ms rank, 99.9% availability, error budget 0.1%/week. Violations trigger autoscale, circuit breakers to a simpler model, or traffic shed to popularity fallback — state the fallback explicitly in interviews (rules beat a timing-out DCN). Memory hook Batch = cheap and stale; online = fresh and expensive; streaming = fresh features without scoring everything offline. Interview angle Ask latency and freshness before picking inference. Recsys at 100ms almost always means precomputed item side + online user side. Rapid fire — Inference Batch for scale and staleness tolerance. Online for request-time decisions with SLOs. Streaming for evolving counters/state. Most systems blend batch + real-time features. # Feature stores and point-in-time correctness A feature store serves the same feature definitions in training and serving, keyed by entity ID and timestamp. Point-in-time correctness means: for a label at time , every feature must reflect only information available before . Violations are Data Leakage — the model learns the future. Implementation pattern: store feature snapshots or event-time aggregations with as_of joins in training SQL; in serving, read the latest committed feature vector up to request_time . Offline backfills must use the same transformation code path (often packaged as a shared library). Typical layout: offline store (warehouse tables for training sets) + online store (Redis/Dynamo for low-latency reads) fed by the same stream processors. Time-travel APIs let researchers request get_features(entity_id, timestamp=t) for backtests without rewriting SQL. Concern Training Serving Join key (user_id, event_time) (user_id, request_id) Aggregation window Closed intervals ending at label time Rolling as of now Freshness Backfill OK SLO-driven (seconds–hours) Feature ownership matters organizationally: central platform teams ship transforms; product teams own entity definitions. Version features in the model registry next to weights so rollback reverts both. Common mistake Joining current user profile to historical labels — profiles were updated after the label event; offline metrics inflate. # Training-serving skew Skew is any systematic difference between the distribution or computation of features at train vs serve time. Cause Example Fix Different code paths Python training, Java serving Shared feature lib; CI contract tests Missing defaults Null imputation differs Explicit default sentinel; monitoring Logging vs live features Trained on stale batch only Serve what you logged; parity checks Normalization drift Stats from old window Versioned stats; refresh job Candidate universe Train on exposed items only Importance weight or multi-stage replay Prevention: snapshot serving features in logs, daily train-serve parity jobs comparing distributions, and shadow mode deployment (see below). Deep dive card: Training-Serving Skew . Add golden request tests : replay recorded production payloads through offline transform code and assert bitwise or epsilon equality on numerics before each release. This catches the subtle bugs — timezone on day of week, off-by-one in sequence windows, off-by-float in embedding norms — that dashboards miss until revenue moves. For ranking, log the candidate set ID list and retrieval scores at serve time so offline replay evaluates the same slate distribution the ranker saw live; retraining on reshuffled candidates without matching retrieval is a silent skew source. Rapid fire — Skew Same transforms, same defaults, same time semantics. Log served features for training replay. Parity tests between offline batch and online RPC. # Deployment patterns and rollback Shadow deployment: new model runs in parallel, predictions discarded or compared — zero user risk; validates latency and skew. Canary: small % of traffic on new model; watch error rate, latency, business metrics; auto-rollback on breach. Blue/green: two full stacks; instant switch; rollback = flip traffic back — good when infra allows duplicate capacity. A/B test: randomized experiment for causal metric lift — required when claiming improvement, not just safety. See A/B Testing Experimentation . Rollback triggers: SLO latency regression, error spikes, guardrail metrics (fraud FP, toxicity reports), and pre-agreed business KPI floors. Keep previous model version hot in the registry. Experimentation ethics: ramp canaries slowly on revenue-critical paths; pre-define duration and stopping rules to avoid p-hacking. When offline and online disagree, trust online for product metrics but mine offline for regression localization (which slice broke). For batch systems, deployment is often pointer flip on output tables (Blue dataset / Green dataset) with downstream consumers reading versioned paths — same conceptual pattern as online blue/green. Memory hook Shadow = observe; canary = trust a little; blue/green = switch; A/B = prove causally. Rapid fire — Deploy Shadow for parity; canary for gradual risk; blue/green for fast revert; A/B for proof. Roll back on latency, errors, guardrails — not vibes. # Model registry, versioning, reproducibility A model registry stores artifacts: weights, feature manifest, training data hash, hyperparameters, metrics, and approval state. Semantic versioning or content hashes tie a served endpoint to an immutable artifact. Reproducibility checklist: seed control, pinned dependencies, logged data snapshots, git SHA of training code, and documented data filters (time windows, bot removal). For regulated domains, retain lineage from prediction → model version → training set. Promotion workflow. Train job completes → offline metrics on holdout → comparison to champion → human approval for high-risk domains → artifact upload → integration tests (schema of features, max latency dry-run) → canary deploy. Reject promotion if slice regressions appear even when global AUC rises — a classic fairness and robustness trap. Champion/challenger terminology: production serves champion; challenger runs in shadow or small canary until statistically significant lift on pre-registered metrics. Document minimum detectable effect so you do not ship noise. Interview angle Name the registry when asked how do you roll back? — serve v42 from registry while v43 trains beats vague we keep old weights. # Monitoring: drift, labels, and proxies Production monitoring spans data , model , infrastructure , and business layers. # Drift taxonomy Covariate shift (data drift): changes; stable — e.g. new user geography after marketing campaign. Prior shift (label drift): changes — e.g. fraud rate spikes in holiday season. Concept drift: changes — the same feature vector means something different (new fraud tactic, UI redesign). Card: Data Drift vs Concept Drift . # Detection methods Compare reference window (training or last week) to production on marginals or predictions: Method Idea Typical use PSI Bucketed distribution shift Categorical / binned numerics KS test Max CDF gap Continuous univariate KL / JS divergence Information distance between distributions Embedding or score distributions Population Stability Index (PSI) on bins ​ with reference proportion ​ and actual ​ : ∑ k ​ ( A i ​ − E i ​ ) ln E i ​ A i ​ ​ Rule of thumb: PSI 0.1 stable; 0.1–0.25 watch; 0.25 investigate (thresholds vary by domain). PSI is one-dimensional — pair with multivariate tests and slice monitors (country, app version). Prediction drift (score distribution shift) often precedes label drift — cheap early warning when labels are delayed. Multivariate drift. Univariate PSI on 500 features triggers false alarms; use random projections , PCA subspace tests, or tree-based drift detectors (e.g. classifying reference vs production on features — AUC means separable shift). In interviews, say you'd combine univariate PSI for alerting with multivariate triage on top movers. KS test uses the supremum of ​ ( x ) − F act ​ ( x ) ∣ ; sensitive to location/scale shifts in continuous scores. Jensen–Shannon is symmetric and bounded compared to raw KL, useful when comparing softmax score vectors bucketed over impressions. # Delayed labels and proxy metrics Fraud, churn, and LTV labels arrive days or weeks late. Operate on proxy metrics (click, session start) with known lag structure while backfilling true labels. Counterfactual evaluation on exploration traffic helps when logs are biased. Interview angle Strong: distinguish input drift from concept drift and say what you'd retrain vs what you'd revert (bad deploy vs world change). Rapid fire — Monitoring Covariate = ; prior = ; concept = . PSI on binned features; KS on continuous; JS for scores. Prediction drift is the fast signal. Proxies when labels lag. # Retraining strategies Scheduled retrain (daily/weekly): simple ops; risks learning stale patterns between runs. Triggered retrain when PSI/KS breaches, online metric drop, or data volume threshold — saves compute but needs automation. Continual learning updates weights online; rare in regulation-heavy or non-stationary-tabular settings due to catastrophic forgetting and audit requirements — more common in ads with incremental linear models or small adapter updates. Cadence trade-off: faster domains (short-video, ads) → daily + streaming features; slow domains (credit) → monthly with heavy validation. Data volume triggers: retrain when new labeled volume crosses a threshold or when active learning queues human labels for uncertain slices — common in moderation and fraud. Evaluation before promote: hold out the most recent time window (for time-series, never random split — see Time-Series Validation Backtesting ). For classifiers, check Precision Recall at the production threshold, not only ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC . # Observability and the feedback loop Log request_id , model_version , feature_version , inputs (hashed or bucketed), outputs, and downstream outcomes when labels arrive. Pipelines: clickstream → label joiner → training table → registry → serve — close the loop deliberately, not accidentally amplifying bias. Dashboards worth naming in interviews: feature null rate, score distribution, latency p50/p99, cache hit rate, GPU utilization, and business KPI by model slice. Alert on compound conditions (PSI high and CTR down), not single metrics alone. Connect training to Regularization and data freshness: retraining on stale windows without reweighting recent events behaves like an overly strong prior. # Latency and cost optimization Levers interviewers recognize: Distillation — teacher → student with softer targets ( LLM Inference patterns apply at scale). Quantization (INT8) and pruning for GPU/CPU throughput. Caching — user embeddings, frequent queries, partial ranker outputs. Batching — dynamic batching on GPU serving (TensorRT/Triton). Two-stage — cheap retrieve, expensive rank on thousands not billions (see Recommender Systems ). Cost-aware serving picks model size to p99 latency , not mean — tail drives time-outs. # Serving topologies Embedded in app (mobile on-device): tiny models, INT8, no network — drift handled via OTA model bundle updates. Sidecar / microservice: language-agnostic RPC (gRPC), autoscaling replicas per model. Multi-model bin packing: Triton schedules heterogeneous models on shared GPUs. LLM-specific: continuous batching, prefix caching, speculative decoding — see LLM Inference ; analogies (cache KV, batch requests) apply to rankers at smaller scale. Testing before prod: contract tests on feature schemas, load tests at peak QPS, and chaos drills (feature store timeout → defaults). Load test the p99 tail , not average QPS alone. Rapid fire — Efficiency Distill, quantize, cache embeddings, batch GPU calls. Funnel cheap stages before expensive cross-models.
