Optimize p99, not average. # Fairness and explainability checks Pre-launch and ongoing: slice metrics (demographic, region, new vs power users), disparate impact on allocation rates (ads, loans, moderation), and explainability where regulated (SHAP on tabular, attention ≠ explanation for deep nets — state limits). Fairness fixes intersect product policy: thresholds per slice, human review queues, and constraint optimization in re-ranking — not only train a fairer model. Explainability in interviews: for tree models, SHAP for local attributions; for deep models, admit limitations — surface-level attention weights are not faithful explanations. Regulated use cases may require adverse action notices tied to top features. # Batch vs online retraining coordination Many stacks run nightly batch retrain while serving hourly refreshed linear calibration layers on top — decouple slow full retrains from fast adapter updates. Document which artifact each layer reads so rollback does not leave mismatched pairs. Rapid fire — MLOps loop Log → label → feature store → train → evaluate → register → canary → monitor → trigger/schedule retrain. Version everything. Never promote without slice checks. # Incident checklist: metrics dropped — what now? Structured response beats retraining randomly: Confirm the signal — not a dashboard bug, seasonal weekday effect, or external outage (ads inventory, upstream API). Segment — which metric, which slice (platform, country, model version), start time vs deploy time. Infra — latency, error rate, feature store freshness, null rates on key features. Skew check — compare logged serve features to training distributions (PSI per feature). Model version — correlate with canary/rollback; if post-deploy, rollback first , analyze second. Data pipeline — broken ETL, changed schema, bot traffic spike. Concept drift — real world changed (competitor, UI test) → needs retrain or policy fix, not rollback. Communication — incident owner, ETA, guardrails if disabling ML fallback to rules. Playbook extensions for ranking/recsys (ties to Recommender Systems ): check retrieval ANN health (index version, empty recall), explore rate changes, and creator-level impression drops. For ads, verify auction inputs and calibration layer — metric drops may be revenue mix not model quality. Post-incident: write a blameless note capturing detection gap (why PSI did not fire), fix (registry rollback vs retrain), and preventive monitor. Interviewers love hearing we added a null-rate alert on feature X after incident Y. Memory hook Roll back deploys before you retrain the world. Interview angle Walk the checklist out loud — interviewers reward operational muscle, not I'd retrain on more data. Rapid fire — Incidents Validate alert → slice → infra → feature PSI → version correlation → rollback if deploy → pipeline → concept drift → comms. Rollback beats blind retrain. # Putting it together: ads click model slice Walk a concrete path: training reads impression logs from the warehouse with point-in-time user stats; positives are clicks within 24h; features include creative embedding (batch), user segment (batch), and session counters (stream). Serving fetches the same three families from the online store; a logistic or shallow DNN runs at 30ms p99. Shadow a new GBDT champion against the live linear model; canary at 2% traffic; monitor CTR, revenue per mille, and PSI on bid floor features. Labels delay hours — early warning from predicted CTR distribution shift. Roll back if canary RPM drops beyond a pre-set guardrail while global latency stays green. Rapid fire — End-to-end slice Warehouse labels + streaming counters → shared transforms → registry versions → shadow → canary → PSI on inputs and scores → delayed label refresh → scheduled daily retrain. # One-page summary Concept The one thing to remember Inference modes Batch cheap/stale; online fresh/expensive; streaming for live features. Feature store Point-in-time joins — features only from before label time. Skew Train and serve must share code, defaults, and semantics. Deploy Shadow observe; canary risk; blue/green revert; A/B prove. Registry Immutable artifacts + lineage for audit and rollback. Drift Covariate vs prior vs concept — different fixes. PSI ​ − E i ​ ) ln ( A i ​ / E i ​ ) on bins; investigate ~0.25. Retrain Scheduled vs triggered; proxies when labels lag. Efficiency Distill, quantize, cache, funnel before heavy rank. Incidents Rollback deploys first; PSI features; don't panic-retrain. # Related ML System Design Framework Training-Serving Skew Data Drift vs Concept Drift Data Leakage Model Evaluation Validation Calibration A/B Testing Experimentation Recommender Systems LLM Inference

heads: Deep & Cross Network — DCN (Google, 2017) → DCN v2 (2020)
All Loss Functions You Need to Know
text: # Problem Type → Baseline → Advanced Model Problem Type Baseline Advanced Binary classification (tabular) Logistic regression LightGBM / XGBoost → DNN Click prediction / ads ranking Logistic regression Wide Deep → DCN v2 Candidate retrieval (rec sys) Matrix factorization (ALS) Two-tower DNN + FAISS ANN Feed / search ranking LightGBM DCN v2, DLRM, MMoE (multi-task) Session-based recs Popularity baseline SASRec / BERT4Rec (Transformer) NLP: classification TF-IDF + LR Fine-tuned BERT / RoBERTa NLP: ranking / retrieval BM25 Bi-encoder (two-tower) → Cross-encoder Fraud detection LightGBM LightGBM + GNN (transaction graph) Image classification Linear on features ResNet → ViT Multimodal (text + image) Separate models, concat features CLIP-style dual encoder Time series / forecasting ARIMA, moving average LSTM → Temporal Fusion Transformer Graph problems (social, fraud) Node degree features + LR GraphSAGE, PinSage, GNN # Wide Deep vs. Deep Cross # Wide Deep (Google, 2016) Wide side : linear model on manually specified feature crosses (you write user_app × search_query ) Deep side : embedding + MLP for generalization Limitation : the cross features on the wide side must be hand-engineered When to use : you have strong domain knowledge about which specific interactions matter # Deep Cross Network — DCN (Google, 2017) → DCN v2 (2020) Replaces the wide side with a cross network that automatically learns bounded-degree feature interactions DCN v2 uses a matrix-based cross layer (more expressive than the original vector-based one) Reduces (not eliminates) manual cross engineering A strong upgrade over Wide Deep when you don't know which crosses matter When to use : large feature spaces, ranking problems where you don't know which crosses matter; a strong, common default for ranking, alongside DLRM/DeepFM # Summary Wide Deep → DCN → DCN v2 (manual crosses) (auto crosses, vector) (auto crosses, matrix — best) # All Loss Functions You Need to Know Loss Formula Symbols MSE 1 ​ ∑ ( y − y ^ ​ ) 2 ​ ∈ R MAE 1 ​ ∑ ∣ y − y ^ ​ ∣ robust regression Huber quadratic if , else linear ​ BCE , CCE ​ y i ​ lo g p i ​ one-hot / soft , Hinge Focal ​ ( 1 − p t ​ ) γ lo g p t ​ hard-example emphasis BPR ​ − s neg ​ ) pairwise scores Triplet anchor/pos/neg, margin NT-Xent / InfoNCE ​ e sim ( i , k ) / τ e sim ( i , j ) / τ ​ in-batch negatives, temperature KL ​ p ( x ) lo g q ( x ) p ( x ) ​ target, model Full taxonomy and traps: Loss Functions . # Classification Binary Cross-Entropy (Log Loss) L = -[y·log(p) + (1-y)·log(1-p)] Use: click prediction, fraud, any binary label Output: sigmoid → probability Default choice for binary problems Categorical Cross-Entropy (Softmax Loss) L = -Σ y_i · log(p_i) Use: multi-class (mutually exclusive), intent detection, NLP classification Output: softmax → probability distribution Focal Loss L = -α_t (1-p_t)^γ · log(p_t) (p_t = probability assigned to the true class) Use: severe class imbalance (fraud, safety, object detection) The (1-p_t)^γ term downweights easy examples (of either class), focuses training on hard examples γ=2 is typical; originated in RetinaNet Often helps when easy negatives dominate; probabilities need recalibration # Regression MSE (Mean Squared Error) L = (y - ŷ)² Penalizes large errors heavily (squared) Sensitive to outliers Use: when large errors are disproportionately bad MAE (Mean Absolute Error) L = |y - ŷ| More robust to outliers than MSE Use: when outliers are common and you don't want them to dominate Huber Loss L = 0.5(y-ŷ)² if |y-ŷ| ≤ δ L = δ·|y-ŷ| - 0.5δ² otherwise Best of both: MSE for small errors, MAE for large ones Use: default regression loss when you're unsure (bid prediction, ETA) # Ranking BPR Loss (Bayesian Personalized Ranking) — pairwise L = -log(σ(ŷ_pos - ŷ_neg)) Pushes score of positive item above negative item Use: implicit feedback (clicks, watches) where you have user-item pairs Common in recommendation systems Hinge Loss — pairwise L = max(0, margin - (ŷ_pos - ŷ_neg)) Similar to BPR but with a hard margin Use: ranking when you want a minimum score gap LambdaRank / LambdaMART — listwise Pairwise gradients weighted by the NDCG change from swapping the pair (a listwise-aware heuristic); LambdaMART is the GBDT version Used inside LightGBM/XGBoost for ranking ( objective=lambdarank ) Use: when you care about the full ranked list quality, not just pairwise order ApproxNDCG / SoftNDCG — listwise Differentiable approximation of NDCG Used in neural ranking models Use: training neural rankers end-to-end # Embedding / Contrastive Triplet Loss L = max(0, d(anchor, pos) - d(anchor, neg) + margin) Pulls anchor closer to positive, pushes away from negative Use: face recognition, image similarity, early recommendation embedding work Problem: hard to mine good triplets NT-Xent Loss (SimCLR / Contrastive) L = -log( exp(sim(z_i, z_j)/τ) / Σ_k exp(sim(z_i, z_k)/τ) ) In-batch negatives: all other samples in the batch are negatives τ = temperature (lower = sharper, higher = softer) Use: self-supervised pretraining, two-tower models, sentence embeddings More efficient than triplet loss (no triplet mining needed) In-Batch Softmax (used in two-tower models) Same idea as NT-Xent but applied to user-item retrieval All other items in batch = negatives for each user Watch out: popular items appear often as negatives → popularity bias in training, correct with logQ correction (subtract log sampling probability from the logits) # Knowledge Distillation KL Divergence L = Σ p(x) · log(p(x)/q(x)) Measures how distribution p (teacher soft labels) differs from q (student predictions) Student loss = task loss + α·KL(teacher || student) Use: compressing large models to smaller ones for serving # Quick Lookup Situation Loss Binary, balanced Binary cross-entropy Binary, imbalanced (fraud, safety) Focal loss Multi-class Categorical cross-entropy Regression, clean data MSE Regression, noisy/outliers Huber or MAE Pairwise ranking (implicit feedback) BPR loss Listwise ranking (optimize NDCG) LambdaRank / ApproxNDCG Embedding learning NT-Xent (in-batch) or Triplet Model compression KL divergence Multi-task Weighted sum of per-task losses # title: ML System Design Framework
text: The repeatable spine for any ML system design prompt. The strongest answers spend the first third scoping and never jump straight to a model. Drive this structure yourself — don't wait to be asked. # The 6 steps # 1. Clarify frame (~5 min) Turn the vague prompt into a concrete ML problem. Pin down: Business goal and who the user is Scale — DAU, # items, QPS Latency budget (e.g. ~100ms for ranking) Freshness requirements What good actually means Open with: First I'll align on the goal and success metric, then scale and latency, then ask what data we have. # 2. ML task metrics What does the model predict ? Framing: ranking vs classification vs retrieval. Offline metrics (AUC, NDCG, recall@k) AND online metrics (CTR, watch time, revenue) AND guardrails. The key move: the proxy you optimize ≠ the thing you actually care about. Tune proxy weights against an online north-star (e.g. D7/D30 retention) via A/B tests. # 3. Data features Sources, labels (explicit vs implicit), leakage, cold start. Feature families: user · item · user×item cross · context. The cross features are where ranking earns its keep. Implicit-feedback bias — name all three: Exposure / selection bias (feedback loop — you only see labels for what you showed) Position bias (rank drives clicks regardless of quality) Noisy negatives (a skip ≠ a confirmed dislike) Fixes: negative sampling, inverse propensity weighting / position-as-feature (zeroed at serving), exploration traffic to break the loop. # 4. Model Start with a baseline , then justify complexity. For large scale: multistage — retrieval → ranking → re-ranking. Discuss tradeoffs , not just the fanciest option. # 5. Serving scale Retrieval: two-tower model + ANN index (HNSW / ScaNN / FAISS). Item embeddings precomputed offline indexed; user tower runs once per request → single ANN lookup. The decoupling is the serving win. Multiple retrieval sources unioned (personalized + trending + social + fresh-exploration). Feature store, online vs batch inference, caching. # 6. Evaluation iteration Offline: ranking metric (NDCG), check calibration if probs feed downstream. Online: A/B test vs north-star (retention) + guardrail metrics (reports, diversity, creator health). Post-launch: monitor feature prediction drift , watch online metrics decay, retrain regularly (daily/continuous for fast domains). Continuous retraining on biased logs amplifies bias → exploration matters long-term. # Back-of-envelope math Pin numbers in the first five minutes — interviewers use them to see if serving is realistic. Quantity Rule of thumb Average QPS Peak QPS often average (traffic shape, geography) Ranking compute — serial ms adds; parallel width = how many cores/GPUs you need inside the latency budget Embedding table RAM ​ × d × bytes_per_param (e.g. 100M IDs × 128-dim × 4 B ≈ 51 GB in fp32) Feature / log storage events/day × bytes/event × retention; separate hot online store vs cold warehouse Experiment sample size see [[ab-testing-and-experimentation Worked example — 100M DAU feed, 50 requests/user/day, rank 500 items at 1 ms scoring each (per candidate, one core): Average QPS × 50/86 , 400 ≈ 5.8 × 1 0 4 . Peak QPS. Scoring load at peak × 500 × 1 ms ≈ 7.2 × 1 0 7 CPU-ms/s cores if every candidate is scored serially on a CPU — in practice batch on GPUs, approximate models, and two-stage retrieval shrink this by orders of magnitude; the envelope tells you whether you need retrieval + light ranker vs one giant GPU ranker. # Two-stage architecture cheat Stage Catalog → out Job Model Retrieval billions → thousands recall, cheap two-tower + ANN Ranking thousands → hundreds precision heavy multi-task (MMoE) Re-rank hundreds → ~10 diversity, policy rules + light model # Cold start Item: content embeddings at upload → retrievable immediately (also = freshness story). User: onboarding preferences + popular/trending prior, let real interactions take over. # Common ways people fail Jump straight to the model. Never define metrics properly (or don't connect offline ↔ online). Ignore data/serving reality. Circle instead of committing — state the structured answer up front. Use generic language instead of canonical component names. # Related ML System Design Interview Prep Recommender Systems ML in Production: Serving, Monitoring MLOps A/B Testing Online Experimentation MOC - System Design · Home

title: Two-Tower Retrieval
text: Say it in 30s: Two-tower retrieval learns separate user and item embeddings so the score is a dot product. Train with sampled softmax and in-batch negatives; correct with logQ so popular items are not oversampled as negatives. At serve time, precompute all item vectors, index them with ANN (HNSW/FAISS), run the user tower once per request, and retrieve top- — that's how you hit billion-scale catalogs under ~20ms. Key points Decoupled serving: item tower offline → ANN; user tower online → one lookup. Ranking with full crosses happens only on candidates. Loss: contrastive / sampled softmax over positive + negatives; in-batch negatives scale with batch size. logQ correction: subtract from negative logits so head items do not dominate the denominator. Complements: graph retrieval, BM25, trending — union before the ranker. The math Score (often L2-normalized cosine). In-batch softmax for positive ) : ) / τ + ∑ j ∈ N ​ e s ( u , i j ​ ) / τ e s ( u , i + ) / τ ​ . logQ correction: use ​ ( u , i j ​ ) = s ( u , i j ​ ) − ln Q ( i j ​ ) on negatives ( item frequency). Subtracting down-weights logits of items that appear often as in-batch negatives, debiasing the partition function toward tail items. Serve: MIPS / ANN on precomputed ; one forward pass for per request. Common follow-ups / traps Why not score all pairs with a cross-encoder? → Quadratic cost; cross-encoders are for rerank/hundreds, not billions. What if the user embedding is stale? → Blend batch user vector with real-time session features in the user tower or a small ranker boost. See depth: Recommender Systems (§Two-tower retrieval). Related: Embeddings Vector Search , Loss Functions .

title: Cold Start
text: Say it in 30s: Cold start is missing interaction history — for new users or new items. Fix users with priors (onboarding, demographics, trending) and exploration until clicks exist. Fix items with content-based signals: metadata, text/image embeddings computed at upload so the item is immediately in ANN retrieval. Pure collaborative filtering fails until impressions accumulate; hybrid systems are mandatory at scale. Key points Item cold start: content tower produces ​ before any clicks; same index as warm items. User cold start: popular/trending prior + onboarding interests; ε exploration to learn fast. New creator / tail: re-ranking boosts and coverage metrics so retrieval does not ignore them. Bandits and explore buckets trade short-term CTR for information. The math Bayesian CTR shrinkage for a new item: = impressions + α + β clicks + α ​ (Beta prior mean). Example: 3 clicks / 100 impressions with = ( 3 + 1 ) / ( 100 + 2 ) ≈ 0.039 against a raw rate of — , so the pull toward the prior mean is small; it dominates only when impressions are tiny. Explore: UCB1 arm score ​ a ​ + c ln t / n a ​ ​ (bonus for few pulls); Thompson sampling draw ​ ∼ Beta ( α a ​ , β a ​ ) from posterior and pick ​ θ a ​ — balances exploit vs learn. Common follow-ups / traps Is cold start only a data problem? → Also architecture: without content embeddings, new SKUs/videos are invisible to CF retrieval. How do you evaluate? → Slice offline recall@k on young items; online new-user retention. See depth: Recommender Systems (§Cold start, diversity, freshness, exploration). Related: Embeddings Vector Search , ML System Design Framework .

title: Training-Serving Skew
text: Say it in 30s: Training-serving skew means the model sees different features or distributions offline than online — separate code paths, wrong imputation, stale normalization stats, or training on logged features you no longer serve. It shows up as good offline metrics and broken live performance. Fix with a shared feature library, log served vectors for replay, point-in-time training joins, and shadow/canary parity checks. Key points Code skew: Java serve vs Python train → one transform implementation in both. Default skew: missing categoricals map to different buckets train vs serve. Temporal skew: training uses current profile joined to old events → leakage and phantom gains. Selection skew: ranker trained only on retrieved items must match live retrieval distribution. The math Distribution skew: for the same entity and decision time, training features should match served features: ​ ( x features ​ ) ≈ p serve ​ ( x features ​ ) Violations (different imputation, code paths, or joins) break even when labels and model weights are fixed. Feature parity: on logged entity IDs, monitor rate ​ ( x ) − f serve ​ ( x ) ∣ ε ) per feature — skew alarms when the rate jumps. Point-in-time join: for label time , only use features with timestamp ​ ≤ t (and the same horizon as production). Training on “current” attributes attached to past events inflates offline metrics and diverges at serve. Common follow-ups / traps Isn't skew the same as drift? → Skew is a static pipeline bug; drift is time-varying population change — both hurt, different fixes. How do you test? → Nightly compare histograms of served vs offline-replayed features on the same entity IDs. See depth: ML in Production (§Training-serving skew). Related: Data Leakage , Data Drift vs Concept Drift , Calibration .

title: Data Drift vs Concept Drift
text: Say it in 30s: Data (covariate) drift is when input features change but the label relationship is stable — e.g. new traffic mix. Label (prior) drift is when shifts. Concept drift is when changes — the same features mean different outcomes after a UI change or new fraud pattern. Detection uses PSI/KS/JS on features or scores; the fix for concept drift is retrain or change the product, not just normalize inputs. Key points Covariate shift → calibration/slice review; concept drift → new labels / model refresh. Prediction drift (score distribution) is an early warning when labels lag. PSI on score/feature histograms vs a training reference — common alert thresholds (watch) and (act). Monitor slices (country, app version), not only global averages. The math PSI (bins , actual fraction ​ , expected ​ from reference): ∑ ​ ( a i ​ − e i ​ ) ln e i ​ a i ​ ​ KS statistic: ​ ∣ F test ​ ( x ) − F train ​ ( x ) ∣ (max CDF gap). KL ​ p i ​ ln q i ​ p i ​ ​ ; JS 1 ​ KL ( p ∥ m ) + 2 1 ​ KL ( q ∥ m ) , 1 ​ ( p + q ) (symmetric, bounded). Covariate shift importance weights: ​ ( x ) p test ​ ( x ) ​ reweights train loss toward the serve distribution. Label / prior shift: changes while may be stable — recalibrate thresholds and slice metrics. PSI example: bin proportions expected , observed → (well below ). Common follow-ups / traps Is seasonal traffic drift? → Often covariate + prior shift; concept drift if user behavior given features changed. Retrain on every PSI alert? → Tune thresholds; rollback bad deploys before mass retrain. See depth: ML in Production (§Monitoring). Related: Training-Serving Skew , Model Evaluation Validation , A/B Testing Experimentation .

title: Coding Round: ML From Scratch
heads: 1. Linear regression: closed form and gradient descent
6. Decision tree: best split by Gini
9. Scaled dot-product attention with causal mask, then multi-head
11. Batch norm forward: train versus eval
text: Fourteen problems that keep reappearing in ML coding rounds, each with a complete solution and the pitfalls an interviewer probes. An ML coding round tests three things at once: whether the math is internalised (can the gradient be written without notes), whether numerical hygiene is automatic (log-sum-exp, stable sigmoid, solving instead of inverting), and whether the code is checked before being declared done. Every solution below is NumPy (PyTorch for attention and the training loop) and ends with a tiny sanity check against a reference implementation. The habit worth copying is that last step: state the check out loud, then run it. What you'll be able to say after this chapter Write OLS, logistic regression, softmax cross-entropy and their gradients without numerical blow-ups. Implement k-means, k-NN, naive Bayes and a Gini split, and name the failure mode of each. Compute ROC-AUC and PR-AUC with tied scores, and NDCG with the right ideal ranking. Write causal multi-head attention, a correct training loop, batch-norm forward, PCA via SVD and an AdamW step. Explain why convolution is a matrix multiply (im2col) and what it costs. # How to run the round Clarify the interface (shapes, dtypes, labels in or ), write the vectorised version directly, state complexity, then test on a case with a known answer. Compare against a reference when one exists, and check gradients numerically when it does not. Interview angle Weak: a correct-looking loop that overflows on large logits and is never run. Strong: the stable formulation from the first line, a two-line assertion against sklearn or torch , and a sentence on what breaks (ties, empty clusters, k n ). # 1. Linear regression: closed form and gradient descent Problem. Fit by least squares, once with the normal equations and once with gradient descent. Approach. The normal equations X + λ R ) w = X ⊤ y cost + d 3 ) . Gradient descent costs per step and needs standardised features, otherwise the loss surface is a ravine and the learning rate is dictated by the largest-scale feature. See Gradient Descent . import numpy as np def fit_ols ( X, y, l2= 0.0 ): Closed form with intercept. Solve, never invert. Xb = np.hstack([np.ones(( len (X), 1 )), X]) R = l2 * np.eye(Xb.shape[ 1 ]); R[ 0 , 0 ] = 0 # do not penalise the intercept return np.linalg.solve(Xb.T @ Xb + R, Xb.T @ y) def fit_gd ( X, y, lr= 0.1 , steps= 2000 ): mu, sd = X.mean( 0 ), X.std( 0 ) Z = (X - mu) / sd # standardise: conditions the problem w, b, n = np.zeros(X.shape[ 1 ]), y.mean(), len (y) for _ in range (steps): err = Z @ w + b - y w -= lr * ( 2 / n) * Z.T @ err b -= lr * ( 2 / n) * err. sum () w_orig = w / sd # undo the scaling return np.r_[b - mu @ w_orig, w_orig] # --- sanity check rng = np.random.default_rng( 0 ) X = rng.normal(size=( 200 , 3 )) * [ 1 , 10 , 100 ] y = 4 + X @ [ 2.0 , - 0.5 , 0.03 ] + rng.normal(scale= 0.1 , size= 200 ) ref = np.linalg.lstsq(np.hstack([np.ones(( 200 , 1 )), X]), y, rcond= None )[ 0 ] assert np.allclose(fit_ols(X, y), ref) assert np.allclose(fit_gd(X, y), ref, atol= 1e-3 ) print ( ok , fit_ols(X, y). round ( 3 )) Pitfalls np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) is slower and less accurate than solve ; with collinear columns both fail, and lstsq or ridge is the answer. Penalising the intercept shifts predictions; the code zeroes that entry of the regulariser. Gradient descent without standardisation needs a tiny learning rate; forgetting to undo the scaling returns coefficients in the wrong units. # 2. Logistic regression with gradient descent Problem. Binary classifier trained by minimising log-loss, with no overflow for large . Approach. The gradient of the mean log-loss with respect to the logit is , so ​ = X ⊤ ( σ ( X w + b ) − y ) / n . Compute the sigmoid by branching on the sign of , and the loss as via logaddexp . Cost per step. See Cross-Entropy Loss . import numpy as np def log_softmax ( z ): z = z - z. max (axis=- 1 , keepdims= True ) # shift: softmax is shift-invariant return z - np.log(np.exp(z). sum (axis=- 1 , keepdims= True )) # log-sum-exp def cross_entropy ( logits, y ): return -log_softmax(logits)[np.arange( len (y)), y].mean() def ce_grad ( logits, y ): p = np.exp(log_softmax(logits)); p[np.arange( len (y)), y] -= 1 return p / len (y) # (softmax - onehot) / N # --- sanity check rng = np.random.default_rng( 0 ) z = rng.normal(size=( 4 , 5 )) * 50 ; y = rng.integers( 0 , 5 , 4 ) assert np.isfinite(cross_entropy(z, y)) f = lambda z: cross_entropy(z, y) num = np.zeros_like(z); eps = 1e-6 for i in np.ndindex(*z.shape): d = np.zeros_like(z); d[i] = eps num[i] = (f(z + d) - f(z - d)) / ( 2 * eps) assert np.allclose(num, ce_grad(z, y), atol= 1e-6 ) import torch, torch.nn.functional as F assert np.isclose(F.cross_entropy(torch.tensor(z), torch.tensor(y)).item(), cross_entropy(z, y)) print ( ok ) Pitfalls Computing softmax then log loses precision; fuse them as above. See Naive Bayes . import numpy as np class MultinomialNB : def fit ( self, X, y, alpha= 1.0 ): self .classes = np.unique(y) self .log_prior = np.log(np.array([(y == c).mean() for c in self .classes])) counts = np.array([X[y == c]. sum ( 0 ) for c in self .classes]) + alpha # Laplace smoothing self .log_lik = np.log(counts / counts. sum ( 1 , keepdims= True )) return self def predict_log_proba ( self, X ): jll = X @ self .log_lik.T + self .log_prior # sum of logs, never a product of probs return jll - np.logaddexp.reduce(jll, axis= 1 , keepdims= True ) def predict ( self, X ): return self .classes[ self .predict_log_proba(X).argmax( 1 )] # --- sanity check from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB as SK rng = np.random.default_rng( 0 ) y = (rng.random( 200 ) .5 ).astype( int ) X = rng.poisson(np.where(y[:, None ] == 1 , 2.0 , 0.5 ) * rng.uniform( .2 , 1.5 , 30 )) mine = MultinomialNB().fit(X, y); sk = SK(alpha= 1.0 ).fit(X, y) assert np.allclose(mine.predict_log_proba(X), sk.predict_log_proba(X)) assert (mine.predict(X) == sk.predict(X)). all () print ( ok , (mine.predict(X) == y).mean()) Pitfalls k-NN: unscaled features, even with ties, and the cost at serving time (an index such as an ANN structure is the production answer). For a feature matrix and integer labels, find the (feature, threshold) pair minimising weighted Gini impurity ​ p c 2 ​ . Approach. Sort each feature, then consider thresholds only between distinct consecutive values. The version below recomputes impurity per candidate, ) overall, which is fine for an interview; the production version keeps running class counts while sweeping, giving . See Decision Trees, Random Forests Gradient Boosting . import numpy as np def gini ( y ): if len (y) == 0 : return 0.0 p = np.bincount(y) / len (y) return 1 - (p ** 2 ). sum () def best_split ( X, y ): Return (feature, threshold, weighted_gini). ROC-AUC and PR-AUC with ties Problem. Compute both areas from scores and binary labels without a library, correct when scores repeat. Approach. ROC-AUC equals the probability that a random positive outscores a random negative, counting ties as one half. That is the Mann-Whitney statistic: rank all scores (average ranks inside tie groups) and use ​ n − ​ ∑ i ∈ + ​ r i ​ − n + ​ ( n + ​ + 1 ) /2 ​ . Average precision sweeps the threshold and sums ​ − R k − 1 ​ ) P k ​ , emitting one point per distinct score. Cost . See ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC . import numpy as np def roc_auc ( y, s ): Mann-Whitney form: P(score_pos score_neg) + 0.5 P(tie). Average ranks handle ties. y = np.asarray(y); s = np.asarray(s, float ) order = np.argsort(s, kind= stable ); ss = s[order] ranks = np.empty( len (s)); i = 0 while i len (s): j = i while j + 1 len (s) and ss[j + 1 ] == ss[i]: j += 1 ranks[order[i:j + 1 ]] = (i + j) / 2 + 1 # average rank of the tie block i = j + 1 n1 = y. sum (); n0 = len (y) - n1 return (ranks[y == 1 ]. sum () - n1 * (n1 + 1 ) / 2 ) / (n1 * n0) def average_precision ( y, s ): Step-wise PR-AUC: sum (R_k - R_{k-1}) * P_k, one point per distinct threshold. y = np.asarray(y); s = np.asarray(s, float ) order = np.argsort(-s, kind= stable ); ys, ss = y[order], s[order] tp = np.cumsum(ys); fp = np.cumsum( 1 - ys) last = np.r_[ss[ 1 :] != ss[:- 1 ], True ] # keep only the last row of each tie group tp, fp = tp[last], fp[last] prec, rec = tp / (tp + fp), tp / y. sum () return np. sum (np.diff(np.r_[ 0 , rec]) * prec) # --- sanity check (with ties on purpose) from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score rng = np.random.default_rng( 0 ) y = (rng.random( 300 ) 0.2 ).astype( int ); s = np. round (rng.normal(size= 300 ) + 1.2 * y, 1 ) assert np.isclose(roc_auc(y, s), roc_auc_score(y, s)) assert np.isclose(average_precision(y, s), average_precision_score(y, s)) print ( round (roc_auc(y, s), 4 ), round (average_precision(y, s), 4 )) Pitfalls Treating tied scores as separate thresholds inflates or deflates both curves; ties must collapse to one point.
